questions.title: Decision-specific capacity
questions.stem: In Ontario, a client with mild dementia consistently explains a wound treatment, its risks and what may happen if it is declined. The daughter asks to sign instead. What should the nurse do?
options: Seek substitute consent because dementia is documented
Assess and support the client's consent for this treatment
Use the consent recorded for the previous admission
Defer every treatment decision until cognition is normal
why: A diagnosis alone does not establish inability to decide this treatment.
Understanding and appreciation relate to the particular decision.
Prior admission consent does not establish current treatment consent.
Cognitive impairment does not necessarily prevent this specific decision.
questions.takeaway: Assess capacity for the particular decision.
questions.learningObjective: Assess capacity for the particular decision.

questions.title: Adolescent treatment choice
questions.stem: In an Ontario clinic, a 16-year-old accurately explains a proposed treatment and its consequences. They prefer not to involve a parent. What should guide the nurse's consent approach?
options: Require parental consent before discussing treatment
Ask the adolescent to return with an adult supporter
Proceed through the capable adolescent's treatment decision
Obtain both parent and adolescent signatures in every case
why: Ontario does not impose a fixed minimum age for treatment consent.
Support can help but is not a prerequisite for capable consent.
Ontario treatment consent depends on capacity, not a fixed minimum age.
A blanket dual-signature rule incorrectly overrides decision-specific capacity.
questions.takeaway: Capacity, rather than a fixed age, governs Ontario treatment consent.
questions.learningObjective: Capacity, rather than a fixed age, governs Ontario treatment consent.

questions.title: Sedation before consent
questions.stem: A client received a sedative and cannot explain a planned elective procedure. The consent discussion has not occurred. What next?
options: Ask the client to repeat the procedure name and sign
Accept the preoperative checklist as evidence of consent
Ask the family to sign without verifying substitute authority
Pause and contact the responsible practitioner
why: Repeating a name does not establish understanding after sedation.
A checklist cannot replace the missing discussion and capacity assessment.
Relationship alone does not establish a lawful substitute pathway.
Elective care permits clarification of capacity and valid consent.
questions.takeaway: Resolve impaired understanding before elective treatment.
questions.learningObjective: Resolve impaired understanding before elective treatment.

questions.title: Consent under pressure
questions.stem: A capable client has signed consent but quietly says, "My caregiver threatened to stop feeding me unless I agreed." What should the nurse do first?
options: Pause to assess coercion and the client's immediate safety
Arrange another teaching session about treatment benefits
Ask the caregiver to reassure the client before proceeding
Rely on the signed form unless the client explicitly cancels
why: Threats may undermine voluntariness and indicate abuse.
More teaching does not first address the threat undermining voluntariness.
The reported coercer may intensify pressure rather than permit free choice.
A signature cannot resolve the newly disclosed concern about coercion.
questions.takeaway: Consent must be voluntary.
questions.learningObjective: Consent must be voluntary.

questions.title: New procedure scope
questions.stem: Before an elective procedure, the plan changes from superficial biopsy to a more extensive intervention. The client consented only to the biopsy. What should the nurse do?
options: Proceed because the revised procedure treats the same diagnosis
Pause preparation until consent for the revised plan is established
Confirm that the original consent form is still on the chart
Ask the family to approve the change while the capable client rests
why: Treating the same condition does not make substantially different procedures interchangeable.
Consent must relate to the actual proposed treatment.
Presence of the form does not establish authorization for revised treatment.
Family approval does not replace the capable client's treatment decision.
questions.takeaway: Verify consent when the treatment plan changes materially.
questions.learningObjective: Verify consent when the treatment plan changes materially.

questions.title: Hearing support
questions.stem: A hard-of-hearing client appears confused during a treatment explanation. What should occur before assuming incapacity?
options: Ask the family to consent because conversation is difficult
Postpone teaching until a relative can explain the treatment
Optimize hearing and communication
Use orientation questions alone to determine treatment capacity
why: Difficulty hearing should be addressed before substituting decision-makers.
A relative may help, but available communication supports should first be optimized.
Accessible communication permits a fair assessment of understanding.
Orientation does not test understanding of the specific treatment decision.
questions.takeaway: Remove communication barriers before judging understanding.
questions.learningObjective: Remove communication barriers before judging understanding.

questions.title: Prior wishes
questions.stem: In Ontario, an incapable 70-year-old client has a most recent, applicable treatment wish documented while capable at age 65. The authorized substitute reports that relatives now favour a different treatment. What should guide the response?
options: Choose the option with the greatest expected survival benefit
Ask all relatives to reach a majority decision
Follow the substitute's personal treatment preference
The applicable prior capable wish
why: Benefit alone does not override an applicable prior capable wish.
Family consensus is not the statutory decision-making test.
The substitute must consider the client's applicable wishes rather than personal preference.
The most recent applicable wish expressed while capable at age 16 or older guides Ontario substitute treatment decisions.
questions.takeaway: Prior capable wishes can guide substitute decisions.
questions.learningObjective: Prior capable wishes can guide substitute decisions.

questions.title: Property attorney
questions.stem: In Ontario, a visitor presents only a power of attorney for property and requests authority over treatment. What next?
options: Verify the lawful treatment decision-maker
Accept it because property and treatment affect the same person's welfare
Ask the visitor to confirm verbally that they know the client's wishes
Delay routine care until a new power of attorney is created
why: Property authority does not itself establish personal-care authority.
Authority over finances does not itself confer treatment authority.
Knowledge of wishes is relevant but does not establish legal authority.
The existing lawful substitute pathway should be verified before assuming new documents are needed.
questions.takeaway: Verify authority for the specific decision domain.
questions.learningObjective: Verify authority for the specific decision domain.

questions.title: Regained capacity
questions.stem: An Ontario client previously incapable of a treatment decision now demonstrates understanding and appreciation. What should the nurse arrange?
options: Use a normal orientation score alone to declare treatment capacity restored
Reassessment and direct client participation
Ask the substitute whether the client may resume making decisions
Continue relying on substitute consent until the current treatment course ends
why: Orientation alone does not establish treatment-specific understanding and appreciation.
Regained capacity may restore the client's own decision-making role.
The substitute does not determine whether capable autonomy may resume.
Changed capacity warrants timely reassessment even during an ongoing course.
questions.takeaway: Revisit consent when capacity changes.
questions.learningObjective: Revisit consent when capacity changes.

questions.title: Questions remain
questions.stem: A client says the procedural benefits are clear but asks about alternatives. Which actions support informed choice? Select all that apply.
options: Arrange answers from the responsible practitioner
Allow decision time when clinically possible
Ask the client to sign now and obtain answers immediately before treatment
Explore what information remains unclear
why: The practitioner can address treatment-specific alternatives.
Time supports deliberation when urgency allows.
Signing first risks bypassing information needed for the current choice.
Clarifying gaps focuses the remaining consent discussion.
questions.takeaway: Informed choice includes alternatives and opportunities for questions.
questions.learningObjective: Informed choice includes alternatives and opportunities for questions.

questions.title: Public corridor
questions.stem: A team begins discussing a client's cancer results beside visitors in a corridor. What is the best response?
options: Omit the name and continue discussing the uncommon diagnosis
Move the discussion to a private area
Complete the discussion quickly to minimize exposure
Ask the family present whether discussion may continue
why: Context may identify the client even without a name.
A private location limits unnecessary disclosure.
Shortening a public disclosure does not remove the avoidable privacy risk.
Other visitors remain within hearing and may not be authorized recipients.
questions.takeaway: Choose a private setting for clinical discussion.
questions.learningObjective: Choose a private setting for clinical discussion.

questions.title: Misdirected fax
questions.stem: A nurse discovers a care summary was faxed to the wrong clinic. What should happen first?
options: Wait for the receiving clinic to confirm whether anyone read it
Correct the fax directory and document the new number
Activate the privacy breach response promptly
Notify the client before contacting the privacy response lead
why: Containment should begin before unauthorized access can be established.
Correction helps future transmissions but does not address the current breach.
Prompt containment and reporting support the required breach response.
The approved response process should promptly coordinate containment and required notification.
questions.takeaway: Report and contain unintended disclosure promptly.
questions.learningObjective: Report and contain unintended disclosure promptly.

questions.title: Personal phone image
questions.stem: A colleague suggests photographing a wound on a personal phone because the approved camera is unavailable. What should the nurse do?
options: Use a personal phone if the client verbally agrees
Send the image through an encrypted personal messaging account
Store the photograph offline until the approved camera returns
Use an approved secure documentation process
why: Client agreement alone does not establish secure storage and handling.
Encryption alone does not establish an authorized documentation system.
Personal storage still bypasses required clinical information safeguards.
Approved processes address consent, access, retention and security.
questions.takeaway: Use authorized systems for clinical images.
questions.learningObjective: Use authorized systems for clinical images.

questions.title: Shared password
questions.stem: A temporary nurse cannot log in and requests a colleague's password. Which response protects accountability?
options: Arrange authorized access through support
Share access briefly and supervise every entry
Enter all temporary staff notes under the shift leader's account
Delay all documentation until the temporary nurse's next shift
why: Individual credentials preserve access control and attribution.
Supervision does not preserve individual credential accountability.
The entries would not reliably identify the person providing care.
Authorized support or downtime processes should maintain timely records.
questions.takeaway: Clinical system access must be individually authorized.
questions.learningObjective: Clinical system access must be individually authorized.

questions.title: Voicemail detail
questions.stem: A client permits callback but has not authorized detailed voicemail. What is the safest message?
options: Leave results because the client requested a callback
A minimal callback request
Ask the answering person to relay the diagnosis
Send detailed findings to the first email address in the old chart
why: Callback permission does not necessarily authorize detailed voicemail.
A minimal message limits disclosure while enabling contact.
The answering person's authority to receive health information is unverified.
The current authorized communication route has not been established.
questions.takeaway: Match messages to the client's communication permissions.
questions.learningObjective: Match messages to the client's communication permissions.

questions.title: Chart disposal
questions.stem: Printed handover sheets containing identifiers remain after shift. What should the nurse do?
options: Place them face down in the staff recycling bin
Keep them in a work bag until the next shift
Use approved confidential disposal
Leave them at the desk for the incoming nurse indefinitely
why: Ordinary recycling does not provide confidential destruction.
Unnecessary transport increases loss and unauthorized access risk.
Secure disposal limits unauthorized access after use.
Retention should follow need and approved secure disposal practices.
questions.takeaway: Dispose of clinical working papers securely.
questions.learningObjective: Dispose of clinical working papers securely.

questions.title: Research request
questions.stem: A researcher outside the care team requests identifiable records. No authorization pathway has been confirmed. What next?
options: Release the records after the researcher signs a confidentiality statement
Remove the names but retain exact dates and rare diagnoses
Accept a colleague's assurance that the project sounds worthwhile
Refer through the approved privacy and research process
why: A confidentiality promise alone does not establish lawful access.
Partial removal may leave the records readily identifiable.
Clinical interest cannot substitute for approved research and privacy authorization.
Approved review establishes lawful access and necessary safeguards.
questions.takeaway: Verify research access before releasing identifiable information.
questions.learningObjective: Verify research access before releasing identifiable information.

questions.title: Privacy at bedside
questions.stem: During bedside handover, a capable client asks that a sensitive history be discussed elsewhere. What should the nurse do?
options: Arrange a private discussion of that information
Finish the bedside script because consistency prevents omissions
Ask the roommate to turn away during the report
Leave the sensitive history out of the receiving team's handover
why: Privacy preferences can be respected while preserving relevant communication.
Consistency does not require sensitive disclosure against the client's stated preference.
Turning away does not prevent hearing confidential information.
Relevant information still needs secure transfer to support care.
questions.takeaway: Adapt handover to protect privacy without losing essential information.
questions.learningObjective: Adapt handover to protect privacy without losing essential information.

questions.title: Release preferences
questions.stem: A client permits updates to a sibling but excludes one sensitive diagnosis. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Clarify the permitted information
Record the disclosure limits
Treat permission for general updates as permission for the full record
Verify identity before telephone updates
why: Specific limits guide what can be disclosed.
Accessible documentation supports consistent team practice.
The client explicitly limited the disclosure scope.
Identity verification reduces disclosure to the wrong person.
questions.takeaway: Respect the scope of permission to share information.
questions.learningObjective: Respect the scope of permission to share information.

questions.title: Social media reflection
questions.stem: A nurse proposes a private social-media post about the only client admitted locally with a rare injury that week. The name is omitted. What is the primary privacy concern?
options: Whether the client would probably feel positively about the story
Whether contextual details permit others to identify the client
Whether the post omits exact admission dates
Whether the account is restricted to nursing colleagues
why: Assumed approval is not authorization to disclose identifiable information.
Unusual contextual details can reveal identity without a name.
Other contextual details may still permit recognition.
A professional audience does not establish a legitimate care purpose.
questions.takeaway: Removing a name does not guarantee anonymity.
questions.learningObjective: Removing a name does not guarantee anonymity.

questions.title: Late entry
questions.stem: A nurse recalls an omitted observation from 0900 while charting at 1400. How should it be documented?
options: Use 0900 as the entry time so the chart stays chronological
Record the observation at 1400 without identifying it as earlier
Mark a late entry with both times
Ask the next nurse to include it in their end-of-shift summary
why: That would conceal the actual time the note was made.
Readers may incorrectly treat it as a current assessment.
Both event and entry times preserve chronology.
That loses accurate authorship and delays useful documentation.
questions.takeaway: Clearly distinguish event time from late-entry time.
questions.learningObjective: Clearly distinguish event time from late-entry time.

questions.title: Unobserved treatment
questions.stem: A colleague asks the nurse to chart a dressing change the colleague performed. There is no emergency. What is appropriate?
options: Sign the colleague's description after verbally confirming completion
Use the same treatment note entered on the previous day
Document the procedure as completed under the nurse's own name
Ask the colleague to document their care
why: Confirmation does not make it the nurse's personally provided care.
The previous entry does not establish today's actions or findings.
That falsely attributes another person's care to the signing nurse.
The person providing care normally documents it.
questions.takeaway: Document care with accurate attribution.
questions.learningObjective: Document care with accurate attribution.

questions.title: Precharting
questions.stem: A nurse prepares morning care notes before seeing clients. Which approach is appropriate?
options: Document completed assessments after care
Mark routine tasks complete unless the client later refuses
Copy normal findings and correct exceptions after rounds
Sign a prepared note with a plan to review it later
why: Documentation should reflect care actually provided.
Expected completion cannot be recorded as an accomplished fact.
Unverified normal findings may be acted on before correction.
A signed entry should accurately reflect care already provided.
questions.takeaway: Do not document planned care as completed care.
questions.learningObjective: Do not document planned care as completed care.

questions.title: Quoting a threat
questions.stem: A client states, 'My partner said they would hurt me tonight.' Which documentation is best?
options: Write that the client reports a stressful relationship
Record the words and relevant assessment
Document suspected partner violence without the actual statement
Record that safety resources were discussed without describing the threat
why: That description omits the specific threatened harm and timing.
Direct words and assessment communicate the specific concern.
The concern matters, but the client's exact report provides essential context.
Intervention documentation alone does not convey the reason for urgent assessment.
questions.takeaway: Record significant client statements accurately and in context.
questions.learningObjective: Record significant client statements accurately and in context.

questions.title: Copy-forward allergy
questions.stem: A copied admission note says no allergies, but the client describes previous penicillin anaphylaxis. What next?
options: Retain the no-allergy alert until old hospital records arrive
Record the report only in the narrative progress note
Clarify and update the active allergy information promptly
Ask the client to remind each nurse during medication rounds
why: The credible severe-reaction history needs prompt active clarification while corroborating records are sought.
A buried note may not update the alert used for prescribing and administration.
Accurate active alerts support immediate prescribing and administration decisions.
Client reminders supplement but cannot replace accurate active allergy information.
questions.takeaway: Resolve clinically important copied-record discrepancies promptly.
questions.learningObjective: Resolve clinically important copied-record discrepancies promptly.

questions.title: Downtime notes
questions.stem: The electronic record fails during a shift. What should the nurse use?
options: Keep notes from memory and enter them after recovery
Record events in a personal encrypted note application
Write a unit-wide list without client identifiers
Approved downtime documentation
why: Delay and memory dependence risk omitted time-sensitive information.
Personal encryption does not make the application an approved clinical record.
Unidentified entries cannot reliably connect observations and treatment to clients.
Downtime procedures preserve care records and later reconciliation.
questions.takeaway: Use the approved record process during system downtime.
questions.learningObjective: Use the approved record process during system downtime.

questions.title: Recording escalation
questions.stem: After reporting a worsening wound, what should the nurse include in the clinical record? Select all that apply.
options: Relevant wound findings
Person contacted and response
Describe the other clinician as careless for not attending immediately
Follow-up care and reassessment
why: Findings explain why escalation was required.
The response establishes the resulting care plan.
A judgment about motive or character is not a factual account of the response.
Follow-up demonstrates whether the concern was addressed.
questions.takeaway: Document the concern, communication and subsequent response.
questions.learningObjective: Document the concern, communication and subsequent response.

questions.title: Neutral language
questions.stem: A client missed a wound appointment after accessible transport was cancelled and asks to reschedule. Which entry best supports the next nurse's care planning?
options: Missed again despite repeated reminders
Transport unavailable; client requests rescheduling
Unable to follow the recommended treatment plan
Family failed to bring client as expected
why: The wording omits the known transportation barrier needed for planning.
The entry identifies an actionable access problem.
This broad conclusion exceeds the specific missed-transport event.
This assigns blame without explaining the reported access problem.
questions.takeaway: Document observed barriers rather than assumed motives.
questions.learningObjective: Document observed barriers rather than assumed motives.

questions.title: Client record correction
questions.stem: A client says the chart lists the wrong emergency contact. What is the best response?
options: Tell the client only a physician can change demographic fields
Keep the old contact until that person authorizes removal
Verify and use the approved correction process
Add the new contact to a personal handover sheet only
why: An approved administrative correction pathway may address this factual error.
An outdated contact does not determine the capable client's preferences.
Verification and correction improve accuracy and privacy.
The authoritative record would remain inaccurate for other staff.
questions.takeaway: Support correction of inaccurate demographic information.
questions.learningObjective: Support correction of inaccurate demographic information.

questions.title: Abbreviation ambiguity
questions.stem: A handover note contains an unfamiliar abbreviation affecting a treatment plan. What should the nurse do?
options: Use the most common meaning in the specialty
Follow the previous shift's actions without clarification
Treat the abbreviation as optional because it is unclear
Clarify with the author or responsible clinician
why: A common interpretation may still be wrong in this treatment plan.
Repeated use does not establish that the original interpretation was correct.
Omission could miss an important treatment instruction.
Direct clarification prevents acting on an incorrect interpretation.
questions.takeaway: Clarify ambiguous documentation before acting on it.
questions.learningObjective: Clarify ambiguous documentation before acting on it.

questions.title: Task report-back
questions.stem: A trained care provider will measure routine intake for a stable client. Which instruction is most useful?
options: Specify what, when and how to report
Ask for a total only if the client appears dehydrated
Request a verbal total whenever the care provider has time
Tell the care provider to decide whether the fluid plan needs adjustment
why: Clear expectations permit timely nursing interpretation and follow-up.
Clinical dehydration may develop after useful early intake information was missed.
Unspecified timing makes planned nursing review unreliable.
Interpreting and revising the clinical plan requires nursing judgment.
questions.takeaway: Assignment includes clear reporting expectations.
questions.learningObjective: Assignment includes clear reporting expectations.

questions.title: New worker competence
questions.stem: A care provider says they have never used the unit's transfer device. What should guide assignment?
options: Assign the transfer because the worker uses other hoists
Verified task competence and required support
Assign the worker to lead after a demonstration without a supervised competence check
Permit the transfer if the client says the worker seems confident
why: Competence with other equipment does not establish competence with this model.
Task-specific competence protects both client and worker.
Observation alone does not establish safe independent operation of this transfer device.
Confidence and client reassurance do not verify safe device operation.
questions.takeaway: Verify competence for the specific assigned task.
questions.learningObjective: Verify competence for the specific assigned task.

questions.title: Outcome responsibility
questions.stem: A nurse assigns a stable client's routine meal assistance according to policy. What responsibility remains with the nurse?
options: Check only that the task box was signed as completed
Review the outcome only if a formal complaint is received
Evaluate whether the care met the plan
Assume intake goals were met because the worker accepted the task
why: A completed task box does not establish the intake or response required by the care plan.
Evaluation should not depend on a complaint after a care problem develops.
Evaluation confirms effectiveness and detects changing needs.
Task acceptance does not establish the client's actual response.
questions.takeaway: Evaluate the outcomes of assigned care.
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate the outcomes of assigned care.

questions.title: Staffing mix
questions.stem: Two nurses have equal workloads; only one is competent in a required specialty procedure. What should assignment consider first?
options: Give the procedure to the longest-serving nurse
Keep equal client numbers even if needed expertise is unavailable
Assign by room location to reduce walking time
Client needs and relevant competence
why: Seniority alone does not demonstrate this procedure-specific competence.
Equal numbers may hide unequal clinical demands and skill requirements.
Efficiency cannot outweigh the competence needed for the procedure.
Matching expertise to care needs supports safe allocation.
questions.takeaway: Assign according to client needs and staff competence.
questions.learningObjective: Assign according to client needs and staff competence.

questions.title: Conflicting instructions
questions.stem: A care provider receives different fluid-measurement instructions from two nurses. What is the best response by the responsible nurse?
options: Clarify one coordinated plan with the team
Ask the worker to follow whichever nurse gave instructions most recently
Use the previous day's instructions until the next shift
Collect only oral intake and leave other sources unresolved
why: A coordinated plan removes ambiguity in ongoing care.
Recency alone does not establish the intended care plan.
The current disagreement may reflect a needed change requiring clarification.
An incomplete plan may undermine the intended fluid-balance assessment.
questions.takeaway: Resolve conflicting team instructions explicitly.
questions.learningObjective: Resolve conflicting team instructions explicitly.

questions.title: Relief handover
questions.stem: A nurse leaves for a scheduled break while a client needs reassessment in 15 minutes. What should occur?
options: Ask the client to ring if they feel worse before reassessment
Confirm a qualified nurse accepts the reassessment
Ask a care provider to decide whether nursing review is necessary
Document the due time without identifying who will respond
why: Symptoms alone do not replace the planned clinical review.
Explicit acceptance establishes continuity during the absence.
The required reassessment involves nursing judgment.
Documentation alone does not establish accepted coverage.
questions.takeaway: Arrange clear coverage for time-sensitive care.
questions.learningObjective: Arrange clear coverage for time-sensitive care.

questions.title: Unexpected assignment limit
questions.stem: An LPN in BC is assigned care beyond their individual competence despite available expert help. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Explain the specific competence limit
Seek qualified collaboration
Proceed because the activity falls somewhere within the profession's legal scope
Arrange a safe division of care
why: Specific limits allow the assignment to be adjusted.
Expert collaboration can support care within appropriate boundaries.
Legal scope does not establish the individual nurse's competence for this client.
A revised plan maintains care while managing the limitation.
questions.takeaway: Competence limits require a safe collaborative care plan.
questions.learningObjective: Competence limits require a safe collaborative care plan.

questions.title: Student supervision
questions.stem: A supervised student is about to use a technique that may contaminate a wound. What should the nurse do first?
options: Allow completion and discuss the technique privately afterward
Interrupt and guide a safe correction
Ask the student to explain the technique while continuing
Observe closely and record the issue for formal evaluation
why: Delayed feedback permits the contamination risk to reach the client.
Immediate coaching protects the client and supports learning.
Explanation should not prolong an action that threatens sterility.
Observation alone does not prevent the immediate breach.
questions.takeaway: Intervene promptly when a learner's action threatens safety.
questions.learningObjective: Intervene promptly when a learner's action threatens safety.

questions.title: Unresolved task completion
questions.stem: At handover, a needed dressing assessment has no documentation and staff are unsure whether it occurred. What next?
options: Assume the dressing was assessed because other tasks were documented
Mark the task complete after asking the previous shift to recall it later
Verify the client's current needs and arrange assessment
Wait until the next scheduled dressing change without examining the client
why: Completion of other care does not establish this assessment occurred.
Unverified completion can conceal an ongoing care need.
Current assessment resolves the care gap and directs follow-up.
The current assessment gap needs resolution based on present risk.
questions.takeaway: Resolve uncertain task completion through verification and current assessment.
questions.learningObjective: Resolve uncertain task completion through verification and current assessment.

questions.title: Feedback on reporting
questions.stem: A care provider delayed reporting low intake. Which feedback best improves future practice?
options: Tell the care provider to be more attentive next time
Repeat the fluid-balance policy without discussing the missed threshold
Ask the worker to report only once the client shows symptoms
Report intake below the agreed threshold before shift end
why: General advice does not clarify what or when to report.
Policy review alone may leave the specific performance gap unresolved.
Waiting for symptoms may delay useful early nursing intervention.
Specific reporting expectations support timely follow-up.
questions.takeaway: Give feedback that describes the required observable action.
questions.learningObjective: Give feedback that describes the required observable action.

questions.title: Transfer essentials
questions.stem: A rehabilitation client transfers with a pending culture and new mobility restrictions. Which items need handover? Select all that apply.
options: Pending result and follow-up responsibility
Current transfer assistance required
The previous assistance level as the sole mobility description
Relevant recent treatment changes
why: Unassigned follow-up can allow abnormal results to be missed.
Receiving staff need the present safe mobility plan.
The receiving team needs current restrictions and assistance rather than a superseded baseline alone.
Recent changes affect ongoing treatment and monitoring.
questions.takeaway: Transfer information should identify active needs and unfinished work.
questions.learningObjective: Transfer information should identify active needs and unfinished work.

questions.title: Referral urgency
questions.stem: A dietitian referral is pending for chronic poor appetite, but the client now coughs with every sip. What should happen first?
options: Ask the dietitian to review calories before changing the plan
Pause oral intake and arrange prompt swallowing assessment
Offer small sips through a straw while awaiting the referral
Complete the meal record and reassess at the next meal
why: Nutrition review does not resolve the immediate swallowing safety concern.
Stopping the current exposure and escalating protects the airway.
An unassessed technique may continue aspiration exposure.
Documentation alone delays response to repeated coughing with intake.
questions.takeaway: New safety findings can change referral priority.
questions.learningObjective: New safety findings can change referral priority.

questions.title: Discharge equipment gap
questions.stem: A client requires a prescribed walker at home, but none is available at the planned discharge time. What next?
options: Discharge with advice to minimize walking until delivery
Use a family member's walker without checking fit and suitability
Coordinate a safe equipment and discharge plan
Ask transport staff to support the client through the first doorway
why: Essential safe mobility needs an achievable plan, not an unassessed restriction.
Availability does not establish safe equipment selection.
Essential equipment should be addressed before a safe transition.
Help at arrival does not meet the continuing home mobility need.
questions.takeaway: Resolve essential equipment barriers during discharge planning.
questions.learningObjective: Resolve essential equipment barriers during discharge planning.

questions.title: Home caregiver limits
questions.stem: A spouse expected to provide complex home care says they cannot manage it. What is the best nursing action?
options: Schedule another demonstration before exploring the spouse's concerns
Ask the spouse to agree temporarily because home care is limited
Send written instructions and proceed with the existing discharge plan
Reassess supports and coordinate alternatives
why: Teaching alone may not address physical, emotional or practical caregiving limits.
Agreement under pressure does not create a sustainable support plan.
Written material does not establish caregiver ability or willingness.
A realistic plan considers caregiver capacity and available services.
questions.takeaway: Confirm caregiver capacity before relying on home support.
questions.learningObjective: Confirm caregiver capacity before relying on home support.

questions.title: Pending result ownership
questions.stem: A client leaves hospital before a pathology result returns. What best prevents loss to follow-up?
options: Document who will review and communicate the result
Tell the client to call if no result arrives within several weeks
Rely on the laboratory's automatic forwarding to the original prescriber
List the pending test without specifying a follow-up pathway
why: Named responsibility creates an actionable follow-up pathway.
Client follow-up alone leaves professional review responsibility unresolved.
Forwarding does not confirm accepted clinical responsibility after transition.
An item on the summary may still be overlooked without ownership.
questions.takeaway: Assign ownership of pending results at transitions.
questions.learningObjective: Assign ownership of pending results at transitions.

questions.title: Follow-up access
questions.stem: A client misses follow-up because the clinic is inaccessible by available transport. What is the best next step?
options: Emphasize the clinical importance of attending the same appointment
Explore accessible follow-up arrangements
Give a reminder call on the morning of the appointment
Ask the client to rebook only when transport becomes reliable
why: The client already identifies a transport barrier, not a knowledge deficit.
Alternatives can make the required care achievable.
A reminder does not provide an accessible route to care.
The required clinical follow-up may need a supported alternative now.
questions.takeaway: Adapt follow-up plans to practical access barriers.
questions.learningObjective: Adapt follow-up plans to practical access barriers.

questions.title: Teach-back gap
questions.stem: A client repeats written discharge words but cannot describe what to do if symptoms worsen. What next?
options: Accept accurate reading aloud as evidence the plan is understood
Give a longer written explanation of every possible complication
Reteach the action plan and reassess understanding
Ask the client to promise to call if uncertain
why: Reading does not demonstrate when or how the client would act.
More volume may obscure the specific response the client cannot explain.
Focused reteaching addresses the identified decision gap.
A promise does not establish recognition of the warning signs.
questions.takeaway: Evaluate whether teaching supports action, not memorization.
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate whether teaching supports action, not memorization.

questions.title: Care conference goals
questions.stem: An interdisciplinary conference proposes several treatments. The capable client has not been asked their priorities. What should the nurse do?
options: Rank the options by predicted functional improvement before asking the client
Implement the team consensus and explain it at discharge
Ask the family to identify goals without involving the capable client
Invite the client's goals into the discussion
why: Professional estimates need to be considered alongside the client's own priorities.
Late explanation prevents meaningful participation in choosing the plan.
Family input can support but not replace the client's own goals.
Client goals help align treatment choices with meaningful outcomes.
questions.takeaway: Include the client's goals in interdisciplinary planning.
questions.learningObjective: Include the client's goals in interdisciplinary planning.

questions.title: Access to food
questions.stem: A client prescribed a meal-dependent medication reports no reliable food supply. Which actions support a workable plan? Select all that apply.
options: Assess access to regular meals
Connect with food and social supports
Reinforce medication timing without addressing meal availability
Inform the team of the treatment barrier
why: The regimen depends on an unmet practical need.
Support services may improve the ability to follow treatment.
Instructions cannot resolve the reported barrier to safely following the regimen.
The team may need to adapt the care plan safely.
questions.takeaway: Identify social barriers that make treatment plans unworkable.
questions.learningObjective: Identify social barriers that make treatment plans unworkable.

questions.title: Return precautions
questions.stem: At home after discharge, a client develops sudden severe breathlessness at rest and cannot speak full sentences. Which action reflects appropriate use of return precautions?
options: Contact the usual clinic when it next opens for severe breathlessness
For new severe breathing difficulty, call emergency services
Use the next scheduled appointment to discuss new severe symptoms
Try the routine home plan and wait an hour before seeking help
why: A routine callback pathway may dangerously delay emergency assessment.
A specific urgent symptom is linked to an appropriate action.
Scheduled follow-up is not appropriate for severe acute breathing difficulty.
An arbitrary delay can be unsafe when breathing difficulty is severe.
questions.takeaway: Link warning symptoms to a clear action and contact.
questions.learningObjective: Link warning symptoms to a clear action and contact.

questions.title: Personal loan request
questions.stem: A current client asks the nurse for a personal loan. What is the best response?
options: Provide a small loan and document repayment expectations
Explain the boundary and explore formal supports
Ask another nurse to lend the money privately
End the visit immediately to avoid discussing money
why: A documented personal debt can still distort the therapeutic relationship.
Clear boundaries preserve the relationship while addressing need.
Moving the loan to a colleague retains a professional boundary concern.
The underlying financial need can be addressed without a personal loan.
questions.takeaway: Address financial needs through appropriate support channels.
questions.learningObjective: Address financial needs through appropriate support channels.

questions.title: Supplier commission
questions.stem: A nurse receives commission for referring clients to a supply company. What should guide recommendations?
options: Recommend the supplier if its prices match competitors
Offer the supplier first and disclose the commission only if asked
Client needs and transparent conflict management
Stop discussing equipment options whenever a financial conflict exists
why: Equivalent prices do not remove the nurse's financial conflict.
Clients need relevant conflict information before relying on the recommendation.
Recommendations require impartial clinical reasoning and conflict disclosure.
Appropriate conflict management can preserve useful, impartial care planning.
questions.takeaway: Manage financial conflicts and prioritize client interests.
questions.learningObjective: Manage financial conflicts and prioritize client interests.

questions.title: Expensive gift
questions.stem: A client offers a costly watch after receiving home care. What is the best response?
options: Accept it after recording that the client initiated the gift
Accept it only after the final scheduled visit
Return it without discussing the meaning with the client
Discuss appreciation and follow gift-boundary policy
why: Client initiation does not eliminate a costly gift's boundary implications.
The relationship and potential obligation do not necessarily end at that visit.
A respectful explanation can preserve trust while setting the boundary.
Policy and professional guidance help respond respectfully without exploitation.
questions.takeaway: Respond to gifts without creating obligation or preferential care.
questions.learningObjective: Respond to gifts without creating obligation or preferential care.

questions.title: Personal social invitation
questions.stem: A current client repeatedly invites a nurse on a private weekend trip. What should the nurse do?
options: Maintain the therapeutic boundary and discuss the request
Accept only after confirming no care will be provided during the trip
Ask a colleague to cover care while the nurse travels with the client
Agree to a shorter social visit instead
why: A clear response preserves the professional purpose of care.
A social trip with a current client still changes the professional relationship.
Coverage does not resolve the dual relationship and power imbalance.
Reducing duration does not address the reason for maintaining the boundary.
questions.takeaway: Maintain professional boundaries beyond scheduled shifts.
questions.learningObjective: Maintain professional boundaries beyond scheduled shifts.

questions.title: Care for a friend
questions.stem: A nurse is assigned a close friend and another qualified nurse is available. What is the best action?
options: Continue the assignment but avoid documenting the prior friendship
Disclose the conflict and request reassignment
Ask the friend whether they believe the nurse can remain objective
Exchange assignments without explaining the reason to the coordinator
why: Concealing the relationship prevents appropriate conflict assessment.
Reassignment can protect objectivity and privacy.
Client reassurance does not replace professional evaluation of the conflict.
The coordinator needs enough information to manage assignment and privacy appropriately.
questions.takeaway: Disclose relationships that may compromise objective care.
questions.learningObjective: Disclose relationships that may compromise objective care.

questions.title: Product endorsement
questions.stem: A vendor asks a nurse to recommend a device using a script that omits limitations. What should the nurse do?
options: Use the script if the device has regulatory approval
Offer the script together with the vendor's satisfaction testimonials
Provide balanced evidence-based information
Ask the client to direct all clinical questions to the salesperson
why: Approval does not justify omitting relevant limitations from counselling.
Testimonials do not provide balanced information about limitations.
Balanced information supports choice without commercial distortion.
The nurse retains responsibility for impartial nursing advice.
questions.takeaway: Keep clinical advice independent of promotional pressure.
questions.learningObjective: Keep clinical advice independent of promotional pressure.

questions.title: Self-disclosure
questions.stem: During wound care, a nurse spends most of the visit describing their own divorce. What is the main concern?
options: The nurse shared information before obtaining written client permission
Home visits require more personal conversation than clinic appointments
The client did not clearly request that the conversation stop
Attention shifted away from the client's needs
why: Written permission is not the central issue when disclosure displaces client care.
The care setting does not justify shifting the focus to the nurse.
Responsibility for therapeutic boundaries remains with the nurse.
Extended personal disclosure can burden the client and displace care.
questions.takeaway: Self-disclosure should serve the client's therapeutic needs.
questions.learningObjective: Self-disclosure should serve the client's therapeutic needs.

questions.title: Fitness to practise
questions.stem: A nurse feels slowed and dizzy after a new prescribed medication before a shift. What should happen?
options: Disclose impairment concerns and arrange safe coverage
Start with lower-acuity clients and reassess dizziness after rounds
Avoid procedures but continue independently administering medications
Wait for the symptoms to recur during care before notifying anyone
why: Early disclosure permits risk assessment and safe staffing.
Even routine care may be unsafe when impairment is already apparent.
Medication administration also requires unimpaired judgment and coordination.
Waiting exposes clients to a foreseeable impairment risk.
questions.takeaway: Assess and act on impairment that may affect safe practice.
questions.learningObjective: Assess and act on impairment that may affect safe practice.

questions.title: Observed impairment
questions.stem: A colleague slurs speech and repeatedly drops prepared medications. What is the immediate priority?
options: Ask the colleague to finish only routine medications while being observed
Protect clients and notify the responsible supervisor
Confront the colleague privately before arranging coverage for clients
Record the observations at shift end if another error occurs
why: Continued medication handling may expose clients before fitness is assessed.
Observed impairment needs immediate risk containment and escalation.
Client protection and supervisory support should not wait for a private confrontation.
Current observable impairment warrants prompt action rather than waiting for harm.
questions.takeaway: Respond to observed impairment with immediate safety measures.
questions.learningObjective: Respond to observed impairment with immediate safety measures.

questions.title: Conscientious concern
questions.stem: A nurse has a personal objection to a lawful, authorized service. Which actions support professional care? Select all that apply.
options: Communicate the concern early through policy
Arrange continuity with an appropriate colleague
Arrange a replacement only after leaving the active assignment
Provide respectful information within the nursing role
why: Early communication permits a safe staffing plan.
Continuity prevents the objection from becoming a care gap.
Continuity should be established before withdrawing from ongoing care.
Respectful care preserves dignity and access.
questions.takeaway: Manage personal objections while maintaining safe continuity.
questions.learningObjective: Manage personal objections while maintaining safe continuity.

questions.title: Discriminatory comment
questions.stem: A colleague uses a racial stereotype to dismiss a client's pain report. What should the nurse do?
options: Ask a second colleague whether the stereotype usually predicts pain behaviour
Assess pain and challenge the discriminatory behaviour
Discuss the comment later while accepting the existing pain plan
Tell the client to submit a complaint before changing care
why: Stereotypes cannot substitute for individual clinical assessment.
The response addresses both the care need and harmful conduct.
The biased assessment may leave the current pain need unmet.
A complaint process should not delay appropriate clinical assessment.
questions.takeaway: Challenge discrimination and assess the individual clinical need.
questions.learningObjective: Challenge discrimination and assess the individual clinical need.

questions.title: Name and pronouns
questions.stem: A client's legal record name differs from their stated name. What supports respectful safe care?
options: Use the legal name exclusively until the record is formally amended
Replace all identification fields with the stated name immediately
Use the stated name while preserving accurate identification
Ask the family to confirm which name staff should use
why: Respectful conversation need not wait for a legal record change.
Uncoordinated identifier changes could disrupt reliable record matching.
Respect and accurate record matching can coexist.
A capable client's own stated preference should guide respectful interaction.
questions.takeaway: Respect identity while maintaining reliable clinical identification.
questions.learningObjective: Respect identity while maintaining reliable clinical identification.

questions.title: Religious observance
questions.stem: A stable client wishes to schedule routine care around prayer. What is the best approach?
options: Move every treatment to after prayer without reviewing timing requirements
Use a standard faith-specific schedule without asking further questions
Ask relatives to negotiate the schedule on the client's behalf
Collaborate on timing consistent with clinical needs
why: Some treatments may be time-sensitive and need collaborative adjustment.
An assumed group practice may not reflect this client's preferences.
The capable client can participate directly in planning.
Collaboration balances observance with essential treatment timing.
questions.takeaway: Individualize routine care around meaningful client preferences.
questions.learningObjective: Individualize routine care around meaningful client preferences.

questions.title: Accessible instructions
questions.stem: A client with low vision receives discharge instructions in small print. What should the nurse do?
options: Arrange an accessible format and check usability
Read the material once and record that instructions were provided
Ask the client to rely on memory for medication changes
Send the same small-print document to a family member
why: Accessible information supports independent use after discharge.
One reading does not ensure the client can access the plan at home.
A durable accessible format is safer for a complex ongoing plan.
Family availability does not replace supporting the client's own access.
questions.takeaway: Provide information in a format the client can use.
questions.learningObjective: Provide information in a format the client can use.

questions.title: Client-chosen supporter
questions.stem: A capable adult asks a trusted friend to join a care meeting. What should guide inclusion?
options: Invite only people listed as next of kin
The client's permission and stated role
Allow the friend to make treatment decisions because they attend
Discuss only information previously shared with the friend
why: A client may authorize a chosen supporter beyond formal kinship.
Client permission defines appropriate involvement and disclosure.
Attendance and support do not establish substitute decision authority.
The client can authorize additional relevant information for this meeting.
questions.takeaway: Include client-chosen supporters with appropriate permission.
questions.learningObjective: Include client-chosen supporters with appropriate permission.

questions.title: Competing goals
questions.stem: A rehabilitation team targets independent stairs, but the client prioritizes safe wheelchair access to work. What next?
options: Continue the original goal until the client demonstrates poor progress
Increase motivational teaching about why stair climbing matters
Revisit goals collaboratively
Suspend all therapy until the client accepts the team's goal
why: Delay leaves rehabilitation directed at a goal the client does not prioritize.
Education alone does not address the client's stated participation goal.
Collaboration can align rehabilitation with participation needs.
Rehabilitation can be adapted instead of made conditional on agreement.
questions.takeaway: Align measurable care goals with the client's priorities.
questions.learningObjective: Align measurable care goals with the client's priorities.

questions.title: Trauma-informed preparation
questions.stem: A client becomes distressed when staff enter without warning. Which plan best supports participation?
options: Increase staff visits to help the client become accustomed to entry
Explain that unscheduled entry is necessary for staff efficiency
Limit visits to medication administration only
Explain visits and seek permission before approaching
why: Repeated unexpected approaches may intensify distress.
Efficiency alone does not justify ignoring an adaptable trigger.
Avoiding other care leaves needs unmet instead of improving predictability.
Predictability and choice can reduce loss of control.
questions.takeaway: Use predictability and choice to support a sense of safety.
questions.learningObjective: Use predictability and choice to support a sense of safety.

questions.title: Resource allocation
questions.stem: Two clients need the same limited mobility aid. What should guide temporary allocation?
options: Assessed urgency and a safe alternative plan
Give the aid to whichever client has waited longer regardless of risk
Prioritize the client whose family can arrange early discharge
Alternate use on a fixed schedule without reassessing individual needs
why: Clinical need and alternatives support fair, safe allocation.
Waiting time alone may overlook urgent safety needs.
Discharge convenience does not automatically outweigh the other client's mobility risk.
A fixed split may fail to protect a client needing the aid at a specific time.
questions.takeaway: Allocate scarce care resources using relevant clinical need.
questions.learningObjective: Allocate scarce care resources using relevant clinical need.

questions.title: Uncertain evidence
questions.stem: A colleague recommends a new dressing based only on a sales brochure. What is the best next step?
options: Trial the dressing on every client before reading the evidence
Check credible evidence and local authorization
Continue the old product solely because staff know it best
Ask clients to choose from the brochure before clinical review
why: Broad adoption exposes clients before suitability has been appraised.
Evidence and policy support an informed practice decision.
Familiarity alone is not a sufficient evidence-based decision.
Promotional choice cannot replace assessment of clinical suitability.
questions.takeaway: Appraise evidence before changing clinical practice.
questions.learningObjective: Appraise evidence before changing clinical practice.

questions.title: Learning after incident
questions.stem: After a medication near miss, which actions support learning? Select all that apply.
options: Examine workflow contributors
Share learning through authorized channels
Limit review to reminding the involved nurse to be more careful
Identify practical safeguards
why: Workflow review can reveal recurring risk conditions.
Appropriate sharing helps others prevent similar events.
Individual reminders alone may leave workflow contributors unchanged.
Specific safeguards translate review into safer practice.
questions.takeaway: Use near misses to improve the care system.
questions.learningObjective: Use near misses to improve the care system.

questions.title: Outcome measure
questions.stem: A unit changes discharge teaching to reduce confusion. Which measure best evaluates client understanding?
options: Number of revised leaflets given to clients
Proportion of nurses attending the teaching workshop
Clients accurately explaining the action plan
Average minutes spent delivering the instructions
why: Distribution measures process completion rather than understanding.
Staff attendance does not establish client comprehension.
An accurate explanation assesses the intended learning outcome.
Time spent does not demonstrate usable learning.
questions.takeaway: Choose measures that match the intended care outcome.
questions.learningObjective: Choose measures that match the intended care outcome.

questions.title: Small improvement test
questions.stem: A team trials a new handover checklist on one shift. What should happen before wider adoption?
options: Adopt it permanently if no incident occurs during the trial
Survey only the nurse who designed the checklist
Expand it immediately because the team likes its appearance
Review omissions, usability and unintended problems
why: Absence of one observed incident does not establish effectiveness.
That misses independent user feedback and unintended problems.
Appearance does not demonstrate communication quality.
Review determines whether the change improves communication safely.
questions.takeaway: Evaluate a small change before expanding it.
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate a small change before expanding it.

questions.title: Incident versus chart
questions.stem: Following a transfer injury, what belongs in the clinical record?
options: Assessment, care and client response
The safety-report identifier without assessment details
The nurse's conclusion about who caused the injury
A recommendation for staff discipline
why: Clinical facts support treatment and continuity.
A reporting reference cannot communicate the client's current clinical needs.
Causal attribution should not replace factual care documentation.
Personnel recommendations do not document the client's assessment or treatment.
questions.takeaway: Clinical records document care; reporting systems support separate review.
questions.learningObjective: Clinical records document care; reporting systems support separate review.

questions.title: Disclosure after harm
questions.stem: A client received delayed treatment after a missed order. What is the nurse's appropriate contribution to disclosure?
options: Explain which staff member is probably legally responsible
Provide known facts within the team disclosure process
Promise that the event cannot affect recovery
Wait until the investigation identifies every contributing factor
why: Speculation may be inaccurate and does not clarify known clinical facts.
Accurate, coordinated disclosure supports honesty and follow-up.
The nurse cannot guarantee an outcome that has not been established.
Initial honest communication need not await complete causal certainty.
questions.takeaway: Communicate known facts honestly through the disclosure process.
questions.learningObjective: Communicate known facts honestly through the disclosure process.

questions.title: Audit confidentiality
questions.stem: A nurse collects data for an approved care-quality audit. What principle applies?
options: Collect full records so additional questions can be explored later
Share identifiable findings with all unit staff through an open link
Use only necessary information with secure handling
Retain a personal copy to make future audits easier
why: Convenience does not justify unnecessary identifiable information.
Audit access should be limited and secured appropriately.
Purpose-limited collection protects privacy during improvement work.
Personal retention may bypass organizational privacy controls.
questions.takeaway: Quality improvement still requires privacy safeguards.
questions.learningObjective: Quality improvement still requires privacy safeguards.

questions.title: Policy conflict
questions.stem: A unit routine appears inconsistent with a current professional safety standard. What should the nurse do?
options: Follow the old routine until a formal complaint forces review
Replace the unit procedure independently without informing the team
Stop all related care while awaiting a policy committee meeting
Raise the discrepancy and arrange safe interim practice
why: Known professional concerns should be raised before harm occurs.
Uncoordinated changes can create new inconsistencies and safety gaps.
A safe interim plan may preserve needed care during review.
Escalation can reconcile the conflict while protecting current clients.
questions.takeaway: Address conflicts between routine practice and professional requirements.
questions.learningObjective: Address conflicts between routine practice and professional requirements.

questions.title: Competence maintenance
questions.stem: A nurse has not performed a rare authorized skill for years. What best supports safe return to it?
options: Review current guidance and demonstrate competence with support
Rely on the initial certification because the procedure name is unchanged
Watch a brief demonstration and declare competence without practice
Perform independently and request help only if a complication occurs
why: Updated learning and supervised assessment identify skill gaps.
Equipment and guidance may have changed, and skill can decay.
Observation alone may not verify the ability to perform safely.
Support should address the identified gap before exposing a client.
questions.takeaway: Maintain current competence for infrequently used skills.
questions.learningObjective: Maintain current competence for infrequently used skills.

questions.title: Seeking consultation
questions.stem: A stable client's needs exceed the nurse's expertise. Which actions support effective consultation? Select all that apply.
options: State the specific concern
Provide relevant assessment findings
Assume the consultant now owns every aspect of the client's care
Clarify the recommended follow-up
why: A focused question makes consultation actionable.
Findings allow informed advice about this client.
A focused consultation does not transfer all nursing responsibilities.
Agreed follow-up closes the communication loop.
questions.takeaway: Consult with a focused question and clear follow-up plan.
questions.learningObjective: Consult with a focused question and clear follow-up plan.

questions.title: Read-back confirmation
questions.stem: During an emergency, a clinician gives a clear verbal instruction allowed by policy. What communication best reduces misunderstanding?
options: Acknowledge with a nod while carrying out the instruction
Repeat the instruction and obtain confirmation
Write the order after acting without repeating it
Ask another staff member to repeat their interpretation instead
why: A nod does not confirm the instruction was heard accurately.
Closed-loop confirmation detects differences before action.
Later documentation cannot catch a hearing error before action.
The receiving nurse should confirm directly with the person giving the instruction.
questions.takeaway: Use closed-loop communication for urgent instructions.
questions.learningObjective: Use closed-loop communication for urgent instructions.

questions.title: Handover interruption
questions.stem: A nonurgent telephone call interrupts transfer handover before allergy information is discussed. What is best?
options: Finish remaining items and assume the omitted information is in the chart
Ask the sending nurse to email omitted information after transport leaves
Resume from a clear checkpoint and verify missing items
Restart only if the receiving nurse notices a missing item
why: The interruption has left a known communication gap.
A delayed message may arrive after receiving staff begin treatment.
A checkpoint prevents interruption-related information loss.
The sender also has responsibility to verify interrupted content.
questions.takeaway: Recover deliberately after interrupted handover.
questions.learningObjective: Recover deliberately after interrupted handover.

questions.title: Urgent versus routine request
questions.stem: A client reports crushing chest pressure while another needs a routine discharge signature. What should the nurse do?
options: Complete the nearly finished discharge paperwork before assessing
Ask the symptomatic client to rest while the nurse finishes the signature
Delegate the chest-pain assessment to an available care provider
Assess the chest symptoms and activate urgent support
why: Routine paperwork should not delay evaluation of possible acute cardiac symptoms.
Rest alone does not replace prompt assessment and escalation.
Initial clinical assessment of new chest pressure requires qualified nursing support.
New crushing pressure warrants immediate assessment and escalation.
questions.takeaway: Time-sensitive symptoms outrank routine administrative work.
questions.learningObjective: Time-sensitive symptoms outrank routine administrative work.

questions.title: Time-critical medication conflict
questions.stem: A nurse must administer a time-critical prescribed medication and attend a routine meeting. What best preserves care?
options: Arrange medication coverage or adjust meeting attendance
Move the dose to the next routine round without checking timing
Give the dose substantially early so the nurse can attend
Leave the prepared medication for whoever becomes available
why: Explicit arrangements prevent a predictable treatment delay.
A time-critical medication may be harmed by an unreviewed delay.
Early administration may be unsafe without reviewing the prescribed timing.
An unaccepted task does not establish safe administration coverage.
questions.takeaway: Plan coverage when schedules conflict with time-critical care.
questions.learningObjective: Plan coverage when schedules conflict with time-critical care.

questions.title: Transport delay
questions.stem: A diagnostic department requests immediate transport, but the client is newly unstable. What should the nurse do?
options: Send the client with a copy of the latest observations
Stabilize and coordinate with the responsible team
Ask the porter to call if the client worsens en route
Recheck only after the diagnostic test because the slot is scarce
why: Written observations do not resolve the new instability or transport needs.
Assessment and coordination determine safe timing and transport support.
A porter cannot replace the required level of clinical monitoring.
Scheduling pressure does not justify delaying assessment of instability.
questions.takeaway: Reassess transport safety when clinical status changes.
questions.learningObjective: Reassess transport safety when clinical status changes.

questions.title: Simultaneous calls
questions.stem: One client requests a blanket; another calls that their tracheostomy feels blocked. Which should the nurse attend first?
options: Finish the nearby blanket request before checking the airway concern
Ask the client with the tracheostomy to try coughing and wait
Possible airway obstruction
Call respiratory therapy and continue routine care until they arrive
why: Convenience should not delay a possible obstruction assessment.
Self-care advice should not replace prompt assessment of reported blockage.
A blocked artificial airway may threaten ventilation immediately.
Consultation does not replace the nurse's immediate response.
questions.takeaway: Prioritize potential airway obstruction over comfort requests.
questions.learningObjective: Prioritize potential airway obstruction over comfort requests.

questions.title: Risk during waiting
questions.stem: A stable client waits hours for transport and a scheduled meal and medication are due. What should the nurse do?
options: Use the discharge order as the endpoint for all unit care
Tell the client to take the medication after arriving home
Withhold the meal in case transport arrives shortly
Reassess needs and coordinate interim care
why: The client still has needs while waiting under the service's care.
An uncertain delay may make that plan unsafe or ineffective.
Convenience alone is not a reason to leave nutrition needs unmet.
Interim planning prevents gaps during delayed transitions.
questions.takeaway: Continue needed care while a transition is delayed.
questions.learningObjective: Continue needed care while a transition is delayed.

questions.title: Unanswered referral
questions.stem: A referral marked urgent has no response and the client's condition is worsening. What is most appropriate?
options: Escalate through an available urgent pathway
Resend the same message with a reminder for the next business day
Discuss the referral at the next scheduled team conference
Ask the client to call the referral office personally
why: Worsening status requires a more immediate response pathway.
The worsening condition requires a pathway matching current urgency.
A routine meeting may occur too late for the changing condition.
Client self-advocacy does not replace urgent clinical escalation.
questions.takeaway: Escalation must match the current clinical urgency.
questions.learningObjective: Escalation must match the current clinical urgency.

questions.title: Safe shift planning
questions.stem: A nurse organizes care for four clients. Which practices support safe time management? Select all that apply.
options: Identify time-sensitive treatments
Leave room for reassessment
Complete the original schedule before responding to new findings
Coordinate shared team tasks
why: Time-critical care requires deliberate scheduling.
Reassessment detects whether priorities have changed.
Changing client status may require immediate reprioritization.
Coordination reduces duplication and missed care.
questions.takeaway: Plan care flexibly around urgency and reassessment.
questions.learningObjective: Plan care flexibly around urgency and reassessment.

questions.title: Alarm responsibility
questions.stem: A monitoring alarm sounds while the assigned nurse is occupied with another emergency. What should a nearby qualified nurse do?
options: Page the assigned nurse and wait beside the station
Respond and coordinate assistance
Silence the alarm while looking for the assigned nurse
Ask the monitor observer to decide whether bedside care is necessary
why: Notification alone may delay assessment while that nurse manages another emergency.
Prompt response establishes whether urgent care is needed.
Silencing without assessing the client can conceal deterioration.
The alarm may require direct qualified assessment to establish safety.
questions.takeaway: Respond to immediate safety needs through coordinated teamwork.
questions.learningObjective: Respond to immediate safety needs through coordinated teamwork.

questions.title: Unclear resuscitation documentation
questions.stem: A stable client has conflicting resuscitation documents. What should happen before a crisis?
options: Follow whichever document has the most signatures
Ask the family which form they prefer without involving the capable client
Clarify current wishes and valid orders through the team
Leave both forms visible so emergency staff can decide later
why: Signature count does not establish the current valid treatment plan.
The client's current capable wishes require direct attention.
Timely clarification prevents uncertainty during an emergency.
The stable period is the opportunity to resolve ambiguity deliberately.
questions.takeaway: Resolve conflicting goals-of-care documentation proactively.
questions.learningObjective: Resolve conflicting goals-of-care documentation proactively.

questions.title: Do-not-resuscitate meaning
questions.stem: A client with a valid no-CPR plan develops treatable pain. What does the plan imply for nursing care?
options: Limit care to mouth care because resuscitation is excluded
Withhold prescribed analgesia until the no-CPR order is rescinded
Require family permission before treating any new symptom
Continue care consistent with the broader goals
why: A CPR decision does not automatically define all other treatment limits.
Pain treatment can be entirely consistent with the client's goals.
The CPR plan does not itself transfer every treatment decision to family.
The overall plan determines appropriate ongoing treatment.
questions.takeaway: A CPR decision is not a blanket refusal of care.
questions.learningObjective: A CPR decision is not a blanket refusal of care.

questions.title: Family requests secrecy
questions.stem: A capable adult asks about results; relatives privately request that staff hide a serious diagnosis. What should guide response?
options: Explore the client's own information preferences
Follow the family's request because they know the client best
Provide only reassuring findings to reduce immediate distress
Postpone disclosure until every relative agrees
why: The client's wishes govern their involvement in information sharing.
Family knowledge does not override the capable client's information preferences.
Selective withholding may prevent informed participation.
Family agreement is not required to determine a capable client's wishes.
questions.takeaway: Ask capable clients how they want health information shared.
questions.learningObjective: Ask capable clients how they want health information shared.

questions.title: Ethics consultation
questions.stem: The team and substitute disagree about whether a burdensome treatment fits the client's known values. What support is appropriate?
options: Obtain additional family votes to settle the disagreement
An ethics consultation alongside the clinical process
Ask the bedside nurse to choose because they know the client best
Proceed with the team's preferred plan before discussing the conflict
why: A vote cannot replace the applicable values and decision framework.
Ethics support can clarify values, obligations and disagreement.
Familiarity does not confer unilateral treatment decision authority.
Acting first may bypass unresolved consent and values concerns.
questions.takeaway: Use structured ethics support for unresolved values conflicts.
questions.learningObjective: Use structured ethics support for unresolved values conflicts.

questions.title: Comfort goal evaluation
questions.stem: A palliative client prioritizes being awake enough to speak with family while maintaining tolerable pain. What best evaluates the plan?
options: Use the pain score as the sole success measure
Compare medication use with the previous day's total
Comfort and desired alertness together
Count completed nursing comfort interventions
why: A low pain score may coexist with unwanted sedation.
Dose volume does not measure the client's desired balance.
Both outcomes reflect the client's stated treatment balance.
Completed tasks do not establish whether the client's goals were achieved.
questions.takeaway: Evaluate outcomes against the client's expressed goals.
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate outcomes against the client's expressed goals.

questions.title: Advance planning discussion
questions.stem: A stable client asks how future care wishes can be recorded. What should the nurse do?
options: Tell the client a general statement will settle every future decision
Record the nurse's recommended choices as the client's plan
Defer discussion until the client becomes seriously ill
Explain local planning resources and facilitate discussion
why: Applicability depends on the future decision and governing law.
Planning should reflect the client's values and informed preferences.
Earlier planning permits participation before a crisis affects capacity.
Accurate resources support informed planning and documentation.
questions.takeaway: Support advance planning through accurate local resources.
questions.learningObjective: Support advance planning through accurate local resources.

questions.title: Cultural support request
questions.stem: An Indigenous client requests access to an Elder during admission. What is the most appropriate response?
options: Ask how to facilitate the requested support
Arrange a generic spiritual visit without asking the client
Wait until discharge planning to explore the request
Contact an Elder selected by staff without checking the client's preference
why: Client-directed support respects individual cultural preferences.
A generic service may not meet the requested cultural support.
Delaying without a clinical reason may deny meaningful support during admission.
