Client direction is needed to avoid assumptions about appropriate support.
questions.takeaway: Facilitate requested cultural supports collaboratively.
questions.learningObjective: Facilitate requested cultural supports collaboratively.

questions.title: Interpreter role clarity
questions.stem: During interpreted teaching, the interpreter begins answering questions for the client. What should the nurse do?
options: Accept the answers if they appear consistent with the care plan
Clarify that responses should reflect the client's own words
Switch to unassisted English to avoid the role confusion
Ask the interpreter to choose what information the client needs
why: Apparent agreement does not establish that the client expressed those views.
Role clarification protects accurate communication and autonomy.
Removing needed interpretation recreates a communication barrier.
Clinical explanation and client choice remain with the appropriate participants.
questions.takeaway: Interpreters facilitate communication rather than decide for clients.
questions.learningObjective: Interpreters facilitate communication rather than decide for clients.

questions.title: Supported decision-making
questions.stem: A client with an intellectual disability wants a supporter present while deciding about care. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Use accessible explanations
Address the client directly
Ask the supporter to consent before attempting accessible explanation
Check the client's understanding with support
why: Adapted communication can support meaningful participation.
Direct engagement respects the client's own decision role.
Disability and support needs do not automatically establish incapacity.
Understanding should be assessed after communication needs are addressed.
questions.takeaway: Support participation without presuming incapacity.
questions.learningObjective: Support participation without presuming incapacity.

questions.title: Refusal documentation detail
questions.stem: A capable client declines a scheduled test after discussion. Which detail best supports continuity?
options: Document that the client was uncooperative with the plan
Record only that the scheduled test was not completed
Stated concern, information discussed and follow-up plan
Record the family's disappointment with the refusal
why: A judgmental label does not explain the decision or next steps.
Completion status omits the discussion, concern and follow-up.
Specific content informs subsequent care without judgment.
Family reaction does not establish the client's decision-making process.
questions.takeaway: Document refusal as a clinical decision with context and follow-up.
questions.learningObjective: Document refusal as a clinical decision with context and follow-up.

questions.title: Professional disagreement
questions.stem: Two nurses disagree about a stable client's care plan. What is the best approach?
options: Continue debating at the bedside so the client hears every disagreement
Each nurse follows their own approach until shift change
Ask the client to choose between nurses without explaining the clinical options
Review findings and standards privately, then agree a plan
why: An unstructured argument may confuse the plan and undermine trust.
Inconsistent care leaves the clinical disagreement unresolved.
Client participation requires meaningful information, not choosing staff personalities.
Focused review promotes a defensible shared plan.
questions.takeaway: Resolve clinical disagreements through evidence and respectful communication.
questions.learningObjective: Resolve clinical disagreements through evidence and respectful communication.

questions.title: Unsafe shortcut pressure
questions.stem: A senior colleague pressures a new nurse to skip a required verification step. What should the new nurse do?
options: Complete the verification and raise the concern appropriately
Follow the senior nurse's instruction and document who directed it
Omit the step once while requesting a policy review later
Ask another novice nurse whether the shortcut is usually accepted
why: Required safeguards remain despite interpersonal pressure.
Attribution does not remove the nurse's own safety accountability.
A later review does not protect the client during this omission.
Common practice does not establish that skipping the required safeguard is safe.
questions.takeaway: Professional accountability includes resisting unsafe shortcuts.
questions.learningObjective: Professional accountability includes resisting unsafe shortcuts.

questions.title: Competing specialist orders
questions.stem: Two specialists prescribe conflicting fluid limits for the same stable client. Both orders are active. What should the nurse do?
options: Use the most restrictive limit
Use the most recent signature automatically
Clarify one coordinated plan before implementing the conflict
Average the two amounts
why: The strictest limit may not match the combined clinical needs.
Recency alone may not resolve competing treatment goals.
The responsible team must reconcile the incompatible instructions.
Averaging creates an unprescribed plan.
questions.takeaway: Resolve conflicting active orders through coordinated clarification.
questions.learningObjective: Resolve conflicting active orders through coordinated clarification.

questions.title: Unmet refrigeration need
questions.stem: A client is prescribed a treatment requiring refrigerated storage but lives without a reliable refrigerator. What is the best discharge action?
options: Repeat storage teaching
Ask the client to improvise a cooler indefinitely
Record that storage advice was given
Coordinate a feasible storage or treatment arrangement
why: Knowledge does not create refrigeration access.
An unvalidated cooler plan may not maintain required conditions.
Documenting advice leaves the practical barrier unresolved.
The team must make the treatment workable in the actual environment.
questions.takeaway: Assess whether treatment requirements can be met after discharge.
questions.learningObjective: Assess whether treatment requirements can be met after discharge.

questions.title: Home-care entry plan
questions.stem: A home-care client cannot reach the door after surgery. The first visit is booked, but no access arrangement exists. What next?
options: Confirm an authorized, reliable entry plan before the visit
Ask the nurse to wait outside until someone passes
Tell the client to leave the door unlocked all day
Assume the visiting nurse has a universal key
why: A planned access method prevents missed care without compromising security.
Chance access is not a reliable continuity plan.
Leaving the home unsecured creates a new safety risk.
Service access cannot be assumed without confirmation.
questions.takeaway: Plan practical access before essential home-care visits.
questions.learningObjective: Plan practical access before essential home-care visits.

questions.title: Interpreter confidentiality concern
questions.stem: A client declines a local interpreter because they know them socially and fear disclosure. What should the nurse arrange?
options: Continue because interpreters sign confidentiality agreements
Offer another qualified interpreter, including remote options
Ask the local interpreter to persuade the client
Use the client's limited English for the complex decision
why: Formal confidentiality does not remove the expressed barrier to participation.
An alternative can preserve language access and the client's comfort.
Persuasion by the person of concern may deepen mistrust.
Complex decision-making still requires effective communication.
questions.takeaway: Address interpreter concerns while preserving language access.
questions.learningObjective: Address interpreter concerns while preserving language access.

questions.title: Aphasia and choice
questions.stem: After stroke, a client understands simple instructions but struggles to speak. Which approaches support involvement? Select all that apply.
options: Allow extra response time
Treat speech difficulty as proof of incapacity
Offer validated yes/no or visual choices
Ask only family for the client's preferences
why: Extra time reduces pressure on impaired expression.
Expressive difficulty does not itself establish lack of understanding.
Alternative communication can reveal the client's own choices.
Family knowledge should not replace accessible direct engagement.
questions.takeaway: Distinguish impaired expression from inability to participate.
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish impaired expression from inability to participate.

questions.title: Conflicting discharge lists
questions.stem: A client has two discharge summaries from the same admission with different follow-up dates. What is most useful?
options: Keep the earlier date because it is sooner
Ask the client to attend both
Verify the intended appointment and provide one clear plan
Cross out both dates and advise calling later
why: Earlier is not necessarily the correct service arrangement.
Two visits may be unnecessary or unavailable.
Verification resolves the contradiction before the client must act.
Removing information without arranging follow-up creates a care gap.
questions.takeaway: Resolve contradictory transition instructions before relying on them.
questions.learningObjective: Resolve contradictory transition instructions before relying on them.

questions.title: Emergency contact versus consent
questions.stem: A capable client's chart lists a neighbour as emergency contact. The neighbour asks to approve a treatment change. What should the nurse explain?
options: Emergency contact status authorizes all urgent decisions
Any listed contact may sign for treatment
The neighbour can approve if staff witnessed the request
Contact designation alone does not establish treatment decision authority
why: Contact details do not automatically confer substitute authority.
Listing a person is not equivalent to lawful consent authority.
Witnessing cannot create a decision-making role.
The capable client normally decides; substitute authority requires separate verification.
questions.takeaway: Do not confuse communication contacts with decision-makers.
questions.learningObjective: Do not confuse communication contacts with decision-makers.

questions.title: Care refusal and dependence
questions.stem: A client declines a shower but accepts washing at the sink. Staff describe the client as refusing all hygiene. What should the nurse do?
options: Clarify the accepted alternative and adapt the care plan
Schedule a mandatory shower before breakfast
Record total refusal because the shower was planned
Ask family to persuade acceptance of the shower
why: The client is selecting a different way to meet the care need.
A routine schedule does not override a capable preference.
The record should reflect accepted and declined care accurately.
Persuasion is unnecessary before considering the reasonable alternative.
questions.takeaway: Distinguish refusal of one method from refusal of the care goal.
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish refusal of one method from refusal of the care goal.

questions.title: Client-held medicines list
questions.stem: A client brings a handwritten medication list with uncertain dates and several crossed-out drugs. What should inform reconciliation?
options: Use the neatest entries as current
Compare client report with pharmacy and current prescribing information
Discard the list because it is handwritten
Treat every listed drug as active
why: Legibility does not establish whether treatment is current.
Multiple sources help resolve changes and actual use.
The list may contain useful information despite uncertainty.
Old or discontinued entries may cause duplication.
questions.takeaway: Reconcile actual medication use using more than one reliable source.
questions.learningObjective: Reconcile actual medication use using more than one reliable source.

questions.title: Shared care ownership
questions.stem: A client receives wound care from two agencies. Each assumes the other will order supplies. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Ask the client to negotiate responsibility alone
Agree who orders and who checks availability
Document the agreed coordination plan
Continue visits until supplies run out before deciding
why: Professional coordination should not be shifted entirely to the client.
Explicit ownership prevents predictable interruptions.
A shared record supports consistent follow-through.
Waiting converts a foreseeable gap into missed care.
questions.takeaway: Assign responsibility across services explicitly.
questions.learningObjective: Assign responsibility across services explicitly.

questions.title: Missed interpreter booking
questions.stem: An elective teaching appointment begins without the booked interpreter. The client cannot understand the explanation. What is best?
options: Use a consent signature as evidence teaching can continue
Speak slowly and complete all material
Rebook or obtain qualified interpretation before complex teaching
Give only the usual English leaflet
why: A signature does not establish present comprehension.
Slower English may not overcome the language barrier.
Complex teaching requires a usable communication channel.
Written English may reproduce the same access barrier.
questions.takeaway: Resolve language access before relying on complex teaching.
questions.learningObjective: Resolve language access before relying on complex teaching.

questions.title: Nonurgent family call during crisis
questions.stem: During active care of a deteriorating client, another client's family calls for a routine update. What should the nurse arrange?
options: Interrupt the urgent assessment to prevent dissatisfaction
Give a hurried update without verifying the caller
Ask the deteriorating client to wait
Have an authorized colleague manage the callback process
why: Routine communication should not interrupt urgent assessment.
Haste does not remove identity and privacy requirements.
Deterioration requires continued timely care.
Delegated communication logistics preserve both urgent care and follow-up.
questions.takeaway: Coordinate routine communication while protecting urgent clinical work.
questions.learningObjective: Coordinate routine communication while protecting urgent clinical work.

questions.title: Unexpected absence of caregiver
questions.stem: A client requires supervised transfers at home; the planned caregiver is unexpectedly hospitalized on discharge day. What next?
options: Reassess discharge supports before proceeding
Ask the client to avoid transfers until tomorrow
Keep the original plan because teaching was complete
Send a transfer leaflet with transport staff
why: The support plan has materially changed and must be made safe.
Basic needs will still require movement.
Completed teaching does not replace unavailable physical assistance.
Written information cannot supply the required helper.
questions.takeaway: Reassess discharge readiness when essential support changes.
questions.learningObjective: Reassess discharge readiness when essential support changes.

questions.title: Visit priority in home care
questions.stem: A home-care nurse has a routine supply delivery and a call from a client whose caregiver cannot wake them normally. What should the nurse do?
options: Deliver supplies before returning the call
Direct immediate emergency assessment and coordinate response
Book a longer visit next week
Ask the caregiver to let the client sleep
why: Routine logistics should not delay an altered-responsiveness emergency.
Difficulty arousing the client may signal an immediate threat.
Future scheduling does not address current deterioration.
Assuming ordinary sleep may delay life-saving treatment.
questions.takeaway: Telephone descriptions of impaired responsiveness require urgent action.
questions.learningObjective: Telephone descriptions of impaired responsiveness require urgent action.

questions.title: Remote assessment limits
questions.stem: During a video visit, image quality prevents assessment of a rapidly spreading wound redness. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Acknowledge the assessment limitation
Arrange timely in-person evaluation based on symptoms
Document a normal wound based on prior photographs
Provide clear escalation instructions while care is arranged
why: The nurse must recognize what cannot be assessed reliably.
An appropriate modality is needed for the changing finding.
Old images cannot establish the current wound status.
Interim instructions support safety during the transition to assessment.
questions.takeaway: Change the care modality when remote assessment is inadequate.
questions.learningObjective: Change the care modality when remote assessment is inadequate.

questions.title: Interpreter dialect mismatch
questions.stem: A remote interpreter and client repeatedly misunderstand each other because their dialects differ. What next?
options: Continue because the interpreter speaks the named language
Ask the client to guess unfamiliar terms
Arrange a better-matched interpreter and verify understanding
Use the interpreter's summary without client confirmation
why: A shared language label does not guarantee effective communication.
Guessing undermines informed participation.
Matching actual communication needs improves accuracy.
An unverified summary may conceal misunderstanding.
questions.takeaway: Verify effective interpretation rather than relying on language labels.
questions.learningObjective: Verify effective interpretation rather than relying on language labels.

questions.title: Family demands additional treatment
questions.stem: A capable client chooses comfort-focused care, but family requests burdensome monitoring that the client declines. What guides the nurse?
options: The family member who visits most often
The most intensive available treatment
An automatic return to curative goals
The client's informed preferences within the agreed plan
why: Visiting frequency does not confer decision authority.
Treatment intensity does not inherently improve goal alignment.
A family request does not cancel the client's chosen goals.
The capable client's choices direct the agreed approach.
questions.takeaway: Align ongoing care with capable, informed goals.
questions.learningObjective: Align ongoing care with capable, informed goals.

questions.title: Escalation communication precision
questions.stem: A nurse needs urgent review for new hypotension after bleeding. Which request best communicates the needed response?
options: Please assess now; blood pressure is falling with ongoing bleeding
Please look at the chart when convenient
The client seems different today
Family would appreciate an update
why: The request links objective deterioration to explicit urgency.
A routine chart review does not convey the need for bedside action.
Vague change omits the key threat.
An update request understates the clinical emergency.
questions.takeaway: State the clinical concern and requested urgency explicitly.
questions.learningObjective: State the clinical concern and requested urgency explicitly.

questions.title: Conflicting client reports
questions.stem: A client tells one nurse they took a home medication and tells another they did not. What should the team do?
options: Choose the account given to the senior nurse
Clarify the uncertainty before any potentially duplicate dose
Average the reported doses
Chart whichever report came last as certain
why: Seniority does not establish which report is accurate.
A possible duplicate dose requires reconciliation and a safe plan.
Averaging creates unsupported administration.
Recency cannot justify documenting uncertainty as fact.
questions.takeaway: Resolve uncertain prior administration before adding treatment.
questions.learningObjective: Resolve uncertain prior administration before adding treatment.

questions.title: Care-plan goal quality
questions.stem: Which outcomes are suitable for evaluating a client's agreed mobility plan? Select all that apply.
options: Staff will encourage activity
Client transfers with the agreed level of assistance by review time
Nurse will provide excellent care
Client identifies when to request transfer help
why: Encouragement describes staff activity rather than client outcome.
Observable performance and timing permit meaningful evaluation.
A broad aspiration is not a measurable client outcome.
The client can demonstrate the planned safety behaviour.
questions.takeaway: Use observable client outcomes to evaluate the plan.
questions.learningObjective: Use observable client outcomes to evaluate the plan.

questions.title: Medication access at discharge
questions.stem: A client cannot afford a newly prescribed essential medication and plans to skip it. What is the nurse's best action?
options: Emphasize that prescriptions must be followed
Suggest using a friend's remaining supply
Coordinate pharmacy/prescriber review of affordable access options
Mark the client as unwilling to cooperate
why: Repetition does not resolve the financial barrier.
Another person's supply may be inappropriate or unsafe.
The team can explore assistance or suitable alternatives.
A judgmental label misses the stated cause.
questions.takeaway: Address treatment affordability before assuming nonadherence.
questions.learningObjective: Address treatment affordability before assuming nonadherence.

questions.title: Community service mismatch
questions.stem: A referral for daily dressing care is accepted by a service that can visit only weekly. What next?
options: Treat acceptance as proof the plan is covered
Reduce dressing frequency independently
Ask the client to improvise the remaining care
Reconcile the required care with actual service capacity
why: Acceptance does not ensure the specified frequency is available.
Changing frequency requires appropriate clinical review.
Improvisation may exceed the client's ability or instructions.
The plan must match real resources or be clinically revised.
questions.takeaway: Verify that a referral supplies the care actually required.
questions.learningObjective: Verify that a referral supplies the care actually required.

questions.title: Unregulated observer report
questions.stem: A trained observer reports that a high-risk client made a new statement about self-harm. What is the nurse's immediate role?
options: Assess the client and activate appropriate safety support
Ask the observer to determine intent independently
Save the report for the next care conference
Request that the observer avoid discussing it further
why: New risk information requires qualified assessment and timely action.
Determining clinical risk is not merely an observation task.
Conference timing may delay urgent protection.
Suppressing communication loses important safety information.
questions.takeaway: Act on new risk reports with qualified assessment.
questions.learningObjective: Act on new risk reports with qualified assessment.

questions.title: Client asks for another opinion
questions.stem: A capable client remains uncertain about an elective treatment and requests a second opinion. What response supports decision-making?
options: Explain that another opinion cancels current care
Help identify the appropriate request pathway
Ask family to decide instead
Require a final refusal before discussing options
why: Seeking another opinion does not inherently end care.
Facilitating a reasonable request supports informed participation.
Uncertainty does not transfer a capable client's authority.
A client can explore options before deciding.
questions.takeaway: Support reasonable requests for additional treatment information.
questions.learningObjective: Support reasonable requests for additional treatment information.

questions.title: Handover to unfamiliar team
questions.stem: An incoming nurse has not used a client's new communication device. Which handover actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Demonstrate how the client indicates urgent needs
Document only the device brand
Verify that the receiving nurse can use the agreed signals
Assume family will remain to interpret
why: Practical demonstration supports immediate communication access.
Brand alone does not explain the client's personalized signals.
Verification identifies whether continuity is functional.
Family presence and availability cannot be assumed.
questions.takeaway: Transfer practical communication methods as part of handover.
questions.learningObjective: Transfer practical communication methods as part of handover.

questions.title: Unfinished care at shift change
questions.stem: A dressing task is due now, but the outgoing nurse must respond to an emergency. What is the best handover action?
options: Mark it complete because supplies are ready
Leave supplies as the only reminder
Explicitly transfer the unfinished task and confirm acceptance
Assume the scheduled chart time guarantees completion
why: Preparation does not establish completed care.
Supplies do not communicate priority or accepted responsibility.
Explicit transfer prevents the task from disappearing between shifts.
A charted schedule does not guarantee someone will act.
questions.takeaway: Identify and transfer unfinished care explicitly.
questions.learningObjective: Identify and transfer unfinished care explicitly.

questions.title: Family translation of sensitive issue
questions.stem: An adult client looks uncomfortable when a relative answers questions about intimate symptoms. What should the nurse offer?
options: Allow the relative to answer to reduce embarrassment
Skip the sensitive assessment entirely
Ask the relative to decide if privacy is necessary
Private assessment with appropriate language support
why: Family answers may conceal the client's own concerns.
Avoidance leaves a relevant clinical need unexplored.
The client should have the opportunity to express privacy preferences.
Privacy and qualified support promote direct, accurate disclosure.
questions.takeaway: Offer private communication when family presence limits disclosure.
questions.learningObjective: Offer private communication when family presence limits disclosure.

questions.title: Refused discharge destination
questions.stem: A capable client declines the facility placement recommended by the team. There is no immediate emergency. What should happen?
options: Explore reasons and discuss feasible alternatives and risks
Arrange transport there because a bed is available
Ask family to sign admission without further assessment
Withhold all discharge information until agreement
why: Discussion supports an informed and workable transition decision.
Bed availability does not establish the client's consent.
Family cannot automatically replace a capable admission decision.
Withholding information undermines informed choice.
questions.takeaway: Explore a capable client's concerns about a proposed care destination.
questions.learningObjective: Explore a capable client's concerns about a proposed care destination.

questions.title: Community follow-up language
questions.stem: A client understands discharge teaching through an interpreter, but the follow-up service provides English-only telephone calls. What should the nurse do?
options: Assume discharge understanding is enough
Arrange language access for the continuing service
Ask the client to memorize likely answers
Cancel follow-up unless a relative is available
why: Language access is needed during ongoing care as well.
Coordinated support makes the follow-up usable.
Memorization cannot cover changing clinical questions.
Family availability should not be the sole access condition.
questions.takeaway: Plan communication access across the entire care transition.
questions.learningObjective: Plan communication access across the entire care transition.

questions.title: Clinical summary relevance
questions.stem: A client transfers for rehabilitation after a complicated admission. Which information most directly supports immediate care? Select all that apply.
options: Every normal result from the admission
Current restrictions and assistance needs
Active risks and the response plan
A chronological transcript of every conversation
why: Excess unfiltered data can obscure current priorities.
Restrictions direct safe daily care.
Active risks guide monitoring and escalation.
A complete transcript is less useful than a focused summary.
questions.takeaway: Prioritize current actionable information in transition summaries.
questions.learningObjective: Prioritize current actionable information in transition summaries.

questions.title: Client preference conflict in records
questions.stem: The care plan says morning bathing; the capable client consistently requests evenings. What should the nurse do?
options: Treat the written schedule as permanent
Ask every shift to negotiate from the beginning
Update the plan collaboratively if clinically feasible
Document each request as nonadherence
why: A routine schedule can be revised with client input.
Repeated negotiation suggests the shared plan needs updating.
A current shared plan reduces conflict and supports preferences.
A timing preference is not inherently treatment nonadherence.
questions.takeaway: Keep routine care plans aligned with current agreed preferences.
questions.learningObjective: Keep routine care plans aligned with current agreed preferences.

questions.title: Delegation terminology
questions.stem: A team uses the word delegation for every shared task. In BC, before arranging a restricted activity with an unregulated worker, what must the nurse verify?
options: That the task appears in the worker's job title
That the client has seen it performed before
That another worker performed it last year
Current regulatory requirements, worker competence and client-specific conditions
why: Job title alone does not establish authority for a restricted activity.
Client familiarity does not establish a lawful delegation process.
Previous practice may not meet current requirements.
Restricted activities require the applicable current framework and safeguards.
questions.takeaway: Distinguish task assignment from the requirements for restricted activities.
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish task assignment from the requirements for restricted activities.

questions.title: Escalating a resource barrier
questions.stem: A required pressure-relieving surface is unavailable and the client has increasing tissue risk. What should the nurse communicate?
options: The specific clinical risk and interim protection needed
Only that supplies are inconvenient
A request to replace every mattress immediately
That no care can occur until delivery
why: Specific risk supports prioritization and a safe temporary plan.
Convenience language understates the client's need.
A blanket request may obscure the urgent individual case.
Other protective care remains possible and necessary.
questions.takeaway: Describe resource shortages in terms of client risk and interim needs.
questions.learningObjective: Describe resource shortages in terms of client risk and interim needs.

questions.title: Family meeting consent
questions.stem: A capable client wants to discuss prognosis without relatives present. The family has travelled far. What should the nurse do?
options: Include relatives because of their travel effort
Arrange the private discussion the client requests
Ask relatives to vote on attendance
Share the discussion afterward without asking
why: Travel effort does not establish permission to receive confidential information.
The client's requested privacy should guide attendance.
Family voting does not replace consent to disclosure.
Private discussion does not authorize later unrestricted disclosure.
questions.takeaway: Respect capable clients' choices about meeting participation.
questions.learningObjective: Respect capable clients' choices about meeting participation.

questions.title: Client safety complaint
questions.stem: A client reports that a transfer technique frightened them and felt unstable. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Assess the reported event and current needs
Defend the staff technique before hearing details
Explain the concern-reporting pathway
Use the feedback to review the transfer plan
why: The client's account may identify a clinically important hazard.
Premature defence can suppress useful information.
Clients should be able to raise concerns safely.
Feedback can reveal whether the plan needs adjustment.
questions.takeaway: Treat safety complaints as information for assessment and improvement.
questions.learningObjective: Treat safety complaints as information for assessment and improvement.

questions.title: Missing consent interpreter record
questions.stem: A procedure consent form is signed, but the client says the earlier explanation was in a language they did not understand. What next?
options: Rely on the signature because it is recent
Ask the client to copy the signature again
Pause and arrange an understandable consent discussion
Ask the witness whether the client appeared agreeable
why: A recent signature does not establish informed understanding.
Another signature would not resolve the information gap.
The expressed comprehension problem requires clarification before proceeding.
Appearance of agreement cannot establish informed consent.
questions.takeaway: Investigate a credible understanding gap despite a signed form.
questions.learningObjective: Investigate a credible understanding gap despite a signed form.

questions.title: Nursing plan versus prescription
questions.stem: A nurse identifies that a prescribed intervention may be inappropriate after a new assessment. The client is stable. What should happen?
options: Carry it out because it is prescribed
Cancel all related treatment permanently
Ask a care provider to decide
Clarify the concern with the responsible practitioner before proceeding
why: Orders do not remove the duty to consider new clinical findings.
Permanent cancellation may exceed the nurse's authority.
The decision requires qualified clinical judgment.
Clarification reconciles the prescription with the changed assessment.
questions.takeaway: Question a treatment order when new findings affect its safety.
questions.learningObjective: Question a treatment order when new findings affect its safety.

questions.title: Quality data interpretation
questions.stem: Falls increased after a unit changed its reporting system to capture near falls. What should the team examine before concluding care worsened?
options: Whether the event definitions and reporting completeness changed
Only the total count
Whether staff preferred the old forms
The colour of the new reporting dashboard
why: Changed measurement can alter counts without equivalent change in harm.
Totals alone may compare unlike event definitions.
Preference does not establish event comparability.
Display colour does not explain clinical performance.
questions.takeaway: Check measurement consistency before interpreting outcome trends.
questions.learningObjective: Check measurement consistency before interpreting outcome trends.

questions.title: Care bundle completion
questions.stem: An audit shows every fall-prevention box checked, but several clients cannot reach their walking aids. What should the nurse conclude?
options: Documentation proves the intervention worked
Direct observation reveals a gap between recorded and actual care
The checklist should be abandoned immediately
Clients should be excluded from the audit
why: Checked boxes do not guarantee the intended conditions exist.
Observed access tests whether care was implemented effectively.
The tool may need correction rather than immediate abandonment.
Client experience is relevant to evaluating real care.
questions.takeaway: Evaluate implementation at the bedside, not only in the record.
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate implementation at the bedside, not only in the record.

questions.title: Error follow-up communication
questions.stem: After an identified care error, which communication practices support ongoing safety? Select all that apply.
options: State verified facts and current care needs
Give an exact prognosis before assessment is complete
Clarify who will provide further updates
Document the client's questions and the follow-up plan
why: Verified facts help the team and client understand current care.
An unsupported prognosis may mislead the client.
Named update responsibility prevents communication gaps.
Questions and follow-up support continuity and transparency.
questions.takeaway: Pair honest error communication with a clear follow-up process.
questions.learningObjective: Pair honest error communication with a clear follow-up process.

questions.title: Research versus care choice
questions.stem: A client believes joining an optional study is required to receive usual treatment. What should the nurse do?
options: Let the study team recruit first and clarify afterward
Encourage participation to preserve rapport
Clarify voluntariness and access to usual care through the study process
Ask family to sign quickly
why: The misunderstanding should be addressed before a decision.
Rapport should not depend on research participation.
A voluntary choice requires understanding the distinction from usual care.
Family signing cannot cure the client's misunderstanding.
questions.takeaway: Separate optional research participation from access to usual care.
questions.learningObjective: Separate optional research participation from access to usual care.

questions.title: Community visit unsafe entry
questions.stem: A home-care nurse arrives to find an aggressive visitor blocking the doorway. The client has no reported emergency. What is appropriate?
options: Enter to avoid missing the appointment
Ask the visitor to supervise the treatment
Conduct care through the partially open doorway
Withdraw to safety and coordinate an alternative safe visit
why: An unsecured threat may endanger both nurse and client.
The aggressive visitor does not provide appropriate safety support.
Improvised doorway care may be unsafe and compromise privacy.
A planned alternative preserves care without entering the immediate hazard.
questions.takeaway: Coordinate continuity when the care environment is unsafe.
questions.learningObjective: Coordinate continuity when the care environment is unsafe.

questions.title: Unclear accountability after transfer
questions.stem: A client physically arrives on a new unit, but no receiving nurse has accepted handover. What should the sending team do?
options: Confirm receiving responsibility and communicate essential care
Assume arrival transfers every responsibility automatically
Leave the chart on the bed and depart
Ask the client to tell staff what happened
why: Explicit acceptance prevents a period without responsible care.
Location alone does not establish a completed handover.
Records without direct transfer may miss urgent needs.
Client participation supplements rather than replaces professional handover.
questions.takeaway: Transfer responsibility explicitly, not solely by changing location.
questions.learningObjective: Transfer responsibility explicitly, not solely by changing location.

questions.title: Health literacy without stigma
questions.stem: A client says they forgot their glasses whenever asked to read care instructions. What is a helpful response?
options: Ask directly whether they can read at all in front of visitors
Offer plain-language explanation and demonstration privately
Document intentional avoidance
Provide a more detailed technical booklet
why: A public challenge may embarrass the client and impede disclosure.
An accessible approach supports understanding without requiring a label.
The reason has not been established.
Greater complexity may deepen the barrier.
questions.takeaway: Use accessible teaching without requiring clients to disclose literacy difficulty.
questions.learningObjective: Use accessible teaching without requiring clients to disclose literacy difficulty.

questions.title: Plan evaluation after trial
questions.stem: A client trials a new toileting schedule for two days but still experiences urgency before planned visits. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Review the actual timing pattern
Keep the schedule unchanged until discharge
Adjust timing collaboratively and evaluate again
Record the plan as effective because it was implemented
why: Observed patterns reveal whether the intervention matches need.
Persisting failure indicates the plan needs review.
A revised trial links evaluation to improvement.
Implementation alone does not establish effectiveness.
questions.takeaway: Revise care plans when measured outcomes remain unmet.
questions.learningObjective: Revise care plans when measured outcomes remain unmet.

questions.title: Disability accommodation in clinic
questions.stem: A client uses a wheelchair; the examination room cannot safely accommodate it, although another suitable room is free. What next?
options: Ask the client to transfer in the corridor
Complete only a verbal assessment
Move the appointment to the accessible room
Require the client to rebook elsewhere
why: A corridor transfer may compromise privacy and safety.
Avoiding needed examination can reduce care quality.
An available suitable space removes the access barrier.
Unnecessary redirection delays accessible care.
questions.takeaway: Use available accommodations to provide equivalent access to care.
questions.learningObjective: Use available accommodations to provide equivalent access to care.

questions.title: Conflicting family updates
questions.stem: Different relatives receive inconsistent updates from several staff members, with the client's permission. What is the best correction?
options: Stop all updates indefinitely
Ask relatives to compare stories themselves
Provide every staff member's interpretation separately
Coordinate a consistent factual update and contact plan
why: Halting communication does not resolve current confusion.
Relatives should not reconcile professional discrepancies alone.
More uncoordinated interpretations may worsen confusion.
A shared communication plan preserves clarity and accountability.
questions.takeaway: Coordinate permitted updates to prevent contradictory information.
questions.learningObjective: Coordinate permitted updates to prevent contradictory information.

questions.title: High-risk result telephone call
questions.stem: A laboratory caller reports a critical result but the client identifiers do not match the nurse's record. What first?
options: Verify identity and result through the approved critical-result process
Record it under the most similar name
Notify the family before verifying
Ignore it because the spelling differs
why: Verification preserves urgency while preventing action on the wrong client.
Similarity is not reliable identification.
Disclosure before verification may harm the wrong client and breach privacy.
The result still needs prompt clarification and appropriate routing.
questions.takeaway: Verify identity while preserving urgency of critical information.
questions.learningObjective: Verify identity while preserving urgency of critical information.

questions.title: Team member speaks up
questions.stem: A junior team member identifies a possible error during an otherwise smooth procedure setup. What response best supports safety?
options: Continue unless a senior person agrees
Pause to examine the specific concern
Discuss it only after the client leaves
Ask the junior member to stop interrupting
why: Rank does not determine whether a risk is valid.
A focused pause permits verification before harm occurs.
Delayed discussion may miss the chance to prevent an error.
Suppressing concerns undermines timely error detection.
questions.takeaway: Respond to safety concerns according to evidence, not hierarchy.
questions.learningObjective: Respond to safety concerns according to evidence, not hierarchy.

questions.title: Consent conversation teach-back
questions.stem: A capable client accurately describes benefits but says treatment has no possible disadvantages after a risk discussion. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Clarify the misunderstood material risks
Treat the signed form as resolving the discrepancy
Ask the responsible practitioner to address remaining questions
Verify understanding before elective treatment proceeds
why: The statement identifies a specific informed-consent gap.
A form cannot replace meaningful understanding.
The practitioner can provide treatment-specific clarification.
Elective timing permits correction of the misunderstanding.
questions.takeaway: Use the client's explanation to identify missing consent information.
questions.learningObjective: Use the client's explanation to identify missing consent information.

questions.title: Gloves between tasks
questions.stem: After perineal care, the nurse must clean the same client's mouth. What should occur before oral care?
options: Keep gloves because it is one client
Remove gloves, clean hands and use fresh gloves
Wipe gloves with antiseptic
Use a clean towel over the gloves
why: The gloves carry organisms from a heavily contaminated site.
Changing barriers and cleaning hands prevents transfer to the mouth.
Disinfecting disposable gloves is not a substitute for changing them.
A towel does not remove contamination from the gloves.
questions.takeaway: Change gloves and clean hands between contaminated and clean tasks.
questions.learningObjective: Change gloves and clean hands between contaminated and clean tasks.

questions.title: Visible soil
questions.stem: A nurse's hands are visibly soiled after removing gloves. What is appropriate?
options: Apply alcohol rub over the soil
Use a disinfectant surface wipe
Wash with soap and water
Put on clean gloves first
why: Visible soil requires physical removal rather than alcohol rub alone.
Surface products may damage skin and are not hand cleansers.
Soap and water remove visible contamination.
New gloves do not remove contamination already on hands.
questions.takeaway: Use soap and water when hands are visibly soiled.
questions.learningObjective: Use soap and water when hands are visibly soiled.

questions.title: Patient-zone contact
questions.stem: A nurse adjusts a client's bedside table without touching the client, then prepares another client's medication. What is required?
options: Clean hands only after medication preparation
Use gloves during medication preparation
Treat table contact as clean
Perform hand hygiene before moving to the next task
why: Contamination should not enter the medication preparation area.
Gloves cannot replace hand hygiene after environmental contact.
Patient surroundings can carry transmissible organisms.
Hand hygiene interrupts transfer from the patient environment.
questions.takeaway: Patient surroundings can contaminate hands without direct client contact.
questions.learningObjective: Patient surroundings can contaminate hands without direct client contact.

questions.title: Wet alcohol rub
questions.stem: After applying alcohol hand rub, the nurse's hands remain wet. What next?
options: Rub until dry before donning gloves
Wipe dry on clothing
Add gloves immediately
Rinse off the product
why: Drying through rubbing completes the intended application and avoids trapped moisture.
Clothing can recontaminate cleaned hands.
Wet product under gloves may irritate skin and impair use.
Rinsing prematurely interrupts product use instructions.
questions.takeaway: Allow hand rub to dry before putting on gloves.
questions.learningObjective: Allow hand rub to dry before putting on gloves.

questions.title: Hand skin damage
questions.stem: A nurse develops cracked skin after frequent hand cleansing. What is the best response?
options: Use gloves instead of hand hygiene
Seek occupational guidance and compatible skin care
Stop cleansing between routine contacts
Use an unapproved oil before every glove change
why: Gloves do not replace hand hygiene and may aggravate damage.
Skin care and product assessment support safe sustained hand hygiene.
Skipping hygiene increases transmission risk.
Unapproved products may affect gloves or antiseptic compatibility.
questions.takeaway: Address skin damage while maintaining effective hand hygiene.
questions.learningObjective: Address skin damage while maintaining effective hand hygiene.

questions.title: Glove tear
questions.stem: A glove tears while the nurse handles soiled linen; no skin injury occurs. What next?
options: Finish all room tasks first
Cover the tear with another glove
Remove gloves, clean hands and replace as needed
Use alcohol rub on the torn glove
why: The barrier breach requires prompt hand hygiene.
Covering the tear does not remove possible hand contamination.
This restores hand cleanliness and the needed barrier.
Glove disinfection does not address contamination beneath the tear.
questions.takeaway: Respond to a glove breach by cleaning hands and replacing barriers.
questions.learningObjective: Respond to a glove breach by cleaning hands and replacing barriers.

questions.title: Mask front contact
questions.stem: While removing a used mask, a nurse touches its front with bare fingers. What should happen?
options: Wipe the mask and reuse it
Continue directly to charting
Use clean gloves over the hands
Clean hands before touching clean surfaces
why: Cleaning the mask does not clean contaminated fingers.
Charting may contaminate shared equipment.
Gloves over unclean hands do not resolve the contamination.
The mask front may transfer organisms to fingers.
questions.takeaway: Correct removal errors with prompt hand hygiene.
questions.learningObjective: Correct removal errors with prompt hand hygiene.

questions.title: PPE preparation
questions.stem: A nurse plans care involving uncontrolled diarrhoea and possible splashing. Which steps are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Assess contact and splash exposure
Gather required barriers before entering
Use only the precaution sign to decide every barrier
Plan safe removal and hand hygiene
why: The task adds specific exposure risks.
Preparation avoids leaving with contaminated equipment or clothing.
Signs do not replace the point-of-care risk assessment.
Removal planning reduces self-contamination after care.
questions.takeaway: Combine posted precautions with a task-specific exposure assessment.
questions.learningObjective: Combine posted precautions with a task-specific exposure assessment.

questions.title: Respirator seal
questions.stem: Before entering an airborne-precaution room, a fit-tested nurse cannot obtain a seal with the assigned respirator. What next?
options: Enter briefly without adjusting it
Obtain suitable respiratory protection before entry
Tighten the surgical mask over it
Rely on the previous fit test
why: A brief exposure can still occur through a poor seal.
Effective protection requires an appropriate device and seal.
Layering a mask does not establish respirator fit.
Fit testing does not replace a seal check at each use.
questions.takeaway: Do not enter an airborne-risk area with an inadequate respirator seal.
questions.learningObjective: Do not enter an airborne-risk area with an inadequate respirator seal.

questions.title: Respirator versus mask
questions.stem: A transport worker plans to enter a room under airborne precautions using a surgical mask. What should the nurse do?
options: Permit entry if the client is masked
Ask the worker to hold their breath
Arrange required respiratory protection and instruction
Open the door to improve circulation
why: Client masking does not replace required worker protection inside the room.
Breath-holding is not a reliable protective measure.
The worker needs protection appropriate to the airborne risk.
Opening the door may impair containment.
questions.takeaway: Match worker respiratory protection to the exposure route.
questions.learningObjective: Match worker respiratory protection to the exposure route.

questions.title: TB transport
questions.stem: A client with suspected infectious pulmonary tuberculosis needs essential imaging. What should accompany the transport plan?
options: Remove precautions for the hallway
Send without notifying imaging
Have the client wear the nurse's respirator
Use source-control masking if tolerated and notify imaging
why: Transport does not eliminate transmission risk.
The receiving area needs advance preparation.
The nurse's respirator is not a client-specific source-control plan.
Masking and coordination reduce exposure during essential movement.
questions.takeaway: Coordinate source control and receiving-area precautions during transport.
questions.learningObjective: Coordinate source control and receiving-area precautions during transport.

questions.title: Measles waiting area
questions.stem: A child with fever, cough and a new rash has a known measles exposure. What is the priority in a crowded clinic?
options: Separate promptly using the airborne-risk pathway
Wait for laboratory confirmation before placement
Seat beside other coughing children
Complete registration before precautions
why: Compatible symptoms and exposure justify immediate containment measures.
Waiting can expose susceptible people before confirmation.
Similar symptoms do not establish the same infection.
Administrative tasks should not delay exposure reduction.
questions.takeaway: Begin indicated precautions from clinical suspicion, not only confirmed tests.
questions.learningObjective: Begin indicated precautions from clinical suspicion, not only confirmed tests.

questions.title: Disseminated zoster
questions.stem: An immunocompromised client has widespread suspected zoster lesions. Which precaution plan should the nurse verify?
options: Contact precautions alone
Airborne and contact precautions
Droplet precautions alone
Routine practices only after covering one lesion
why: Widespread zoster also presents airborne transmission concerns.
Combined precautions address airborne and lesion-contact exposure.
Droplet precautions do not adequately address the indicated routes.
Covering one lesion cannot contain widespread disease.
questions.takeaway: Disseminated zoster requires combined route-specific precautions.
questions.learningObjective: Disseminated zoster requires combined route-specific precautions.

questions.title: Uncontained drainage
questions.stem: A dressing repeatedly leaks purulent drainage onto bedding. What should guide initial infection-control action?
options: Culture result alone
Absence of fever
Contain drainage and add indicated contact precautions
Use a larger shared linen hamper only
why: Precautions may be needed before the organism is identified.
Lack of fever does not prevent environmental contamination.
Uncontained drainage raises contact-transmission risk.
Hamper size does not address exposure during care.
questions.takeaway: Uncontained secretions can require additional contact precautions.
questions.learningObjective: Uncontained secretions can require additional contact precautions.

questions.title: New diarrhoea cluster
questions.stem: Three residents develop vomiting and diarrhoea over one shift. What should the nurse do first?
options: Wait for every stool culture
Continue communal meals pending a diagnosis
Compare menus before changing care
Notify the outbreak/IPAC lead and institute indicated precautions
why: Waiting for confirmation can permit further transmission.
Group activities may spread an infectious syndrome.
Dietary review may help investigation but should not delay containment.
A cluster warrants prompt coordinated assessment and precautions.
questions.takeaway: Recognize clusters early and initiate the outbreak response pathway.
questions.learningObjective: Recognize clusters early and initiate the outbreak response pathway.

questions.title: Suspected C. difficile
questions.stem: A client develops frequent unformed stools after antibiotics. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Initiate the local enteric-precaution pathway
Use dedicated toileting equipment where feasible
Wait for confirmation before changing room practices
Promptly communicate the symptoms for assessment
why: The clinical presentation warrants early transmission precautions.
Dedicated equipment reduces indirect spread.
Delay may expose others while tests are pending.
Assessment is needed for causes, hydration and treatment planning.
questions.takeaway: Act on suspected infectious diarrhoea while assessment proceeds.
questions.learningObjective: Act on suspected infectious diarrhoea while assessment proceeds.

questions.title: Precaution discontinuation
questions.stem: A client colonized with a resistant organism has no symptoms and requests removal of precautions. What should the nurse do?
options: Stop because colonization is not illness
Follow local IPAC discontinuation criteria
Stop after one shower
Use the client's room preference alone
why: Asymptomatic carriage may still transmit organisms.
Criteria depend on organism, setting and current policy.
Bathing does not establish clearance.
Preference matters but cannot determine transmission status.
questions.takeaway: Use organism- and setting-specific criteria to stop precautions.
questions.learningObjective: Use organism- and setting-specific criteria to stop precautions.

questions.title: Isolation-related missed care
questions.stem: A client on contact precautions reports fewer staff visits and delayed toileting. What is the best response?
options: Explain that isolation reduces all contact
Remove precautions without review
Plan reliable care contacts using required precautions
Ask family to provide all bedside care
why: Precautions should not justify unmet nursing needs.
Stopping precautions may expose others.
Organized visits maintain care quality while controlling transmission.
Family support does not replace the service's care responsibilities.
questions.takeaway: Additional precautions must not reduce access to necessary care.
questions.learningObjective: Additional precautions must not reduce access to necessary care.

questions.title: Visitor PPE teaching
questions.stem: A visitor is unsure how to leave a contact-precaution room safely. What is most useful?
options: Hand them the policy manual
Tell them to copy other visitors
Remove precautions while family visits
Demonstrate removal and hand hygiene, then observe return demonstration
why: A manual alone may not build practical removal skill.
Other visitors may use incorrect technique.
Family presence does not eliminate transmission risk.
Demonstration and observation identify contamination errors.
questions.takeaway: Evaluate PPE teaching through observed performance.
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate PPE teaching through observed performance.

questions.title: Shared room diarrhoea
questions.stem: A newly incontinent client with suspected infectious diarrhoea shares a room with a highly vulnerable client. What should happen?
options: Request placement review and begin indicated precautions
Wait for a positive test before acting
Separate beds with a curtain only
Transfer the roommate's supplies but keep shared toileting
why: Contamination risk and roommate vulnerability require prompt placement review.
Clinical suspicion can justify action before confirmation.
A curtain does not address shared contact surfaces.
Shared toileting remains a major exposure route.
questions.takeaway: Consider source containment and roommate vulnerability in placement.
questions.learningObjective: Consider source containment and roommate vulnerability in placement.

questions.title: Cohorting uncertainty
questions.stem: Two clients have vomiting but no confirmed diagnosis. What should guide cohorting?
options: Identical symptom duration
IPAC assessment of likely organism and compatibility
Availability of one double room
Both clients' normal temperatures
why: Similar timing does not establish the same pathogen.
Cohorting requires consideration of transmission and other risks.
Bed availability alone cannot determine safe cohorting.
Afebrile clients can still carry different infections.
questions.takeaway: Do not assume matching symptoms establish safe cohorting.
questions.learningObjective: Do not assume matching symptoms establish safe cohorting.

questions.title: Respiratory source control
questions.stem: A coughing client arrives for a nonurgent clinic appointment. What should the nurse do first?
options: Wait for the full examination
Send directly to a crowded waiting area
Apply respiratory hygiene and separation measures per risk assessment
Ask the client to suppress every cough
why: Initial containment should not await the complete assessment.
Crowding increases opportunities for exposure.
Early source control and placement reduce transmission during assessment.
Cough suppression is not a practical infection-control strategy.
questions.takeaway: Apply respiratory source control at first presentation.
questions.learningObjective: Apply respiratory source control at first presentation.

questions.title: Aerosol procedure planning
questions.stem: A required procedure may generate infectious aerosols; the team lacks the required room and respiratory protection. What next?
options: Use extra surgical masks
Proceed quickly with fewer staff
Open a window and proceed
Escalate to arrange the required controls and safe timing
why: Additional surgical masks do not replace appropriate respiratory protection.
Short duration does not establish safe exposure control.
A window is not a verified substitute for required engineering controls.
Planning should match clinical urgency with suitable protective resources.
questions.takeaway: Resolve required aerosol-procedure controls before proceeding when feasible.
questions.learningObjective: Resolve required aerosol-procedure controls before proceeding when feasible.

questions.title: Exposure notification
questions.stem: A staff member learns of an unprotected exposure to a communicable infection. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Report through occupational health promptly
Provide timing and nature of exposure
Wait for symptoms before seeking advice
Follow individualized work and follow-up instructions
why: Prompt assessment may enable time-sensitive prevention.
Exposure details guide risk evaluation.
Some interventions are useful before symptoms appear.
Work restrictions and monitoring depend on the specific exposure.
questions.takeaway: Use occupational health assessment after unprotected exposure.
questions.learningObjective: Use occupational health assessment after unprotected exposure.

questions.title: Sick food handler
questions.stem: A nurse with active vomiting is scheduled to help with resident meal service. What should occur?
options: Attend with gloves only
Notify the supervisor and follow illness-exclusion guidance
Work if no fever is present
Restrict work to preparing cold foods
why: Gloves alone do not control all enteric transmission risks.
Illness management protects residents and supports appropriate return-to-work decisions.
Vomiting illness can be infectious without fever.
Cold-food preparation can still contaminate ready-to-eat food.
questions.takeaway: Report potentially infectious illness before direct care or food handling.
questions.learningObjective: Report potentially infectious illness before direct care or food handling.

questions.title: Laundry handling
questions.stem: A linen sheet is heavily contaminated with stool. What handling best limits spread?
options: Shake it before bagging
Carry it against the uniform
Contain it at the point of use without shaking
Rinse it in the handwashing sink
why: Shaking can disperse contaminated material.
Uniform contact can spread organisms beyond the room.
Containment limits environmental and clothing contamination.
The handwashing sink should not become a soiled-linen processing area.
questions.takeaway: Contain soiled linen without dispersing contamination.
questions.learningObjective: Contain soiled linen without dispersing contamination.

questions.title: Leaking waste bag
questions.stem: A bag of contaminated waste leaks during removal. What should the nurse do?
options: Compress it to reduce volume
Carry it quickly through the unit
Place it beside clean supplies
Contain the leak using approved packaging and cleanup procedures
why: Compression can expel contaminated fluid.
Speed does not prevent environmental contamination.
Clean supplies should be protected from leaking waste.
Appropriate containment and cleanup address the actual exposure route.
questions.takeaway: Contain leaking contaminated material before transporting it.
questions.learningObjective: Contain leaking contaminated material before transporting it.

questions.title: Contact time
questions.stem: A disinfectant label requires the surface to remain wet for a specified contact time. The surface dries early. What next?
options: Reapply as directed to achieve the required wet time
Assume wiping completed disinfection
Dry it further with a towel
Dilute the product to slow evaporation
why: Label-directed wet exposure is necessary for the claimed disinfection.
Wiping alone may not achieve the required microbial effect.
Early drying shortens the intended exposure.
Unapproved dilution changes effectiveness and safety.
questions.takeaway: Meet the disinfectant's labelled concentration and contact time.
questions.learningObjective: Meet the disinfectant's labelled concentration and contact time.

questions.title: Visible soil on equipment
questions.stem: A reusable device has visible organic material before disinfection. What should happen first?
options: Apply extra disinfectant over the soil
Clean according to device instructions
Sterilize the entire bedside cart
Store it until the soil dries
why: Organic material can interfere with effective disinfection.
Cleaning removes material that impairs subsequent processing.
The required process should match the actual device and risk.
Drying may make contamination harder to remove.
questions.takeaway: Cleaning precedes effective disinfection or sterilization.
questions.learningObjective: Cleaning precedes effective disinfection or sterilization.

questions.title: Cleaning cloth transfer
questions.stem: A staff member uses the same cloth for a toilet and then a bedside table. What should the nurse do?
options: Approve if the table looks dry
Add perfume to the cleaning product
Stop and use appropriate fresh cleaning materials
Move the table closer to the toilet
why: Dry appearance does not establish absence of transferred organisms.
Fragrance does not correct cross-contamination.
Fresh materials prevent spread from heavily contaminated to cleaner areas.
Location does not make the contaminated technique appropriate.
questions.takeaway: Prevent dirty-to-clean transfer during environmental cleaning.
questions.learningObjective: Prevent dirty-to-clean transfer during environmental cleaning.

questions.title: Dilution uncertainty
questions.stem: A bottle of disinfectant lacks concentration and preparation information. What is the safest action?
options: Use it if the smell is familiar
Add water until it looks usual
Apply twice as much
Replace it with a correctly identified approved preparation
why: Odour does not establish identity or concentration.
Appearance cannot guide a safe dilution.
Extra volume cannot compensate for unknown strength.
Verified preparation is needed for safe effective use.
questions.takeaway: Do not use an unidentified or unverified cleaning preparation.
questions.learningObjective: Do not use an unidentified or unverified cleaning preparation.

questions.title: Dedicated commode
questions.stem: A unit uses a dedicated commode for a client with infectious diarrhoea. Which practices remain necessary? Select all that apply.
options: Clean and disinfect according to protocol
Prevent access by other clients
Skip hand hygiene because equipment is dedicated
Use appropriate barriers for emptying and cleaning
why: Dedicated equipment still becomes contaminated through use.
Dedication reduces transfer only if others do not share it.
Hands can become contaminated while handling the commode.
Waste handling creates contact and possible splash exposure.
questions.takeaway: Dedicated equipment complements rather than replaces routine precautions.
questions.learningObjective: Dedicated equipment complements rather than replaces routine precautions.

questions.title: Single-use device
questions.stem: An unopened device package states 'single use.' A colleague proposes reusing it after a quick wipe. What should the nurse do?
options: Reuse if it looks intact
Follow the approved single-use and disposal instructions
Soak it in hand rub
Reserve it for another client with the same diagnosis
why: Visual integrity does not establish reprocessing suitability.
Labelled use and authorized processing determine safe reuse decisions.
Hand rub is not a validated device reprocessing method.
Matching diagnoses does not prevent cross-infection.
questions.takeaway: Do not improvise reprocessing for single-use devices.
questions.learningObjective: Do not improvise reprocessing for single-use devices.

questions.title: Sterile package moisture
questions.stem: A sterile dressing package is damp although unopened. What should the nurse do?
options: Dry the outside and use it
Open it beside the client to inspect
Replace the compromised package
Use it only on a small wound
why: Drying does not restore a compromised sterile barrier.
Visual inspection cannot establish retained sterility.
Moisture may compromise the package's protective barrier.
Wound size does not make compromised sterility acceptable.
questions.takeaway: Reject sterile supplies with compromised packaging.
questions.learningObjective: Reject sterile supplies with compromised packaging.

questions.title: Sterile field unseen
questions.stem: A sterile setup is left unattended outside the nurse's view. What is the safest interpretation?
options: It remains sterile if no one reports touching it
Only the outer edge needs replacement
A new sterile drape restores certainty
Sterility cannot be assured; establish a new setup
why: Absence of a reported touch does not verify the field.
An unobserved breach may involve the centre too.
A drape does not reliably undo unknown contamination.
A fresh setup restores a verifiable sterile process.
questions.takeaway: Maintain observation of a sterile field throughout use.
questions.learningObjective: Maintain observation of a sterile field throughout use.

questions.title: Reaching across field
questions.stem: During sterile preparation, a nurse needs an item beyond the field. What is appropriate?
options: Reposition or obtain help without reaching nonsterile clothing over it
Reach quickly to reduce exposure
Cover the sleeve with a clean towel
Ask the client to pass it across the centre
why: Changing access protects the sterile working area.
Speed does not prevent contamination from nonsterile clothing.
A clean towel is not necessarily a sterile barrier.
The client's hands may contaminate the field during transfer.
questions.takeaway: Arrange supplies to avoid reaching nonsterile items over sterile areas.
questions.learningObjective: Arrange supplies to avoid reaching nonsterile items over sterile areas.

questions.title: Sterile glove boundary
questions.stem: A sterile glove touches the bed rail before catheter insertion. What next?
options: Continue if the rail was recently cleaned
Replace the contaminated glove using aseptic technique
Apply alcohol rub to the glove
Use that hand only to hold the catheter
why: A cleaned rail is not a sterile surface.
Replacing the glove restores the required sterile barrier.
Hand rub does not re-sterilize the glove.
Holding the catheter would transfer contamination to an invasive device.
questions.takeaway: Replace a sterile glove after contact with a nonsterile surface.
questions.learningObjective: Replace a sterile glove after contact with a nonsterile surface.

questions.title: Catheter system break
questions.stem: An indwelling urinary drainage system disconnects accidentally. What should the nurse do?
options: Reconnect the exposed ends immediately
Wipe only the outside and reconnect
Follow the sterile replacement protocol for the compromised system
Leave it open until the next emptying
why: Reconnecting exposed components can introduce organisms.
External wiping does not restore internal sterility.
A break in the closed system requires appropriate aseptic correction.
An open system prolongs contamination risk.
questions.takeaway: Treat a urinary drainage-system break as a contamination event.
questions.learningObjective: Treat a urinary drainage-system break as a contamination event.

questions.title: Drainage bag position
questions.stem: A urinary drainage bag is resting on the floor and raised above bladder level during transfer. What should be corrected?
options: Only the visible floor contact
Only the tubing colour
Only the bag label
Keep it off the floor and below bladder level
why: Position also affects drainage and backflow risk.
Tubing colour is not the identified hazard.
Labelling does not correct contamination or reflux risk.
Both environmental contamination and drainage direction require correction.
questions.takeaway: Protect a urinary drainage bag from floor contact and backflow.
questions.learningObjective: Protect a urinary drainage bag from floor contact and backflow.

questions.title: Urinary catheter prevention
questions.stem: A client's catheter was inserted for a short procedure that is now complete. Which actions reduce infection risk? Select all that apply.
options: Review whether the indication remains
Maintain a closed drainage system
Disconnect routinely for easier movement
Remove when authorized and no longer needed
why: Ongoing need should be reassessed rather than assumed.
A closed system limits organism entry.
Routine disconnection creates avoidable contamination opportunities.
Reducing unnecessary catheter duration reduces exposure risk.
questions.takeaway: Review device necessity and preserve closed drainage.
questions.learningObjective: Review device necessity and preserve closed drainage.

questions.title: Specimen from catheter
questions.stem: A urine culture is prescribed for a catheterized client. Which collection approach is appropriate?
options: Take urine from the drainage bag
Use the disinfected sampling port with aseptic technique
Disconnect the catheter from the tubing
Collect urine from the floor spill
why: Bag urine may not represent a fresh uncontaminated specimen.
The designated port permits sampling while preserving the closed system.
Disconnection needlessly breaks the drainage system.
Spilled urine is unsuitable for reliable culture interpretation.
questions.takeaway: Collect catheter specimens aseptically through the designated port.
questions.learningObjective: Collect catheter specimens aseptically through the designated port.

questions.title: Injection preparation area
questions.stem: A nurse prepares injections beside a sink used for dirty equipment. What should change?
options: Use more frequent wiping only
Prepare fewer syringes at once
Move preparation to a designated clean area
Cover the sink drain during preparation
why: Wiping alone does not separate clean preparation from contamination sources.
Smaller batches do not resolve the unsuitable location.
A clean area protects medications and sterile supplies.
A drain cover does not control all nearby splash contamination.
questions.takeaway: Separate clean medication preparation from contaminated processing areas.
questions.learningObjective: Separate clean medication preparation from contaminated processing areas.

questions.title: Multidose vial entry
questions.stem: Before accessing a multidose vial again, which action is required?
options: Reuse the previous syringe for the same client
Change only the needle on the used syringe
Enter through an untouched part of the stopper
Use a new sterile needle and syringe with stopper disinfection
why: A previously used syringe may contaminate the vial.
Changing the needle does not make a used syringe sterile.
An apparently untouched spot does not replace disinfection.
Fresh sterile equipment and aseptic access protect vial contents.
questions.takeaway: Use new sterile equipment for every vial entry.
questions.learningObjective: Use new sterile equipment for every vial entry.

questions.title: Injection safety breach
questions.stem: A used syringe was accidentally re-entered into a shared vial. What should the nurse do?
options: Remove the vial from use and report the breach promptly
Reserve it for the next client only
Disinfect the stopper and continue
Use a filter needle for later doses
why: The vial may be contaminated and requires exposure assessment.
Changing the recipient does not remove contamination.
Stopper cleaning cannot sterilize the vial's contents.
A filter needle does not reliably remove infectious risk.
questions.takeaway: Quarantine a potentially contaminated shared medication vial.
questions.learningObjective: Quarantine a potentially contaminated shared medication vial.

questions.title: Sharps container capacity
questions.stem: A sharps container has reached its marked fill line during a busy medication round. What next?
options: Push contents down with forceps
Close and replace it through the approved process
Leave new sharps on the cart temporarily
Continue until the lid cannot close
why: Manipulating contents increases puncture and exposure risk.
Timely replacement preserves safe point-of-use disposal.
Loose sharps create injury risk for others.
Overfilling compromises safe closure and disposal.
questions.takeaway: Replace sharps containers at the indicated fill limit.
questions.learningObjective: Replace sharps containers at the indicated fill limit.

questions.title: Unexpected sharp in linen
questions.stem: A nurse sees a used needle in a linen pile. What is the safest action?
options: Shake the linen into the hamper
Pick it up by hand through thick gloves
Secure the area and use the approved sharps retrieval method
Ask laundry staff to find it later
why: Shaking can hide or propel the sharp.
Gloves do not reliably prevent puncture.
Controlled retrieval avoids blind handling and exposure.
Deferring the hazard transfers risk to other workers.
questions.takeaway: Do not blindly handle linen containing an exposed sharp.
questions.learningObjective: Do not blindly handle linen containing an exposed sharp.

questions.title: Blood splash to eye
questions.stem: Blood splashes into a nurse's eye during care. What is the immediate action?
options: Apply alcohol around the eyelid
Finish the procedure before responding
Cover the eye with a dry dressing
Irrigate promptly and activate the exposure pathway
why: Alcohol can injure ocular tissues.
Delay prolongs contact and delays exposure assessment.
A covering does not remove the contaminant.
Immediate irrigation and prompt assessment address exposure and follow-up.
questions.takeaway: Irrigate exposed mucous membranes and seek prompt exposure assessment.
questions.learningObjective: Irrigate exposed mucous membranes and seek prompt exposure assessment.

questions.title: Sharps disposal setup
questions.stem: A nurse prepares a bedside injection where no sharps container is within reach. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
