options: Arrange safe point-of-use disposal before starting
Keep the disposal route unobstructed
Plan to recap before walking to the utility room
Use the approved container rather than an improvised cup
why: Preparation avoids handling an exposed sharp unnecessarily.
An accessible route supports immediate disposal.
Recapping introduces avoidable needlestick risk.
Approved containers provide puncture-resistant containment.
questions.takeaway: Plan sharps disposal before beginning the procedure.
questions.learningObjective: Plan sharps disposal before beginning the procedure.

questions.title: Specimen transport leak
questions.stem: A blood specimen tube is leaking inside its transport bag. What should the nurse do?
options: Send it rapidly before more leaks
Contain it and follow laboratory recollection/transport guidance
Wipe the requisition and send everything
Place it with food samples in a larger bag
why: Speed does not make a leaking specimen safe or reliable.
Containment and laboratory guidance address exposure and specimen integrity.
A contaminated requisition and leaking tube remain problematic.
Mixed-purpose packaging does not meet specimen transport requirements.
questions.takeaway: Contain compromised specimens and verify safe laboratory handling.
questions.learningObjective: Contain compromised specimens and verify safe laboratory handling.

questions.title: Clean supply contamination
questions.stem: A nurse places unused dressings from a contact-precaution room back on the shared clean cart. What should be reviewed?
options: Whether the packages match stock labels
Whether the client touched each package
Room-exposed supply handling under local IPAC policy
Whether the packages are the largest size
why: Correct stock labels do not establish uncontaminated packaging.
Room exposure can occur without direct client touch.
Local handling rules account for contamination of outer packaging.
Size does not determine contamination risk.
questions.takeaway: Protect shared clean supplies from patient-room contamination.
questions.learningObjective: Protect shared clean supplies from patient-room contamination.

questions.title: Fall despite low score
questions.stem: A client scored low risk at admission but is now sedated after a procedure. What should guide mobility assistance?
options: The original score until tomorrow
The current sedation and functional assessment
The client's usual independence alone
Whether a fall has already occurred
why: Admission scoring may no longer reflect present function.
A new impairment requires updated precautions.
Baseline independence does not establish post-sedation safety.
Prevention should begin before an injury occurs.
questions.takeaway: Reassess fall risk after a clinical or medication change.
questions.learningObjective: Reassess fall risk after a clinical or medication change.

questions.title: Unwitnessed fall
questions.stem: A nurse finds a client on the floor reporting hip pain. What should happen before moving them routinely?
options: Obtain the incident form
Ask them to walk to test strength
Assess injury and summon appropriate help
Transfer immediately to preserve dignity
why: Documentation follows immediate assessment and care.
Weight bearing may worsen an unrecognized injury.
Assessment determines a safe response and transfer method.
Dignity matters, but unassessed movement can cause harm.
questions.takeaway: Assess for injury before routine movement after a fall.
questions.learningObjective: Assess for injury before routine movement after a fall.

questions.title: Fall without pain
questions.stem: After an unwitnessed fall, an anticoagulated client denies pain and requests to return to bed. What is the priority?
options: Accept the absence of pain as reassurance
Complete only the mobility score
Wait for bruising before reporting
Assess and escalate possible occult injury under protocol
why: Serious injury may initially be painless.
Mobility scoring does not assess bleeding or head injury.
Visible bruising may appear after clinically important bleeding.
Anticoagulation increases concern for hidden injury after a fall.
questions.takeaway: Absence of pain does not exclude serious post-fall injury.
questions.learningObjective: Absence of pain does not exclude serious post-fall injury.

questions.title: Alarm as sole precaution
questions.stem: A confused client repeatedly tries to stand despite a bed alarm. What is the best plan?
options: Assess unmet needs and provide individualized observation and assistance
Increase alarm volume only
Place the alarm out of the client's reach
Rely on the alarm to prevent standing
why: Addressing causes and timely assistance reduces risk before movement.
Louder alarms do not address why the client gets up.
Alarm placement alone does not meet the client's needs.
An alarm alerts staff but cannot physically prevent a fall.
questions.takeaway: Alarms supplement individualized fall prevention.
questions.learningObjective: Alarms supplement individualized fall prevention.

questions.title: Footwear mismatch
questions.stem: A client walks safely with an aid but wears loose slippers that slide during turns. What is the best adjustment?
options: Add another walking aid
Arrange secure, well-fitting nonslip footwear
Reduce all activity for the day
Ask the client to shuffle without turning
why: An extra aid does not correct slipping footwear.
Appropriate fit and traction address the observed hazard.
Unnecessary inactivity does not solve the footwear problem.
An altered gait may increase instability.
questions.takeaway: Match fall prevention to the specific observed hazard.
questions.learningObjective: Match fall prevention to the specific observed hazard.

questions.title: Post-fall review
questions.stem: A client fell while reaching for a hearing aid. Which actions help prevent recurrence? Select all that apply.
options: Review item placement and reach
Assess why assistance was not accessed
Attribute the fall solely to age
Revise the individualized plan with the client
why: Accessible items reduce unsafe reaching.
Understanding the sequence identifies modifiable barriers.
Age alone does not explain the event's mechanism.
A targeted revised plan addresses the actual circumstances.
questions.takeaway: Use the event sequence to guide post-fall prevention.
questions.learningObjective: Use the event sequence to guide post-fall prevention.

questions.title: New visual deficit
questions.stem: A client has a new visual field deficit and repeatedly bumps the walker against doorframes. What next?
options: Practice faster walking to improve confidence
Remove the walker permanently
Reassess mobility with rehabilitation support
Keep the previous independence designation
why: Speed increases collision risk before compensatory strategies are learned.
Removing an aid without assessment may increase instability.
The new deficit requires an adapted mobility approach.
The prior designation no longer matches observed function.
questions.takeaway: Reassess safe mobility after sensory or neurological change.
questions.learningObjective: Reassess safe mobility after sensory or neurological change.

questions.title: Unsafe bathroom urgency
questions.stem: A client receiving a diuretic rushes to the bathroom before help arrives. Which change most directly addresses this pattern?
options: Repeat the fall-risk leaflet
Use continuous bed rest
Move the call bell farther away
Coordinate toileting assistance with expected urgency
why: Information alone may not overcome urgent need.
Bed rest may add harm and is not individualized.
Reduced access to help increases risk.
Anticipating timing addresses the reason for unsafe rushing.
questions.takeaway: Align assistance with predictable care needs.
questions.learningObjective: Align assistance with predictable care needs.

questions.title: Wheelchair transfer brakes
questions.stem: A client is ready to stand from a wheelchair, but one brake does not hold. What should the nurse do?
options: Use a functioning chair or approved safe alternative
Hold the wheel while the client stands
Ask the client to move quickly
Place the chair against a curtain rail
why: A reliable stable surface is required for transfer.
Manual holding may fail during weight transfer.
Speed reduces control without fixing the defect.
A curtain rail is not a verified restraint for the chair.
questions.takeaway: Do not transfer from equipment with unreliable stabilization.
questions.learningObjective: Do not transfer from equipment with unreliable stabilization.

questions.title: Transfer reassessment
questions.stem: A client normally uses a sit-to-stand device but cannot follow instructions today. What should guide transfer?
options: Yesterday's equipment plan
Current ability and an appropriate revised method
The client's usual body weight alone
The quickest available device
why: A previous plan may be unsafe after a functional change.
The device must match present participation and physical ability.
Weight is only one factor in safe device selection.
Availability does not establish suitability.
questions.takeaway: Choose transfer equipment using current client function.
questions.learningObjective: Choose transfer equipment using current client function.

questions.title: Hoist sling tear
questions.stem: A small tear is found in a sling before lifting a dependent client. What next?
options: Use it for a shorter lift
Reinforce it with a towel
Remove it from use and obtain compatible intact equipment
Ask a second worker to hold the tear
why: Even a short lift loads the damaged material.
A towel is not a validated repair.
An intact compatible sling preserves the designed support.
Manual support cannot reliably compensate for sling failure.
questions.takeaway: Remove damaged lifting components from service.
questions.learningObjective: Remove damaged lifting components from service.

questions.title: Hoist preparation
questions.stem: Before lifting a dependent client, which checks are necessary? Select all that apply.
options: Compatibility and condition of sling and lift
Required staff and client-specific plan
A sling chosen only by colour
Equipment capacity and attachment security
why: Compatibility and integrity are essential to safe loading.
Staffing and technique should match the assessed transfer.
Colour alone does not establish correct size or model.
Capacity and secure attachment prevent mechanical failure.
questions.takeaway: Check the full lifting system before loading it.
questions.learningObjective: Check the full lifting system before loading it.

questions.title: Client begins to collapse
questions.stem: During assisted walking, a client's knees buckle. What should a trained nurse do?
options: Pull sharply upward by the arms
Try to keep the client standing alone
Step away to obtain a wheelchair
Use trained techniques to guide safely downward and call for help
why: Arm traction can injure the client and nurse.
Trying to hold full body weight may injure both people.

A controlled descent reduces injury risk while assistance is obtained.
questions.takeaway: Use trained fall-response techniques rather than lifting a collapsing client.
questions.learningObjective: Use trained fall-response techniques rather than lifting a collapsing client.

questions.title: Heavy repositioning
questions.stem: Two nurses cannot reposition a dependent client without excessive force. What is the best response?
options: Obtain appropriate repositioning equipment and assistance
Pull harder on the drawsheet
Ask the client to tolerate a quick lift
Use the bed rails as lifting handles
why: Equipment reduces hazardous manual loading.
Additional force increases worker and client injury risk.
Speed does not reduce the load's hazards.
Bed rails may not be designed for that force or technique.
questions.takeaway: Escalate equipment needs when manual effort is unsafe.
questions.learningObjective: Escalate equipment needs when manual effort is unsafe.

questions.title: Slide-sheet use
questions.stem: A worker proposes leaving a low-friction transfer sheet beneath a mobile client after repositioning. What should be checked?
options: Whether the sheet matches the bedding
Manufacturer instructions and sliding risk in this situation
Whether the client prefers the colour
Whether the next shift usually removes it
why: Appearance does not determine intended use.
Some devices are not safe for continued use under an independently moving client.
Colour is unrelated to stability.
Custom does not establish device safety.
questions.takeaway: Follow device instructions and reassess unintended sliding risk.
questions.learningObjective: Follow device instructions and reassess unintended sliding risk.

questions.title: Bed exit and rails
questions.stem: A confused client climbs over fully raised bed rails. What is the best next step?

Add more rails without reassessment
Review restrictive equipment and use a safer individualized plan
Tell the client the rails make climbing safe
why: A higher fall can increase injury severity.
More barriers may intensify climbing or entrapment risk.
Reassessment can address the behaviour using less hazardous measures.
Rails do not make climbing safe.
questions.takeaway: Bed rails can create hazards and require individualized assessment.
questions.learningObjective: Bed rails can create hazards and require individualized assessment.

questions.title: Restraint request
questions.stem: Family requests wrist restraints because a restless client touches a dressing. The client is not causing immediate serious harm. What first?

An order alone does not establish necessity.

questions.learningObjective: Assess causes and alternatives before restrictive interventions.

questions.title: Restrictive-device monitoring

Monitor circulation, skin and comfort

questions.learningObjective: Authorization does not remove ongoing restraint assessment and care.

questions.learningObjective: Respond immediately to possible restraint-related neurovascular compromise.

questions.learningObjective: Match elopement precautions to the person's risk and environment.

questions.learningObjective: Act promptly when a vulnerable client is unexpectedly missing.

questions.title: Seizure environment

questions.learningObjective: Prepare the environment and team for the known seizure pattern.

The room's routine cleaning time

The number of visitors yesterday

Assess the client, correct the sensor and verify appropriate settings

Ask the client to remove jewellery only
Pause and notify MRI staff for device-specific verification

Maintain safe therapy during replacement
Discard all pumps without reviewing model details
Follow the notice and organizational response instructions

questions.title: Wrong-client screen

Resolve the identity mismatch before proceeding

Follow identification-error and recollection policy

options: Assess and provide wound care
Review skin fragility and removal technique
Treat the absence of bleeding as proof of no injury
Adjust product and handling choices when indicated
why: The actual tissue injury requires assessment and treatment.
Risk and technique review identify preventive changes.
A skin tear may require care even with little bleeding.
A tailored plan can reduce recurrence.
questions.takeaway: Use injury findings to improve the next care episode.
questions.learningObjective: Use injury findings to improve the next care episode.

questions.title: Bed entrapment gap
questions.stem: A mattress replacement leaves a large gap beside the rail for a frail client. What next?
options: Fill it with loose pillows
Use the rail only at night
Remove the unsafe configuration from use and obtain an approved fit
Ask the client to stay centred
why: Loose pillows are not a validated entrapment correction.
Night use still exposes the client to the gap.
Compatible equipment reduces entrapment risk.
Position reminders cannot reliably prevent movement into the gap.
questions.takeaway: Assess compatibility when bed components change.
questions.learningObjective: Assess compatibility when bed components change.

questions.title: Accessible call system
questions.stem: A client with severe hand weakness cannot press the standard call bell. What should the nurse arrange?
options: Tell them to call loudly
Place the same button closer
Rely solely on scheduled rounds
An accessible call device with verified successful use
why: Voice may not carry or remain strong during distress.
Proximity does not overcome inability to activate the button.
Rounds supplement but do not replace access to urgent help.
A suitable device restores the client's ability to summon assistance.
questions.takeaway: Verify that the client can actually activate the call system.
questions.learningObjective: Verify that the client can actually activate the call system.

questions.title: Post-sedation escort
questions.stem: A client remains drowsy after a procedure and plans to leave alone by public transit. What should happen?
options: Reassess recovery and arrange discharge support per protocol
Provide coffee and proceed
Accept a promise to stay awake
Shorten instructions to speed departure
why: Residual impairment requires a safe recovery and transport plan.
Coffee does not establish restored judgment or coordination.
A promise does not reverse sedation.
Less teaching does not reduce the transport risk.
questions.takeaway: Discharge safety includes recovery status and practical support.
questions.learningObjective: Discharge safety includes recovery status and practical support.

questions.title: Recognize a silent chest during asthma
questions.stem: A client with severe asthma was wheezing loudly. They now have barely audible breath sounds, exhaustion and difficulty speaking. What is the priority interpretation?
options: Another routine assessment can wait until the next inhaler time
Airflow may be critically reduced despite quieter breathing
Bronchospasm is resolving because the wheeze decreased
Anxiety is the main issue because wheezing is absent
why: Potential ventilatory failure requires immediate escalation.
Diminished sounds with exhaustion can signal impending respiratory failure.
Quieter sounds are not reassuring when speech and effort deteriorate.
The physical deterioration indicates a respiratory threat requiring urgent support.
questions.takeaway: Diminished sounds with exhaustion can signal impending respiratory failure.
questions.learningObjective: Recognize a silent chest during asthma.

questions.title: Evaluate a short-lived reliever response
questions.stem: A client's prescribed asthma reliever briefly improves breathing, but severe dyspnea returns within minutes and they can speak only a few words. What should the nurse do?
options: Coach slower breathing before deciding whether more help is needed
Offer a sedative to reduce work of breathing
Escalate urgently while continuing the authorized emergency plan
Plan routine outpatient review because the medicine had some effect
why: Coaching must not delay care for severe respiratory compromise.
Sedation may impair ventilation and is not routine initial asthma care.
A brief response followed by severe symptoms suggests inadequate control.
Transient benefit does not establish safe recovery.
questions.takeaway: A brief response followed by severe symptoms suggests inadequate control.
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate a short-lived reliever response.

questions.title: Evaluate new drowsiness during COPD treatment
questions.stem: A client treated for a COPD exacerbation becomes drowsy after oxygen was increased. Saturation is above the prescribed target. What should the nurse do?
options: Remove all oxygen until the client is fully awake
Accept the high saturation as proof of adequate ventilation
Reduce observations because the client is finally resting
Urgently assess ventilation and titrate oxygen to the ordered target under protocol
why: Abrupt withdrawal can cause dangerous hypoxemia.
Pulse oximetry measures oxygenation, not carbon dioxide clearance.
New altered alertness is deterioration rather than reassuring rest.
Drowsiness may indicate hypercapnia; controlled oxygen and urgent review are needed.
questions.takeaway: Drowsiness may indicate hypercapnia; controlled oxygen and urgent review are needed.
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate new drowsiness during COPD treatment.

questions.title: Interpret oxygenation with worsening effort
questions.stem: A client with pneumonia maintains saturation on increasing oxygen but becomes exhausted and uses accessory muscles. Which conclusion is best?
options: Respiratory status is worsening despite the maintained saturation
Treatment is effective because the displayed saturation is unchanged
Anxiety alone explains the effort because oxygenation is supported
The oxygen device can be removed to test independence now
why: Rising support needs and fatigue can precede ventilatory failure.
The same saturation on more oxygen does not establish improvement.
Work of breathing and fatigue need physiological assessment.
Reducing support during deterioration may worsen hypoxemia.
questions.takeaway: Rising support needs and fatigue can precede ventilatory failure.
questions.learningObjective: Interpret oxygenation with worsening effort.

questions.title: Recognize pneumonia deterioration in an older adult
questions.stem: An older adult with pneumonia has a temperature of 37.4°C but is newly inattentive, breathing faster and eating little. What should guide the nurse's response?
options: Focus first on completing a nutrition supplement
Treat the change from baseline as possible acute deterioration
Wait for a fever above 38°C before reporting
Attribute inattention to the unfamiliar room alone
why: Immediate physiological assessment takes priority over supplement intake.
Older adults may deteriorate without a marked fever.
Absence of high fever does not exclude serious illness.
A new cognitive change with respiratory symptoms needs assessment.
questions.takeaway: Older adults may deteriorate without a marked fever.
questions.learningObjective: Recognize pneumonia deterioration in an older adult.

questions.title: Respond to vomiting during noninvasive ventilation
questions.stem: A client wearing a tight noninvasive ventilation mask begins vomiting and cannot clear the contents. What should happen first?
options: Keep the mask sealed until an antiemetic takes effect
Lower the head of the bed to stop the leak
Remove the mask and protect the airway while summoning help
Increase mask pressure to maintain the oxygen saturation
why: Waiting leaves the airway exposed to vomit.
Flat positioning can further compromise airway protection.
The interface traps vomit and creates an immediate aspiration threat.
More pressure does not clear the airway and may worsen aspiration risk.
questions.takeaway: The interface traps vomit and creates an immediate aspiration threat.
questions.learningObjective: Respond to vomiting during noninvasive ventilation.

questions.title: Escalate an obstructed tracheostomy
questions.stem: A tracheostomy-dependent client suddenly struggles to breathe, and the trained nurse cannot pass the suction catheter through the tube. What is appropriate?
options: Repeatedly force the catheter through the resistance
Instill repeated saline boluses until the catheter passes
Wait for the next scheduled respiratory therapy visit
Call emergency help and follow the tracheostomy obstruction algorithm
why: Force may cause trauma without restoring ventilation.
Routine repeated instillation may delay definitive airway care.
An obstructed artificial airway is an immediate emergency.
Failure to pass the catheter suggests obstruction requiring a structured airway response.
questions.takeaway: Failure to pass the catheter suggests obstruction requiring a structured airway response.
questions.learningObjective: Escalate an obstructed tracheostomy.

questions.title: Select a response to retained tracheal secretions
questions.stem: A client with a tracheostomy has audible gurgling, visible secretions and an ineffective cough. Oxygen saturation has fallen from baseline. What is the most appropriate initial intervention by a competent nurse?
options: Assess and perform suctioning according to the airway protocol
Increase oxygen only and postpone secretion assessment
Give a cough suppressant before attempting clearance
Increase humidification and delay airway clearance until the next round
why: The findings indicate retained secretions compromising airway clearance.
Oxygen does not remove an obstructing secretion burden.
Suppressing the cough can further impair secretion removal.
Humidification may support ongoing care but does not promptly remove the current obstructing secretions.
questions.takeaway: The findings indicate retained secretions compromising airway clearance.
questions.learningObjective: Select a response to retained tracheal secretions.

questions.title: Respond to bradycardia during suctioning
questions.stem: During tracheal suctioning, a client's pulse falls markedly and oxygen saturation drops. What should the nurse do first?
options: Repeat immediately with stronger suction pressure
Stop suctioning and support oxygenation while reassessing
Complete the planned suction time before stopping
Advance the catheter farther to clear more secretions
why: Greater suction can increase trauma and oxygen loss.
Suction-related hypoxemia or vagal stimulation requires ending the stimulus.
Continuing may worsen bradycardia and hypoxemia.
Additional stimulation can compound the instability.
questions.takeaway: Suction-related hypoxemia or vagal stimulation requires ending the stimulus.
questions.learningObjective: Respond to bradycardia during suctioning.

questions.title: Evaluate expanding subcutaneous emphysema
questions.stem: A client with a chest drain develops increasing neck and chest swelling that crackles on palpation, with new dyspnea. What is the priority?
options: Document expected postoperative swelling without reassessment
Clamp the tube until the swelling stops
Assess breathing and urgently report possible drainage failure or air leak
Massage the swelling to disperse trapped air
why: The progression and dyspnea make this finding clinically important.
Clamping may trap intrathoracic air and worsen pressure.
Expanding subcutaneous air with dyspnea can signal a significant thoracic complication.
Massage does not correct the source or restore effective drainage.
questions.takeaway: Expanding subcutaneous air with dyspnea can signal a significant thoracic complication.
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate expanding subcutaneous emphysema.

questions.title: Manage an accidental chest-drain disconnection
questions.stem: A chest drain disconnects from its drainage system while still in the client's chest. What should guide immediate care?
options: Leave the tubing open while obtaining the routine dressing tray
Clamp the tube for the rest of the shift
Reconnect contaminated ends without any assessment
Protect the connection and restore drainage using the local emergency protocol
why: An open system can permit air entry and worsen respiratory status.
Prolonged clamping can create dangerous intrathoracic pressure.
Restoring connection must account for contamination and client condition.
A prompt protocol-based response limits air entry and loss of drainage function.
questions.takeaway: A prompt protocol-based response limits air entry and loss of drainage function.
questions.learningObjective: Manage an accidental chest-drain disconnection.

questions.title: Recognize an acute post-procedure pneumothorax
questions.stem: Soon after central venous catheter placement, a client has sudden dyspnea, falling blood pressure and markedly reduced breath sounds on one side. What is the priority?
options: Activate emergency assessment for a possible tension pneumothorax
Wait for routine post-procedure imaging before escalating
Give the scheduled anxiolytic and reassess later
Encourage forceful coughing to re-expand the lung
why: The combination suggests rapidly worsening ventilation and circulation.
Clinical instability requires action before routine confirmation.
Sedation can obscure deterioration without correcting the thoracic problem.
Coughing does not treat a pressurized pleural air collection.
questions.takeaway: The combination suggests rapidly worsening ventilation and circulation.
questions.learningObjective: Recognize an acute post-procedure pneumothorax.

questions.title: Prioritize active hemoptysis
questions.stem: A client coughs up increasing amounts of bright blood and struggles to clear the airway. The bleeding source is not known. What takes priority?
options: Encourage the client to lie flat for a full examination
Summon urgent help and support airway clearance and oxygenation
Collect a complete sputum history before requesting help
Offer warm fluids to ease throat irritation
why: Flat positioning can impair clearance and worsen aspiration of blood.
Active airway flooding can threaten ventilation before total blood loss is large.
History must not delay response to airway compromise.
Oral intake is unsafe during major active airway bleeding.
questions.takeaway: Active airway flooding can threaten ventilation before total blood loss is large.
questions.learningObjective: Prioritize active hemoptysis.

questions.title: Support a symptomatic pleural effusion
questions.stem: A client with a known large pleural effusion is breathless when supine but more comfortable sitting. Prescribed drainage is being arranged. What is appropriate now?
options: Encourage a large fluid intake to thin secretions
Begin vigorous chest percussion over the effusion
Support an upright position and monitor respiratory response
Keep the client flat to spread pleural fluid evenly
why: Pleural fluid is not airway mucus and extra intake may not help.
Percussion does not remove fluid from the pleural space.
Positioning can reduce breathing difficulty while definitive treatment is prepared.
The position already worsens this client's breathlessness.
questions.takeaway: Positioning can reduce breathing difficulty while definitive treatment is prepared.
questions.learningObjective: Support a symptomatic pleural effusion.

questions.title: Respond to postoperative thoracic bleeding
questions.stem: After lung surgery, chest drainage changes from a small serosanguineous amount to rapidly increasing bright-red output. The client becomes pale and tachycardic. What is appropriate?
options: Clamp the drain to prevent further blood loss
Empty the chamber and wait for the next scheduled total
Encourage ambulation to mobilize retained drainage
Urgently assess circulation and notify the surgical team
why: Clamping does not stop internal bleeding and may conceal accumulation.
Delaying review risks worsening hemorrhage.
An unstable potentially bleeding client should not be mobilized.
Rapid fresh drainage with systemic signs suggests significant postoperative bleeding.
questions.takeaway: Rapid fresh drainage with systemic signs suggests significant postoperative bleeding.
questions.learningObjective: Respond to postoperative thoracic bleeding.

questions.title: Deliver oxygen after total laryngectomy
questions.stem: A client with a total laryngectomy becomes hypoxemic. A colleague places oxygen at the nose, but saturation does not improve. What change is needed?
options: Deliver oxygen through the neck stoma using appropriate equipment
Increase nasal flow before checking the stoma
Ask the client to breathe more deeply through the mouth
Cover the stoma to direct oxygen through the face
why: After total laryngectomy, the lungs receive air through the stoma.
Higher nasal flow cannot reach the surgically separated airway.
The mouth is no longer connected to the lower airway.
Occluding the stoma obstructs the client's only airway.
questions.takeaway: After total laryngectomy, the lungs receive air through the stoma.
questions.learningObjective: Deliver oxygen after total laryngectomy.

questions.title: Manage ineffective clearance in cystic fibrosis
questions.stem: A client with cystic fibrosis reports thicker sputum and difficulty clearing secretions. They are stable enough to follow the established airway-clearance plan. What is appropriate?
options: Limit activity solely because coughing is uncomfortable
Use the individualized prescribed airway-clearance regimen and reassess
Suppress the productive cough before clearance therapy
Delay all clearance until antibiotics have finished
why: A blanket restriction does not address retained secretions or the individualized plan.
The plan targets mobilization and removal of retained secretions.
Reducing an effective cough may worsen secretion retention.
Secretion management remains important during treatment of exacerbations.
questions.takeaway: The plan targets mobilization and removal of retained secretions.
questions.learningObjective: Manage ineffective clearance in cystic fibrosis.

questions.title: Evaluate a bronchiectasis exacerbation
questions.stem: A client with bronchiectasis reports increased purulent sputum, worsening breathlessness and less ability to perform usual activities. What is most appropriate?
options: Wait for complete loss of appetite before seeking review
Recommend stopping airway clearance to reduce coughing
Promptly assess and report a possible exacerbation
Reassure because chronic productive cough is expected
why: Additional deterioration is not needed to justify assessment.
Withholding clearance may increase secretion retention.
Changes from the established sputum and functional baseline suggest worsening disease.
The change in quantity, quality and function is significant.
questions.takeaway: Changes from the established sputum and functional baseline suggest worsening disease.
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate a bronchiectasis exacerbation.

questions.title: Respond to aspiration during feeding
questions.stem: During tube feeding, a client develops sudden coughing, wet respirations and falling saturation. What should the nurse do first?
options: Increase the feeding rate to finish before repositioning
Flush the tube before assessing the client
Give a sedative to reduce distress from coughing
Stop feeding and assess/support the airway and breathing
why: More feed may increase exposure and worsen the event.
Tube care should not delay airway and respiratory assessment.
Sedation may further impair airway protection.
Continuing delivery can worsen aspiration while respiratory compromise is assessed.
questions.takeaway: Continuing delivery can worsen aspiration while respiratory compromise is assessed.
questions.learningObjective: Respond to aspiration during feeding.

questions.title: Recognize airway risk after a burn
questions.stem: A client rescued from an enclosed fire has facial burns, soot around the mouth and a newly hoarse voice. Saturation is initially 97%. What is the priority?
options: Urgent airway assessment because swelling may progress
Complete burn-size calculations before calling for airway review
Use the normal saturation to exclude inhalation injury
Provide oral fluids before assessing swallowing
why: Voice change and inhalation exposure can precede airway obstruction.
Detailed burn assessment must not delay a threatened airway.
Initial oxygenation does not establish future airway patency.
Evolving airway injury can make oral intake unsafe.
questions.takeaway: Voice change and inhalation exposure can precede airway obstruction.
questions.learningObjective: Recognize airway risk after a burn.

questions.title: Interpret oximetry after smoke exposure
questions.stem: A client from an enclosed garage is confused and has a headache after engine exhaust exposure. Routine pulse oximetry reads 99%. What should the nurse do?
options: Observe until the oxygen reading begins to fall
Escalate suspected carbon monoxide exposure despite the reading
Rule out poisoning because saturation exceeds 95%
Focus on oral hydration before respiratory assessment
why: Waiting for a misleading measurement to change can delay care.
Standard pulse oximetry can appear normal with carboxyhemoglobin present.
The displayed saturation cannot reliably exclude carbon monoxide poisoning.
Potential toxic hypoxia needs urgent assessment and treatment.
questions.takeaway: Standard pulse oximetry can appear normal with carboxyhemoglobin present.
questions.learningObjective: Interpret oximetry after smoke exposure.

questions.title: Recognize worsening ventilation after chest trauma
questions.stem: After blunt chest trauma, a client has painful shallow breaths, a segment of chest moving abnormally and increasing fatigue. What is most urgent?
options: Encourage vigorous coughing before addressing severe pain
Wait for bruising to fully develop before reassessing
Escalate for respiratory support and effective prescribed analgesia
Bind the entire chest tightly to prevent movement
why: Uncontrolled pain limits useful coughing and respiratory effort.
Fatigue and abnormal movement already indicate significant injury.
Chest instability and pain can impair ventilation and lead to exhaustion.
Circumferential restriction can further reduce ventilation.
questions.takeaway: Chest instability and pain can impair ventilation and lead to exhaustion.
questions.learningObjective: Recognize worsening ventilation after chest trauma.

questions.title: Avoid excluding embolism from normal oximetry
questions.stem: A postoperative client develops pleuritic pain and unexplained tachycardia. Saturation is 96% on room air. A colleague says embolism is excluded. Which response is best?
options: An embolism always causes audible wheezing first
Only clients with swollen legs can have an embolism
Pulse oximetry determines whether chest pain is cardiac
Normal saturation does not exclude pulmonary embolism
why: Wheezing is not required for pulmonary embolism.
Visible leg findings may be absent.
Oximetry cannot identify the cause of chest pain.
An embolism can be present without marked resting hypoxemia.
questions.takeaway: An embolism can be present without marked resting hypoxemia.
questions.learningObjective: Avoid excluding embolism from normal oximetry.

questions.title: Identify improvement after respiratory support
questions.stem: A client receives treatment for acute respiratory distress. Which changes support improvement when compared with the pretreatment state? Select all that apply.
options: A normal saturation maintained only by increasing oxygen
A quieter chest accompanied by increasing drowsiness
A lower respiratory rate with worsening exhaustion
Less accessory-muscle use with more comfortable speech
Stable oxygenation on a lower prescribed oxygen requirement
why: Increasing support may hide worsening gas exchange.
Reduced sounds with declining alertness can indicate ventilatory failure.
A falling rate from fatigue is not a reassuring recovery sign.
Reduced work and improved speech suggest better respiratory function.
Less support for the same oxygenation suggests improvement.
questions.takeaway: Reduced work and improved speech suggest better respiratory function.
questions.learningObjective: Identify improvement after respiratory support.

questions.title: Recognize respiratory acidosis during COPD deterioration
questions.stem: An acutely drowsy client has pH 7.28, PaCO2 58 mmHg and HCO3 26 mmol/L. Reference ranges are 7.35–7.45, 35–45 and 22–26, respectively. What is most consistent?
options: A normal blood gas because bicarbonate is in range
Respiratory acidosis requiring urgent ventilatory assessment
Metabolic acidosis from a low bicarbonate level
Respiratory alkalosis from excessive ventilation
why: The abnormal pH and carbon dioxide remain clinically important.
Acidemia with elevated carbon dioxide indicates impaired ventilation.
Bicarbonate is not reduced below the supplied reference range.
Excess ventilation would lower carbon dioxide rather than raise it.
questions.takeaway: Acidemia with elevated carbon dioxide indicates impaired ventilation.
questions.learningObjective: Recognize respiratory acidosis during COPD deterioration.

questions.title: Resolve a changed-strength barcode alert
questions.stem: A client's tablet strength was changed this morning. Scanning the evening tablet produces a wrong-strength alert, although the drug name matches. What should the nurse do next?
options: Give it and ask pharmacy to update the barcode
Compare the current order with the supplied product
Split the tablet to match yesterday's dose
Use the barcode from the morning package
why: The discrepancy must be resolved before an uncertain dose is given.
The alert may reflect an outdated supply after the dose change.
Yesterday's dose does not establish the current prescription or tablet suitability.
A different package's barcode cannot verify the tablet being administered.
questions.takeaway: The alert may reflect an outdated supply after the dose change.
questions.learningObjective: Resolve a changed-strength barcode alert.

questions.title: Replace a contaminated controlled medication
questions.stem: While preparing a prescribed controlled analgesic, a tablet falls onto the floor. The client reports severe pain. What is the best action?
options: Place the dropped tablet in the client's drawer for later disposal
Discard it now and request replacement at the next scheduled dose
Arrange documented disposal and a replacement dose promptly
Document the dropped tablet as administered and obtain another
why: Unsecured storage leaves an unidentified controlled medication accessible.
Waiting until the next dose unnecessarily leaves the current pain untreated.
This maintains safe medication handling while addressing pain without unnecessary delay.
Incorrect administration documentation can create a false cumulative dose record.
questions.takeaway: This maintains safe medication handling while addressing pain without unnecessary delay.
questions.learningObjective: Replace a contaminated controlled medication.

questions.title: Investigate uncertain prior administration
questions.stem: An antihypertensive is due. The client says another nurse already gave it, but the administration record is blank. Blood pressure is stable. What should happen first?
options: Give it because the electronic record is blank
Mark it refused because the client questioned it
Wait one hour and give it if pressure is unchanged
Verify administration with the nurse and available records
why: A blank entry does not exclude an undocumented dose.
Questioning prior administration is different from declining treatment.
Blood pressure alone cannot establish whether the earlier dose occurred.
A stable client allows clarification that prevents duplicate dosing.
questions.takeaway: A stable client allows clarification that prevents duplicate dosing.
questions.learningObjective: Investigate uncertain prior administration.

questions.title: Select an accurate oral measuring device
questions.stem: A child is prescribed 1.8 mL of an oral liquid. The caregiver's cup has 5-mL markings. What should the nurse provide?
options: A calibrated oral syringe with suitable graduations
A second cup with the same graduations
Instructions to fill just below the cup's first mark
Instructions to round to 2.5 mL for convenience
why: Fine mL markings allow measurement of the small prescribed volume.
Another coarsely marked cup does not improve measurement accuracy.
Visual estimation below 5 mL is imprecise for 1.8 mL.
Rounding the prescribed volume this far changes the intended dose.
questions.takeaway: Fine mL markings allow measurement of the small prescribed volume.
questions.learningObjective: Select an accurate oral measuring device.

questions.title: Review redosing after vomiting
questions.stem: Ten minutes after an oral antibiotic, a child vomits. No intact medicine is visible and the child is now comfortable. What should the nurse do?
options: Reschedule the next dose sooner without consultation
Assess timing and obtain drug-specific redosing guidance
Repeat the full dose because vomiting was early
Give half a dose as a compromise
why: Changing the interval can unintentionally increase exposure.
Some medication may have been absorbed, so replacement needs specific guidance.
Early vomiting does not prove that none of the dose was absorbed.
An arbitrary half-dose does not resolve uncertainty about absorption.
questions.takeaway: Some medication may have been absorbed, so replacement needs specific guidance.
questions.learningObjective: Review redosing after vomiting.

questions.title: Address a tolerability-related refusal
questions.stem: A client declines a scheduled antibiotic because the last dose caused nausea without rash or breathing symptoms. What is the best response?
options: Document refusal and leave the concern for discharge teaching
Recommend stopping the course until all nausea resolves
Assess the nausea and discuss an acceptable treatment plan
Record an allergy and request permanent avoidance of the class
why: Deferring discussion misses a current barrier to necessary treatment.
Unreviewed interruption may leave the infection inadequately treated.
A manageable adverse effect may be addressed while respecting the refusal.
Isolated nausea does not establish an immune-mediated allergy.
questions.takeaway: A manageable adverse effect may be addressed while respecting the refusal.
questions.learningObjective: Address a tolerability-related refusal.

questions.title: Handle a single-dose vial remainder
questions.stem: A nurse withdraws a dose from a vial labelled single-dose. A second dose for the same client is due that evening. What should happen to the remainder?
options: Refrigerate it because only one client will receive it
Label it with the usual multidose discard date
Withdraw the evening dose into a labelled syringe for bedside storage
Discard it according to policy after preparation
why: Same-client use does not change the container's single-dose designation.
A multidose beyond-use policy does not apply to this vial.
Future preparation and storage require an approved process, not repurposing opened single-dose supply.
Single-dose packaging is not intended for storage after opening.
questions.takeaway: Single-dose packaging is not intended for storage after opening.
questions.learningObjective: Handle a single-dose vial remainder.

questions.title: Verify a client-owned product
questions.stem: A client brings a weekly organizer after admission. One tablet does not match the current medication list. The client says it is the usual heart medicine. What is appropriate?
options: Have the medication identified and the intended order verified
Give it because it was placed in today's compartment
Use the old discharge list as the active prescription
Omit only the unfamiliar tablet for the entire admission
why: Both product identity and current treatment intent remain uncertain.
Organizer placement is not independent verification of the product.
An older list may omit subsequent changes or discontinued therapy.
An unresolved omission may interrupt necessary treatment.
questions.takeaway: Both product identity and current treatment intent remain uncertain.
questions.learningObjective: Verify a client-owned product.

questions.title: Prevent transdermal duplication
questions.stem: A client using a daily medicated patch sometimes forgets where yesterday's patch was placed. Which strategies are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Apply the new patch first and search later
Use the same small skin area every day
Write a replacement schedule from memory each morning
Check for and remove the old patch before replacement
Record the application time and site
why: This permits unintended overlapping exposure while the old patch remains.
Repeated placement can irritate skin and does not ensure old-patch removal.
Reconstructing timing from memory is unreliable when forgetfulness is the problem.
An old patch may continue delivering medication after a new one is applied.
A simple record helps identify patches and prevents duplicate applications.
questions.takeaway: An old patch may continue delivering medication after a new one is applied.
questions.learningObjective: Prevent transdermal duplication.

questions.title: Maintain eye-drop sterility
questions.stem: During teaching, a client repeatedly steadies an eye-drop bottle by resting its tip on the lower lashes. Which correction is most useful?
options: Hold the bottle farther away and squeeze several drops
Aim at the centre of the eye to avoid the lashes
Support the hand on the face while keeping the tip clear
Wipe the tip after each contact and continue
why: A distant, forceful technique wastes medicine and reduces accuracy.
Direct corneal placement causes discomfort and does not solve contamination risk.
Hand support can improve control without contaminating the dropper tip.
Post-contact wiping does not reliably restore sterility.
questions.takeaway: Hand support can improve control without contaminating the dropper tip.
questions.learningObjective: Maintain eye-drop sterility.

questions.title: Perform an independent dose check
questions.stem: Policy requires an independent check of a high-alert infusion. Which actions preserve independence? Select all that apply.
options: The second nurse verifies only that the pump is running
The second nurse signs after reviewing yesterday's dose
Each nurse calculates from the original prescription
Both compare results before administration begins
One nurse states the answer while the other calculates
why: Pump operation does not establish that the programmed dose is correct.
Yesterday's treatment cannot verify the current preparation and order.
Separate calculations reduce the chance of carrying forward the same arithmetic error.
Differences can then be resolved before the client is exposed.
Knowing the first answer can bias the second calculation.
questions.takeaway: Separate calculations reduce the chance of carrying forward the same arithmetic error.
questions.learningObjective: Perform an independent dose check.

questions.title: Administer verified medicines through a tube
questions.stem: A client receives four immediate-release medicines through a gastric tube. Pharmacy has confirmed each formulation is suitable for the tube; mixing them has not been assessed. Which practices support safe administration? Select all that apply.
options: Flush between medicines using the prescribed fluid plan
Combine all preparations to reduce nursing time
Add the medicines to the full feeding container
Use the same flushing volume for every client
Give each prepared medicine separately
why: Flushing clears residual medicine while respecting the client's fluid allowance.
Compatibility for individual tube use does not establish mixture compatibility.
The client may not receive the complete dose if feeding is interrupted.
Fluid restrictions and tube characteristics require an individualized plan.
Separate administration reduces interaction and blockage risks and supports complete dosing.
questions.takeaway: Separate administration reduces interaction and blockage risks and supports complete dosing.
questions.learningObjective: Administer verified medicines through a tube.

questions.title: Relate renal decline to drug exposure
questions.stem: A frail adult's creatinine rises during dehydration. A scheduled medicine is eliminated mainly by the kidneys, and the client is newly drowsy. What concern should guide review?
options: A dosing error is the only possible explanation
Accumulation despite an unchanged prescribed dose
Reduced absorption caused by the creatinine rise
Tolerance requiring a higher dose
why: Correctly administered doses can accumulate when organ function changes.
Reduced clearance can increase exposure even when administration has not changed.
The main stated change affects elimination rather than proving poor absorption.
New drowsiness during renal decline suggests increased effect, not reduced response.
questions.takeaway: Reduced clearance can increase exposure even when administration has not changed.
questions.learningObjective: Relate renal decline to drug exposure.

questions.title: Evaluate additive sedation
questions.stem: A client stable on an opioid becomes unusually sleepy after a sedative is added. Respirations are currently 14/min and regular. What is the best next action?
options: Reduce only the opioid without reviewing the new drug
Reassess after the client has completed a full sleep cycle
Assess sedation and breathing before further sedating doses
Give the next sedative because respirations exceed 12/min
why: Both agents may contribute, and independent dose changes lack a treatment plan.
Waiting may miss progressive sedation and ventilatory impairment.
Combined effects can progress, so current safety and the regimen need review.
A single respiratory rate does not establish safety with increasing sedation.
questions.takeaway: Combined effects can progress, so current safety and the regimen need review.
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate additive sedation.

questions.title: Recognize a mistimed trough level
questions.stem: An antibiotic trough was ordered immediately before the next dose, but the sample was drawn just after infusion completion. What should the nurse do?
options: Interpret it using the usual trough range
Delay all future doses until the number decreases
Request a dose reduction based only on the reported number
Report the exact sampling and infusion times
why: A post-infusion concentration cannot be treated as a trough.
Dosing decisions require review of the mistimed result and clinical context.
A misleading sampling time can produce an inappropriate dose adjustment.
Accurate timing allows the team to determine whether repeat sampling is needed.
questions.takeaway: Accurate timing allows the team to determine whether repeat sampling is needed.
questions.learningObjective: Recognize a mistimed trough level.

questions.title: Evaluate an antiemetic beyond sedation
questions.stem: After a prescribed antiemetic, a client is mildly sleepy but wakes easily and remains alert during conversation. They can swallow safely and have no intake restriction but have not attempted fluids. Which assessment best determines the intended therapeutic response?
options: Ask about nausea and assess tolerance of a small permitted intake
Record sleep as proof that nausea resolved
Measure respiratory rate as the only evidence of nausea relief
Wait for a full meal before reassessing
why: This measures the target symptom and its functional effect.
Sedation can occur without relief of nausea.
Respiratory rate assesses safety rather than the intended antiemetic outcome.
A smaller permitted intake can evaluate response sooner and more tolerably.
questions.takeaway: This measures the target symptom and its functional effect.
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate an antiemetic beyond sedation.

questions.title: Resolve uncertain Y-site compatibility
questions.stem: A maintenance infusion runs through the only available lumen. A new IV medicine is due, but Y-site compatibility is not documented. The client is stable. What comes first?
options: Stop the maintenance fluid without assessing its purpose
Verify compatibility and an appropriate administration method
Run the medicine slowly through the Y-site
Look for cloudiness after starting the medicine
why: Interrupting an essential infusion may itself be harmful and needs planning.
The nurse needs a safe plan before the solutions contact each other.
A slower rate cannot establish chemical compatibility.
Some incompatibilities are not visible, and exposure has already occurred.
questions.takeaway: The nurse needs a safe plan before the solutions contact each other.
questions.learningObjective: Resolve uncertain Y-site compatibility.

questions.title: Identify the correct infusion pathway
questions.stem: Two similar clear infusions run through separate lumens. A replacement bag is ready, but one tubing label has detached. What should the nurse do?
options: Choose the bag whose remaining volume matches the record
Replace the label using the previous shift's diagram
Trace the relevant tubing from bag to client
Use the pump positioned nearest the correct lumen
why: Estimated volume cannot verify the tubing connection.
A diagram may not reflect connections changed since handover.
Physical tracing confirms the actual connections before the bag is changed.
Equipment position does not reliably identify the connected pathway.
questions.takeaway: Physical tracing confirms the actual connections before the bag is changed.
questions.learningObjective: Identify the correct infusion pathway.

questions.title: Respond to resistance during flushing
questions.stem: A peripheral catheter flushed easily earlier but now resists flushing and causes pain. What is the safest next action?
options: Use a smaller syringe to generate more pressure
Reposition the arm and start the medicine without reassessment
Flush until blood return appears
Stop using the catheter and assess the site and patency
why: Higher pressure can damage the catheter or surrounding tissue.
Repositioning alone does not resolve unexplained pain and resistance.
Continuing against resistance can worsen a catheter complication.
New pain and resistance suggest a complication requiring assessment.
questions.takeaway: New pain and resistance suggest a complication requiring assessment.
questions.learningObjective: Respond to resistance during flushing.

questions.title: Differentiate phlebitis from infiltration
questions.stem: A peripheral IV site is warm and red, with tenderness tracking along the vein. There is no cool swelling. Which problem is most consistent?
options: Phlebitis
Simple nonvesicant infiltration
A dressing-related skin reaction only
Systemic fluid overload
why: Vein-tracking warmth and tenderness favour venous inflammation.
Infiltration more often causes localized swelling and coolness.
A localized adhesive pattern would not explain tenderness along the vein.
Fluid overload does not explain this focal vein-tracking inflammation.
questions.takeaway: Vein-tracking warmth and tenderness favour venous inflammation.
questions.learningObjective: Differentiate phlebitis from infiltration.

questions.title: Teach a sublingual formulation
questions.stem: A client prescribed a sublingual tablet says they will swallow it quickly to avoid the taste. What should the nurse explain?
options: It can be mixed into a drink if the full drink is taken
It should dissolve under the tongue as directed
Chewing is equivalent to letting it dissolve
Taking it after food gives the same onset
why: This converts the intended route to gastrointestinal administration.
The prescribed formulation relies on absorption through oral mucosa.
Chewing changes intended administration and may affect absorption.
Swallowing with food does not reproduce the sublingual route.
questions.takeaway: The prescribed formulation relies on absorption through oral mucosa.
questions.learningObjective: Teach a sublingual formulation.

questions.title: Address inhaler coordination difficulty
questions.stem: A client presses a metered-dose inhaler before starting inhalation despite repeated coaching. Hand strength is adequate. What is the most useful next step?
options: Repeat written instructions without observing technique
Switch directly to a dry-powder device without assessment
Trial a compatible spacer with return demonstration
Add extra puffs to compensate for estimated loss
why: The barrier is demonstrated coordination rather than missing written information.
A different device requires adequate inspiratory ability and technique assessment.
A spacer reduces the timing coordination required for delivery.
The delivered amount remains uncertain and the prescription is altered.
questions.takeaway: A spacer reduces the timing coordination required for delivery.
questions.learningObjective: Address inhaler coordination difficulty.

questions.title: Prevent wrong-route liquid delivery
questions.stem: An oral liquid must be given through a feeding tube while the client also has an IV line. Which preparation best reduces a route mix-up?
options: Use an IV syringe but place it beside the feeding pump
Prepare it early in an unlabelled oral syringe
Ask another nurse to give it without identifying the route
Use a labelled enteral syringe and trace the tube
why: Location alone cannot prevent connection to vascular access.
Dedicated equipment does not remove the need for identification.
Handover must include the medication and intended route.
Dedicated equipment and tracing reduce wrong-route connection risk.
questions.takeaway: Dedicated equipment and tracing reduce wrong-route connection risk.
questions.learningObjective: Prevent wrong-route liquid delivery.

questions.title: Manage an unavailable time-critical dose
questions.stem: A client's prescribed time-critical medicine is due, but the dispensing cabinet is empty. The previous dose was given on time. What should the nurse do?
options: Contact pharmacy promptly and escalate any anticipated delay
Document omission immediately and wait for routine restocking
Move the dose to the next medication round independently
Use a similar medicine available in the cabinet
why: Timely supply coordination protects continuity and allows an alternate plan if needed.
The supply problem may be resolved before a clinically important delay.
Changing timing may reduce therapeutic coverage without review.
Therapeutic substitution requires an authorized plan.
questions.takeaway: Timely supply coordination protects continuity and allows an alternate plan if needed.
questions.learningObjective: Manage an unavailable time-critical dose.

questions.title: Apply a localized topical order
questions.stem: A topical corticosteroid is prescribed twice daily to one small elbow lesion. The client asks for it on new undiagnosed facial redness too. What is appropriate?
options: Use the facial rash response to confirm its diagnosis
Treat the ordered area and arrange review of the facial rash
Apply a thinner layer to the face using the same order
Use a weaker steroid left from a previous prescription on the face
why: An empiric steroid response does not establish a safe diagnosis.
A new site and diagnosis require assessment before extending therapy.
Less product does not authorize a new treatment site.
An old prescription does not establish the new diagnosis or current treatment authorization.
questions.takeaway: A new site and diagnosis require assessment before extending therapy.
questions.learningObjective: Apply a localized topical order.

questions.title: Respond to possible ACE inhibitor angioedema
questions.stem: A client taking ramipril for several months develops a swollen tongue and muffled voice. There is no rash. What is the priority?
options: Observe until a rash develops to confirm allergy
Withhold tomorrow's ramipril and arrange routine follow-up
Activate emergency help and assess airway patency
Give an oral antihistamine before deciding whether to escalate
why: ACE inhibitor angioedema may occur without an itchy rash.
Stopping future exposure does not manage the current airway threat.
Tongue swelling and voice change may rapidly progress to airway obstruction.
Oral treatment can delay airway care and may be unsafe to swallow.
questions.takeaway: Tongue swelling and voice change may rapidly progress to airway obstruction.
questions.learningObjective: Respond to possible ACE inhibitor angioedema.

questions.title: Evaluate a new cough during ACE therapy
questions.stem: A client has a persistent dry cough after starting an ACE inhibitor. Temperature, oxygenation and weight are unchanged, and there is no dyspnea. What is most appropriate?
options: Begin fluid restriction for presumed pulmonary congestion
Advise stopping all antihypertensives until the cough disappears
Request antibiotics based on cough duration alone
Report the cough for medication review
why: The assessment does not demonstrate congestion warranting that intervention.
An indiscriminate interruption may destabilize blood pressure control.
A persistent dry cough alone does not establish bacterial infection.
The timing and otherwise stable assessment support considering an ACE inhibitor effect.
questions.takeaway: The timing and otherwise stable assessment support considering an ACE inhibitor effect.
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate a new cough during ACE therapy.

questions.title: Assess potassium-sparing therapy safely
questions.stem: A client taking spironolactone plans to replace table salt with a potassium-based substitute. Potassium is currently 4.8 mmol/L, reference 3.5–5.0. What is best?
options: Review the substitute with the prescriber or pharmacist first
Approve it because today's potassium is within range
Separate the salt substitute from spironolactone by two hours
Start it now and review potassium at the usual annual visit
why: Spironolactone and added potassium can together cause hyperkalemia.
A current normal value does not predict safety after potassium intake increases.
Dose separation does not remove the potassium-retaining effect of spironolactone.
A substantial new potassium source warrants review before routine use.
questions.takeaway: Spironolactone and added potassium can together cause hyperkalemia.
questions.learningObjective: Assess potassium-sparing therapy safely.

questions.title: Assess possible digoxin accumulation
questions.stem: A client's pulse falls from 76 to 48/min after several days of poor intake and worsening kidney function. Digoxin is due; nausea and yellow-tinged vision are new. What should happen?
options: Encourage oral fluids and reassess after the next dose
Withhold the dose and arrange urgent rhythm and toxicity assessment
Give it because the serum level was therapeutic last week
Treat nausea first and give digoxin once it settles
why: Giving another dose before review may worsen toxicity.
Renal decline, bradycardia and characteristic symptoms suggest possible digoxin accumulation.
A previous level does not reflect the current renal and clinical changes.
Suppressing one symptom does not address possible cardiac toxicity.
questions.takeaway: Renal decline, bradycardia and characteristic symptoms suggest possible digoxin accumulation.
questions.learningObjective: Assess possible digoxin accumulation.

questions.title: Assess severe muscle symptoms on a statin
questions.stem: A client taking atorvastatin reports diffuse muscle pain, weakness and tea-coloured urine after no unusual exercise. What is appropriate?
options: Encourage exercise to distinguish stiffness from medication effects
Wait for the next scheduled lipid panel before reporting
Arrange prompt assessment for muscle injury and renal complications
Suggest taking the next dose with food to reduce intolerance
why: Exertion may worsen injury and delay assessment.
Lipid results do not assess an acute muscle-injury complication.
This symptom combination is concerning for serious statin-associated muscle injury.
Food does not address muscle breakdown or dark urine.
questions.takeaway: This symptom combination is concerning for serious statin-associated muscle injury.
questions.learningObjective: Assess severe muscle symptoms on a statin.

questions.title: Clarify nitrate use after a PDE5 inhibitor
questions.stem: A client with chest discomfort has a nitroglycerin order and reports sildenafil use earlier today. Blood pressure is 116/72 mmHg. What should the nurse do?
options: Give nitrate because systolic pressure is above 100 mmHg
Give half the nitrate dose before seeking advice
Wait for the sildenafil effect to wear off before assessing pain
Withhold nitrate and urgently notify the chest-pain team
why: The initial pressure does not remove the drug interaction.
An unprescribed partial dose does not establish interaction safety.
Chest discomfort still needs immediate assessment and an alternative plan.
The combination can cause severe hypotension despite an initially normal pressure.
questions.takeaway: The combination can cause severe hypotension despite an initially normal pressure.
questions.learningObjective: Clarify nitrate use after a PDE5 inhibitor.

questions.title: Distinguish diuretic benefit from adverse effects
questions.stem: A client receives furosemide for congestion. Which follow-up findings support benefit rather than excessive diuresis? Select all that apply.
options: Ankle edema decreases while standing blood pressure remains stable
Weight falls and the client becomes faint on standing
Urine output rises but oxygen needs also rise
Serum potassium falls below the supplied reference range
Breathlessness decreases at the same activity level
why: Reduced edema without postural instability supports useful fluid removal.
Faintness suggests potentially excessive volume loss despite weight reduction.
Diuresis alone does not demonstrate improving pulmonary status.
Electrolyte depletion is an adverse effect rather than a treatment goal.
Improved exertional breathing supports reduced pulmonary congestion.
questions.takeaway: Improved exertional breathing supports reduced pulmonary congestion.
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish diuretic benefit from adverse effects.

questions.title: Respond to symptomatic thiazide-associated hyponatremia
questions.stem: A client taking hydrochlorothiazide is newly confused. Sodium is 124 mmol/L, reference 135–145, and the next dose is due. What is the priority?
options: Plan repeat sodium testing at the next routine visit
Withhold the dose pending urgent assessment of symptomatic hyponatremia
Encourage additional plain water for presumed dehydration
Give the dose because blood pressure remains elevated
why: New confusion makes routine delayed reassessment inadequate.
Neurological symptoms with markedly low sodium require prompt review.
Free water can worsen a dilutional sodium problem.
Blood pressure alone does not outweigh this acute electrolyte concern.
questions.takeaway: Neurological symptoms with markedly low sodium require prompt review.
questions.learningObjective: Respond to symptomatic thiazide-associated hyponatremia.

questions.title: Explain safe beta-blocker continuation
questions.stem: A client taking metoprolol for angina wants to stop because there has been no chest pain for weeks. What is the best response?
options: Stop now and restart if the pulse rises
Take it on alternating days until the supply is gone
Discuss any change with the prescriber and avoid abrupt withdrawal
Use it only when chest pain returns
why: A reactive restart does not safely manage withdrawal risk.
An improvised taper is not an individualized discontinuation plan.
Symptom control may reflect treatment, and abrupt withdrawal can provoke ischemia.
Changing maintenance therapy to symptom-triggered use may reduce protection.
questions.takeaway: Symptom control may reflect treatment, and abrupt withdrawal can provoke ischemia.
questions.learningObjective: Explain safe beta-blocker continuation.

questions.title: Address postural symptoms after treatment
questions.stem: After a first antihypertensive dose, a client becomes light-headed on standing. Supine pressure is 128/76 and standing pressure is 98/60 mmHg. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Help the client sit or lie safely and reassess symptoms
Report the positional readings for regimen review
Reassure because the supine pressure is normal
Give a large glass of water and immediately repeat standing without checking restrictions
Independently omit all future antihypertensive doses
why: Positioning limits immediate fall risk during symptomatic pressure reduction.
The measurable symptomatic change can guide treatment adjustment.
A normal supine reading does not explain away postural instability.
A fluid intervention requires context and does not replace safe positioning and reassessment.
Longer-term changes require a treatment plan rather than blanket withdrawal.
questions.takeaway: Positioning limits immediate fall risk during symptomatic pressure reduction.
questions.learningObjective: Address postural symptoms after treatment.

questions.title: Tailor once-daily diuretic timing
questions.stem: A client takes prescribed once-daily furosemide at 22:00 and wakes repeatedly to urinate. There is no prescribed bedtime requirement. What should be discussed?
options: Move dosing earlier with the treatment team's timing guidance
Reduce the prescribed dose to reduce nighttime urine
Avoid daytime fluid intake so less is excreted at night
Take the dose only after a day of ankle swelling
why: Earlier administration can reduce nocturnal diuresis while preserving therapy.
Dose reduction may compromise congestion control.
Unnecessary restriction can cause dehydration without resolving timing.
Symptom-triggered use changes the prescribed maintenance schedule.
questions.takeaway: Earlier administration can reduce nocturnal diuresis while preserving therapy.
questions.learningObjective: Tailor once-daily diuretic timing.

questions.title: Recognize heparin-associated thrombosis
questions.stem: Six days after starting heparin, a client's platelets fall by more than half and a new painful swollen leg develops. What should the nurse do?
options: Apply compression and repeat platelets tomorrow
Stop heparin and urgently escalate under protocol
Give the next heparin dose while awaiting routine review
Request a lower heparin dose to reduce bruising risk
why: Local measures do not address a potentially serious medication reaction.
Thrombocytopenia with new thrombosis raises concern for heparin-induced thrombocytopenia.
Continued exposure can worsen immune-mediated thrombosis.
The concern is a prothrombotic immune reaction, not simply excessive anticoagulation.
questions.takeaway: Thrombocytopenia with new thrombosis raises concern for heparin-induced thrombocytopenia.
questions.learningObjective: Recognize heparin-associated thrombosis.

questions.title: Evaluate head injury during anticoagulation
questions.stem: A client taking apixaban strikes the head in a fall. They deny headache and are alert with equal pupils. What should the nurse do?
options: Check INR before deciding whether assessment is needed
Withhold one dose and consider the injury managed
Arrange urgent head-injury assessment and follow the escalation pathway
Continue usual checks unless a headache develops
why: INR does not reliably measure apixaban's anticoagulant effect.
Medication review alone does not evaluate possible internal injury.
Early normal findings do not exclude anticoagulant-associated intracranial bleeding.
Waiting for symptoms may delay recognition of occult bleeding.
questions.takeaway: Early normal findings do not exclude anticoagulant-associated intracranial bleeding.
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate head injury during anticoagulation.

questions.title: Respond to possible antiplatelet-related bleeding
questions.stem: A client taking clopidogrel reports black sticky stools and dizziness. They have not taken iron or bismuth. What is the priority?
options: Provide constipation advice and review stool appearance tomorrow
Request a routine outpatient fecal screening test
Give the scheduled dose and report symptoms at handover
Assess circulation and urgently report suspected gastrointestinal bleeding
why: This presentation suggests bleeding rather than simple constipation.
A screening pathway is inappropriate for possible active symptomatic bleeding.
Administration and delayed reporting may worsen an unresolved bleeding event.
Melena with dizziness may indicate clinically significant blood loss.
questions.takeaway: Melena with dizziness may indicate clinically significant blood loss.
questions.learningObjective: Respond to possible antiplatelet-related bleeding.

questions.title: Obtain a procedure-specific anticoagulant plan
questions.stem: A client taking a direct oral anticoagulant has surgery in two days but no interruption instructions. Kidney function has recently declined. What is appropriate?
options: Obtain a plan incorporating the drug, renal function and procedure
Use the interruption schedule from a different anticoagulant
Continue because the latest INR is normal
Ask the client to choose whether bleeding or clotting is more concerning
why: These factors affect interruption and restart decisions.
Drug-specific elimination and bleeding risk differ.
A normal INR does not establish absent direct-anticoagulant effect.
The client needs an informed clinical plan, not an unsupported risk choice.
questions.takeaway: These factors affect interruption and restart decisions.
questions.learningObjective: Obtain a procedure-specific anticoagulant plan.

questions.title: Apply anticoagulant precautions to daily care
questions.stem: A client starting anticoagulation describes their usual routines. Which planned changes are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Use a normal INR to decide whether a dose is needed
Take a missed dose together with the next one routinely
Use a soft toothbrush for gentle oral care
Check before adding nonprescription anti-inflammatory medicines
Stop anticoagulation for every small bruise
why: Not all anticoagulants are titrated by INR.
Missed-dose instructions are drug specific, and automatic doubling may be unsafe.
Reducing gum trauma helps limit preventable bleeding.
Many NSAIDs increase bleeding risk when combined with anticoagulation.
Unplanned interruptions can increase thrombosis risk.
questions.takeaway: Reducing gum trauma helps limit preventable bleeding.
questions.learningObjective: Apply anticoagulant precautions to daily care.

questions.title: Explain direct anticoagulant follow-up
questions.stem: A client taking apixaban believes no follow-up is necessary because INR tests are not scheduled. Which response is best?
options: Check only for large visible bruises
Monitor only if the prescribed dose changes
Bleeding, kidney function and medication changes still need review
Ask for weekly INR tests to confirm effectiveness
why: Important bleeding can occur internally without large bruises.
Renal function and interacting therapy can change exposure at the same dose.
Absence of routine INR titration does not eliminate safety monitoring.
INR is not used to routinely titrate apixaban.
questions.takeaway: Absence of routine INR titration does not eliminate safety monitoring.
questions.learningObjective: Explain direct anticoagulant follow-up.

questions.title: Recognize clinically important nitrate hypotension
questions.stem: After prescribed nitrate treatment, chest pain improves but pressure falls to 78/44 mmHg and the client feels faint. What is the priority?
options: Give another dose because some discomfort remains
Repeat the blood pressure in the other arm before calling for help
Recheck at the usual medication-effect interval
Activate urgent assessment and support circulation under protocol
why: Additional vasodilation can worsen circulatory instability.
Rapid confirmation can accompany but must not delay response to severe symptomatic hypotension.
The new instability requires immediate reassessment rather than routine timing.
Severe symptomatic hypotension threatens perfusion despite pain improvement.
questions.takeaway: Severe symptomatic hypotension threatens perfusion despite pain improvement.
questions.learningObjective: Recognize clinically important nitrate hypotension.

questions.title: Identify possible excessive diuresis
questions.stem: A client treated for edema loses weight rapidly, develops dry mouth and becomes dizzy on standing. Lung sounds are now clear. What should guide the next review?
