options: Possible intravascular depletion despite reduced edema
Persistent fluid overload because some ankle edema remains
Successful treatment requiring no further assessment
A need to increase diuretic frequency
why: Improved congestion can coexist with excessive circulating-volume loss.
Residual peripheral edema does not exclude depleted circulating volume.
Postural symptoms suggest an adverse physiological effect.
More diuresis may worsen the symptoms of depletion.
questions.takeaway: Improved congestion can coexist with excessive circulating-volume loss.
questions.learningObjective: Identify possible excessive diuresis.

questions.title: Evaluate amlodipine-associated edema
questions.stem: A client develops bilateral ankle edema after an amlodipine increase. Weight, lung sounds and exercise tolerance are unchanged. What is most appropriate?
options: Delay reporting until breathlessness develops
Assess and report possible medication-related peripheral edema
Request an automatic diuretic increase for heart failure
Tell the client to stop amlodipine permanently
why: A medication adverse effect can warrant review before respiratory compromise.
The timing and absence of pulmonary symptoms support reviewing amlodipine.
The assessment does not establish systemic congestion as the cause.
Medication changes need an individualized blood-pressure treatment plan.
questions.takeaway: The timing and absence of pulmonary symptoms support reviewing amlodipine.
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate amlodipine-associated edema.

questions.title: Prioritize a rate-slowing drug combination
questions.stem: A client taking diltiazem and metoprolol has new near-syncope and pulse 42/min. Both morning doses are due. What should happen?
options: Give only diltiazem because it is not a beta-blocker
Give metoprolol alone because diltiazem was added more recently
Withhold pending urgent assessment of symptomatic bradycardia
Give both because blood pressure is within range
why: Diltiazem can also slow cardiac conduction and rate.
Both slow the heart rate, and an arbitrary selection does not resolve symptomatic bradycardia.
Combined rate-slowing effects may be contributing to instability.
A normal pressure does not remove the danger of symptomatic bradycardia.
questions.takeaway: Combined rate-slowing effects may be contributing to instability.
questions.learningObjective: Prioritize a rate-slowing drug combination.

questions.title: Plan ACE inhibitor safety monitoring
questions.stem: A client starts an ACE inhibitor while also receiving a diuretic. Which follow-up information is particularly relevant? Select all that apply.
options: Creatinine and potassium trends
Only a single pretreatment kidney result
Repeat only serum sodium because a diuretic is prescribed
Medication review only if edema appears
Blood pressure and postural symptoms
why: ACE inhibitors can affect renal function and potassium balance.
A baseline does not show changes after therapy begins.
Sodium alone misses the relevant potassium, renal and hemodynamic changes.
Relevant adverse effects can develop without peripheral swelling.
Combined therapy can produce clinically important hypotension.
questions.takeaway: Combined therapy can produce clinically important hypotension.
questions.learningObjective: Plan ACE inhibitor safety monitoring.

questions.title: Explain a prescribed nitrate-free interval
questions.stem: A client removes a nitrate patch for a prescribed daily interval but worries this means treatment is failing. What explanation is most useful?
options: The interval helps preserve nitrate responsiveness
The interval is needed only when a rash appears
An extra patch before the interval provides lasting protection
The interval means chest symptoms need no action
why: Continuous nitrate exposure can produce tolerance and reduce effect.
Its purpose includes limiting tolerance, independently of local irritation.
Extra exposure changes the dose and can cause hypotension.
New or worsening symptoms still require the client's acute-care plan.
questions.takeaway: Continuous nitrate exposure can produce tolerance and reduce effect.
questions.learningObjective: Explain a prescribed nitrate-free interval.

questions.title: Clarify an undocumented anticoagulant transition
questions.stem: A transfer list contains both warfarin and a direct oral anticoagulant, without a transition plan. The client cannot explain the change. What is appropriate?
options: Hold both for several days to ensure clearance
Clarify the intended transition before uncertain doses
Continue both until the next routine INR result
Choose the medicine the client used longest
why: An arbitrary interruption may create avoidable thrombosis risk.
Unplanned overlap can cause bleeding, while an incorrect omission can leave thrombosis untreated.
The list alone does not authorize overlap and INR may be insufficient.
Duration of prior use does not establish current treatment intent.
questions.takeaway: Unplanned overlap can cause bleeding, while an incorrect omission can leave thrombosis untreated.
questions.learningObjective: Clarify an undocumented anticoagulant transition.

questions.title: Address a timing barrier to adherence
questions.stem: A client skips antihypertensive doses because rotating shifts make the schedule difficult. They understand the purpose and can afford the medicine. What is the most useful intervention?
options: Arrange financial assistance as the first step
Add a fixed-time alarm without discussing the rotating shifts
Develop a feasible prescribed schedule with the client and team
Repeat the explanation of long-term stroke risk only
why: Cost is not the barrier reported in this scenario.
A reminder alone may not make the prescribed schedule feasible.
This directly addresses the identified timing barrier.
The client already understands the purpose; practical scheduling remains unresolved.
questions.takeaway: This directly addresses the identified timing barrier.
questions.learningObjective: Address a timing barrier to adherence.

questions.title: Apply a type 1 diabetes sick-day plan
questions.stem: A client with type 1 diabetes has influenza and poor appetite. They plan to stop both basal and mealtime insulin until eating normally. What needs clarification first?
options: Whether all glucose checks can wait until normal meals resume
Whether the client can simply use yesterday's mealtime doses
Whether the client should exercise whenever glucose rises
How to maintain necessary insulin and monitor during illness
why: Illness increases the need for monitoring rather than justifying a pause.
Changed intake and illness require the prescribed adjustment plan.
Exercise is not an appropriate substitute for insulin during acute illness.
Basal insulin deficiency can precipitate ketoacidosis even when intake is poor.
questions.takeaway: Basal insulin deficiency can precipitate ketoacidosis even when intake is poor.
questions.learningObjective: Apply a type 1 diabetes sick-day plan.

questions.title: Address lipohypertrophy before dose escalation
questions.stem: A client has erratic glucose despite prescribed insulin use. They inject into the same firm abdominal lump because it hurts less. What is the most useful next step?
options: Assess injection sites and teach rotation into healthy tissue
Request an immediate dose increase based only on high readings
Switch every dose to a different body region without a plan
Teach deeper injections into the same lump
why: Lipohypertrophy can cause unpredictable absorption and needs correction before assuming dose failure.
Increasing insulin without addressing absorption may increase subsequent hypoglycemia risk.
Unsystematic changes can add variation in absorption and make patterns harder to interpret.
Changing depth does not restore normal absorption in damaged tissue.
questions.takeaway: Lipohypertrophy can cause unpredictable absorption and needs correction before assuming dose failure.
questions.learningObjective: Address lipohypertrophy before dose escalation.

questions.title: Explain why insulin pens are individual devices
questions.stem: Two spouses use the same insulin product and ask to share a pen with separate needles. What is the best explanation?
options: Cleaning the outer pen permits sharing
Blood contamination may occur inside the pen
Sharing is acceptable when neither has a known infection
Sharing is acceptable if both prescribed doses match
why: External cleaning does not disinfect its internal fluid pathway.
Changing the needle does not make a pen safe for another person.
Unrecognized bloodborne infection still makes shared use unsafe.
Matching doses does not address contamination inside the device.
questions.takeaway: Changing the needle does not make a pen safe for another person.
questions.learningObjective: Explain why insulin pens are individual devices.

questions.title: Verify a concentrated insulin transition
questions.stem: A client's insulin prescription changes to a concentrated pen. They want to withdraw the insulin using their old syringe because it feels familiar. What is appropriate?
options: Ask the client to calculate the conversion from memory
Use the old pen's appearance to identify equivalent settings
Verify the product-specific administration method and reteach with demonstration
Use the same syringe volume as the previous product
why: Device-specific safety should not rely on an improvised home conversion.
Appearance cannot establish product or delivery equivalence.
Transferring concentrated insulin to an unsuitable syringe can cause major dosing error.
Different concentrations contain different amounts in the same volume.
questions.takeaway: Transferring concentrated insulin to an unsuitable syringe can cause major dosing error.
questions.learningObjective: Verify a concentrated insulin transition.

questions.title: Link a sulfonylurea to skipped-meal symptoms
questions.stem: A client taking gliclazide reports shakiness during a shift after missing lunch. They have a glucose meter available. What should the nurse advise first?
options: Wait until dinner because the morning dose has already passed
Skip tomorrow's dose and continue today's shift without assessment
Treat only if the client loses consciousness
Check glucose and follow the prescribed low-glucose plan if needed
why: Its glucose-lowering effect can persist beyond the morning meal.
A future medication change does not address the current symptoms.
Waiting permits a potentially manageable episode to become severe.
Gliclazide can cause hypoglycemia, especially when food intake is missed.
questions.takeaway: Gliclazide can cause hypoglycemia, especially when food intake is missed.
questions.learningObjective: Link a sulfonylurea to skipped-meal symptoms.

questions.title: Review metformin during acute renal decline
questions.stem: A client taking metformin is admitted with vomiting, dehydration and new acute kidney injury. A usual dose is due. What is appropriate?
options: Seek prompt medication review before administering the dose
Give it because the long-term prescription has not changed
Give half the dose without contacting the team
Give it with food and defer the kidney result
why: Acute renal impairment and dehydration can change metformin safety.
The acute illness changes the assessment required before administration.
An arbitrary reduction is not an authorized renal-adjustment plan.
Food does not remove the accumulation concern from acute renal impairment.
questions.takeaway: Acute renal impairment and dehydration can change metformin safety.
questions.learningObjective: Review metformin during acute renal decline.

questions.title: Recognize possible euglycemic ketoacidosis
questions.stem: A client taking empagliflozin has persistent vomiting, abdominal pain and deep breathing. Glucose is only moderately elevated. What should the nurse do?
options: Give an extra empagliflozin dose for the elevated glucose
Arrange urgent assessment including consideration of ketoacidosis
Use the glucose value to exclude a diabetic emergency
Encourage oral fluid intake and review at the next clinic visit
why: Further dosing is not an appropriate response to possible ketoacidosis.
SGLT2-related ketoacidosis may occur without extreme glucose elevation.
Glucose alone cannot rule out ketoacidosis in this context.
The breathing pattern and persistent symptoms require timely acute assessment.
questions.takeaway: SGLT2-related ketoacidosis may occur without extreme glucose elevation.
questions.learningObjective: Recognize possible euglycemic ketoacidosis.

questions.title: Evaluate severe symptoms during GLP-1 therapy
questions.stem: A client taking semaglutide reports severe persistent upper abdominal pain and repeated vomiting. Mild nausea had occurred previously. What is best?
options: Delay one meal and continue the dose escalation schedule
Wait to report until symptoms have lasted a full week
Arrange prompt clinical assessment before the next dose
Repeat the prior advice to eat smaller meals only
why: Continuing escalation before assessment may worsen an unresolved complication.
Persistence and severity already justify assessment.
Severe persistent pain requires evaluation beyond expected mild gastrointestinal intolerance.
Dietary advice alone is insufficient for this change in severity.
questions.takeaway: Severe persistent pain requires evaluation beyond expected mild gastrointestinal intolerance.
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate severe symptoms during GLP-1 therapy.

questions.title: Assess hyperglycemia after glucocorticoids
questions.stem: A client starts systemic prednisone and subsequently has thirst and repeatedly elevated glucose despite no prior diabetes diagnosis. What interpretation best guides care?
options: A previous normal glucose rules out a medication contribution
The client must have permanently lost all insulin production
Thirst is sufficient evidence to reduce prednisone independently
The steroid may have increased glucose and monitoring needs
why: Normal pretreatment values do not exclude steroid-associated hyperglycemia.
This presentation does not establish irreversible pancreatic failure.
Treatment changes require review of the indication and glucose management plan.
Glucocorticoids can raise glucose even without previously diagnosed diabetes.
questions.takeaway: Glucocorticoids can raise glucose even without previously diagnosed diabetes.
questions.learningObjective: Assess hyperglycemia after glucocorticoids.

questions.title: Verify practical insulin readiness
questions.stem: An older adult is preparing to manage a new insulin pen independently at home. Which findings support readiness? Select all that apply.
options: The client accurately demonstrates selecting and delivering the prescribed dose
The client explains when and how to treat low glucose
The client agrees with every instruction but cannot show dose selection
The client identifies the pen only by cap colour
The client relies on a family member who will not be present
why: Return demonstration tests practical ability rather than verbal agreement.
Recognizing and responding to hypoglycemia supports safer independent use.
Agreement alone does not demonstrate the ability to administer insulin.
Colour cannot reliably establish the prescribed insulin product.
A plan dependent on unavailable assistance does not support independent use.
questions.takeaway: Return demonstration tests practical ability rather than verbal agreement.
questions.learningObjective: Verify practical insulin readiness.

questions.title: Plan discontinuation after prolonged steroid use
questions.stem: A client has taken systemic prednisone daily for months and wants to stop because symptoms improved. What is the best response?
options: Continue indefinitely because tapering is never possible
Arrange a prescriber-directed taper and discuss adrenal suppression
Stop when the current package is finished regardless of dose
Alternate full doses and no doses based on daily symptoms
why: Discontinuation may be possible with an individualized monitored plan.
Prolonged therapy can suppress endogenous cortisol, making abrupt withdrawal hazardous.
Package completion does not establish a safe discontinuation schedule.
An improvised schedule does not address adrenal recovery reliably.
questions.takeaway: Prolonged therapy can suppress endogenous cortisol, making abrupt withdrawal hazardous.
questions.learningObjective: Plan discontinuation after prolonged steroid use.

questions.title: Improve levothyroxine administration consistency
questions.stem: A client takes levothyroxine with iron on some mornings and without breakfast on others. Thyroid results have become variable. What is the best teaching focus?
options: Take all missed tablets with the next iron dose
Request a higher dose before addressing administration technique
Use consistent instructed timing and separate interacting supplements
Adjust the tablet dose to each morning's energy level
why: Unreviewed catch-up and iron interaction can further destabilize exposure.
Correcting inconsistent administration may prevent unnecessary dose escalation.
Variable food and iron exposure can alter levothyroxine absorption.
Daily symptoms cannot safely determine replacement dosing.
questions.takeaway: Variable food and iron exposure can alter levothyroxine absorption.
questions.learningObjective: Improve levothyroxine administration consistency.

questions.title: Recognize possible thyroid overreplacement
questions.stem: After a levothyroxine increase, a client develops palpitations, heat intolerance and tremor. What should the nurse do?
options: Recommend taking it later in the day without reporting
Explain that these symptoms must occur before benefit
Advise reducing food intake to control the symptoms
Report symptoms for thyroid and cardiovascular assessment
why: Timing alone does not address potentially excessive hormone exposure.
Palpitations and tremor are not required signs of successful replacement.
Dietary restriction does not correct excessive thyroid hormone effect.
The temporal pattern suggests possible overreplacement requiring review.
questions.takeaway: The temporal pattern suggests possible overreplacement requiring review.
questions.learningObjective: Recognize possible thyroid overreplacement.

questions.title: Report fever during antithyroid treatment
questions.stem: A client taking methimazole develops fever and a sore throat. They ask whether to treat it as a usual cold. What is appropriate?
options: Promptly contact the treatment team for assessment and blood-count guidance
Use cold remedies and report only if symptoms persist a week
Continue monitoring thyroid symptoms without discussing the fever
Treat it as an allergy solely because fever followed treatment
why: Agranulocytosis is uncommon but serious and must be considered.
Delayed assessment may miss a serious drug-associated infection risk.
Thyroid symptom control does not exclude marrow toxicity.
Fever and sore throat require evaluation rather than an assumed mechanism.
questions.takeaway: Agranulocytosis is uncommon but serious and must be considered.
questions.learningObjective: Report fever during antithyroid treatment.

questions.title: Evaluate oral bisphosphonate suitability
questions.stem: A client prescribed oral alendronate cannot remain upright because of an acute back condition. What should the nurse do before administration?
options: Crush it into a small volume of food
Clarify an appropriate treatment plan or alternative
Give it with breakfast to protect the esophagus
Give it just before sleep to minimize discomfort
why: Changing formulation does not establish safety and can increase irritation.
Upright positioning is part of reducing esophageal injury with oral alendronate.
Food reduces absorption and does not replace positioning requirements.
Recumbency increases the risk of esophageal exposure.
questions.takeaway: Upright positioning is part of reducing esophageal injury with oral alendronate.
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate oral bisphosphonate suitability.

questions.title: Recognize desmopressin-associated water retention
questions.stem: A client taking desmopressin drinks unusually large amounts of water and develops headache, confusion and weight gain. What is the priority concern?
options: An expected adaptation requiring no laboratory review
A need for an additional dose because headache persists
Water retention with possible hyponatremia
Insufficient desmopressin causing dehydration
why: New neurological symptoms require prompt assessment.
Further antidiuretic effect could worsen water retention.
Antidiuretic action plus excess intake can dilute sodium and affect the brain.
Weight gain and high intake favour water retention rather than untreated water loss.
questions.takeaway: Antidiuretic action plus excess intake can dilute sodium and affect the brain.
questions.learningObjective: Recognize desmopressin-associated water retention.

questions.title: Escalate failed oral adrenal replacement
questions.stem: A client with adrenal insufficiency cannot keep prescribed hydrocortisone down during gastroenteritis and feels increasingly weak. What is appropriate?
options: Wait until the next routine tablet time
Take smaller bites of food before retrying for several hours
Replace the missed medicine with extra salt and water
Urgently follow the emergency sick-day replacement plan
why: Delay can allow adrenal crisis to develop.
A prolonged trial of oral intake can delay necessary parenteral replacement.
Fluids and salt cannot replace deficient glucocorticoid activity.
Vomiting can prevent absorption when illness increases cortisol needs.
questions.takeaway: Vomiting can prevent absorption when illness increases cortisol needs.
questions.learningObjective: Escalate failed oral adrenal replacement.

questions.title: Prepare for new exercise with insulin
questions.stem: An insulin-treated client plans to start prolonged evening exercise. Which elements belong in a safe individualized plan? Select all that apply.
options: Continue exercising through shakiness until a planned break
Monitor glucose around activity and afterward as instructed
Keep rapid carbohydrate readily available
Assume an adequate pre-exercise meal prevents every low
Omit all basal insulin on exercise days
why: Symptoms require timely assessment rather than continued exertion.
Exercise can alter glucose during activity and later recovery.
Accessible treatment supports a prompt response to low glucose.
Delayed hypoglycemia can still occur despite prior food intake.
Blanket basal omission can create significant insulin deficiency.
questions.takeaway: Exercise can alter glucose during activity and later recovery.
questions.learningObjective: Prepare for new exercise with insulin.

questions.title: Plan insulin use across time zones
questions.stem: A client using basal and mealtime insulin will cross several time zones. Which preparations are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Use home-clock timing for every dose without reviewing meal changes
Pack all insulin with ice directly against the cartridges
Estimate new doses after arrival based only on hunger
Obtain an individualized dosing and monitoring schedule
Carry accessible supplies and hypoglycemia treatment
why: Rigid timing may mismatch local meals and dose intervals.
Freezing can damage insulin and make it unreliable.
Hunger is not an adequate measure of insulin requirements.
Time changes can alter intervals between doses and meals.
Lost checked luggage should not interrupt essential treatment.
questions.takeaway: Time changes can alter intervals between doses and meals.
questions.learningObjective: Plan insulin use across time zones.

questions.title: Evaluate emergency glucagon teaching
questions.stem: A partner receives training with the client's prescribed glucagon rescue device. Which statement shows appropriate understanding?
options: I will try to give a drink before using it even if swallowing is unsafe
I will practise by partly discharging the real rescue device
I will use the device as taught and call for emergency help
If the person wakes, no further glucose checks are needed
why: Oral intake during impaired consciousness creates aspiration risk.
A partially used single-use device may not provide the intended emergency dose.
Severe hypoglycemia needs rescue treatment plus assessment and continued monitoring.
Low glucose can recur and the cause still needs review.
questions.takeaway: Severe hypoglycemia needs rescue treatment plus assessment and continued monitoring.
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate emergency glucagon teaching.

questions.title: Assess abnormal insulin appearance
questions.stem: A clear insulin product now contains visible particles after being left near a heater. What should the nurse advise?
options: Use it if the next glucose reading is normal
Increase the dose to compensate for possible loss of potency
Refrigerate it again and assume potency is restored
Do not use it and arrange a verified replacement
why: A glucose result cannot verify the damaged product's reliability.
The degree of damage is unknown, making dose compensation unsafe.
Cooling cannot reverse damage already caused by improper storage.
Unexpected particles and heat exposure raise concern about product integrity.
questions.takeaway: Unexpected particles and heat exposure raise concern about product integrity.
questions.learningObjective: Assess abnormal insulin appearance.

questions.title: Respond to interrupted pump delivery
questions.stem: A client with type 1 diabetes finds that insulin pump delivery stopped several hours ago. They feel well but glucose is rising. What should happen?
options: Check glucose and ketones as directed and activate the backup insulin plan
Wait for symptoms before using the backup plan
Give a correction through the same unverified malfunctioning system
Reconnect and postpone all monitoring until bedtime
why: Pump interruption can quickly lead to insulin deficiency and ketoacidosis.
Feeling well does not exclude evolving insulin deficiency.
The intended dose may not be delivered until function is confirmed.
Restored connection alone does not show that glucose and ketones are safe.
questions.takeaway: Pump interruption can quickly lead to insulin deficiency and ketoacidosis.
questions.learningObjective: Respond to interrupted pump delivery.

questions.title: Distinguish antithyroid benefit from excessive suppression
questions.stem: A client starts treatment for hyperthyroidism. Which change best supports the intended response?
options: The client reports a new sore throat and fever
Resting tachycardia and tremor decrease without new cold intolerance
Weight rises rapidly with profound lethargy and cold intolerance
Palpitations persist but the client is less worried
why: These can indicate an important adverse effect requiring assessment.
This suggests reduced excess hormone effect without clear hypothyroid symptoms.
These findings may suggest excessive suppression rather than balanced treatment.
Reduced anxiety does not establish a physiological treatment response.
questions.takeaway: This suggests reduced excess hormone effect without clear hypothyroid symptoms.
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish antithyroid benefit from excessive suppression.

questions.title: Clarify an incomplete correction scale
questions.stem: A client's premeal glucose lies above the highest range on the prescribed insulin correction scale. The client is alert and the meal is available. What should the nurse do?
options: Use the highest listed dose as the final plan
Withhold all insulin and omit repeat glucose testing
Contact the authorized prescriber or follow the escalation instruction
Extend the scale by repeating its last numerical increment
why: That dose may be insufficient or inappropriate for the unlisted range.
Uncertainty about one dose does not remove ongoing assessment needs.
The incomplete scale does not authorize extrapolation to an unlisted range.
A pattern in listed doses is not a prescription for higher values.
questions.takeaway: The incomplete scale does not authorize extrapolation to an unlisted range.
questions.learningObjective: Clarify an incomplete correction scale.

questions.title: Recognize complications during chronic corticosteroid therapy
questions.stem: A client taking long-term systemic corticosteroids is reviewing when to call the clinic. Which findings need prompt reporting? Select all that apply.
options: New fever with a worsening cough
Black sticky stools with new light-headedness
Joint pain improves enough to walk farther
The prescribed morning administration routine remains consistent
Mild appetite improvement without other changes
why: Immunosuppression raises concern about infection and its progression.
This pattern may indicate gastrointestinal bleeding.
Functional improvement may be an intended anti-inflammatory benefit.
Consistent timing alone is not evidence of a complication.
This can occur with corticosteroids and is less urgent than the listed red flags.
questions.takeaway: Immunosuppression raises concern about infection and its progression.
questions.learningObjective: Recognize complications during chronic corticosteroid therapy.

questions.title: Obtain cultures without an avoidable antibiotic delay
questions.stem: A stable client has orders for a urine culture and a first antibiotic dose for suspected infection. The specimen can be collected now. What is appropriate?
options: Collect the specimen promptly before the first dose
Give the dose and collect urine after symptoms improve
Wait for the culture result before giving the ordered antibiotic
Collect the sample from a previously filled drainage bag
why: Antibiotic exposure can reduce culture yield when sampling is easily obtained first.
Treatment may reduce the chance of identifying the organism.
Specimen collection does not require delaying treatment until results return.
Old bag urine may not reliably represent a fresh diagnostic specimen.
questions.takeaway: Antibiotic exposure can reduce culture yield when sampling is easily obtained first.
questions.learningObjective: Obtain cultures without an avoidable antibiotic delay.

questions.title: Reassess therapy when susceptibility results arrive
questions.stem: A client improving on an empiric broad-spectrum antibiotic has a culture identifying a susceptible organism. What should the nurse anticipate?
options: Adding another antibiotic solely because a culture is positive
Team review for the most targeted effective regimen
Continuing broad coverage is always required after improvement
Stopping immediately because the organism is identified
why: A positive culture does not automatically justify duplicate coverage.
Susceptibility results can support narrowing therapy while maintaining effectiveness.
Clinical improvement does not eliminate the value of targeted treatment.
Identification alone does not establish completion of treatment.
questions.takeaway: Susceptibility results can support narrowing therapy while maintaining effectiveness.
questions.learningObjective: Reassess therapy when susceptibility results arrive.

questions.title: Clarify an incomplete allergy history
questions.stem: A client reports 'a penicillin allergy' before receiving a newly prescribed antibiotic. No reaction details are recorded. What is the best next step?
options: Remove the allergy because no written proof is available
Conclude that every antibiotic is contraindicated
Ask what happened, when it occurred and what treatment was needed
Assume nausea and airway swelling carry the same risk
why: An undocumented history still needs investigation before removal.
An allergy to one drug does not establish allergy to all antimicrobials.
Reaction characteristics help the team assess the allergy and antibiotic plan.
Different reaction types require different clinical interpretation.
questions.takeaway: Reaction characteristics help the team assess the allergy and antibiotic plan.
questions.learningObjective: Clarify an incomplete allergy history.

questions.title: Respond to severe antibiotic-associated diarrhea
questions.stem: A client taking antibiotics develops frequent watery stools and abdominal cramping. What is most appropriate?
options: Recommend loperamide before evaluating the cause
Reassure that diarrhea means the antibiotic is working
Skip only the next meal and continue without reassessment
Assess hydration and promptly report possible antibiotic-associated infection
why: Suppressing diarrhea may be inappropriate with suspected infectious colitis.
The symptom can represent a clinically important adverse complication.
Dietary changes alone do not address dehydration or possible infection.
Significant diarrhea may require testing, treatment review and transmission precautions.
questions.takeaway: Significant diarrhea may require testing, treatment review and transmission precautions.
questions.learningObjective: Respond to severe antibiotic-associated diarrhea.

questions.title: Interpret antibiotic response using trends
questions.stem: After antibiotics begin for pneumonia, which findings most clearly support improvement? Select all that apply.
options: Temperature trend and respiratory symptoms improve
Usual activity becomes easier at the same oxygen requirement
One normal temperature while an antipyretic is active
Less coughing accompanied by increasing somnolence
A falling white count with worsening hypotension
why: The infection's clinical manifestations should lessen with effective treatment.
Functional improvement adds meaningful evidence of recovery.
This alone can mask fever without establishing infection control.
Reduced cough with declining alertness may indicate deterioration.
Laboratory improvement does not outweigh new circulatory compromise.
questions.takeaway: The infection's clinical manifestations should lessen with effective treatment.
questions.learningObjective: Interpret antibiotic response using trends.

questions.title: Recognize aminoglycoside ototoxicity
questions.stem: A client receiving gentamicin reports new ringing in the ears and unsteadiness. The next dose is due. What is appropriate?
options: Wait until the antibiotic course is complete to arrange testing
Promptly report the symptoms and clarify the next dose
Give the dose because hearing loss has not been confirmed
Treat dizziness with a sedative before administration
why: Delay may allow potentially irreversible injury to progress.
Aminoglycosides can cause auditory and vestibular toxicity.
Early symptoms warrant review before further potentially harmful exposure.
Sedation can obscure neurological assessment without addressing ototoxicity.
questions.takeaway: Aminoglycosides can cause auditory and vestibular toxicity.
questions.learningObjective: Recognize aminoglycoside ototoxicity.

questions.title: Review aminoglycoside clearance during renal decline
questions.stem: During gentamicin therapy, urine output falls and creatinine rises. The most recent drug level predates these changes. What is appropriate?
options: Increase the dose because less drug reaches the urine
Measure only fluid intake before deciding the dose is safe
Request prompt review of current levels and dosing
Use the prior drug level to approve the next several doses
why: Reduced elimination generally raises systemic accumulation concerns.
Intake alone does not assess drug clearance or nephrotoxicity.
Reduced clearance can increase exposure after a previously acceptable level.
An earlier level may no longer represent the client's exposure.
questions.takeaway: Reduced clearance can increase exposure after a previously acceptable level.
questions.learningObjective: Review aminoglycoside clearance during renal decline.

questions.title: Assess a vancomycin infusion reaction
questions.stem: During IV vancomycin, a client develops flushing and itching over the neck and chest. Blood pressure and breathing remain stable. What should the nurse do first?
options: Continue unchanged because blood pressure is normal
Label all future glycopeptides as confirmed anaphylactic allergies
Give the remaining infusion faster to shorten exposure
Pause the infusion and assess/report the reaction
why: Stable pressure does not justify ignoring a new infusion reaction.
The current findings do not establish that specific immune mechanism.
Faster delivery can worsen an infusion-related reaction.
The pattern may be infusion related, but assessment is needed before a revised plan.
questions.takeaway: The pattern may be infusion related, but assessment is needed before a revised plan.
questions.learningObjective: Assess a vancomycin infusion reaction.

questions.title: Recognize a severe cutaneous drug reaction
questions.stem: After starting trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, a client develops fever, a spreading painful rash and mouth sores. What is appropriate?
options: Urgently escalate and withhold further doses pending review
Give the next dose with an antihistamine only
Treat the mouth sores and wait for the skin to peel
Reduce the dose independently and reassess next week
why: Painful rash with mucosal involvement suggests a potentially severe drug reaction.
Symptom suppression does not address possible severe mucocutaneous injury.
Waiting for further progression delays necessary assessment.
An unprescribed reduction is inadequate for a serious suspected reaction.
questions.takeaway: Painful rash with mucosal involvement suggests a potentially severe drug reaction.
questions.learningObjective: Recognize a severe cutaneous drug reaction.

questions.title: Respond to tendon pain during fluoroquinolone use
questions.stem: A client taking ciprofloxacin reports new Achilles tendon pain without trauma. What should the nurse advise?
options: Take the antibiotic with food and monitor only nausea
Avoid stressing the tendon and promptly contact the prescriber
Stretch forcefully before the next dose
Continue usual running unless swelling becomes visible
why: Changing food timing does not address the tendon complaint.
Fluoroquinolones can cause tendon injury that needs treatment review.
Loading a potentially injured tendon may increase rupture risk.
Pain can precede marked swelling or rupture.
questions.takeaway: Fluoroquinolones can cause tendon injury that needs treatment review.
questions.learningObjective: Respond to tendon pain during fluoroquinolone use.

questions.title: Address tetracycline chelation
questions.stem: A client takes doxycycline together with calcium supplements and an antacid each morning. What instruction is most useful?
options: Crush all products together to improve absorption
Take them together only when a full meal is eaten
Check the product-specific separation interval with the pharmacist
Take an extra doxycycline tablet with the supplements
why: Mixing does not prevent mineral binding.
A meal does not reliably remove this interaction.
Minerals can bind doxycycline and reduce its absorption.
Additional dosing is not a safe solution to impaired absorption.
questions.takeaway: Minerals can bind doxycycline and reduce its absorption.
questions.learningObjective: Address tetracycline chelation.

questions.title: Differentiate expected rifampin discoloration from danger
questions.stem: A client taking rifampin reports orange urine but no pain, jaundice or systemic symptoms. What is the best response?
options: Stop the medicine until urine becomes clear
Assume orange urine confirms dehydration
Report it as confirmed urinary bleeding
Explain expected discoloration and review symptoms requiring reporting
why: An expected effect alone does not justify interrupting essential therapy.
The medication itself can account for the colour change.
Orange discoloration without assessment is not proof of hematuria.
Rifampin can discolour body fluids without indicating organ injury.
questions.takeaway: Rifampin can discolour body fluids without indicating organ injury.
questions.learningObjective: Differentiate expected rifampin discoloration from danger.

questions.title: Report vision changes on ethambutol
questions.stem: A client taking ethambutol says colours look different and reading is newly blurred. What is appropriate?
options: Promptly contact the treatment team before further dosing
Wait for the next routine eye appointment in several months
Recommend stronger reading glasses first
Reassure because the client has no eye pain
why: Ethambutol-associated optic toxicity needs timely assessment.
A new change requires earlier review to limit potential injury.
A prescription change should not precede evaluation of possible drug toxicity.
Optic toxicity can occur without pain.
questions.takeaway: Ethambutol-associated optic toxicity needs timely assessment.
questions.learningObjective: Report vision changes on ethambutol.

questions.title: Evaluate neuropathic symptoms during isoniazid
questions.stem: A client taking isoniazid reports new tingling in both feet and has not been taking prescribed pyridoxine. What is most appropriate?
options: Double isoniazid to complete the course sooner
Assess symptoms and report the missed pyridoxine and possible neuropathy
Advise permanently stopping all tuberculosis medicines
Treat tingling as proof the infection is resolving
why: Increasing exposure may worsen adverse effects and changes the prescription.
Isoniazid-related neuropathy risk and supplementation need review.
Uncoordinated interruption can compromise treatment.
Peripheral tingling is not a marker of tuberculosis cure.
questions.takeaway: Isoniazid-related neuropathy risk and supplementation need review.
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate neuropathic symptoms during isoniazid.

questions.title: Support a complex tuberculosis regimen
questions.stem: A client finds the tuberculosis regimen difficult to manage and is considering taking only the tablet that causes least nausea. Which responses are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Explore adverse effects and arrange regimen support
Explain why the prescribed combination should not be self-selected
Recommend taking only one medicine until appetite returns
Suggest saving omitted tablets to add after treatment ends
Assume missed doses are resolved once symptoms improve
why: Addressing tolerability and practical barriers supports effective combination treatment.
Unplanned partial treatment can promote failure and resistance.
Selective therapy can undermine the intended regimen.
A delayed self-designed course is not an appropriate treatment plan.
Symptom improvement does not establish completion or cure.
questions.takeaway: Addressing tolerability and practical barriers supports effective combination treatment.
questions.learningObjective: Support a complex tuberculosis regimen.

questions.title: Explain oral vancomycin for intestinal infection
questions.stem: A client prescribed oral vancomycin for C. difficile asks why an IV route is not automatically stronger. What is the best explanation?
options: IV medicines are always more effective than oral medicines
The routes can be exchanged dose for dose without review
Oral treatment is chosen only because it has no adverse effects
The prescribed oral route delivers treatment to the intestinal site
why: Route alone does not establish effectiveness at a specific site.
Routes have different drug distribution and treatment roles.
Oral therapy can still have adverse effects and requires monitoring.
Route effectiveness depends on the target infection, not simply IV access.
questions.takeaway: Route effectiveness depends on the target infection, not simply IV access.
questions.learningObjective: Explain oral vancomycin for intestinal infection.

questions.title: Administer oral nystatin for local effect
questions.stem: A client prescribed nystatin oral suspension immediately swallows it without distributing it in the mouth. What teaching is most useful?
options: Follow the prescribed directions for contact with affected oral surfaces
Mix it into a full drink to eliminate the taste
Stop treatment as soon as the first patch disappears
Use it immediately before rinsing vigorously with water
why: Local contact is important when treating oral candidiasis.
Dilution and rapid swallowing may reduce useful oral contact.
Visible improvement does not automatically establish course completion.
Immediate rinsing may remove medicine from the treatment area.
questions.takeaway: Local contact is important when treating oral candidiasis.
questions.learningObjective: Administer oral nystatin for local effect.

questions.title: Review fluconazole with anticoagulation
questions.stem: A client stable on warfarin is newly prescribed fluconazole. What should the nurse ensure?
options: Advise extra vitamin K foods to offset the new drug
Interaction review and an appropriate anticoagulation-monitoring plan
Continue usual monitoring because both doses are standard
Separate the medicines by two hours as the only precaution
why: Unplanned dietary compensation makes anticoagulation less predictable.
Fluconazole can increase warfarin effect and bleeding risk.
Standard doses do not exclude a clinically significant interaction.
Spacing does not prevent the metabolic interaction.
questions.takeaway: Fluconazole can increase warfarin effect and bleeding risk.
questions.learningObjective: Review fluconazole with anticoagulation.

questions.title: Assess a QT-risk antibiotic combination
questions.stem: A client prescribed azithromycin takes another QT-prolonging medicine and has potassium below the supplied reference range. What is appropriate?
options: Separate the two medicines by one hour
Monitor only for a skin rash after administration
Clarify the regimen and electrolyte correction/monitoring plan
Give the antibiotic because there is no current chest pain
why: Timing separation does not reliably remove their electrophysiological interaction.
A rash check does not address the identified cardiac risk.
Combined QT risk and hypokalemia can increase dysrhythmia risk.
Dysrhythmia risk can exist without chest pain.
questions.takeaway: Combined QT risk and hypokalemia can increase dysrhythmia risk.
questions.learningObjective: Assess a QT-risk antibiotic combination.

questions.title: Review clarithromycin with a statin
questions.stem: A client taking a statin is newly prescribed clarithromycin. The pharmacist flags a clinically important interaction for that product. What should the nurse do?
options: Give both because the antibiotic course is short
Advise spacing doses across morning and evening only
Tell the client to halve both medicines independently
Clarify the planned alternative or temporary medication adjustment
why: Short exposure can still cause a significant interaction.
Spacing does not necessarily remove a metabolic interaction.
Arbitrary dose changes can reduce efficacy and do not establish safety.
The flagged combination requires an authorized plan before uncertain coadministration.
questions.takeaway: The flagged combination requires an authorized plan before uncertain coadministration.
questions.learningObjective: Review clarithromycin with a statin.

questions.title: Identify a potassium-raising antibiotic interaction
questions.stem: A client taking ramipril develops weakness after starting trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole. Potassium is elevated. Which information is most relevant to report?
options: The combination can contribute to hyperkalemia
The antibiotic must have caused potassium loss
Weakness is unrelated if blood pressure is normal
The interaction can be excluded because administration times differ
why: Trimethoprim and renin-angiotensin system inhibition can both increase potassium.
That interpretation conflicts with the elevated result and recognized interaction.
Normal pressure does not exclude an important electrolyte disturbance.
Dose spacing does not remove the potassium-retaining effects.
questions.takeaway: Trimethoprim and renin-angiotensin system inhibition can both increase potassium.
questions.learningObjective: Identify a potassium-raising antibiotic interaction.

questions.title: Clarify antibiotic delivery with continuous feeds
questions.stem: A client receives continuous enteral nutrition and a new antibiotic through the tube. Pharmacy identifies an interaction with the feed's minerals. What is appropriate?
options: Increase the antibiotic amount to compensate for reduced absorption
Obtain a product-specific timing or alternative-route plan
Interrupt feeding for an arbitrary full day
Mix the antibiotic directly into the feed to dilute minerals
why: Unprescribed dose compensation is unreliable and potentially unsafe.
The interaction and nutrition requirements need coordinated management.
An unnecessarily long hold compromises nutrition without a tailored plan.
Mixing may worsen binding and make dosing incomplete.
questions.takeaway: The interaction and nutrition requirements need coordinated management.
questions.learningObjective: Clarify antibiotic delivery with continuous feeds.

questions.title: Reassess presumed lower urinary infection
questions.stem: A client treated with nitrofurantoin for cystitis develops fever, flank pain and vomiting. What should the nurse do?
options: Give a second dose to improve kidney penetration
Treat only the nausea and continue the same plan
Promptly report possible upper urinary infection and treatment failure
Encourage completion without reporting until the last capsule
why: Extra dosing does not establish adequate treatment of renal infection.
Symptom relief alone may mask worsening infection.
New systemic and flank symptoms suggest a condition needing a different assessment and regimen.
Progression beyond lower urinary symptoms requires earlier review.
questions.takeaway: New systemic and flank symptoms suggest a condition needing a different assessment and regimen.
questions.learningObjective: Reassess presumed lower urinary infection.

questions.title: Plan antibiotic use after discharge
questions.stem: A client leaves hospital with an antibiotic course and asks what to do if symptoms settle or adverse effects develop. Which instructions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Keep remaining doses for a similar illness months later
Share unused doses with someone who has the same symptoms
Restart the entire course independently after a missed dose
Take the medicine for the prescribed course unless the team changes the plan
Report severe adverse effects promptly for treatment advice
why: Future symptoms may have a different cause requiring reassessment.
Similar symptoms do not establish the same infection or prescription.
Missed-dose management does not usually mean an unreviewed new course.
Duration should follow the individualized treatment plan rather than symptom-based guessing.
Serious reactions may require urgent review and an altered regimen.
questions.takeaway: Duration should follow the individualized treatment plan rather than symptom-based guessing.
questions.learningObjective: Plan antibiotic use after discharge.

questions.title: Assess home IV antibiotic readiness
questions.stem: A client will manage home IV antibiotic therapy with nursing support. Which demonstrations support safe discharge planning? Select all that apply.
options: The client explains how to report fever, rash or line problems
The client follows the taught aseptic connection procedure
The client plans to change infusion speed whenever running late
The client recognizes the bag by colour but cannot confirm its label
The client expects the pump alarm to identify every site complication
why: Recognizing complications supports timely contact and reassessment.
Observed technique helps establish practical ability to handle the system.
Unprescribed rate changes can cause adverse effects or delivery problems.
Appearance alone does not verify drug, dose or intended client.
Infiltration or inflammation may occur without a reliable pump alarm.
questions.takeaway: Recognizing complications supports timely contact and reassessment.
questions.learningObjective: Assess home IV antibiotic readiness.

questions.title: Contralateral cane support
questions.stem: A client prescribed a cane for painful left-knee arthritis walks farther when the knee is unloaded. Which technique should the nurse reinforce?
options: Hold the cane in the left hand
Use whichever hand feels easiest each step
Change to two-handed walker use without reassessment
Hold the cane in the right hand
why: Same-side use provides less effective unloading of the painful knee.
Inconsistent technique reduces predictable support during gait.
A device change requires assessment rather than substituting for cane teaching.
Contralateral support reduces loading of the painful left knee.
questions.takeaway: Use a cane on the side opposite the weaker leg.
questions.learningObjective: Use a cane on the side opposite the weaker leg.

questions.title: Walker rising
questions.stem: A client safely walks with a walker but it tips toward them when they rise from a chair. The chair has armrests. Which change should the nurse teach?
options: Have a helper stabilize the walker for every rise
Rock several times while holding the walker
Push from the chair armrests before grasping the walker
Place the walker farther ahead before rising
why: This may limit movement but does not teach the independent technique the client can use.
Momentum while pulling can still tip the walker toward the client.
The stable chair supports rising without pulling the walker backward.
Extra reaching reduces stability and does not remove the pulling force.
questions.takeaway: Rise using the chair before grasping the walker.
questions.learningObjective: Rise using the chair before grasping the walker.

questions.title: Crutch pressure
questions.stem: An adult using axillary crutches develops hand tingling after walking. The nurse observes body weight resting on the pads. Which correction addresses the observed problem?
options: Encourage a tighter hand grip only
Transfer weight through the handgrips
Add thicker padding beneath each armpit
Schedule shorter walks without changing technique
why: Grip strength alone does not change weight resting on the axillary pads.
This relieves the observed nerve-compressing axillary pressure.
Padding does not eliminate pressure from body weight on the axillae.
Rest may reduce symptoms temporarily but leaves the cause in place.
questions.takeaway: Keep body weight off the axillary crutch pads.
questions.learningObjective: Keep body weight off the axillary crutch pads.

questions.title: Wheelchair footplates
questions.stem: A client cleared for a stand-pivot transfer is seated in a wheelchair. The brakes are locked, but the feet remain on the footplates. What should happen next?
options: Move footplates aside and place the feet securely
Apply a transfer belt and start the stand
Move the chair closer while the client begins rising
Recline the backrest before the stand
why: Stable floor contact is needed before initiating the stand.
A belt does not remove the footplate obstruction.
Chair position should be set before the client starts moving.
Reclining does not correct foot placement for this transfer.
questions.takeaway: Clear wheelchair footplates before a standing transfer.
questions.learningObjective: Clear wheelchair footplates before a standing transfer.

questions.title: Stroke shoulder support
questions.stem: A client with a flaccid arm after stroke reports shoulder discomfort during repositioning. Which change best addresses the likely mechanical cause?
options: Reposition less often to avoid all discomfort
Give the next prescribed analgesic before every turn
Encourage the client to lift with the weak arm
Support the affected arm throughout movement
why: Reduced movement leaves pressure risks and the mechanical cause unresolved.
Analgesia may help but does not correct unsupported limb traction.
A flaccid arm cannot provide reliable weight-bearing support.
Support limits traction on the weak shoulder.
questions.takeaway: Protect a weak shoulder from traction during movement.
questions.learningObjective: Protect a weak shoulder from traction during movement.

questions.title: Passive range
questions.stem: During prescribed passive elbow movement, a client with limited mobility reports pulling discomfort at the same point each time. What should the nurse do?
options: Increase repetitions while keeping the same painful range
Repeat after the next analgesic without changing the endpoint
Stop at the comfortable limit and reassess
Move slightly beyond the limit to lengthen the muscle
why: More repetitions do not make the painful endpoint appropriate.
Pain relief alone does not make the previously painful range appropriate.
The painful limit guides safe movement and may require plan revision.
Pushing through pain may injure restricted tissues.
questions.takeaway: Perform passive movement gently within the tolerated range.
questions.learningObjective: Perform passive movement gently within the tolerated range.

questions.title: Active movement choice
questions.stem: After stroke, a client can move the right arm through its full range but needs assistance on the left. Which plan best uses the client's abilities?
options: Complete right-arm exercises only on therapy days
Use active right-arm exercise with individualized left-arm assistance
Use passive movement for both arms to maintain symmetry
Focus exercise only on the weak left arm
why: Unnecessary restriction reduces opportunities for safe practice.
The plan preserves voluntary activity while addressing weaker-side needs.
This removes useful voluntary activity on the stronger side.
The stronger arm also benefits from ongoing functional use.
questions.takeaway: Use active movement when the client can participate.
questions.learningObjective: Use active movement when the client can participate.

questions.title: Logroll alignment
questions.stem: A postoperative client has a prescribed logroll technique. Which actions follow that plan? Select all that apply.
options: Agree on the movement sequence before turning
Keep shoulders and hips aligned during the turn
Raise the shoulders first to make the turn easier
Use a one-person turn because the client is light
why: Coordinated timing supports a controlled movement as one unit.
Alignment limits twisting targeted by the logroll order.
Moving the shoulders separately introduces trunk rotation.
Required assistance depends on alignment needs and ability, not weight alone.
questions.takeaway: Coordinate a logroll to avoid twisting the trunk.
questions.learningObjective: Coordinate a logroll to avoid twisting the trunk.

questions.title: Gait endurance
questions.stem: A rehabilitation client aims to walk to the dining room. They walk 20 metres steadily but become exhausted at 30 metres without chest pain or desaturation. Which plan best supports progress?
options: Complete the full route once daily despite exhaustion
Use a wheelchair for every trip until endurance is normal
Increase gait speed to finish before fatigue occurs
Repeat manageable distances with planned rests
why: Repeated excessive fatigue may undermine safe participation.
Exclusive substitution removes an opportunity to build walking tolerance.
Faster walking may increase exertion rather than reduce it.
Graded practice builds tolerance without repeatedly exceeding it.
questions.takeaway: Progress mobility using observed tolerance and planned rest.
questions.learningObjective: Progress mobility using observed tolerance and planned rest.

questions.title: Weight-bearing clarification
questions.stem: After ankle surgery, an adult has a right non-weight-bearing order and has practised transfers. Which observed action requires correction?
options: Adjusting clothing while seated before transferring
Requesting a rest after a transfer
Briefly loading both feet while standing to adjust clothing
Using the taught transfer device with staff nearby
why: Seated preparation reduces standing demands.
Rest responds appropriately to exertion during restricted mobility.
Even brief right-foot loading violates the current restriction.
The trained method supports adherence to the restriction.
questions.takeaway: Apply the prescribed weight-bearing restriction during every transfer.
questions.learningObjective: Apply the prescribed weight-bearing restriction during every transfer.

questions.title: Seated alignment
questions.stem: A wheelchair user reports thigh discomfort after meals. Their pelvis has slid forward and both feet dangle. Which intervention should the nurse prioritize?
options: Encourage repeated scooting back during every meal
Request seating reassessment and support the feet
Add a softer cushion without reassessing seat height
Shorten meals so the client sits for less time
why: Repeated correction alone does not address an unsuitable fit.
Seat and footrest fit directly affect the observed alignment problem.
A cushion may further raise the client above the footrests.
This limits exposure but leaves the seating cause unresolved.
questions.takeaway: Match wheelchair seating to body dimensions and support needs.
questions.learningObjective: Match wheelchair seating to body dimensions and support needs.

questions.title: Bed mobility cue
questions.stem: A client with mild weakness can bridge safely and wants to regain bed mobility. Which assistance best supports that goal?
options: Give stepwise cues and allow the client to contribute
Complete the turn quickly with two staff
Wait for full independent strength before practising
Use a mechanical aid for every movement regardless of ability
why: Supported practice uses the ability needed for the stated goal.
Staff movement alone does not practise the client's retained skill.
Safe graded participation can begin before complete independence.
Automatic equipment use may bypass feasible active participation.
questions.takeaway: Invite safe participation in bed mobility.
questions.learningObjective: Invite safe participation in bed mobility.

questions.title: Contracture prevention
questions.stem: An immobile client's ankles remain pointed downward on the mattress. Which measures belong in an individualized prevention plan? Select all that apply.
options: Include regular prescribed ankle movement
Place a pillow only beneath the knees
Rely on the mattress to position the feet
Support the ankles in the prescribed neutral alignment
why: Movement helps preserve available joint range.
This does not address the downward ankle position.
The observed resting posture shows the mattress is insufficient.
Neutral positioning limits prolonged shortening in plantar flexion.
questions.takeaway: Combine alignment and movement to reduce contracture risk.
questions.learningObjective: Combine alignment and movement to reduce contracture risk.

questions.title: Hip precautions
questions.stem: A client returning home after hip surgery must follow a specified hip-flexion limit. Which home detail should prompt equipment review?
options: The client has practised using a long-handled aid
The dining chair has firm armrests
The preferred chair is low and deeply cushioned
The toilet has the prescribed raised seat
why: Adaptive equipment can reduce bending during dressing.
Armrests assist a controlled rise without requiring a low seat.
Low seating can require flexion beyond the prescribed limit.
The raised seat supports the ordered movement limit.
questions.takeaway: Match furniture and self-care aids to prescribed movement precautions.
questions.learningObjective: Match furniture and self-care aids to prescribed movement precautions.

questions.title: Transfer belt placement
questions.stem: A client can partly bear weight but a standard transfer belt would cross a painful fresh abdominal incision. The transfer is not urgent. What is the best plan?
options: Use a single-person pivot without any support
Reassess for a suitable alternative transfer method
Place additional gauze under the same tight belt
Give analgesia and use the belt unchanged
why: Removing equipment without reassessment may create a fall risk.
The assistance should avoid injuring the surgical site.
Padding does not reliably remove incisional compression.
Pain relief does not eliminate mechanical stress on the incision.
questions.takeaway: Adapt transfer equipment to wounds and other attachments.
questions.learningObjective: Adapt transfer equipment to wounds and other attachments.

questions.title: Fatigue during grooming
questions.stem: A client with stable chronic lung disease wants to continue grooming independently but becomes breathless while standing. Which plan best meets that goal?
options: Arrange seated grooming with supplies within reach
Have staff complete all grooming
Move grooming to after a full bath
Encourage faster movements to shorten the task
why: Sitting and reduced reaching conserve energy for independent care.
This removes independence the client may retain with adaptation.
Fatigue after bathing may make the task harder.
Rushing can increase breathlessness and reduce control.
questions.takeaway: Conserve energy by pacing and simplifying valued daily activities.
questions.learningObjective: Conserve energy by pacing and simplifying valued daily activities.

questions.title: One-handed dressing
questions.stem: A client with right-arm weakness becomes frustrated trying to insert that arm after dressing the stronger arm. Which change should the nurse suggest?
options: Start with the stronger arm and pull the shirt over the weak elbow
Ask staff to dress both arms routinely
Place the shirt over the head before inserting either arm
Dress the weaker arm first
why: Starting on the strong side restricts fabric available around the weaker arm.
This bypasses an achievable adaptive technique.
This sequence limits access and garment movement around the weaker limb.
The loose garment allows easier placement of the less mobile limb.

questions.learningObjective: Dress the weaker limb first using adaptable clothing.

questions.title: Clothing removal
questions.stem: A client with left-arm weakness struggles to remove a shirt because the stronger arm remains inside it. Which technique should the nurse teach?
options: Ask staff to remove every garment
Pull the shirt over the head before freeing either arm
Remove the stronger arm first
Begin with the weaker arm every time
why: Automatic substitution does not build the available skill.
Freeing the stronger arm first provides assistance around the weak limb.
The freed arm can assist gentle removal from the weak side.
This keeps the useful arm enclosed during the harder part.
questions.takeaway: Undress the stronger limb first to assist the weaker limb.
questions.learningObjective: Undress the stronger limb first to assist the weaker limb.

questions.title: Reacher use
questions.stem: A client under temporary bending restrictions wants to retrieve a dropped sock independently. Which response best supports rehabilitation?
options: Encourage a seated forward reach to the floor
Offer the prescribed reacher and supervise practice
Pick it up immediately each time
Ask the client to wait for movement restrictions to end
why: Seated bending may still breach the prescribed limit.
The aid permits the task without prohibited bending.
Routine substitution prevents practice of a suitable adaptive skill.
The task is possible now with approved equipment.
questions.takeaway: Use adaptive equipment to preserve function within restrictions.
questions.learningObjective: Use adaptive equipment to preserve function within restrictions.

questions.title: Walking aid reassessment
questions.stem: A client who uses a walker safely on vinyl repeatedly catches its legs on the bedroom carpet. What should the nurse do first?

Switch to a cane immediately
Advise the client to take larger steps
Have a helper lift the walker legs at the carpet edge

Larger steps may reduce control without resolving equipment catch.
Ad hoc assistance does not establish route or device suitability.

questions.learningObjective: Reassess equipment and environment when gait performance changes.

questions.title: Resting hand position
questions.stem: An immobile client has an individually fitted hand splint. Which care actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Follow the individual wearing schedule
Extend wearing time after a missed session without advice
Add thick padding to relieve tightness without reassessment
Inspect the skin at scheduled splint removal
why: The schedule balances alignment with tissue tolerance.
Extra wear may exceed skin tolerance.
Padding can further tighten a fitted device.

questions.learningObjective: Monitor skin and comfort with prescribed splints.

questions.title: Turning with tubes

questions.learningObjective: Arrange tubes before movement to prevent traction and obstruction.

questions.title: Supported side lying

questions.learningObjective: Support the limbs and separate bony surfaces in side lying.

questions.title: Bed exercise evaluation

questions.title: Activity after bed rest

questions.learningObjective: Use the response to position changes to progress activity.

questions.title: Denture cleaning
questions.stem: A client removes full dentures for cleaning. Which setup reduces breakage if they slip?
options: Use a deep unlined sink
Clean them over an uncovered bedside table

questions.title: Denture-related soreness

Inspect the mouth and assess fit

questions.learningObjective: Assess oral discomfort before changing the diet.

questions.title: Natural teeth care

Use mouthwash as the only cleaning

questions.title: Oral bleeding risk
questions.stem: A client has fragile, bleeding gums and a revised oral-care plan. Which approach is best?
options: Use a standard firm-bristle brush to clear deposits
Start flossing despite no established flossing routine
Replace all cleaning with an alcohol-containing rinse
Use the ordered gentle oral-care method

questions.learningObjective: Adapt oral care to tissue condition and bleeding risk.

questions.title: Oral appliance storage

Place it in an unlabelled medication cup
Use a labelled denture container
Wrap it in a tissue

questions.title: Dry lips

A compatible lip moisturizer
Frequent alcohol-based mouth rinses
Lemon swabs repeatedly

questions.title: Bathing preferences

Document refusal of all hygiene
Offer a morning bath before breakfast instead
Ask the family to persuade the client to accept mornings

Changing the morning hour does not address the evening preference.

questions.learningObjective: Adapt routine hygiene to the client's preferences when feasible.

questions.title: Bath temperature
questions.stem: A client with reduced foot sensation prepares for a foot wash. Which instruction is appropriate?

Rely on the usual tap setting without testing
Use the clients report that yesterday's water felt safe
Check water with an intact-sensation area or thermometer

Tap settings do not reliably establish the final water temperature.
A previous sensation does not establish today's water temperature.
Impaired sensation can prevent recognition of excessive heat.

questions.learningObjective: Verify water temperature independently when sensation is impaired.

questions.title: Perineal skin care
questions.stem: An adult has frequent urinary leakage and fragile perineal skin. Which actions support comfort? Select all that apply.
options: Use repeated soap washes after every small leak
Apply barrier cream without cleansing visible urine first
Clean gently after leakage
Use the prescribed skin barrier

questions.learningObjective: Use gentle cleansing and moisture protection after incontinence.

questions.title: Foreskin replacement

Return the foreskin to its usual position

questions.title: Eye crust removal
questions.stem: A client has dried secretions on the eyelids. Which technique is appropriate?
options: Use gentle wipes with a clean surface each pass
Use one damp pad until both eyes appear clean
Reuse one dirty corner for both eyes
Start wiping before moistening adherent crusts

questions.title: Hearing aid care

Using alcohol on every component
Applying the cleaning method used for another model

questions.title: Glasses before meals

questions.learningObjective: Address sensory aids before assuming loss of self-care ability.

questions.title: Shaving with fragile skin

Use the disposable wet razor available on the unit

questions.learningObjective: Use gentle shaving methods matched to skin condition.

questions.title: Nail care limits

questions.title: Pruritic skin

questions.title: Skin-fold moisture

Dry the fold gently and assess the skin

questions.title: Perineal dignity

questions.title: Contact lens discomfort
