These may indicate a treatable oral condition.
Painful tissue injury can reduce nutritional intake.
questions.takeaway: Follow up oral lesions that affect comfort or intake.
questions.learningObjective: Follow up oral lesions that affect comfort or intake.

questions.title: Bathing fatigue
questions.stem: Halfway through a bed bath, a stable client reports exhaustion. What is the best response?
options: Ask another staff member to finish immediately while the client rests in bed
Pause and agree on priority areas
Complete every area before allowing rest
Abandon all remaining hygiene without a revised plan
why: Changing caregivers does not reduce the client's immediate fatigue from continued care.
Rest and partial care respect current tolerance.
This ignores the client's stated exhaustion.
Care can be prioritized and rescheduled rather than left unplanned.
questions.takeaway: Adjust hygiene duration to the client's energy level.
questions.learningObjective: Adjust hygiene duration to the client's energy level.

questions.title: Earwax self-care
questions.stem: A client says they use cotton swabs deep inside the ear canal. Which teaching is appropriate?
options: Clean the outer ear and seek advice for blockage
Use a smaller swab to reach farther into the canal
Try wax-softening drops without checking ear symptoms or history
Start home irrigation whenever hearing seems reduced
why: Deep insertion can push wax inward or injure tissue.
A smaller object can still push wax inward or injure the canal.
Pain, drainage, or prior ear procedures may change whether drops are appropriate.
Hearing changes require assessment before assuming wax and irrigating.
questions.takeaway: Avoid inserting objects into the ear canal.
questions.learningObjective: Avoid inserting objects into the ear canal.

questions.title: Skin tear dressing removal
questions.stem: A client's fragile skin pulls when adhesive is removed. Which technique reduces trauma?
options: Remove the tape in one brisk upward motion
Keep the skin taut by pulling it away from the adhesive
Use repeated dry gauze rubbing to remove remaining adhesive
Support the skin while releasing adhesive slowly
why: Upward force can lift fragile epidermis with the adhesive.
This adds tissue tension instead of supporting skin at the release point.
Friction may injure the fragile surface; an appropriate removal method is needed.
Counter-support limits skin stretching and stripping.
questions.takeaway: Support fragile skin during adhesive removal.
questions.learningObjective: Support fragile skin during adhesive removal.

questions.title: Client-led hygiene
questions.stem: A client with arthritis can brush teeth with a built-up handle. Which outcome best indicates effective assistance?
options: The client can name the equipment supplier
The client finishes despite increased hand pain
The client completes brushing comfortably
The nurse finishes faster alone
why: Knowing a supplier does not demonstrate comfortable oral-care performance.
Completion with increased pain suggests the adaptation needs adjustment.
Adaptive support achieved the self-care goal.
Speed alone does not measure client independence.
questions.takeaway: Evaluate adaptive hygiene by comfortable participation.
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate adaptive hygiene by comfortable participation.

questions.title: Mealtime alertness
questions.stem: A client with an established dysphagia plan is unusually drowsy when lunch arrives. What should the nurse do before feeding?
options: Ask family to feed slowly
Assess alertness and swallowing readiness
Offer the usual thickened drink
Begin with the smallest portion
why: Changing feeders does not resolve the clinical change.
Today's reduced alertness may make the established plan insufficient.
Prescribed consistency does not overcome reduced airway protection.
Small portions still require adequate alertness and swallowing.
questions.takeaway: Reassess readiness when alertness changes before oral intake.
questions.learningObjective: Reassess readiness when alertness changes before oral intake.

questions.title: Texture consistency
questions.stem: A client prescribed minced food receives soup containing firm vegetable chunks. Which response best follows the swallowing plan?
options: Replace it with the prescribed texture
Add thickener without altering the chunks
Encourage extra chewing between sips
Serve only the broth without checking consistency
why: Mixed textures may exceed the assessed swallowing ability.
Thickening liquid does not change solid particle size.
Chewing advice does not replace the prescribed texture.
The broth may also fail the prescribed liquid consistency.
questions.takeaway: Verify both food texture and liquid consistency.
questions.learningObjective: Verify both food texture and liquid consistency.

questions.title: Meal supervision
questions.stem: A client has a prescribed slow-paced assisted feeding plan. Which observations indicate appropriate implementation? Select all that apply.
options: The client remains upright as prescribed
The feeder alternates spoonfuls rapidly
Conversation continues while food is swallowed
Each mouthful is swallowed before another
why: Position supports the assessed swallowing strategy.
Rapid alternating can overwhelm the planned swallowing pace.
Divided attention can interfere with this assisted feeding plan.
This prevents accumulating food faster than swallowing allows.
questions.takeaway: Match feeding pace to observed swallowing.
questions.learningObjective: Match feeding pace to observed swallowing.

questions.title: Thickened fluid acceptance
questions.stem: A client dislikes prescribed thickened fluids and drinks very little. What should the nurse do?
options: Thicken drinks further to improve safety
Record intake and wait several days
Discuss acceptable options with the swallowing team
Offer unrestricted thin water immediately
why: Extra thickness may reduce acceptance without addressing the prescription.
Persistent poor intake needs timely reassessment.
Intake and preference need a safe individualized adjustment.
A separate assessed water protocol would be required.
questions.takeaway: Address poor acceptance without independently changing swallowing prescriptions.
questions.learningObjective: Address poor acceptance without independently changing swallowing prescriptions.

questions.title: Food pocketing
questions.stem: A client recovering from stroke finishes lunch with food remaining in one cheek. What is the best next action?
options: Lay the client down for rest
Assist prescribed oral clearance and inspect
Offer another spoonful to stimulate swallowing
Give a large drink to wash it down
why: Residual food remains an aspiration and hygiene concern.
Retained food requires removal using the established safe method.
More food increases the retained bolus.
An unplanned liquid bolus may increase aspiration risk.
questions.takeaway: Check oral clearance after meals when pocketing occurs.
questions.learningObjective: Check oral clearance after meals when pocketing occurs.

questions.title: Neglect at meals
questions.stem: A client with left-sided neglect eats only food on the right. What supports rehabilitation during a supervised meal?
options: Cue scanning toward the overlooked side
Mix every food together centrally
Feed every mouthful from the right
Document poor appetite alone
why: Practice addresses neglect while supporting access to food.
This may improve access but does not practise scanning.
Exclusive right-side feeding reinforces inattention to the left.
Uneaten food reflects an observed perceptual barrier.
questions.takeaway: Use specific cues to address perceptual barriers to eating.
questions.learningObjective: Use specific cues to address perceptual barriers to eating.

questions.title: Tremor and utensils
questions.stem: A client with tremor spills food but can bring a spoon to the mouth. Which intervention best preserves independence?
options: Have staff provide complete feeding
Limit meals to finger foods exclusively
Increase spoonful size to reduce the number of movements
Trial assessed adaptive utensils
why: Full substitution bypasses the client's retained movement.
Some adaptation may help, but unnecessary restriction limits choice.
Larger spoonfuls can increase spillage and do not improve motor control.
Adaptation may improve control while preserving participation.
questions.takeaway: Match eating aids to the observed functional barrier.
questions.learningObjective: Match eating aids to the observed functional barrier.

questions.title: Meal pain barrier
questions.stem: A client leaves most food because mouth ulcers hurt. What should the nurse prioritize?
options: Begin calorie counting as the only intervention
Explain the importance of completing meals
Assess oral pain and coordinate comfort care
Increase portion size at the next meal
why: Measurement identifies deficit but does not relieve the cause.
Education alone does not overcome painful lesions.
The stated intake barrier requires treatment and suitable food.
More food does not address pain with eating.
questions.takeaway: Treat the specific barrier contributing to poor intake.
questions.learningObjective: Treat the specific barrier contributing to poor intake.

questions.title: Early satiety
questions.stem: A client with cancer feels full after several bites but swallows safely. Which plan is most appropriate?
options: Prioritize low-energy bulky foods
Offer small nutrient-dense portions more often
Add large drinks before each meal
Serve one large main meal daily
why: Bulk may fill the stomach without meeting nutritional needs.
This uses limited appetite to improve energy intake.
Premeal volume may worsen early satiety.
A large portion conflicts with the reported tolerance.
questions.takeaway: Use nutrient density when meal volume is limited.
questions.learningObjective: Use nutrient density when meal volume is limited.

questions.title: Protected mealtime
questions.stem: A dependent client misses meals because routine care repeatedly interrupts feeding. Which changes are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Reschedule nonurgent tasks around meals
Arrange reliable feeding assistance
Leave covered trays until the next shift
Record refusal when assistance is unavailable
why: Reducing interruptions protects the opportunity to eat.
Dependence requires planned help when food arrives.
Delay can reduce food quality and intake.
Lack of help is not a client refusal.
questions.takeaway: Plan assistance and timing to make meals accessible.
questions.learningObjective: Plan assistance and timing to make meals accessible.

questions.title: Food preference assessment
questions.stem: A client eats little hospital food but requests familiar foods compatible with the ordered diet. What should the nurse do?
options: Explain that standard menus meet all needs
Require finishing the tray before alternatives
Ask relatives to bring anything without checking restrictions
Coordinate acceptable familiar choices
why: Nutritional adequacy on paper does not ensure consumption.
This may discourage intake without a clinical benefit.
Compatibility with the clinical diet still matters.
Preference-sensitive meals may improve actual intake.
questions.takeaway: Use preferences within the prescribed nutrition plan.
questions.learningObjective: Use preferences within the prescribed nutrition plan.

questions.title: Fluid allowance distribution
questions.stem: A client prescribed a daily fluid limit is thirsty by evening after drinking most of it at breakfast. Which plan helps?
options: Exclude soup from the intake total
Increase the limit whenever thirst occurs
Distribute the allowance across the day
Keep breakfast unchanged and reserve only medication sips for evening
why: Liquid foods contribute to the prescribed allowance.
Changing the restriction requires clinical review.
Planning preserves access to fluid during later hours.
Medication sips may not address avoidable early overuse; the whole-day allocation needs review.
questions.takeaway: Plan fluid timing and count liquid foods consistently.
questions.learningObjective: Plan fluid timing and count liquid foods consistently.

questions.title: Restricted-fluid mouth comfort
questions.stem: A client on a fluid restriction has dry mouth despite receiving the allotted drinks. Which measures fit the plan? Select all that apply.
options: Use alcohol-containing mouth rinse whenever dryness returns
Provide frequent oral hygiene
Count offered ice within the allowance
Provide unlimited ice chips
why: Alcohol-containing rinses may worsen dryness rather than relieve it.
Cleaning and moistening can improve comfort with limited intake.
Melted ice contributes to total fluid consumption.
Ice becomes fluid and can exceed the restriction.
questions.takeaway: Relieve thirst while accounting for all fluid sources.
questions.learningObjective: Relieve thirst while accounting for all fluid sources.

questions.title: Meal intake documentation
questions.stem: A client eats all yogurt but none of the vegetables or meat. Which record best supports nutritional review?
options: Record foods and approximate amounts eaten
Record half the tray eaten only
Record adequate appetite because yogurt was finished
Record refusal of the prescribed diet
why: Specific intake shows which nutrients may be missing.
A single fraction obscures the actual food pattern.
One accepted food does not establish adequate intake.
Selective intake needs description rather than interpretation.
questions.takeaway: Describe actual intake when assessing nutritional adequacy.
questions.learningObjective: Describe actual intake when assessing nutritional adequacy.

questions.title: Vegetarian protein
questions.stem: A client avoiding animal products needs added protein and has no relevant dietary restrictions. Which offered meal best addresses this need?
options: Clear vegetable broth with tea
Fruit salad with juice
White toast with jam
Lentil stew with whole-grain bread
why: This supplies little protein despite being plant based.
Fruit contributes nutrients but little protein.
This does not substantially address the protein goal.
Legumes provide a practical plant protein source.
questions.takeaway: Identify acceptable protein sources within dietary preferences.
questions.learningObjective: Identify acceptable protein sources within dietary preferences.

questions.title: Low-sodium choices
questions.stem: A client prescribed a sodium-restricted diet compares similar packaged soups. Which teaching is useful?
options: Choose the lowest calorie option
Compare sodium per serving without checking servings per container
Compare sodium for the amount actually eaten
Choose the product labelled natural
why: Calories do not reliably predict sodium content.
The amount actually eaten may contain several labelled servings.
Serving sizes affect the sodium consumed.
Natural labelling does not establish low sodium.
questions.takeaway: Use serving size and sodium content together.
questions.learningObjective: Use serving size and sodium content together.

questions.title: Celiac meal review
questions.stem: A client with celiac disease receives grilled meat, rice, and gravy of unknown ingredients. What should the nurse do?
options: Offer ordinary bread instead of the gravy
Verify the gravy ingredients before serving
Remove the rice because it is a grain
Serve gravy separately and let the client decide
why: Standard wheat bread would introduce gluten.
Wheat-containing thickeners may make gravy unsuitable.
Plain rice is naturally gluten free.
Unknown ingredients still prevent an informed food choice.
questions.takeaway: Check hidden ingredients when implementing gluten avoidance.
questions.learningObjective: Check hidden ingredients when implementing gluten avoidance.

questions.title: Lactose intolerance planning
questions.stem: A client reports cramps after milk but tolerates lactose-free milk. Which change best maintains nutrition?
options: Offer the tolerated lactose-free equivalent
Remove all dairy before considering lactose-free milk
Offer cream because the portion is smaller
Use an unfortified plant beverage without reviewing its nutrients
why: This preserves nutritional intake while addressing the trigger.
A tolerated nutritionally similar option avoids unnecessary food restriction.
Tolerance cannot be assumed from portion size alone.
Alternatives vary in protein and calcium; nutritional equivalence needs review.
questions.takeaway: Use tolerated substitutes before broad food elimination.
questions.learningObjective: Use tolerated substitutes before broad food elimination.

questions.title: Nutrition referral evidence
questions.stem: Which observations support dietitian review for a client recovering from a major illness? Select all that apply.
options: Repeated intake below usual portions
Preference for an alternative meal time
One skipped dessert after a full meal
Unintentional weight loss over several weeks
why: Persistent reduced intake can impair recovery.
Timing preference alone does not establish malnutrition.
An isolated omitted dessert is weak evidence of deficit.
A sustained loss suggests nutritional risk.
questions.takeaway: Use intake and weight trends to identify nutrition risk.
questions.learningObjective: Use intake and weight trends to identify nutrition risk.

questions.title: Feeding tube oral care
questions.stem: A client receiving all nutrition through a tube asks whether mouth care is still needed. Which response is best?
options: Only denture cleaning is needed
Use moistened swabs alone instead of brushing natural teeth
Oral tissues still need regular cleaning
Mouth care can stop until eating resumes
why: Gums and other oral surfaces still need care.
Swabs can moisten tissues but do not adequately replace plaque removal by brushing.
Tube feeding does not prevent oral plaque or dryness.
Lack of oral food does not eliminate oral-care needs.
questions.takeaway: Continue oral hygiene during enteral feeding.
questions.learningObjective: Continue oral hygiene during enteral feeding.

questions.title: Feeding schedule tolerance
questions.stem: A client feels nauseated during a prescribed tube-feeding increase. Vital signs are stable. What should the nurse do?
options: Record nausea only at the end of the shift
Assess tolerance and review the prescribed progression
Give the prescribed antiemetic and continue rate increases without reassessment
Dilute formula independently
why: Delayed review prolongs a potentially correctable problem.
Symptoms may require individualized adjustment with the team.
Symptom treatment does not replace tolerance assessment before further progression.
Unordered dilution changes nutrient delivery and contamination risk.
questions.takeaway: Use symptoms to reassess enteral feeding progression.
questions.learningObjective: Use symptoms to reassess enteral feeding progression.

questions.title: Constipation baseline
questions.stem: A client reports bowel movements every other day with soft stools and no discomfort. What is the most appropriate interpretation?
options: This may be the client's normal pattern
Daily laxatives are automatically indicated
The client should have a daily stool regardless of comfort

why: Comfort and stool consistency matter alongside frequency.
A comfortable established pattern does not require routine treatment.
A fixed daily target is unnecessary for a comfortable established pattern.
Soft comfortable alternate-day stools do not establish a need for stimulant treatment.

questions.learningObjective: Assess bowel function against the person's usual pattern.

questions.title: Toileting after breakfast
questions.stem: A client with chronic constipation often feels an urge after breakfast but postpones toileting. Which plan is useful?
options: Schedule toileting only before breakfast
Discourage responding to urges between rounds
Ask the client to strain at bedtime
Protect unhurried toilet time after breakfast
why: This ignores the client's observed urge pattern.
Repeated postponement may worsen constipation.
Forced straining does not use the natural urge.
The established urge offers a practical bowel routine.

questions.learningObjective: Build bowel routines around usual urges and meal responses.

questions.title: Fibre adjustment
questions.stem: A client abruptly doubles fibre intake and develops bloating without alarm symptoms. What teaching is best?
options: Switch immediately to concentrated fibre at the same increased total
Maintain the abrupt increase without reviewing symptoms
Increase fibre gradually with appropriate fluids
Increase fibre further before reviewing fluid intake

Gradual adjustment can reduce gas and improve tolerance.

questions.learningObjective: Introduce fibre gradually and individualize fluid intake.

questions.title: Toileting posture
questions.stem: A client strains while sitting on a high toilet with feet dangling. Which change should the nurse trial?
options: Coach stronger straining while the feet remain unsupported
Provide secure foot support
Ask the client to lean forward while keeping both feet off the floor
Add another raised seat without reviewing foot contact

questions.takeaway: Support the feet during seated toileting.
questions.learningObjective: Support the feet during seated toileting.

questions.title: Apparent diarrhoea
questions.stem: An immobile client with several days of hard stools now leaks small amounts of liquid stool. What should the nurse assess first?
options: Possible retained stool with overflow
Whether the usual fibre goal was reached
Whether a larger continence product fits
Which antidiarrhoeal was previously effective

Diet history matters but does not resolve possible impaction.
Containment does not identify the cause of leakage.
Suppressing stool before assessing retention may worsen the problem.

questions.learningObjective: Assess overflow when liquid leakage follows constipation.

questions.title: Bowel diary
questions.stem: A client has intermittent faecal urgency and wants to identify patterns. Which entries are useful? Select all that apply.
options: Food intake and associated symptoms
Only episodes requiring a linen change
Only foods the client considers unhealthy
Stool consistency and timing
why: These may reveal triggers needing further assessment.
This misses less severe but informative episodes.
Selective recording can obscure relevant associations.
Both help characterize the elimination pattern.
questions.takeaway: Record bowel patterns systematically before attributing triggers.
questions.learningObjective: Record bowel patterns systematically before attributing triggers.

questions.title: Privacy and retention
questions.stem: A postoperative client voids small amounts while repeatedly watching the open curtain. Bladder assessment shows no urgent retention. What should the nurse try?
options: Keep the curtain partly open to monitor progress continuously
Limit fluids until the client voids normally
Provide privacy and the usual safe position
Request catheterization as the first comfort measure

questions.learningObjective: Address privacy and positioning barriers to elimination.

questions.title: Functional incontinence
questions.stem: A client feels urinary urgency but cannot undo small buttons before reaching the toilet. Which change targets the main barrier?
options: Offer the toilet before each staff break
Use easy-release clothing
Begin a bladder diary as the only measure
Offer a continence pad instead of toilet assistance

Recording does not immediately address the observed access problem.
Containment does not remove the functional barrier.
questions.takeaway: Identify and reduce functional barriers to continence.
questions.learningObjective: Identify and reduce functional barriers to continence.

questions.title: Prompted voiding
questions.stem: A cognitively impaired client remains dry when reminded and assisted every few hours. Which care plan is appropriate?
options: Use an individualized prompted-voiding routine
Wait for the client to initiate every request
Provide pads without scheduled toilet offers
Reduce daytime drinks routinely
why: The observed response supports regular cueing and assistance.
The client has demonstrated a need for prompts.

questions.learningObjective: Build continence care on responses to individualized assistance.

questions.title: Stress leakage
questions.stem: A client leaks small amounts of urine when coughing but empties the bladder normally. Which teaching fits a prescribed pelvic-floor programme?
options: Bear down strongly during each contraction
Practise only by interrupting every void
Stop drinking before physical activity
Practise the taught contractions consistently
why: Bearing down increases pressure rather than lifting the pelvic floor.
Repeated interrupted voiding is not the routine exercise method.
Routine dehydration does not address pelvic-floor support.
Regular targeted exercise supports pelvic-floor function.
questions.takeaway: Teach correct pelvic-floor technique within the individualized plan.
questions.learningObjective: Teach correct pelvic-floor technique within the individualized plan.

questions.title: Bladder diary interpretation
questions.stem: A client's diary shows large evening drinks followed by several nocturnal toilet trips. There is no fluid restriction. Which discussion is most useful?
options: Use a larger night-time pad only
Schedule daytime toilet visits but leave evening drinks unchanged
Shift some intake earlier in the day
Eliminate fluids from lunch onward
why: Containment does not address the observed timing pattern.
Daytime toileting does not address the documented nocturnal volume pattern.
Timing may reduce nocturnal volume while preserving hydration.
Broad restriction is unnecessary and may impair hydration.
questions.takeaway: Adjust fluid timing based on the observed voiding pattern.
questions.learningObjective: Adjust fluid timing based on the observed voiding pattern.

questions.title: Commode access
questions.stem: A client can transfer safely with one helper but cannot walk to the bathroom before leakage occurs. Which plan best supports continence?
options: Provide a bedpan for every episode despite preference
Provide a bedside commode with timely assistance
Use an indwelling catheter for convenience
Tell the client to request help only after urgency peaks
why: The client can use a more functional seated option.
Shorter access matches the client's transfer ability.
Invasive drainage is not justified by this access problem.
Late requests increase the chance of leakage.
questions.takeaway: Match toileting access to mobility and urgency.
questions.learningObjective: Match toileting access to mobility and urgency.

questions.title: Urinal positioning
questions.stem: A male client with weak grip spills urine because he cannot hold the urinal steady. Which adaptation is most useful?
options: Assist positioning and support the urinal
Offer fewer drinks before toileting
Document total incontinence
Offer the urinal every two hours without help holding it
why: Targeted help addresses the grip deficit while permitting voiding.
Reducing hydration does not improve handling ability.
Spillage from handling is not proof of loss of bladder control.
Scheduled access does not resolve weak grip and unstable positioning.
questions.takeaway: Distinguish device-handling difficulty from incontinence.
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish device-handling difficulty from incontinence.

questions.title: Comfortable bedpan use
questions.stem: A client permitted head elevation reports difficulty using a bedpan while flat. Which change should the nurse make?
options: Leave the client flat but extend time
Choose a deeper pan solely to increase volume
Delay until the next scheduled round
Raise the head as tolerated and support alignment

Capacity does not correct the difficulty voiding flat.
Postponement may worsen discomfort and urgency.
A more upright position can facilitate elimination.

questions.learningObjective: Use the most natural safe elimination position available.

questions.title: Catheter discomfort
questions.stem: A catheterized client reports pulling discomfort after moving into a chair. The tubing is taut. What should the nurse do first?
options: Increase fluid intake immediately
Begin a urine culture solely for discomfort
Reposition tubing and securement to remove traction
Request a larger catheter

questions.title: Drainage bag emptying
questions.stem: A mobile client manages a catheter bag at home. Which observed practices indicate understanding? Select all that apply.
options: Waits until the bag is tightly distended
Avoids touching the outlet to the container
Secures the closed outlet after emptying
Rests the outlet inside collected urine
why: Overfilling can impair drainage and increase traction.

Closure prevents leakage and maintains device function.

questions.learningObjective: Empty the bag without contaminating or overstretching the system.

questions.title: Catheter hygiene
questions.stem: An adult with a long-term catheter asks how to clean around it. What should the nurse emphasize?
options: Routine gentle hygiene according to the care plan
Use an antiseptic wash for every routine clean without an indication
Apply antibiotic ointment around the meatus routinely
Disconnecting the tubing during every bath
why: Ordinary cleaning removes secretions without unnecessary irritation.

Routine antibiotic application without indication is not required for ordinary catheter hygiene.

questions.learningObjective: Use gentle external catheter hygiene while preserving the closed system.

questions.title: Continence product fit
questions.stem: A client develops groin marks after a new absorbent product is introduced. Which action should the nurse prioritize?
options: Add a second product inside the first
Change products less often to reduce handling
Apply barrier cream without reviewing fit
Reassess size and skin condition
why: Layering may worsen tightness and heat.
Prolonged exposure may worsen skin irritation.
Barrier protection does not remove mechanical pressure.

questions.title: Ostomy pouch timing
questions.stem: A client says the pouch pulls painfully when nearly full. Which teaching addresses this problem?
options: Change the whole appliance after every small output
Tighten the support belt firmly
Empty it before it becomes heavy
Add another layer of adhesive tape

Extra compression does not solve pouch overfilling.
Earlier emptying reduces weight on the skin barrier.

questions.learningObjective: Avoid letting pouch weight strain the skin barrier.

questions.title: Peristomal leakage
questions.stem: A client reports burning beneath a leaking ostomy barrier. What is the best response?
options: Wait until after the next meal for the routine appliance change
Remove the leaking appliance and assess the seal
Tape over the leak until the next routine change

Effluent contact can rapidly irritate peristomal skin.
Trapped effluent continues contacting the skin.

questions.learningObjective: Address leakage promptly to protect peristomal skin.

questions.title: Changing stoma size

Cut the opening larger for ventilation
Fill the enlarged gap with extra paste without remeasuring
why: Postoperative size changes require reassessment of fit.
An outdated opening leaves skin exposed to effluent.
Further exposure increases the area at risk.

questions.learningObjective: Recheck stoma size as postoperative swelling resolves.

questions.title: Ostomy participation

options: Require a complete change immediately
Have family perform all future care
Postpone all teaching until discharge morning
Agree on one manageable participation step
why: The demand exceeds the client's stated readiness.
This may prevent development of the client's own skills.
Delayed practice limits opportunities to gain confidence.

questions.learningObjective: Build ostomy self-care through achievable agreed steps.

questions.title: Ostomy teaching evaluation
questions.stem: Which client actions demonstrate practical pouch-management learning? Select all that apply.

Relies only on the printed instruction sheet
Checks the seal when itching occurs
Shows how to empty and close the pouch

questions.title: Flatus and embarrassment

options: Recommend skipping meals before every outing
Discuss individual food patterns and pouch options

questions.learningObjective: Address ostomy concerns with individualized practical strategies.

questions.title: Bowel regimen evaluation

options: The client's comfort and usual pattern are restored

Bloating persists despite frequent small stools
Stool frequency increases but stools become watery
why: The goal is comfortable function rather than a fixed frequency.
Increased frequency without comfortable passage does not meet the bowel-care goal.
Persistent bloating suggests incomplete relief and warrants review.
Watery stools can cause harm and do not represent comfortable normalized function.
questions.takeaway: Evaluate bowel care using comfort, consistency, and individual pattern.
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate bowel care using comfort, consistency, and individual pattern.

questions.title: Diarrhoea skin comfort
questions.stem: An adult with frequent loose stools reports perianal burning. Which measures belong in the comfort plan? Select all that apply.
options: Apply the recommended moisture barrier
Use vigorous repeated soap scrubbing
Delay cleansing until several episodes accumulate
Clean gently and dry without rubbing
why: Protection reduces contact with subsequent stool.
Frequent friction and detergent can worsen irritation.
Longer contact increases exposure to stool irritants.
Gentle removal of irritants limits additional skin trauma.
questions.takeaway: Protect perianal skin during frequent stool passage.
questions.learningObjective: Protect perianal skin during frequent stool passage.

questions.title: Toilet communication
questions.stem: A client with expressive aphasia cannot reliably request toileting. Which intervention is most useful?
options: Interpret restlessness as refusal of care
Ask spoken questions only after restlessness develops
Provide an accessible agreed toileting signal
Provide a call bell without agreeing on a toileting signal
why: Restlessness may communicate an unmet elimination need.
A reactive series of questions is less reliable than an agreed accessible request.
A consistent signal addresses the communication barrier.
Bell access is helpful but does not establish how the specific need will be communicated.
questions.takeaway: Adapt toileting communication to expressive ability.
questions.learningObjective: Adapt toileting communication to expressive ability.

questions.title: Night-time toileting balance
questions.stem: A resident is awakened by fixed toileting rounds despite remaining dry most nights. What should guide revision?
options: Add fluids at every awakening
Review the diary and individual sleep pattern
Continue the schedule because it fits staffing
Remove night-time assistance entirely
why: Extra nocturnal intake may increase toilet need.
The plan should balance continence needs with restorative sleep.
Staff convenience alone does not justify repeated waking.
The resident may still need help when awake or urgent.
questions.takeaway: Individualize night-time toileting using actual need and sleep effects.
questions.learningObjective: Individualize night-time toileting using actual need and sleep effects.

questions.title: Elimination goal setting
questions.stem: A client wants fewer accidents during afternoon activities. Which goal best measures the success of the continence plan?
options: No more than one afternoon leakage episode over the next seven days
Demonstrate easier clothing fastenings by Friday
Record daily fluid intake for seven days
Describe two continence strategies at the next visit
why: A defined leakage outcome directly measures the goal of fewer afternoon accidents.
This measures a useful skill rather than the requested continence outcome.
This measures monitoring behaviour rather than the frequency of accidents.
This measures knowledge rather than success in preventing afternoon leakage.
questions.takeaway: Measure continence outcomes against the client's chosen activity goals.
questions.learningObjective: Select a time-defined continence outcome matching the client's goal.

questions.title: Pain without speech
questions.stem: A client with advanced dementia grimaces and guards a hip during turning. Which assessment approach is most useful?
options: Record no pain because no rating is available
Use heart rate as the sole pain measure
Ask the family to select a number without assessment
Use an appropriate behavioural tool and collateral history
why: Inability to use numbers does not establish comfort.
Physiological changes are nonspecific and may be absent.
Family knowledge helps but does not replace structured observation.
Observed behaviours and known baseline can indicate pain when speech is limited.
questions.takeaway: Use structured behavioural assessment when reliable self-report is unavailable.
questions.learningObjective: Use structured behavioural assessment when reliable self-report is unavailable.

questions.title: Pain communication aid
questions.stem: An alert intubated client can point accurately but cannot speak. What should the nurse try first for pain assessment?
options: Ask family to estimate the current pain
Wait until extubation to establish a score
Offer an accessible visual pain scale
Use only a behavioural pain score
why: A capable client can report through another communication route.
Communication adaptation allows assessment now.
The client can provide self-report through pointing.
Behavioural observation is secondary when reliable self-report remains possible.
questions.takeaway: Adapt communication before abandoning pain self-report.
questions.learningObjective: Adapt communication before abandoning pain self-report.

questions.title: Different pain quality
questions.stem: A client with stable chronic knee aching now describes burning feet at night. What is the best next step?
options: Record the highest number without location
Assess the new pain separately
Increase knee exercises as the main response
Use the old knee assessment unchanged
why: A score alone obscures the new symptom pattern.
A different site and quality may indicate another mechanism.
The new foot symptoms may have a different cause.
The previous assessment does not characterize burning feet.
questions.takeaway: Assess new pain characteristics separately from an existing pain problem.
questions.learningObjective: Assess new pain characteristics separately from an existing pain problem.

questions.title: Functional comfort goal
questions.stem: A client with persistent back pain wants to sit through dinner with family. Which goal best guides evaluation?
options: Tolerates the chosen sitting period with acceptable symptoms
Reports zero pain at every assessment
Takes every offered analgesic dose
Rests in bed throughout the evening
why: The outcome directly measures the client's meaningful activity.
Complete absence may be unrealistic and misses the functional goal.
Medication use is a process rather than functional outcome.
Avoidance does not meet the client's stated participation goal.
questions.takeaway: Include meaningful function in comfort goals.
questions.learningObjective: Include meaningful function in comfort goals.

questions.title: Fear of movement
questions.stem: A rehabilitation client avoids approved exercise because they expect pain. What should the nurse do?
options: Provide reassurance that exercise never hurts
Require completion before discussing concerns
Cancel all exercise until pain completely disappears
Explore the fear and plan a paced trial
why: Absolute reassurance may be inaccurate and reduce trust.
Coercion may increase fear and reduce participation.
Avoidance may worsen deconditioning without resolving fear.
Collaboration addresses anticipation while respecting movement limits.
questions.takeaway: Address fear and use graded activity within the plan.
questions.learningObjective: Address fear and use graded activity within the plan.

questions.title: Pain diary usefulness
questions.stem: A client has intermittent headaches under assessment. Which diary entries are most useful? Select all that apply.
options: Only the worst episode each month
Only the pain score without duration
Timing, triggers, and associated symptoms
Treatments tried and the observed response
why: Selective recording misses frequency and variation.
Intensity alone omits clinically useful temporal information.
Patterns can guide assessment of the headache episodes.
Response helps judge effectiveness and possible overuse.
questions.takeaway: Record pain context and response as well as intensity.
questions.learningObjective: Record pain context and response as well as intensity.

questions.title: Cold application tolerance
questions.stem: A client prescribed a cold pack for an ankle sprain reports burning beneath it. What should the nurse do first?
options: Encourage distraction from the sensation
Remove the pack and inspect the skin
Add another layer while leaving the pack in place
Wait until the prescribed interval ends
why: Distraction should not conceal a possible tissue injury.
Burning may indicate cold-related tissue injury or intolerance.
Inspection is needed before continuing after a warning symptom.
A scheduled duration does not override skin intolerance.
questions.takeaway: Stop thermal therapy when abnormal sensations suggest injury.
questions.learningObjective: Stop thermal therapy when abnormal sensations suggest injury.

questions.title: Heat precautions
questions.stem: A client with numb feet requests a heating pad for comfort. Which action is best?
options: Assess sensation and choose a safer comfort plan
Use the client's preferred high setting briefly
Ask the client to remove it when too hot
Cover the pad with a thick blanket
why: Reduced sensation can prevent recognition of heat injury.
Brief exposure can still burn insensate skin.
The client may not reliably feel excessive heat.
Insulation can increase heat retention unpredictably.
questions.takeaway: Avoid relying on impaired sensation to regulate heat exposure.
questions.learningObjective: Avoid relying on impaired sensation to regulate heat exposure.

questions.title: Relaxation preference
questions.stem: A client with recurrent tension discomfort dislikes guided imagery but enjoys quiet music. What is the best plan?
options: Continue imagery because it is commonly recommended
Replace all prescribed treatment with music
Ask the family to choose regardless of preference
Offer preferred music as an adjunct
why: A disliked intervention may increase frustration rather than comfort.
Adjunctive comfort does not automatically replace needed treatment.
The client's response should guide individualized comfort measures.
A chosen acceptable strategy is more likely to support relaxation.
questions.takeaway: Match nonpharmacological comfort strategies to client preference.
questions.learningObjective: Match nonpharmacological comfort strategies to client preference.

questions.title: Breakthrough pattern
questions.stem: A client reports pain reliably worsening during evening wound care despite acceptable comfort at rest. What should the nurse report?
options: Only the total daily analgesic amount
That the client is generally comfortable
The predictable procedure-related timing
Only the lowest daytime pain score
why: Amount alone does not show when coverage is inadequate.
A global label hides pain during necessary care.
The team can plan anticipatory relief for that specific event.
That omits the recurrent distressing episode.
questions.takeaway: Identify predictable painful activities when planning comfort care.
questions.learningObjective: Identify predictable painful activities when planning comfort care.

questions.title: Touch consent
questions.stem: A client with chronic pain stiffens when a nurse starts a back rub. What should the nurse do?
options: Ask a family member to perform the same massage
Stop and ask about touch preferences
Continue with lighter pressure without asking
Explain that massage usually reduces pain
why: Changing the person does not resolve the client's preference.
The response suggests the intervention may be unwelcome.
Consent and preference still need clarification.
Average benefit does not establish this client's comfort.
questions.takeaway: Confirm consent and preference for hands-on comfort measures.
questions.learningObjective: Confirm consent and preference for hands-on comfort measures.

questions.title: Nausea environmental trigger
questions.stem: A client receiving treatment reports nausea when strong food odours enter the room. Which plan best targets this trigger?
options: Offer tolerated low-odour foods in a ventilated setting
Provide larger hot meals less often
Remove oral care because it may smell
Encourage finishing food before assessing symptoms
why: This reduces the identified stimulus while supporting intake.
Hot food odours and large portions may worsen symptoms.
Routine gentle oral care can still support comfort.
Pressure to eat does not address the trigger.
questions.takeaway: Modify identified environmental nausea triggers.
questions.learningObjective: Modify identified environmental nausea triggers.

questions.title: Vomiting positioning
questions.stem: An alert weak client in bed begins vomiting and cannot turn independently. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Measure the emesis before repositioning
Offer water to rinse immediately during vomiting
Finish obtaining a detailed nausea history
Assist a safe side or upright position
why: Measurement must not delay airway-protective assistance.
Oral fluid during active emesis may increase aspiration risk.
Immediate positioning precedes extended history taking.
Positioning helps protect the airway during active vomiting.
questions.takeaway: Protect the airway during vomiting before detailed assessment.
questions.learningObjective: Protect the airway during vomiting before detailed assessment.

questions.title: Restless discomfort
questions.stem: A nonverbal client repeatedly pulls at clothing and shifts in the chair. Which assessments may identify treatable discomfort? Select all that apply.
options: Only whether sedating medication is available
Only how long the behaviour interrupts staff
Toileting need and abdominal fullness
Skin pressure and positioning
why: Sedation does not identify the unmet physical need.
Staff inconvenience does not characterize the client's discomfort.
Elimination discomfort can present as restlessness.
Mechanical discomfort may drive repeated shifting.
questions.takeaway: Assess unmet physical needs before interpreting restlessness behaviourally.
questions.learningObjective: Assess unmet physical needs before interpreting restlessness behaviourally.

questions.title: Sleep pattern assessment
questions.stem: A hospitalized client reports poor sleep but naps for several hours each afternoon. What should the nurse explore first?
options: A fixed early bedtime for every client
Usual routine and daytime sleep pattern
The strongest available sleep medicine
Whether the client can tolerate less sleep
why: A generic schedule may conflict with established habits.
The pattern may explain reduced night-time sleep drive.
Medication selection should follow assessment of contributors.
Dismissing the concern does not assess a modifiable pattern.
questions.takeaway: Assess the full sleep-wake pattern before selecting interventions.
questions.learningObjective: Assess the full sleep-wake pattern before selecting interventions.

questions.title: Nocturnal symptom cause
questions.stem: A client repeatedly awakens with shortness of breath and needs extra pillows. What should the nurse do?
options: Assess the respiratory change and escalate
Offer a sleep aid as the first response
Use earplugs and a dark room only
Schedule a longer afternoon nap
why: Sleep interruption may reflect worsening cardiopulmonary status.
Sedation does not address the possible physiological cause.
Environmental changes do not treat breathing-related awakening.
Compensatory sleep does not explain the new symptom.
questions.takeaway: Investigate physiological symptoms causing repeated awakening.
questions.learningObjective: Investigate physiological symptoms causing repeated awakening.

questions.title: Sleep environment choice
questions.stem: A stable client sleeps lightly and is disturbed mainly by hallway conversation. Which agreed intervention targets that cause?
options: Move the bedtime two hours earlier
Encourage a large evening meal
Increase daytime bed rest
Reduce nearby noise and offer acceptable sound protection
why: Earlier sleep does not remove hallway noise.
Meal size does not address the acoustic trigger.
Additional bed rest may reduce night-time sleep drive.
This directly addresses the identified disturbance.
questions.takeaway: Select sleep interventions that match the identified disturbance.
questions.learningObjective: Select sleep interventions that match the identified disturbance.

questions.title: Night-time care scheduling
questions.stem: Which actions can support sleep for a stable client without compromising necessary monitoring? Select all that apply.
options: Omit ordered observations without review
Complete every nonurgent task whenever staff are free
Coordinate compatible nonurgent care tasks
Review whether routine tasks can occur before bedtime
why: Necessary monitoring cannot be removed solely for convenience.
Uncoordinated timing creates unnecessary interruptions.
Clustering reduces avoidable awakenings.
Individual scheduling protects the sleep period.
questions.takeaway: Coordinate routine care around sleep while preserving required monitoring.
questions.learningObjective: Coordinate routine care around sleep while preserving required monitoring.

questions.title: Caffeine and sleep
questions.stem: A client has difficulty falling asleep after several late-evening coffees. Which trial is most reasonable?
options: Take an additional nap before bedtime
Move caffeine earlier and monitor sleep
Replace coffee with caffeinated cola
Stay in bed longer each morning immediately
why: A late nap can reduce sleep pressure.
Timing targets a plausible stimulant-related contributor.
The stimulant exposure remains.
Later rising may perpetuate difficulty falling asleep.
questions.takeaway: Assess stimulant timing when planning sleep improvement.
questions.learningObjective: Assess stimulant timing when planning sleep improvement.

questions.title: CPAP comfort
questions.stem: A client prescribed CPAP removes the mask because it leaves painful marks. What should the nurse do?
options: Assess fit and arrange appropriate adjustment
Tighten straps to stop all mask movement
Accept stopping therapy without discussing alternatives
Place thick unapproved padding under the seal
why: A better interface may preserve therapy and comfort.
Excess pressure may worsen the painful marks.
Untreated symptoms may return despite a correctable fit problem.
This can alter fit and effective pressure delivery.
questions.takeaway: Address interface discomfort to support prescribed sleep therapy.
questions.learningObjective: Address interface discomfort to support prescribed sleep therapy.

questions.title: Palliative positioning choice
questions.stem: A dying client becomes distressed with large turns but tolerates small shifts. Which plan best balances comfort and skin care?
options: Continue large turns on a rigid schedule
Stop all skin assessment because death is near
Use analgesia solely to enforce the same turn size
Agree on tolerated small changes and reassess
why: A fixed routine may impose disproportionate distress.
Skin discomfort can still be identified and relieved.
Medication should support agreed comfort goals, not a rigid routine.
Comfort goals and tissue tolerance should guide individual positioning.
questions.takeaway: Individualize repositioning to comfort and goals at end of life.
questions.learningObjective: Individualize repositioning to comfort and goals at end of life.

questions.title: Family food concerns
questions.stem: A dying client has little desire to eat, and family worry they are causing suffering. What should the nurse explain?
options: Promise artificial feeding always improves comfort
Avoid discussing eating until the family stops asking
Offer desired intake as tolerated and discuss comfort goals
Require fixed portions to demonstrate good care
why: Benefits and burdens depend on the individual situation.
Questions signal a need for sensitive explanation.
Reduced intake may accompany dying; comfort guides support.
Pressure to eat may increase distress.
questions.takeaway: Discuss intake in relation to the dying client's comfort and wishes.
questions.learningObjective: Discuss intake in relation to the dying client's comfort and wishes.

questions.title: Breathlessness positioning
questions.stem: A client with stable chronic breathlessness prefers sitting forward with arms supported. What should the nurse do?
options: Focus only on the saturation number
Support the position and reassess comfort
Require lying flat to save energy
Remove arm support to strengthen muscles
why: Subjective distress matters even when saturation is unchanged.
An individually helpful supported posture can reduce effort.
Supine posture may worsen the client's breathing discomfort.
Unsupported effort may increase breathlessness during rest.
questions.takeaway: Support positions that relieve breathlessness and evaluate the response.
questions.learningObjective: Support positions that relieve breathlessness and evaluate the response.

questions.title: Comfort measure evaluation
questions.stem: A client trialling music for procedural anxiety says pain is unchanged but they feel less tense. What is the best interpretation?
options: The intervention improved one agreed symptom
The strategy failed because pain was unchanged
Music should replace all analgesia now
The client must be reporting inconsistent information
why: A reduced tension response is a meaningful separate outcome.
Comfort includes more than pain intensity alone.
Reduced tension does not establish adequate pain relief.
Pain and tension can change independently.
questions.takeaway: Evaluate each symptom targeted by a comfort intervention.
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate each symptom targeted by a comfort intervention.

questions.title: Fatigue priorities
questions.stem: A client with chronic illness has energy for one morning activity and values attending a family video call. What should guide planning?
options: Complete all hygiene first regardless of tolerance
Cancel the call to preserve energy for staff routines
Encourage doing every task at once
Prioritize the meaningful activity with rest around it
why: Routine task order may exhaust capacity for the valued activity.
This subordinates the client's goal to convenience.
Unpaced activity can exceed the known energy limit.
Energy conservation should support the client's own priorities.
questions.takeaway: Allocate limited energy around the client's meaningful priorities.
questions.learningObjective: Allocate limited energy around the client's meaningful priorities.

questions.title: Unexpected cuff reading
questions.stem: A comfortable client has a new high automated blood pressure. The cuff barely closes around a large upper arm. What should happen first?
options: Request extra antihypertensive medication immediately
Repeat on the same arm with the same cuff
Compare with a reading taken last month only
Repeat using the correct cuff size
why: Treatment should not rely on a visibly unsuitable measurement setup.
Repetition preserves the identified source of error.
Historical values cannot validate today's technique.
An undersized cuff can overestimate pressure.
questions.takeaway: Correct an identified measurement problem before interpreting an isolated result.
questions.learningObjective: Correct an identified measurement problem before interpreting an isolated result.

questions.title: Irregular pulse count
questions.stem: A client reports intermittent palpitations. The radial pulse is irregular during a short count. Which assessment is most useful next?
options: Repeat only after the next scheduled round
Use skin temperature to estimate cardiac rate
Count the apical pulse for a full minute
Multiply a ten-second count by six
why: Symptoms and a new irregularity need timely assessment.
Temperature does not quantify the rhythm abnormality.
A full assessment better characterizes an irregular rhythm.
A brief sample may misrepresent an irregular rate.
questions.takeaway: Use a full-minute assessment for an irregular pulse.
questions.learningObjective: Use a full-minute assessment for an irregular pulse.

questions.title: Respiratory sampling
questions.stem: A postoperative client has shallow irregular breaths after analgesia. Which observation is most useful for detecting deterioration?
options: Whether the client denies pain
Rate, depth, and alertness together
A fifteen-second count alone
Oxygen saturation without examining the client
why: Pain relief does not establish respiratory safety.
Ventilation adequacy involves more than respiratory frequency.
A short count may miss irregularity and reduced depth.
Supplemental oxygen may mask inadequate ventilation.
questions.takeaway: Assess respiratory depth and consciousness alongside rate.
questions.learningObjective: Assess respiratory depth and consciousness alongside rate.

questions.title: Capillary glucose contamination
questions.stem: A well client has an unexpectedly high finger-stick result after peeling an orange. What is the best first response?
options: Wash and dry the hands, then repeat
Administer correction insulin from the unconfirmed result
Wipe only with a dry tissue and repeat
Document the result as the new baseline
why: Sugar residue can falsely elevate a capillary reading.
Treatment could be inappropriate if the sample was contaminated.
A dry wipe may leave surface sugar residue.
A potentially contaminated result requires verification.
questions.takeaway: Use clean dry hands for reliable capillary glucose testing.
questions.learningObjective: Use clean dry hands for reliable capillary glucose testing.

questions.title: Weight trend technique
questions.stem: A client's weight appears to rise sharply, but today's measurement used a different scale and heavy clothing. Which action improves interpretation?
options: Average both measurements immediately
Assume fluid overload without assessment
Disregard all weight measurements this admission
Repeat under comparable measurement conditions
why: Averaging does not correct incompatible conditions.
Measurement differences may explain some of the apparent change.
A repeat standardized measurement can still be useful.
Standardization helps distinguish real change from measurement variation.
questions.takeaway: Use consistent conditions when interpreting weight trends.
questions.learningObjective: Use consistent conditions when interpreting weight trends.

questions.title: Urine trend verification
questions.stem: A stable postoperative client's chart shows no urine for six hours, but a family member reports two toilet visits. What should the nurse do?
options: Give a fluid bolus independently
Enter estimated volumes from memory
Clarify and assess the missing output
Report confirmed anuria from the chart
why: An incomplete record does not authorize unprescribed treatment.
Unmeasured voids should not be documented as measured amounts.
Incomplete recording may mimic reduced renal output.
The chart conflicts with reported voiding and needs verification.
questions.takeaway: Verify missing output without inventing volumes.
questions.learningObjective: Verify missing output without inventing volumes.

questions.title: Platelet result context
questions.stem: A client awaiting an invasive procedure has platelets 48 × 10⁹/L; the laboratory range is 150–400. What should the nurse prioritize?
options: Proceed because haemoglobin is normal
Notify the procedural team before proceeding
Record it for routine discharge teaching
Repeat routine vital signs as the sole response
why: Haemoglobin does not measure platelet-mediated clotting.
Marked thrombocytopenia increases procedural bleeding risk.
The result affects today's procedure safety.
Normal vital signs do not remove the bleeding risk.
questions.takeaway: Escalate abnormal platelets before an invasive procedure.
questions.learningObjective: Escalate abnormal platelets before an invasive procedure.

questions.title: Anaemia trend
questions.stem: A postoperative client's haemoglobin falls from 126 to 89 g/L with increasing dizziness on sitting. What should the nurse do?
options: Assess for bleeding and promptly escalate
Offer an iron-rich snack as the first response
Encourage walking to improve circulation
Wait for the next day's blood test
why: The symptomatic decline needs evaluation for blood loss.
Food does not address possible acute bleeding.
Dizziness increases fall risk and may reflect compromised perfusion.
Delay could miss ongoing blood loss.
questions.takeaway: Interpret haemoglobin changes together with symptoms and timing.
questions.learningObjective: Interpret haemoglobin changes together with symptoms and timing.

questions.title: Renal baseline
questions.stem: A dehydrated adult's creatinine rises from 70 to 145 µmol/L in two days. What information should accompany escalation? Select all that apply.
options: Recent medicines and contrast exposure
Only whether the result has a red flag
Only the client's usual bedtime
Recent urine output and fluid balance
why: Potential renal stressors guide further assessment.
The change from baseline matters beyond software flags.
Bedtime does not explain the renal trend.
These help characterize the acute renal change.
questions.takeaway: Communicate renal trends with output and relevant exposures.
questions.learningObjective: Communicate renal trends with output and relevant exposures.

questions.title: Sodium symptoms
questions.stem: A client has sodium 122 mmol/L (reference 135–145) and new confusion. What is the best response?
options: Provide salty food as definitive treatment
Recheck orientation at the end of shift
Promptly assess neurological status and escalate
Encourage large amounts of plain water
why: Diet alone is not adequate management of symptomatic hyponatraemia.
Delayed reassessment misses potential neurological deterioration.
Neurological change with marked hyponatraemia needs urgent review.
Additional free water may worsen the imbalance.
questions.takeaway: Pair electrolyte results with neurological findings when setting urgency.
questions.learningObjective: Pair electrolyte results with neurological findings when setting urgency.

questions.title: Sample haemolysis
questions.stem: A stable client has an elevated potassium result labelled significantly haemolysed. Which action is most appropriate?
options: Repeat next week if symptoms appear
Assess and urgently arrange verification with the team
File it as normal without follow-up
Treat the value as definitive without noting haemolysis
why: Clinically important potassium changes may be asymptomatic.
Haemolysis may distort potassium, but true elevation must be excluded.
A distorted sample cannot establish a normal potassium.
Sample quality may alter treatment decisions.
questions.takeaway: Investigate unreliable critical results promptly rather than dismissing them.
questions.learningObjective: Investigate unreliable critical results promptly rather than dismissing them.

questions.title: Inflammatory marker limits
questions.stem: A client's white-cell count is mildly elevated after surgery, but they are afebrile and stable. What is the best interpretation?
options: Assess the trend and other clinical findings
Diagnose wound infection immediately
Conclude infection is impossible without fever
Request antibiotics solely from the count
why: A white-cell rise alone does not establish infection.
The isolated result lacks local or systemic infection evidence.
Afebrile clients can still develop infection.
Treatment requires clinical evaluation of a likely cause.
questions.takeaway: Interpret laboratory abnormalities within the clinical picture.
questions.learningObjective: Interpret laboratory abnormalities within the clinical picture.

questions.title: Anticoagulation test relevance
questions.stem: A client taking warfarin has a prescribed INR target documented in the plan. Which information is most useful when a new INR arrives?
options: Compare only with the laboratory's healthy-person range
Assume every elevated INR indicates active haemorrhage
Judge effectiveness from pulse rate alone
Compare it with that target and bleeding findings
why: The intended therapeutic range differs from untreated values.
An elevated result indicates risk, not proof of bleeding.
Pulse does not measure warfarin's anticoagulant effect.
The individual target and symptoms guide escalation.
questions.takeaway: Interpret anticoagulation monitoring against the prescribed therapeutic target.
questions.learningObjective: Interpret anticoagulation monitoring against the prescribed therapeutic target.

questions.title: Low potassium cues
questions.stem: A client on prolonged gastric suction has potassium 2.9 mmol/L (reference 3.5–5.0) and weakness. Which assessment deserves priority?
options: Detailed dietary recall from the previous week
Long-term dietary preferences before vital signs
Cardiac rate and rhythm with escalation
Repeat assessment of bowel motility
why: Intake contributes to cause assessment but is secondary to immediate cardiac risk.
Diet history matters later than immediate assessment.
Potassium depletion can disturb cardiac conduction.
Ileus can accompany depletion, but cardiac conduction effects take priority.
questions.takeaway: Consider cardiac complications when potassium is low.
questions.learningObjective: Consider cardiac complications when potassium is low.

questions.title: Albumin interpretation
questions.stem: A client with inflammation and oedema has low albumin. Which statement is most appropriate?
options: Double dietary protein without team assessment
Use a broader nutrition assessment
Diagnose poor protein intake from albumin alone
Assume normal nutrition because oedema increases weight
why: Nutrition changes should reflect the whole clinical picture.
Albumin is affected by inflammation and fluid status.
The result has important non-nutritional influences.
Fluid weight can hide loss of body tissue.
questions.takeaway: Do not use albumin alone to diagnose malnutrition.
questions.learningObjective: Do not use albumin alone to diagnose malnutrition.

questions.title: Urine culture contamination
questions.stem: A client's urine culture reports mixed flora after collection from an unclean bedpan. The client is stable. What should the nurse do?
options: Discuss recollection using the ordered clean method
Assume several simultaneous infections
Start isolation based on the report alone
Discard symptoms because the sample is poor
why: Contamination limits interpretation of the original sample.
Mixed organisms can reflect collection contamination.
A contaminated culture does not identify a transmission diagnosis.
Symptoms still require assessment despite an unreliable specimen.
questions.takeaway: Link culture interpretation to specimen quality.
questions.learningObjective: Link culture interpretation to specimen quality.

questions.title: Twenty-four-hour collection
questions.stem: A client misses one void during a timed 24-hour urine collection. What should the nurse do?
options: Estimate the missed volume and add water
Extend collection by an arbitrary hour
Send the collection without noting the omission
Notify the laboratory and follow restart instructions
why: Estimated replacement cannot restore the missing analyte content.
An extra hour does not reliably replace the missed sample.
The laboratory needs the limitation to interpret validity.
An incomplete timed sample may invalidate the result.
questions.takeaway: Report omissions in timed specimens rather than concealing them.
questions.learningObjective: Report omissions in timed specimens rather than concealing them.

questions.title: Midstream collection
questions.stem: An adult can independently collect a prescribed midstream urine specimen. Which instructions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Collect from urine already in the toilet
Pour the specimen through a used measuring jug
Begin voiding before collecting the sample
Avoid touching the inside of the container
why: Toilet water contaminates the sample.
Another unclean container can contaminate the sample.
Midstream collection reduces contamination from initial urethral washout.
Contact can introduce organisms into the specimen.
questions.takeaway: Preserve clean collection technique for a midstream specimen.
questions.learningObjective: Preserve clean collection technique for a midstream specimen.

questions.title: Sputum quality
questions.stem: A client submits thin clear saliva for a sputum culture. What should the nurse do?
options: Collect immediately after mouthwash without checking instructions
Coach a deep cough and recollect as ordered
Send it as adequate because volume is sufficient
Add water to reach the laboratory fill line
why: Some collection preparations may affect specimen quality.
A lower-respiratory sample is needed for the requested test.
Volume does not establish respiratory specimen quality.
Dilution does not create sputum and may invalidate testing.
questions.takeaway: Assess whether a sample represents the site being tested.
questions.learningObjective: Assess whether a sample represents the site being tested.

questions.title: Occult-blood instructions
questions.stem: A client has a home stool test kit, but its instructions differ from a previous kit. What should the nurse advise?
options: Follow the current kit's specific instructions
Apply every restriction from the old kit
Collect during visible rectal bleeding without checking guidance
Use the same specimen container from last year
why: Collection and dietary requirements vary by test method.
Unneeded restrictions can confuse or impair completion.
Active bleeding may affect interpretation and requires appropriate advice.
Collection materials must match the current test.
questions.takeaway: Use instructions specific to the test being performed.
questions.learningObjective: Use instructions specific to the test being performed.

questions.title: Blood culture timing
questions.stem: Blood cultures and antibiotics are newly ordered for a deteriorating client. Collection can occur promptly. What should the nurse coordinate?
options: Wait for the next fever peak
Give several antibiotic doses before collecting
Cancel cultures if the temperature falls
Collect cultures before antibiotics without delaying urgent care
why: Waiting can delay needed antimicrobial treatment.
Prior treatment may reduce organism recovery.
Temporary temperature change does not remove the order's purpose.
Pre-treatment sampling improves yield while preserving timely treatment.
questions.takeaway: Coordinate cultures and treatment without unnecessary delay.
questions.learningObjective: Coordinate cultures and treatment without unnecessary delay.

questions.title: Unexpected laboratory identity
questions.stem: A laboratory result lists the correct name but a different date of birth from the client. What should happen before using it?
options: Copy it into the chart and clarify later
Ask the client whether the value seems familiar
Resolve the identification discrepancy
Accept it because names match
why: Incorrect attribution can trigger unsafe decisions.
Client familiarity cannot verify specimen identity.
Treatment requires confirmation that the result belongs to this client.
Names alone do not reliably establish identity.
questions.takeaway: Resolve mismatched identifiers before acting on a laboratory result.
questions.learningObjective: Resolve mismatched identifiers before acting on a laboratory result.

questions.title: Test result follow-through
questions.stem: A client is discharged with an important test still pending. Which actions reduce follow-up risk? Select all that apply.
options: Rely on the client remembering to mention it next year
Confirm who will review and communicate it
Give the client a clear follow-up contact
Assume no telephone call means a normal result
why: Delayed informal follow-up may miss time-sensitive findings.
Named responsibility prevents results being overlooked.
The client needs a route if no result arrives.
Silence does not establish that the result was reviewed.
questions.takeaway: Assign responsibility and a clear contact for pending results.
questions.learningObjective: Assign responsibility and a clear contact for pending results.

questions.title: Specimen transport delay
questions.stem: A freshly collected urine specimen remains unrefrigerated because transport is delayed. What should the nurse do?
options: Check laboratory time and storage requirements
Send it later without noting the delay
Freeze it without laboratory guidance
Transfer it to a larger container
why: Delay can alter results and may require recollection.
Unreported delay prevents assessment of specimen suitability.
Unapproved storage can damage specimen integrity.
Container size does not correct elapsed storage time.
questions.takeaway: Follow test-specific storage requirements when transport is delayed.
questions.learningObjective: Follow test-specific storage requirements when transport is delayed.

questions.title: Laboratory trend communication
questions.stem: Which details belong when reporting a clinically important change in a laboratory result? Select all that apply.
options: Current symptoms and relevant treatment
Only that the computer highlighted the number
The entire unrelated admission history
Previous value and collection times
why: Clinical context helps establish urgency and likely causes.
A flag alone omits essential clinical information.
Unfocused detail can obscure the actionable change.
The magnitude and speed of change influence interpretation.
questions.takeaway: Communicate the result, trend, and current clinical context.
questions.learningObjective: Communicate the result, trend, and current clinical context.

questions.title: Bowel preparation difficulty
questions.stem: A client preparing for colonoscopy vomits repeatedly and cannot finish the prescribed preparation. What should the nurse advise?
options: Skip the remainder without informing the team
Use an over-the-counter substitute independently
Contact the procedural team for an individualized plan
Continue the same volume rapidly
why: The bowel may be inadequately prepared for visualization.
Different preparations have different risks and instructions.
Incomplete preparation and vomiting may require revised instructions.
Faster intake may worsen vomiting and intolerance.
questions.takeaway: Report inability to complete bowel preparation before the procedure.
questions.learningObjective: Report inability to complete bowel preparation before the procedure.

questions.title: After colonoscopy
questions.stem: Several hours after colonoscopy, a client develops worsening abdominal pain and fever. Which action is most appropriate?
options: Wait until the scheduled follow-up visit
Arrange urgent clinical assessment
Encourage walking for presumed retained gas only
Offer food before assessing the abdomen
why: A delayed visit is inappropriate for evolving warning signs.
These findings can indicate a significant procedural complication.
Fever with worsening pain is not routine gas discomfort.
Food does not address possible perforation or other complications.
questions.takeaway: Escalate fever and worsening pain after colonoscopy.
questions.learningObjective: Escalate fever and worsening pain after colonoscopy.

questions.title: Sedated discharge
questions.stem: A client feels alert after procedural sedation and plans to drive home. What should the nurse do?
options: Follow discharge restrictions and confirm safe transport
Allow driving after a short hallway walk
Offer coffee to reverse sedation
Use the client's normal blood pressure as clearance
why: Subjective alertness does not establish restored driving ability.
Walking does not test all effects relevant to driving.
Caffeine does not reliably reverse psychomotor impairment.
Blood pressure does not establish safe reaction time.
questions.takeaway: Apply post-sedation transport instructions despite perceived alertness.
questions.learningObjective: Apply post-sedation transport instructions despite perceived alertness.

questions.title: Upper endoscopy intake
questions.stem: A client returns after throat anaesthetic for upper endoscopy and requests tea. What determines readiness for oral intake?
options: The client's report of thirst alone
Absence of abdominal pain
Completion of the written discharge form
Recovery criteria and swallowing safety per protocol
why: Thirst does not establish recovery of safe swallowing.
Abdominal comfort does not assess pharyngeal sensation.
Administrative completion does not establish physiological readiness.
Pharyngeal anaesthesia can temporarily impair airway protection.
questions.takeaway: Confirm swallowing safety before intake after throat anaesthesia.
questions.learningObjective: Confirm swallowing safety before intake after throat anaesthesia.

questions.title: Endoscopy warning signs
questions.stem: Which post-upper-endoscopy findings require prompt reporting? Select all that apply.
options: Mild temporary throat irritation without other symptoms
Brief bloating that steadily improves
New breathing difficulty
Severe persistent chest or abdominal pain
why: Minor irritation can occur after instrumentation.
Improving transient bloating is less concerning than severe symptoms.
This may indicate an airway or procedural complication.
Severe pain can signal a significant complication.
questions.takeaway: Teach specific warning signs after endoscopy.
questions.learningObjective: Teach specific warning signs after endoscopy.

questions.title: Kidney biopsy bleeding
questions.stem: After kidney biopsy, a client has increasing flank pain, tachycardia, and falling blood pressure. What is the priority?
options: Treat pain alone and reassess tomorrow
Urgently assess and escalate possible bleeding
Offer the next meal to improve strength
Encourage ambulation to relieve stiffness
why: Analgesia alone can delay recognition of deterioration.
The combined findings suggest clinically important haemorrhage.
Eating does not address possible circulatory compromise.
Activity is inappropriate during suspected bleeding.
questions.takeaway: Recognize bleeding through combined post-biopsy trends.
questions.learningObjective: Recognize bleeding through combined post-biopsy trends.

questions.title: Biopsy preparation medicines
questions.stem: Before an elective biopsy, a client mentions an anticoagulant omitted from the medication list. What should the nurse do?
options: Notify the procedural team before proceeding
Assume it is covered by routine fasting
Tell the client to stop it for a week independently
Add it to discharge paperwork only
why: Anticoagulant exposure changes bleeding-risk planning.
Fasting does not reverse anticoagulation.
