Interruption requires a clinician-directed balance of bleeding and clotting risk.
The information is needed before tissue sampling.
questions.takeaway: Reconcile bleeding-risk medicines before invasive testing.
questions.learningObjective: Reconcile bleeding-risk medicines before invasive testing.

questions.title: Cystoscopy aftercare
questions.stem: A client reports inability to urinate and increasing suprapubic discomfort after cystoscopy. What is appropriate?
options: Reassure that every voiding change is expected
Encourage several litres quickly before assessment
Wait until the next day for a urine sample
Promptly assess and contact the procedural team
why: Mild burning differs from painful inability to void.
Large intake can worsen discomfort with retention.
The current retention concern needs earlier evaluation.
Painful inability to void may indicate retention or obstruction.
questions.takeaway: Differentiate mild expected irritation from postprocedure retention.
questions.learningObjective: Differentiate mild expected irritation from postprocedure retention.

questions.title: ERCP complication cue
questions.stem: After ERCP, a client develops persistent severe upper abdominal pain with vomiting. Which response is best?
options: Offer a large meal to settle the stomach
Discharge because the procedure report was normal
Escalate for assessment of a complication
Attribute it solely to preprocedure fasting
why: Feeding does not address the acute warning signs.
A normal procedural report does not exclude later complications.
Pancreatitis and other complications require prompt evaluation.
Fasting does not explain severe persistent pain with vomiting.
questions.takeaway: Monitor for delayed complications after an apparently completed procedure.
questions.learningObjective: Monitor for delayed complications after an apparently completed procedure.

questions.title: Liver biopsy monitoring
questions.stem: A client returning from liver biopsy looks pale and reports new lightheadedness. Which assessments are most relevant? Select all that apply.
options: Only whether the client can eat
Vital signs and their change from baseline
Abdominal discomfort and evidence of bleeding
Only whether the dressing remains dry
why: Eating ability does not establish circulatory stability.
A trend can reveal impaired perfusion after biopsy.
These findings help assess a procedural bleeding complication.
A dry surface dressing does not exclude internal bleeding.
questions.takeaway: Assess for internal as well as visible bleeding after biopsy.
questions.learningObjective: Assess for internal as well as visible bleeding after biopsy.

questions.title: Contrast history
questions.stem: Before contrast-enhanced CT, a client describes wheezing and facial swelling during a previous contrast injection. What should the nurse do?
options: Alert radiology before contrast is given
Record a seafood allergy instead
Proceed because the previous reaction resolved
Ask the client to take a home antihistamine without orders
why: A previous significant reaction changes preparation and risk assessment.
The relevant history is the actual prior contrast reaction.
Resolution does not remove recurrence risk.
Premedication requires an appropriate directed plan.
questions.takeaway: Clarify actual contrast reactions before repeat exposure.
questions.learningObjective: Clarify actual contrast reactions before repeat exposure.

questions.title: Renal function before imaging
questions.stem: A client scheduled for contrast imaging has a newly reported acute decline in kidney function. What is the best action?
options: Assume last month's creatinine remains sufficient
Cancel all future imaging independently
Encourage unrestricted fluids despite a fluid limit
Communicate the change to the imaging team
why: An acute change makes the older result less relevant.
Risks and diagnostic benefits require team evaluation.
Hydration must respect the client's clinical restrictions.
Current renal status may alter imaging and hydration decisions.
questions.takeaway: Share new renal impairment before contrast decisions.
questions.learningObjective: Share new renal impairment before contrast decisions.

questions.title: MRI implant uncertainty
questions.stem: A client scheduled for MRI says they have an implanted device but cannot identify it. What should the nurse do?
options: Ask the client whether magnets usually bother them
Remove jewellery and proceed
Pause entry pending device verification by MRI staff
Assume all recent implants are compatible
why: Subjective experience cannot establish MRI safety.
External metal removal does not resolve implant uncertainty.
Device-specific compatibility must be confirmed before exposure.
Compatibility depends on the particular device and conditions.
questions.takeaway: Verify an implant's MRI conditions before entering the scanner area.
questions.learningObjective: Verify an implant's MRI conditions before entering the scanner area.

questions.title: MRI claustrophobia
questions.stem: A client with severe claustrophobia has an elective MRI tomorrow. Which plan best reduces an avoidable failed examination?
options: Promise the scan will be brief without checking
Notify the team early and plan support
Wait until the scan begins to discuss it
Tell the client to take someone else's sedative
why: Inaccurate reassurance can undermine informed preparation.
Preparation allows individualized strategies or ordered medication planning.
Late disclosure limits preparation options.
Unprescribed sedation creates avoidable risks.
questions.takeaway: Identify procedure tolerance barriers early enough to plan.
questions.learningObjective: Identify procedure tolerance barriers early enough to plan.

questions.title: Pregnancy and imaging
questions.stem: Before planned radiographic imaging, a client of childbearing potential says pregnancy is possible. What should the nurse do?
options: Follow screening policy and notify the imaging team
Assume absence of nausea excludes pregnancy
Cancel the examination permanently
Proceed without communicating because exposure is brief
why: Pregnancy status may affect imaging decisions and preparation.
Symptoms are not a reliable pregnancy screen.
Necessary imaging requires a risk-benefit decision rather than automatic cancellation.
The team needs relevant pregnancy information regardless of duration.
questions.takeaway: Communicate possible pregnancy before radiation-based procedures.
questions.learningObjective: Communicate possible pregnancy before radiation-based procedures.

questions.title: Procedural fasting ambiguity
questions.stem: A client's elective procedure instructions conflict with a new order allowing breakfast. What should the nurse do?
options: Choose whichever instruction is newest without checking
Apply a universal midnight-fast rule
Ask another client what they were told
Clarify with the procedural team before intake
why: The new order may not account for the planned procedure.
Fasting requirements vary by procedure and anaesthetic plan.
Another person's instructions do not resolve this order conflict.
Procedure-specific fasting requirements need a consistent plan.
questions.takeaway: Resolve conflicting preparation instructions before acting.
questions.learningObjective: Resolve conflicting preparation instructions before acting.

questions.title: Procedure communication needs
questions.stem: A client with hearing impairment will need to follow breathing instructions during a biopsy. Which preparation is most useful?
options: Repeat instructions more loudly from behind
Explain the instructions only after sedation
Agree on accessible cues before starting
Remove all communication aids without an alternative
why: Position and accessibility matter more than volume alone.
Sedation may reduce comprehension and recall.
Reliable communication supports cooperation during time-sensitive instructions.
This leaves the client unable to follow essential cues.
questions.takeaway: Plan accessible communication before a cooperative procedure.
questions.learningObjective: Plan accessible communication before a cooperative procedure.

questions.title: Postprocedure baseline
questions.stem: A client with long-standing unequal pupils is scheduled for a procedure requiring sedation. What should the nurse document beforehand?
options: Wait until recovery to record pupil findings
Current neurological findings and established baseline
Only a generic statement that the client is normal
Assume asymmetry means the procedure must be cancelled
why: A recovery-only assessment cannot establish the preprocedure baseline.
Baseline documentation helps distinguish later changes from chronic findings.
That omits the relevant existing asymmetry.
A chronic stable finding needs context rather than automatic cancellation.
questions.takeaway: Record relevant baseline abnormalities before procedures.
questions.learningObjective: Record relevant baseline abnormalities before procedures.

questions.title: Skin preparation reaction
questions.stem: A client awaiting a procedure reports a prior blistering reaction to the planned antiseptic. What is the best action?
options: Clarify the reaction and alert the procedural team
Use less of the same product without discussion
Apply a barrier cream under the antiseptic independently
Proceed if there is no current rash
why: An alternative preparation may be needed to avoid injury.
Dose reduction does not establish tolerance.
This may interfere with preparation and does not resolve allergy assessment.
A prior reaction remains relevant without an active rash.
questions.takeaway: Address preparation-product reactions before exposure.
questions.learningObjective: Address preparation-product reactions before exposure.

questions.title: Sedation reassessment
questions.stem: A client's discharge time has arrived, but they remain difficult to keep awake. What should the nurse do?
options: Discharge if a relative promises close observation
Offer food to force wakefulness
Document the usual recovery time as achieved
Continue monitoring and escalate unmet recovery criteria
why: Home supervision does not replace adequate immediate recovery.
Feeding a drowsy client can increase aspiration risk.
Documentation must reflect the client's actual condition.
A clock time does not establish readiness for discharge.
questions.takeaway: Use recovery criteria rather than elapsed time alone.
questions.learningObjective: Use recovery criteria rather than elapsed time alone.

questions.title: Bronchoscopy bleeding
questions.stem: A client has a small blood streak after bronchoscopy, then develops repeated bright-red expectoration and dyspnoea. What changed the priority?
options: The client's desire for a drink
The scheduled discharge approaching
Increasing bleeding with respiratory symptoms
The mere presence of any cough
why: Thirst is secondary to the respiratory change.
Schedule does not determine clinical urgency.
The new pattern suggests a complication needing urgent assessment.
Some coughing can occur after airway instrumentation.
questions.takeaway: Reassess when minor expected symptoms become progressive or systemic.
questions.learningObjective: Reassess when minor expected symptoms become progressive or systemic.

questions.title: Lumbar puncture headache
questions.stem: After lumbar puncture, a client develops a headache that is much worse upright and improves lying down. What should the nurse do?
options: Assume the pain score is unreliable
Assess and report the positional pattern
Diagnose migraine without further assessment
Encourage prolonged upright walking immediately
why: Position-dependent symptoms can be clinically meaningful.
The pattern helps identify a postprocedural headache and guide treatment.
The temporal and positional features require procedure-related evaluation.
Upright posture aggravates the reported symptoms.
questions.takeaway: Describe positional features when assessing postprocedure headache.
questions.learningObjective: Describe positional features when assessing postprocedure headache.

questions.title: Thoracentesis surveillance
questions.stem: Following thoracentesis, a client develops new pleuritic pain, dyspnoea, and reduced breath sounds on that side. What should the nurse do?
options: Activate urgent assessment for a respiratory complication
Encourage repeated forceful coughing first
Attribute symptoms to anxiety without examination
Offer a meal and repeat observations later
why: The findings may indicate pneumothorax or another complication.
This delays assessment of new respiratory compromise.
Unilateral findings require clinical investigation.
Nutrition is secondary to a new breathing problem.
questions.takeaway: Treat new unilateral respiratory findings after thoracentesis as significant.
questions.learningObjective: Treat new unilateral respiratory findings after thoracentesis as significant.

questions.title: Procedure teaching recall
questions.stem: A client cannot recall discharge warnings after receiving sedation. Which approach is most useful?
options: Repeat the same instructions faster
Rely on the signed discharge sheet
Ask the client to memorize every technical detail
Review written instructions with the support person and client
why: Speed may further reduce comprehension.
A signature does not demonstrate retained understanding.
Essential action instructions are more useful than exhaustive detail.
Sedation can impair recall, so accessible reinforcement matters.
questions.takeaway: Reinforce post-sedation teaching using accessible written and support-person guidance.
questions.learningObjective: Reinforce post-sedation teaching using accessible written and support-person guidance.

questions.title: Procedure handover content
questions.stem: Which information is especially relevant when receiving a client after an invasive procedure? Select all that apply.
options: Only that the procedure was completed
The next routine meal choice alone
Procedure-specific restrictions and monitoring orders
Sedation given and the last observations
why: Completion alone omits current recovery needs.
Meal preference does not communicate procedural risk.
These direct safe immediate recovery care.
These establish exposure and recovery trends.
questions.takeaway: Receive an actionable recovery handover after invasive procedures.
questions.learningObjective: Receive an actionable recovery handover after invasive procedures.

questions.title: Drain output stops
questions.stem: A closed wound drain stops collecting fluid while swelling develops near the incision. What should the nurse do first?
options: Record zero output as improvement
Assess the tubing and operative area promptly
Remove the drain because output has ceased
Increase compression without examining the site
why: The new swelling contradicts uncomplicated improvement.
Obstruction may prevent drainage and allow fluid accumulation.
Cessation with swelling does not establish readiness for removal.
External pressure does not identify the drainage problem.
questions.takeaway: Interpret drain output together with the wound and tubing assessment.
questions.learningObjective: Interpret drain output together with the wound and tubing assessment.

questions.title: Drain suction seal
questions.stem: A prescribed bulb-suction drain repeatedly expands immediately after compression. Which action is most appropriate?
options: Check closure and connections using the device instructions
Measure output only at the usual time
Apply wall suction without a new plan
Replace the dressing without checking the system
why: Loss of seal can prevent the intended suction.
Measurement alone does not correct lost suction.
The device may not be designed for that pressure.
An intact dressing does not ensure a functioning suction circuit.
questions.takeaway: Investigate failure of a closed drain to maintain prescribed suction.
questions.learningObjective: Investigate failure of a closed drain to maintain prescribed suction.

questions.title: Separate drains
questions.stem: A client has two surgical drains with different amounts and colours of output. How should the nurse document drainage?
options: Combine output under one undocumented label
Record only the drain with more output
Estimate both from the larger container
Measure and describe each drain separately
why: Combining obscures clinically useful differences.
The smaller drain may still show an important change.
Estimated substitution misrepresents measured drainage.
Site-specific trends can identify which area has changed.
questions.takeaway: Track each drainage source separately.
questions.learningObjective: Track each drainage source separately.

questions.title: Wound-edge separation
questions.stem: During removal of ordered sutures, a wound edge begins to separate. What should the nurse do?
options: Apply lotion and resume removal
Document the gap only after finishing
Stop and obtain wound assessment
Continue removing the remaining sutures
why: Lotion does not restore wound support.
Delayed recognition may increase the defect.
New separation requires reassessment before further removal.
Further removal may worsen the opening.
questions.takeaway: Stop suture removal if wound edges separate.
questions.learningObjective: Stop suture removal if wound edges separate.

questions.title: Hidden dressing loss
questions.stem: A postoperative client lies on a damp blood-stained sheet despite a small stain on the visible dressing. What should the nurse prioritize?
options: Use the small visible stain to estimate total loss
Assess the full wound area and circulation
Reinforce the visible stain alone
Change the linen before assessment
why: Visible dressing area may underestimate hidden drainage.
Dependent drainage may hide a larger blood loss.
This misses blood that has tracked beneath the client.
Comfort care should not delay evaluation of possible bleeding.
questions.takeaway: Look for concealed bleeding when surface findings do not fit.
questions.learningObjective: Look for concealed bleeding when surface findings do not fit.

questions.title: Gastric suction replacement
questions.stem: A client with gastric suction has increasing thirst, dry mucosa, and rising pulse. Which information is most useful to report?
options: Suction losses and prescribed fluid replacement received
The frequency of mouth care provided
Only whether the suction sounds active
Only the last meal before admission
why: Unreplaced losses may contribute to volume depletion.
Mouth care affects comfort but does not quantify losses contributing to volume depletion.
Sound does not establish the volume removed.
Remote intake is less useful than current measured losses.
questions.takeaway: Compare gastrointestinal losses with replacement and clinical response.
questions.learningObjective: Compare gastrointestinal losses with replacement and clinical response.

questions.title: Tube drainage change
questions.stem: A gastric decompression tube has no output, and abdominal distension increases. What should the nurse do?
options: Clamp it because no output suggests recovery
Begin feeding through the same tube
Increase suction beyond the prescribed setting
Assess position indicators and tubing patency per policy
why: Increasing distension argues against assuming recovery.
The new symptoms require assessment before changing use.
More pressure may injure tissue and does not verify position.
A displaced or obstructed tube may stop effective decompression.
questions.takeaway: Investigate loss of decompression when symptoms worsen.
questions.learningObjective: Investigate loss of decompression when symptoms worsen.

questions.title: Urinary catheter obstruction
questions.stem: A catheterized client develops bladder discomfort and no urine drainage. Tubing is kinked under the thigh. What should the nurse do first?
options: Request increased analgesia as the sole response
Replace the catheter before correcting tubing
Relieve the kink and reassess drainage
Obtain a urine culture before checking drainage
why: Pain relief does not restore urine flow.
Replacement is unnecessary before addressing the visible kink.
A visible mechanical obstruction is immediately correctable.
Culture does not relieve the identified obstruction.
questions.takeaway: Correct visible drainage obstruction and reassess its effect.
questions.learningObjective: Correct visible drainage obstruction and reassess its effect.

questions.title: Post-removal voiding
questions.stem: After catheter removal, a client reports frequent small voids and lower abdominal fullness. Which assessment is most useful?
options: Fluid restriction before assessment
Post-void bladder assessment per protocol
Urine colour alone
A count of toilet visits alone
why: Restriction does not identify or resolve retention.
Small voids can coexist with substantial retained urine.
Colour does not measure bladder emptying.
Frequency does not reveal retained volume.
questions.takeaway: Assess emptying when small frequent voids accompany fullness.
questions.learningObjective: Assess emptying when small frequent voids accompany fullness.

questions.title: Bladder irrigation balance
questions.stem: An ordered bladder irrigation infuses 1200 mL. The drainage bag contains 1650 mL. What urine output should be documented, assuming no other fluid inputs? Use mL.
options: 450 mL
why: Subtracting irrigant from total drainage gives 450 mL.
This includes the 1200 mL of irrigation fluid.
This is the irrigation input, not urine produced.
Adding input to drainage double-counts irrigation.
questions.takeaway: Subtract irrigation input from total drainage to estimate urine output.
questions.learningObjective: Subtract irrigation input from total drainage to estimate urine output.

questions.title: Irrigation obstruction cue
questions.stem: During prescribed bladder irrigation, drainage slows and the client reports suprapubic pressure. What is the priority?
options: Increase inflow before assessing outflow
Document low urine production from bag volume alone
Wait until the scheduled bag change
Assess outflow and follow the obstruction protocol
why: More inflow can worsen distension if drainage is blocked.
Irrigation and possible obstruction confound the measurement.
The symptomatic change needs immediate attention.
Continued inflow against obstruction can distend the bladder.
questions.takeaway: Check drainage promptly when bladder irrigation causes pressure.
questions.learningObjective: Check drainage promptly when bladder irrigation causes pressure.

questions.title: Chest drain positioning
questions.stem: A client with a chest drain is transferred to a chair. Which observations require correction? Select all that apply.
options: The unit is secured upright
Connections remain secured as prescribed
The collection unit lies above chest level
Tubing is compressed beneath the chair leg
why: Upright positioning supports correct system operation.
Secure connections help preserve system integrity.
Elevation can interfere with the intended drainage system.
Compression can obstruct drainage from the pleural space.
questions.takeaway: Maintain unobstructed dependent chest drainage during movement.
questions.learningObjective: Maintain unobstructed dependent chest drainage during movement.

questions.title: Chest drain bubbling
questions.stem: A water-seal chamber develops continuous bubbling that was previously intermittent. The client is stable. What should the nurse do?
options: Increase suction beyond the order
Assess the client and check connections per protocol
Clamp the tube and leave it clamped
Ignore it because all bubbling is expected
why: Changing pressure does not identify the leak source.
A new continuous air leak pattern needs investigation.
Prolonged unplanned clamping can trap pleural air.
Continuous new bubbling differs from some expected intermittent activity.
questions.takeaway: Investigate a changed chest-drain air-leak pattern.
questions.learningObjective: Investigate a changed chest-drain air-leak pattern.

questions.title: Chest drain sudden cessation
questions.stem: A client with a chest drain becomes more breathless as previously active drainage suddenly stops. What should guide the response?
options: Urgent client and system assessment
Assume the lung has fully re-expanded
Empty the collection unit by disconnecting it
Wait for the daily radiograph
why: Symptoms make obstruction or another complication concerning.
Stopped drainage alone does not establish recovery during worsening symptoms.
Unplanned disconnection can compromise the system.
Acute respiratory change cannot await routine imaging.
questions.takeaway: Interpret drainage cessation in the context of the client's condition.
questions.learningObjective: Interpret drainage cessation in the context of the client's condition.

questions.title: Compression device use
questions.stem: A postoperative client has prescribed intermittent pneumatic compression while in bed. Which observations support effective implementation? Select all that apply.
options: The device cycles while prescribed therapy is needed
Sleeves remain rolled down at the ankles
The machine is off for every sleeping period
Sleeves fit according to device instructions
why: A disconnected machine does not provide prophylactic compression.
Bunched sleeves do not provide intended compression.
Unordered long interruptions reduce prescribed prophylaxis.
Correct fit supports intended compression without excessive pressure.
questions.takeaway: Check fit and actual operation of prescribed compression devices.
questions.learningObjective: Check fit and actual operation of prescribed compression devices.

questions.title: New calf finding
questions.stem: A postoperative client reports unilateral calf swelling and tenderness. What is the best action?
options: Increase exercise intensity to reduce swelling
Apply the other client's compression stocking
Assess and promptly notify the clinical team
Massage the calf before walking
why: New symptoms require assessment before progression.
Compression selection requires an appropriate assessed plan.
New unilateral findings may indicate venous thrombosis.
Massage is inappropriate when thrombosis is suspected.
questions.takeaway: Evaluate new unilateral leg symptoms before routine activity.
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate new unilateral leg symptoms before routine activity.

questions.title: Incision splinting
questions.stem: A client avoids coughing after abdominal surgery because of incisional pulling. Which intervention best supports pulmonary hygiene?
options: Delay breathing exercises until stitches are removed
Teach gentle incision support during prescribed coughing
Encourage only shallow breaths until healing
Replace all coughing with throat clearing
why: Necessary respiratory prevention should not wait for complete healing.
Support can reduce discomfort and permit effective clearance.
Shallow breathing can promote retained secretions and atelectasis.
Throat clearing may not mobilize lower-airway secretions.
questions.takeaway: Support the incision to enable prescribed coughing and deep breathing.
questions.learningObjective: Support the incision to enable prescribed coughing and deep breathing.

questions.title: Incentive device technique
questions.stem: A client using an ordered incentive spirometer exhales forcefully into it. Which instruction is correct?
options: Inhale slowly through the mouthpiece as taught
Exhale faster to raise the marker
Keep taking short rapid breaths
Use it only when saturation falls
why: The device encourages sustained inspiratory expansion.
Forceful exhalation does not perform the intended exercise.
Rapid shallow breaths do not achieve sustained expansion.
Prescribed prevention should not depend solely on desaturation.
questions.takeaway: Verify inspiratory technique when evaluating incentive spirometry use.
questions.learningObjective: Verify inspiratory technique when evaluating incentive spirometry use.

questions.title: Postoperative delirium prevention
questions.stem: A high-risk older adult is alert after surgery but has misplaced hearing aids and glasses. Which actions reduce preventable disorientation? Select all that apply.
options: Provide orientation and preserve sleep where feasible
Change rooms repeatedly for convenience
Keep the room continuously dark during daytime
Restore accessible sensory aids
why: Predictable cues and rest support cognitive function.
Frequent environmental change can increase confusion.
Daytime cues help preserve the sleep-wake cycle.
Hearing and vision support environmental interpretation.
questions.takeaway: Support orientation, sensory access, and sleep in at-risk clients.
questions.learningObjective: Support orientation, sensory access, and sleep in at-risk clients.

questions.title: Pressure under oxygen tubing
questions.stem: A client using continuous nasal oxygen has new tenderness behind one ear. What should the nurse do?
options: Tighten tubing to reduce movement
Apply tape over the painful spot without inspection
Inspect and relieve device pressure while maintaining therapy
Stop prescribed oxygen for the entire shift
why: More tension may worsen local pressure.
Concealment can delay recognition of skin injury.
Local pressure can injure skin beneath tubing.
Therapy should continue with an appropriate protective adjustment.
questions.takeaway: Assess and offload device pressure without losing necessary treatment.
questions.learningObjective: Assess and offload device pressure without losing necessary treatment.

questions.title: Wound trajectory
questions.stem: A wound has decreasing dimensions and healthy granulation, with unchanged mild serous drainage. Which interpretation is most appropriate?
options: Stop all care immediately
The trend is consistent with progress
Unchanged drainage proves treatment failure
Granulation means infection is present
why: Improvement still requires the prescribed ongoing plan.
Size reduction and granulation support healing assessment.
Drainage alone does not override the improving wound dimensions.
Healthy granulation is part of tissue repair.
questions.takeaway: Evaluate wound healing using multiple consistent measurements.
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate wound healing using multiple consistent measurements.

questions.title: Drain removal teaching
questions.stem: A client is going home with a prescribed wound drain. Which demonstrations are most useful before discharge? Select all that apply.
options: Measures and records drain-specific output
Shows how to secure tubing during movement
Knows only the original surgical date
Plans to wait for severe pain before checking the site
why: Home trends inform follow-up and removal decisions.
Securement reduces accidental traction at the site.
The date does not demonstrate daily drain-management ability.
Earlier assessment is needed for changes in function or skin.
questions.takeaway: Use return demonstration for home drainage care.
questions.learningObjective: Use return demonstration for home drainage care.

questions.title: Postoperative oral intake
questions.stem: After abdominal surgery, a client prescribed diet advancement develops repeated vomiting and increasing distension. What should the nurse do?
options: Continue the next diet stage on schedule
Offer more fibre immediately
Record nausea without changing the plan
Pause advancement and assess with the team
why: A schedule does not override new intolerance.
Fibre does not address possible postoperative ileus or obstruction.
Repeated vomiting and distension require active review.
New intolerance may indicate impaired gastrointestinal function.
questions.takeaway: Reassess diet progression when postoperative intolerance develops.
questions.learningObjective: Reassess diet progression when postoperative intolerance develops.

questions.title: Neuromuscular baseline
questions.stem: Before applying a prescribed splint, which findings are most useful to document for later comparison? Select all that apply.
options: Only the splint brand
Only the client's dominant hand
Distal movement and sensation
Distal colour, temperature, and circulation findings
why: Brand does not establish the limb's clinical baseline.
Dominance does not measure current neurovascular status.
These establish neurological function before immobilization.
These establish perfusion for comparison after application.
questions.takeaway: Record distal neurovascular findings before immobilization.
questions.learningObjective: Record distal neurovascular findings before immobilization.

questions.title: Cast education evaluation
questions.stem: A client with a new cast says itching makes them want to insert a pen beneath it. Which response is most appropriate?
options: Ignore itching until cast removal
Discuss safe itch relief and assess persistent irritation
Suggest a narrower object
Recommend lotion poured inside
why: Persistent discomfort may indicate a pressure or skin problem.
Objects can injure concealed skin beneath the cast.
Smaller objects can still damage skin and become trapped.
Moisture may damage the lining and macerate skin.
questions.takeaway: Protect concealed skin while investigating persistent cast discomfort.
questions.learningObjective: Protect concealed skin while investigating persistent cast discomfort.

questions.title: Medication review before conception
questions.stem: A client whose epilepsy is controlled with prescribed medication hopes to conceive in three months. They ask what to do about possible fetal medication effects. What should the nurse recommend?
options: Continue the current plan until a preconception medication review is arranged
Reduce medication only during the first trimester
Wait for a positive pregnancy test before requesting advice
Substitute a nonprescription supplement while awaiting assessment
why: Planned review balances fetal exposure concerns against seizure-control needs without abrupt treatment changes.
Unsupervised dose reduction can cause breakthrough seizures and does not establish fetal safety.
Waiting loses an opportunity to optimize treatment before early fetal development.
A supplement does not provide established antiseizure treatment or assured pregnancy safety.
questions.takeaway: Arrange preconception medication review while maintaining prescribed therapy pending advice.
questions.learningObjective: Arrange preconception medication review while maintaining prescribed therapy pending advice.

questions.title: Workplace exposure assessment
questions.stem: A client planning pregnancy works in a laboratory and asks whether to request reassignment. They feel well and cannot name the chemicals handled. What should the nurse do first?
options: Recommend avoiding all laboratory duties immediately
Obtain substance and exposure information for occupational-health review
Recommend changing to an evening shift while awaiting advice
Base advice on coworkers' uncomplicated pregnancies
why: Blanket reassignment precedes assessment of the actual exposure and available controls.
Specific substances, routes and protections are needed for a meaningful occupational assessment.
Changing shifts does not establish or control substance-specific exposure.
Other workers' outcomes do not establish this client's exposure level or risk.
questions.takeaway: Characterize workplace exposures before recommending individualized pregnancy precautions.
questions.learningObjective: Characterize workplace exposures before recommending individualized pregnancy precautions.

questions.title: Discussing an early alcohol exposure
questions.stem: At the first prenatal visit, a client reports drinking before recognizing pregnancy and asks whether anything can still help. Which response best supports health promotion?
options: Focus on whether ultrasound can exclude all effects
Explain that avoiding further alcohol and continuing prenatal care remain useful
Recommend reducing intake gradually without further assessment
Defer the topic until the client can recall every drink
why: Ultrasound cannot exclude every possible effect and does not address preventable ongoing exposure.
Nonjudgmental advice supports prevention and care without predicting an individual fetal outcome.
A reduction plan requires assessment; the safest pregnancy recommendation is to avoid alcohol.
Incomplete recall should not delay supportive assessment and prevention advice.
questions.takeaway: Support abstinence and prenatal follow-up without making unsupported predictions about past exposure.
questions.learningObjective: Support abstinence and prenatal follow-up without making unsupported predictions about past exposure.

questions.title: Planning a vegan prenatal diet
questions.stem: A pregnant vegan client eats beans, grains, vegetables and fruit but takes no supplements. Weight gain is appropriate. Which assessment is most useful next?
options: Whether a higher calorie target is needed solely because the diet is vegan
Whether meat can be added before further counselling
Sources of vitamin B12, iron and other required prenatal nutrients
Whether normal weight gain removes the need for nutritional review
why: Calorie adequacy and micronutrient adequacy are different questions in this scenario.
A nutritionally adequate plan may be developed within the client's dietary preferences.
Appropriate weight gain does not establish adequate intake of B12 or other nutrients.
Weight gain alone cannot rule out a nutrient gap.
questions.takeaway: Assess specific nutrient sources even when prenatal weight gain appears appropriate.
questions.learningObjective: Assess specific nutrient sources even when prenatal weight gain appears appropriate.

questions.title: Pregnancy nausea with preserved intake
questions.stem: At ten weeks, a client reports morning nausea, stable weight and retained fluids. Which teaching is appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Try small meals more frequently
Identify and avoid personal food triggers
Report inability to retain fluids
Drink most fluids together with meals
why: Smaller portions may be more tolerable without unnecessarily restricting overall intake.
Trigger identification allows an individualized rather than blanket dietary adjustment.
Loss of fluid tolerance changes the need for clinical assessment.
Separating fluids from meals may improve tolerance; large combined volumes can worsen nausea.
questions.takeaway: Pair practical nausea strategies with clear advice about worsening intake.
questions.learningObjective: Pair practical nausea strategies with clear advice about worsening intake.

questions.title: Prenatal food insecurity
questions.stem: A pregnant client understands the meal plan but skips lunch to preserve food for their children. What nursing response best addresses the identified barrier?
options: Repeat teaching about fetal nutrient requirements
Set a goal to document every missed meal
Offer referral to accessible food and income supports
Ask the client to purchase smaller prenatal supplement packages
why: The client already understands the advice; limited resources prevent using it.
Tracking alone does not make food available to the household.
Material supports address the stated barrier to adequate intake.
Supplements cannot replace meals, and smaller packages may not improve affordability.
questions.takeaway: Match prenatal interventions to resource barriers rather than assuming a knowledge deficit.
questions.learningObjective: Match prenatal interventions to resource barriers rather than assuming a knowledge deficit.

questions.title: Continuing prenatal activity
questions.stem: A client who walks regularly has an uncomplicated pregnancy and no activity restrictions. They ask how to adapt activity as pregnancy progresses. Which advice is best?
options: Maintain exactly the same distance regardless of symptoms
Stop structured activity and rely only on household tasks
Switch to an unfamiliar intensive exercise program
Adjust activity to comfort and discuss new warning symptoms promptly
why: A fixed distance ignores changing tolerance and emerging clinical concerns.
Uncomplicated pregnancy does not by itself require stopping enjoyable activity.
Unfamiliar intensive training needs assessment rather than routine recommendation.
Individual adaptation supports activity while preserving responsiveness to warning signs.
questions.takeaway: Adapt prenatal activity to tolerance and clinical status.
questions.learningObjective: Adapt prenatal activity to tolerance and clinical status.

questions.title: A symptom during prenatal exercise
questions.stem: During a low-intensity prenatal class, a client reports new vaginal bleeding. They are alert and deny pain. What should the nurse advise first?
options: Stop activity and contact the maternity service promptly
Rest briefly and resume if bleeding stops
Change to seated exercise for the remainder of class
Record the episode for the next routine prenatal visit
why: Bleeding requires timely assessment even without pain or altered consciousness.
Temporary improvement does not establish that continuing exercise is appropriate.
Changing exercise type does not evaluate the cause of bleeding.
A routine future visit may delay needed assessment.
questions.takeaway: Stop prenatal exercise and seek assessment for vaginal bleeding.
questions.learningObjective: Stop prenatal exercise and seek assessment for vaginal bleeding.

questions.title: Dental assessment during pregnancy
questions.stem: A pregnant client has gum bleeding when brushing and has postponed a routine dental visit. Which teaching best addresses the concern?
options: Continue hygiene and arrange an oral-health assessment now
Stop flossing until the postpartum visit
Use mouthwash instead of brushing until bleeding resolves
Increase calcium intake before deciding whether dental care is needed
why: Ongoing hygiene and assessment address oral disease without unnecessary pregnancy-related delay.
Stopping cleaning may worsen plaque-related inflammation.
Mouthwash does not replace mechanical plaque removal or clinical assessment.
Nutrient changes do not identify the cause of gum bleeding.
questions.takeaway: Encourage oral assessment and effective hygiene during pregnancy.
questions.learningObjective: Encourage oral assessment and effective hygiene during pregnancy.

questions.title: Reviewing vaccines before birth
questions.stem: A client says, 'I had my vaccines years ago, so pregnancy should not change anything.' Which review elements are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Document previous doses and reactions
Check current pregnancy-specific recommendations
Explain potential protection of the newborn
Apply the routine adult schedule without checking pregnancy precautions
why: Previous doses and reactions inform what is indicated and safe.
Some recommendations depend specifically on pregnancy and gestational timing.
Maternal immunization can provide protection during early infancy.
Pregnancy may alter vaccine selection and timing, so adult guidance alone is insufficient.
questions.takeaway: Use pregnancy-specific Canadian guidance alongside the client's vaccine history.
questions.learningObjective: Use pregnancy-specific Canadian guidance alongside the client's vaccine history.

questions.title: Sexual health during pregnancy
questions.stem: A pregnant client has a new partner and asks whether condoms are unnecessary now. What is the best response?
options: Discuss condom use and appropriate sexually transmitted infection assessment
Focus only on postpartum contraception
Recommend relying on a partner's lack of symptoms
Delay infection screening until after delivery unless symptoms develop
why: Pregnancy prevents neither exposure nor infection, and screening may be indicated without symptoms.
Future contraception does not address current infection exposure.
Several sexually transmitted infections can be asymptomatic.
Delayed assessment may miss opportunities to protect the client and infant.
questions.takeaway: Include infection prevention and risk-based screening in prenatal sexual-health teaching.
questions.learningObjective: Include infection prevention and risk-based screening in prenatal sexual-health teaching.

questions.title: Preparing for changing birth circumstances
questions.stem: A client strongly prefers a particular labour plan and worries that staff will disregard it. Which nursing response best supports informed preparation?
options: Explain that written preferences remove the need for further consent discussions
Explore priorities and how options will be discussed if circumstances change
Suggest omitting preferences to avoid disappointment
Focus only on the standard unit routine
why: Preferences guide care but do not replace ongoing information and consent.
Understanding priorities supports meaningful shared decisions when the clinical situation evolves.
Avoiding preferences removes useful information about what matters to the client.
Routine information alone does not address the client's concern about participation.
questions.takeaway: Discuss both birth priorities and communication when care options change.
questions.learningObjective: Discuss both birth priorities and communication when care options change.

questions.title: A change in fetal activity
questions.stem: At 33 weeks, a client reports substantially less fetal movement than usual this afternoon. They have no bleeding or pain. What advice is most appropriate?
options: Reassess at tomorrow's usual active time
Bring the concern to the next routine appointment
Contact the maternity service promptly for individualized assessment
Drink something cold and call only if movement has not increased by bedtime
why: Waiting until tomorrow may delay evaluation of a meaningful change.
Absence of pain does not make delayed review sufficient.
A reduction from the established pattern warrants prompt maternity advice and assessment.
Attempts to stimulate movement should not postpone contact for a meaningful change.
questions.takeaway: Act promptly on a meaningful reduction in the usual fetal movement pattern.
questions.learningObjective: Act promptly on a meaningful reduction in the usual fetal movement pattern.

questions.title: Planning a labour support role
questions.stem: A client asks a close friend to support them during birth. The friend feels uncertain about helping. Which preparation is most useful?
options: Practise a fixed breathing schedule before asking about preferences
Ask the friend to select all pain-relief options in advance
Give only the hospital visiting policy
Discuss the client's preferences and practise agreed comfort measures
why: Comfort methods should be adapted to the client rather than fixed in advance.
A support person does not replace the capable client's ongoing decisions.
Visiting information alone does not prepare the friend to provide support.
Shared expectations and practical rehearsal make support responsive to the client.
questions.takeaway: Prepare labour support around the client's preferences and practical comfort needs.
questions.learningObjective: Prepare labour support around the client's preferences and practical comfort needs.

questions.title: Planning accessible prenatal care
questions.stem: A client misses prenatal visits because shifts change weekly and bus service is limited. Which actions address the barriers? Select all that apply.
options: Explore feasible appointment times
Ask about transport assistance
Discuss which follow-up components can safely occur remotely
Offer video visits for every remaining appointment without checking which assessments require in-person care
why: Scheduling flexibility can reduce the identified employment conflict.
Transport assistance addresses a concrete access problem.
Appropriate remote components may improve access while preserving necessary in-person assessment.
Universal remote substitution can miss necessary examinations or tests.
questions.takeaway: Reduce practical barriers when arranging prenatal follow-up.
questions.learningObjective: Reduce practical barriers when arranging prenatal follow-up.

questions.title: Cannabis used for pregnancy nausea
questions.stem: A client uses cannabis edibles for nausea and believes avoiding smoke eliminates pregnancy risks. Which response is most accurate?
options: Edibles are preferred throughout pregnancy because there is no smoke
Cannabis exposure remains; arrange review of safer nausea treatments
Stop all nausea treatments until the next trimester
Use symptom relief as evidence that the product is safe
why: Avoiding smoke does not eliminate exposure to cannabis constituents.
Route changes do not establish fetal safety, and nausea deserves an assessed treatment plan.
Untreated nausea may compromise intake; options can be reviewed now.
A product can relieve symptoms without being appropriate during pregnancy.
questions.takeaway: Explain that edible cannabis does not remove pregnancy exposure concerns.
questions.learningObjective: Explain that edible cannabis does not remove pregnancy exposure concerns.

questions.title: Postpartum practical supports
questions.stem: A client expecting a first baby lives alone and has no nearby family. Which question best guides a useful support plan?
options: Which infant-care techniques would you like demonstrated before discharge?
Would you prefer a telephone check-in at the end of the first week?
'Which daily tasks may be difficult, and who or what services could help?'
'Would reading another parenting booklet settle your concern?'
why: Skill teaching may help but does not first identify the practical support gap.
Follow-up is useful but does not first establish help with daily tasks.
Task-specific assessment identifies feasible help with meals, rest and infant care.
More information alone may not resolve a lack of practical assistance.
questions.takeaway: Assess practical postpartum needs and available supports before birth.
questions.learningObjective: Assess practical postpartum needs and available supports before birth.

questions.title: Rubella protection before conception
questions.stem: A client is not pregnant, plans conception soon and has documented lack of rubella immunity. What should the nurse arrange?
options: Vaccine counselling that includes waiting at least four weeks before conception
Deferring vaccination until after the planned pregnancy
Vaccination without discussing a conception interval
Repeating serology after conception before counselling
why: Canadian guidance recommends delaying conception at least four weeks after rubella-containing vaccination.
A susceptible nonpregnant client can consider protection before conception.
Timing advice is part of safe preconception vaccine counselling.
Waiting loses an opportunity to plan protection before pregnancy.
questions.takeaway: Review rubella vaccination and conception timing before pregnancy.
questions.learningObjective: Review rubella vaccination and conception timing before pregnancy.

questions.title: Health literacy in prenatal information
questions.stem: A client shows two conflicting prenatal supplement advertisements and asks which claim to trust. Which approach best supports independent information appraisal?
options: Choose the advertisement with more testimonials
Compare authorship, evidence, date and relevance with a trusted clinical source
Select the product described as natural
Use the more expensive product as the quality standard
why: Testimonials cannot establish effectiveness or safety for this client.
Source appraisal helps distinguish evidence from marketing and supports future decisions.
Natural origin does not establish supplement safety.
Price is not a reliable measure of clinical evidence.
questions.takeaway: Teach source appraisal when prenatal information is commercially promoted.
questions.learningObjective: Teach source appraisal when prenatal information is commercially promoted.

questions.title: Postpartum follow-up planning
questions.stem: A client will have help overnight for three days after birth but is unsure who will review their feeding concerns after discharge. Which preparations are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Confirm how and when feeding follow-up will occur
Agree on rest opportunities during the available support
Assume the routine later postpartum visit covers every early feeding concern
Arrange an additional support option when the initial help ends
why: A clear follow-up route supports timely assessment of feeding difficulties.
Matching rest to actual available help makes the plan feasible.
New feeding concerns may need earlier assessment than a routine later visit.
Anticipating the end of current support prevents an avoidable gap.
questions.takeaway: Coordinate postpartum support with actual availability and follow-up needs.
questions.learningObjective: Coordinate postpartum support with actual availability and follow-up needs.

questions.title: Observing breastfeeding discomfort
questions.stem: During a home visit, a parent reports pinching pain throughout breastfeeds. The infant feeds frequently but often slips off. What should the nurse do first?
options: Shorten every feed to reduce nipple exposure
Observe a full feed and assess attachment and milk transfer
Recommend a fixed four-hour feeding schedule
Suggest pumping exclusively before observing feeding
why: Shortening feeds may reduce intake without correcting the underlying problem.
Pain and slipping suggest a correctable feeding issue that direct observation can clarify.
Restricting frequency does not address ineffective attachment.
A major feeding change is premature before assessing the parent's chosen method.
questions.takeaway: Observe latch and milk transfer when feeding is painful or ineffective.
questions.learningObjective: Observe latch and milk transfer when feeding is painful or ineffective.

questions.title: Evidence of milk transfer
questions.stem: During a breastfeed, an infant remains attached for 30 minutes. Which additional observation most directly supports effective milk transfer?
options: The parent reports fuller breasts before feeding
The infant's eyes remain closed
Rhythmic sucking followed by audible swallowing
The infant sucks rapidly throughout the feed without observed swallowing
why: Breast fullness alone does not show what the infant receives.
Closed eyes do not establish effective intake.
Swallowing linked to sucking is direct evidence of milk transfer.
Rapid sucking without swallowing does not establish effective milk transfer.
questions.takeaway: Assess swallowing rather than feed duration alone when evaluating milk transfer.
questions.learningObjective: Assess swallowing rather than feed duration alone when evaluating milk transfer.

questions.title: Responsive bottle feeding
questions.stem: A caregiver reports repeatedly encouraging a well-growing infant to finish bottles despite turning away. Which teaching is most appropriate?
options: Pause or stop when the infant shows fullness cues
Prepare a larger bottle to reduce feeding frequency
Increase flow so feeding finishes before the infant turns away
Schedule feeds solely by the printed age guide
why: Responsive feeding respects fullness and avoids pressuring intake beyond cues.
Larger bottles may reinforce the same pressure to finish.
Faster flow can overwhelm coordination and does not address satiety.
Age guides do not replace the individual infant's hunger and fullness signals.
questions.takeaway: Use hunger and satiety cues to guide bottle feeding.
questions.learningObjective: Use hunger and satiety cues to guide bottle feeding.

questions.title: Formula affordability and preparation
questions.stem: A caregiver dilutes formula to make a container last longer. The infant has no current symptoms. What should the nurse prioritize?
options: Change to a more concentrated homemade mixture
Advise smaller feeds without discussing preparation
Wait for the next growth check before intervening
Review correct preparation and connect the family with formula-access support
why: An improvised mixture cannot ensure safe nutrient or electrolyte content.
Smaller feeds do not correct inappropriate concentration or food insecurity.
Preparation errors warrant intervention before symptoms appear.
Correct preparation addresses immediate safety while resource support addresses the cause.
questions.takeaway: Address both unsafe formula dilution and the financial barrier driving it.
questions.learningObjective: Address both unsafe formula dilution and the financial barrier driving it.

questions.title: Synthesizing newborn intake findings
questions.stem: At a day-eight visit, a newborn continues to lose weight, has fewer wet diapers than two days ago and rarely swallows during long feeds. What should the nurse prioritize?
options: Reassure the parent because frequent long feeds indicate adequate intake
Arrange prompt feeding and clinical assessment
Shorten feeds and review growth at the next routine visit
Increase intervals between feeds to strengthen hunger cues
why: Feeding duration does not outweigh the concerning weight, output and transfer pattern.
The combined findings suggest inadequate intake requiring timely assessment and a feeding plan.
Waiting without addressing falling weight and reduced output may delay necessary support.
Longer gaps can further reduce intake and do not correct ineffective transfer.
questions.takeaway: Integrate weight, output and observed transfer when deciding whether newborn intake needs assessment.
questions.learningObjective: Integrate weight, output and observed transfer when deciding whether newborn intake needs assessment.

questions.title: Complementary food selection
questions.stem: A six-month-old sits with support, controls their head and shows interest in food. Which first-food plan best addresses emerging nutritional needs?
options: Fruit juice between milk feeds
Iron-rich soft foods alongside milk feeds
Low-fat milk replacing breastfeeds
Vegetable broth replacing one daily feed
why: Juice supplies little iron and can displace nutritious intake.
Suitable iron-rich foods complement continuing milk nutrition.
Low-fat milk is not an appropriate replacement here.
Broth alone provides inadequate complementary nutrition.
questions.takeaway: Include iron-rich foods when complementary feeding begins.
questions.learningObjective: Include iron-rich foods when complementary feeding begins.

questions.title: Advancing feeding skills
questions.stem: A nine-month-old handles mashed foods comfortably but receives only smooth purées because they lack molars. What should the nurse suggest?
options: Continue smooth foods until molars erupt
Add cereal to every bottle
Introduce suitable soft finger foods under supervision
Delay self-feeding until spoon use is precise
why: Suitable texture progression need not wait for molars.
Bottle cereal does not develop texture-handling skills.
Soft foods allow developmentally appropriate chewing and self-feeding practice.
Waiting for precision removes opportunities to learn.
questions.takeaway: Advance food texture according to feeding ability.
questions.learningObjective: Advance food texture according to feeding ability.

questions.title: Honey in infant food
questions.stem: A caregiver offers homemade yogurt sweetened with honey to an eight-month-old. What ingredient change should the nurse prioritize?
options: Replace honey with suitable mashed fruit
Replace yogurt with fruit juice
Add cereal to thicken the honey
Use pasteurized honey in the recipe
why: Avoiding honey reduces infant botulism exposure during the first year.
Juice substitution does not address the specific honey risk.
Thickening does not remove potential bacterial spores.
Pasteurization does not reliably eliminate the relevant spores.
questions.takeaway: Avoid honey before 12 months of age.
questions.learningObjective: Avoid honey before 12 months of age.

questions.title: Mealtime positioning
questions.stem: A parent feeds an older infant soft pieces while the infant moves around the living room. What is the most useful change?
options: Offer only purées while moving
Give smaller portions but maintain the routine
Allow independent eating in a reclined stroller
Seat the infant upright and supervise the meal
why: Changing texture does not correct an unstable feeding position.
Portion size alone does not address movement-related risk.
Reclining does not support an optimal feeding position.
Stable upright supervised eating supports safer swallowing.
questions.takeaway: Establish upright supervised meals for complementary feeding.
questions.learningObjective: Establish upright supervised meals for complementary feeding.

questions.title: Responsive infant feeding
questions.stem: Which observations suggest a bottle-fed infant may be ready to pause or stop? Select all that apply.
options: Turning away repeatedly
Closing the mouth when offered the nipple
Relaxing after feeding without seeking more
Rooting actively toward the nipple
why: Turning away can communicate fullness or need for a break.
Closing the mouth indicates disengagement rather than permission to insist.
Relaxed satisfaction supports pausing and observing further cues.
Active rooting is more consistent with feeding interest.
questions.takeaway: Recognize satiety cues instead of pressuring bottle completion.
questions.learningObjective: Recognize satiety cues instead of pressuring bottle completion.

questions.title: Coping with infant crying
questions.stem: A tired parent says, 'I am getting so angry I need to put the baby down.' The infant appears well. What is the best immediate advice?
options: Continue holding until the crying ends
Place the infant safely in a crib and take a brief calming break
Leave the infant on a sofa within hearing distance
Begin a detailed feeding diary immediately
why: Continuing while overwhelmed may increase the risk of losing control.
Safe placement permits a brief pause and help-seeking.
A sofa is not a safe unattended infant surface.
Documentation is secondary to immediate caregiver regulation and infant safety.
questions.takeaway: Use safe placement and a calming break when crying overwhelms caregivers.
questions.learningObjective: Use safe placement and a calming break when crying overwhelms caregivers.

questions.title: Infant language interaction
questions.stem: A family speaks two languages and asks how to support early communication. Which activity is most useful?
options: Repeated vocabulary videos
Restrict conversation to the nurse's language
Responsive talking and reading in familiar family languages
Practising word repetition without responding to gestures
why: Passive media do not replace responsive interpersonal language learning.
Comfortable family language supports richer everyday interaction.
Responsive exchanges provide meaningful language and social experience.
Ignoring gestures misses important early communication cues.
questions.takeaway: Encourage responsive communication in languages the family uses comfortably.
questions.learningObjective: Encourage responsive communication in languages the family uses comfortably.

questions.title: An infant hearing concern
questions.stem: An infant rarely turns toward voices despite otherwise alert behaviour. What should the nurse recommend?
options: Timely hearing and developmental assessment
Increasing background music during play
Waiting until speech develops to reassess
Comparing only with the parent's childhood milestones
why: Early assessment can identify barriers to communication development.
Added background sound does not evaluate hearing ability.
Waiting for speech may delay useful early support.
Family history does not replace assessment of this infant.
questions.takeaway: Refer persistent hearing concerns before language delay becomes established.
questions.learningObjective: Refer persistent hearing concerns before language delay becomes established.

questions.title: Loss of toddler skills
questions.stem: A toddler previously used several words but now rarely speaks and no longer points. What is the best action?
options: Suggest a language app and review next year
Attribute the change to a new sibling
Focus solely on increasing vocabulary practice
Arrange prompt developmental and hearing assessment
why: Home practice alone does not evaluate loss of established skills.
A family change should not automatically explain developmental regression.
Regression across communication behaviours requires broader assessment.
Loss of learned skills warrants timely evaluation.
questions.takeaway: Escalate developmental regression rather than reassuring from age alone.
questions.learningObjective: Escalate developmental regression rather than reassuring from age alone.

questions.title: Interpreting growth data
questions.stem: Which information helps interpret an infant's unexpectedly low weight measurement? Select all that apply.
options: Previous measurements and trajectory
Measurement technique and equipment
Feeding history and current health
Whether the infant exceeds a sibling's weight at that age
why: Serial data distinguish a stable pattern from a concerning change.
Technique errors can create misleading apparent growth changes.
Intake and illness provide essential clinical context.
Sibling comparisons do not establish this infant's expected trajectory.
questions.takeaway: Verify measurements and clinical context before interpreting growth change.
questions.learningObjective: Verify measurements and clinical context before interpreting growth change.

questions.title: Development after preterm birth
questions.stem: A four-month-old infant was born eight weeks early. The parent worries because a term-born cousin has more advanced skills. What should guide the nurse's discussion?
options: The cousin's developmental pace
Corrected age and the infant's progress across domains
Birth weight as the sole comparison
The number of weeks spent in hospital
why: Another infant's pace is not an individualized developmental standard.
Corrected age contextualizes early expectations after prematurity.
Birth weight alone cannot determine developmental milestones.
Hospital duration does not replace developmental assessment.
questions.takeaway: Use corrected age and longitudinal progress after premature birth.
questions.learningObjective: Use corrected age and longitudinal progress after premature birth.

questions.title: Stranger distress during assessment
questions.stem: A nine-month-old cries when the nurse approaches but settles with their caregiver. A routine assessment is due. Which approach is best?
options: Complete the examination quickly despite distress
Separate the caregiver to reduce distraction
Begin gradually while the caregiver holds the infant
Postpone all assessments until stranger distress disappears
why: Rushing may intensify distress and reduce useful observations.
Removing familiar support can worsen developmental anxiety.
A familiar secure base improves tolerance of nonurgent assessment.
Care can usually proceed with developmentally appropriate adaptation.
questions.takeaway: Adapt routine assessments to infant stranger anxiety.
questions.learningObjective: Adapt routine assessments to infant stranger anxiety.

questions.title: Chalky changes on primary teeth
questions.stem: A parent reports white chalky areas near a toddler's gumline but no pain. What should the nurse recommend?
options: Arrange dental assessment before pain develops
Review only at the next annual physical
Increase brushing pressure to remove the marks
Wait until permanent teeth replace them
why: Early decay may be painless and benefit from timely treatment.
Delayed review may allow preventable progression.
Excess pressure can injure tissues and does not diagnose the change.
Primary teeth have important functions and warrant care.
questions.takeaway: Refer early tooth changes even when pain is absent.
questions.learningObjective: Refer early tooth changes even when pain is absent.

questions.title: Toothbrushing independence
questions.stem: A four-year-old insists on brushing alone but misses back teeth. Which plan best supports development and oral health?
options: Let the child manage independently to build confidence
Replace brushing with rinsing on difficult evenings
Wait until permanent teeth arrive to correct technique
Let the child practise, then provide adult brushing assistance
why: Independence before adequate dexterity can leave plaque behind.
Rinsing does not replace cleaning tooth surfaces.
Primary teeth also need effective plaque removal.
Shared participation supports skill-building while ensuring cleaning.
questions.takeaway: Combine child participation with adult help until brushing is effective.
questions.learningObjective: Combine child participation with adult help until brushing is effective.

questions.title: Toddler feeding autonomy
questions.stem: Which approaches support a healthy toddler's feeding autonomy? Select all that apply.
options: Offer regular meals and snacks
Provide appropriate nutritious choices
Let appetite guide how much is eaten from offered food
Require a clean plate before leaving every meal
why: Predictable opportunities support appetite and feeding routines.
Adults can structure available choices without coercion.
Respecting appetite supports developing internal intake regulation.
Clean-plate pressure overrides fullness and can create conflict.
questions.takeaway: Provide mealtime structure while respecting the toddler's appetite.
questions.learningObjective: Provide mealtime structure while respecting the toddler's appetite.

questions.title: Toilet learning readiness
questions.stem: A caregiver wants to begin toilet learning, but the toddler cannot signal needs and strongly resists sitting. What is the best advice?
options: Extend toilet sitting until the child urinates
Pause pressure and watch for readiness while using a predictable routine
Remove fluids after lunch to reduce accidents
Start nighttime training before daytime learning
why: Prolonged forced sitting can increase resistance.
Readiness-based practice supports cooperation and avoids unnecessary conflict.
Fluid restriction does not teach toileting skills.
Nighttime control develops differently and is not a prerequisite.
questions.takeaway: Match toilet learning to developmental readiness.
questions.learningObjective: Match toilet learning to developmental readiness.

questions.title: Toddler choice-making
questions.stem: A two-year-old resists dressing before a clinic visit. Which suggestion best supports autonomy within a necessary routine?
options: Ask whether the child wants to get dressed
Explain every future consequence in detail
Offer a choice between two suitable shirts
Let the child decide whether to attend the visit
why: An unrestricted yes-or-no choice can conflict with the required task.
Lengthy explanations exceed typical toddler processing needs.
Limited acceptable choices support autonomy without abandoning the routine.
Attendance decisions remain an adult responsibility.
questions.takeaway: Offer bounded choices during toddler care routines.
questions.learningObjective: Offer bounded choices during toddler care routines.

questions.title: Preschool procedure preparation
questions.stem: A four-year-old needs a routine blood draw later today. Which preparation is most appropriate?
options: Use simple concrete explanations and demonstrate on a doll shortly beforehand
Explain the cellular purpose of each laboratory test
Begin daily detailed explanations several weeks ahead
Avoid mentioning discomfort unless the child asks
why: Concrete play and near-term preparation match preschool understanding.
Cellular explanations exceed the immediate developmental learning need.
Prolonged detailed anticipation may increase worry.
Honest age-appropriate preparation includes expected sensations.
questions.takeaway: Prepare preschoolers with brief concrete play-based explanations.
questions.learningObjective: Prepare preschoolers with brief concrete play-based explanations.

questions.title: Magical thinking about illness
questions.stem: A preschooler says, 'My brother got sick because I was angry at him.' What should the nurse explain?
options: Anger can cause illness when it is strong
The child should apologize before discussing the illness
The family will decide whether the child is responsible
Feelings and thoughts did not cause the brother's illness
why: Confirming the belief reinforces guilt and inaccurate causation.
Apology does not correct the child's developmental misunderstanding.
Responsibility is not a matter for family blame.
A concrete correction addresses preschool magical thinking and guilt.
questions.takeaway: Correct preschool beliefs that thoughts or feelings caused illness.
questions.learningObjective: Correct preschool beliefs that thoughts or feelings caused illness.

questions.title: Supporting a school-age learner
questions.stem: Which teaching approaches fit a school-age child learning routine asthma self-care with caregivers? Select all that apply.
options: Explain cause and effect in concrete terms
Allow supervised skill practice
Agree on manageable responsibilities
Give the child sole responsibility for obtaining refills
why: Concrete explanations connect actions with understandable outcomes.
Practice builds confidence and reveals learning needs.
Shared manageable tasks support developing competence.
Adults remain responsible for ensuring access and appropriate oversight.
questions.takeaway: Build school-age self-care through explanation, practice and shared responsibility.
questions.learningObjective: Build school-age self-care through explanation, practice and shared responsibility.

questions.title: School avoidance assessment
questions.stem: A ten-year-old has recurrent morning abdominal discomfort and missed school; initial medical assessment is reassuring. What should the nurse explore next?
options: Whether the child can be removed permanently from school
School experiences, peer relationships and symptom patterns
Whether all symptoms stop if rewards are withheld
Only the family's preferred dietary supplements
why: Permanent withdrawal precedes understanding the problem.
Contextual assessment may identify stress, bullying or unmet learning needs.
A behavioural assumption may overlook distress or continuing clinical concerns.
Supplements alone do not address the attendance pattern.
questions.takeaway: Explore school and social context when symptoms interfere with attendance.
questions.learningObjective: Explore school and social context when symptoms interfere with attendance.

questions.title: Screen habits in early childhood
questions.stem: A preschooler watches videos during most meals and bedtime routines. Parents want one useful starting change. What should the nurse suggest?
options: Replace all videos with educational content only
Allow screens whenever the child is quiet
Create screen-free meals and a calming bedtime routine
Measure screen size before changing routines
why: Content choice does not address displacement of interaction and sleep routines.
Quiet behaviour alone does not establish a healthy pattern.
Specific routine changes protect interaction and sleep-related habits.
Screen dimensions are less relevant than timing and displacement.
questions.takeaway: Focus screen counselling on routines and activities displaced by use.
questions.learningObjective: Focus screen counselling on routines and activities displaced by use.

questions.title: Childhood activity access
questions.stem: A parent cannot afford organized sports and worries their child cannot be active. Which advice is best?
options: Plan enjoyable free play, walking or community activities
Delay activity until a sports program is affordable
Prioritize exercise equipment purchases over daily play
Use competitive performance as the first activity goal
why: Everyday enjoyable movement can support activity without program fees.
Waiting leaves an unnecessary access barrier in place.
Equipment is not required for many beneficial activities.
Performance goals may reduce enjoyment and participation.
questions.takeaway: Develop feasible enjoyable movement opportunities beyond organized sports.
questions.learningObjective: Develop feasible enjoyable movement opportunities beyond organized sports.

questions.title: A childhood growth conversation
questions.stem: A child is distressed after being called overweight at school. The caregiver requests a diet plan. What should the nurse prioritize?
options: Set a rapid weight-loss goal before assessing growth
Ask the child to weigh daily without support
Discuss appearance as the main reason for change
Assess growth and routines using nonstigmatizing family-centred language
why: Rapid restriction without assessment may be inappropriate during growth.
Frequent unsupervised weighing may intensify distress.
Appearance-focused counselling reinforces the child's experience of stigma.
Growth context and respectful family routines support a safer plan.
questions.takeaway: Discuss childhood growth without stigma or unassessed restrictive dieting.
questions.learningObjective: Discuss childhood growth without stigma or unassessed restrictive dieting.

questions.title: Preparing for puberty
questions.stem: Which topics belong in anticipatory guidance before or during early puberty? Select all that apply.
options: Expected variation in timing of body changes
Private questions about hygiene and menstruation where relevant
Trusted adults and reliable information sources
Comparison with classmates to determine whether development is acceptable
why: Normal variation can reduce unnecessary anxiety about peer differences.
Private practical information supports preparation for body changes.
Accessible trusted support helps the young person seek help.
Peer comparison alone cannot evaluate development or respect privacy.
questions.takeaway: Offer private practical puberty guidance that acknowledges normal variation.
questions.learningObjective: Offer private practical puberty guidance that acknowledges normal variation.

questions.title: Adolescent consultation privacy
questions.stem: A teenager becomes silent when a parent answers sexual-health questions. What is the best initial approach in a routine visit?
options: Continue with the parent to avoid discomfort
Explain the routine opportunity for private discussion and confidentiality limits
Ask the parent to guess the teenager's answers
Postpone sensitive questions until adulthood
why: Continuing without privacy may prevent accurate assessment.
A normalized private discussion supports disclosure while clarifying limits.
Proxy guesses cannot replace the young person's account.
Delayed assessment can miss current health-promotion needs.
questions.takeaway: Provide developmentally appropriate privacy with clear confidentiality limits.
questions.learningObjective: Provide developmentally appropriate privacy with clear confidentiality limits.

questions.title: Sexual-health assessment language
questions.stem: A young adult says they have partners of more than one gender. Which question best guides relevant prevention teaching?
options: 'Which identity should I use to decide your risk?'
'Can we skip details if you have no symptoms?'
'What sexual practices and protection methods are relevant for you?'
'Does one partner seem safer than the others?'
why: Identity alone does not describe exposures or protection.
Absence of symptoms does not rule out infection risk.
Practice-based questions allow individualized and inclusive prevention advice.
Perceived safety is not a substitute for exposure assessment.
