questions.takeaway: Base sexual-health counselling on practices and protection rather than identity assumptions.
questions.learningObjective: Base sexual-health counselling on practices and protection rather than identity assumptions.

questions.title: STI screening without symptoms
questions.stem: A client with a new partner says no testing is needed because both feel well. What should the nurse explain?
options: Some infections are asymptomatic, so testing depends on exposure and current guidance
Testing is useful only when a rash is present
A partner's reassurance replaces screening
Screening is required only when contraception fails
why: Risk-based screening may identify infections without noticeable symptoms.
Symptoms are not required for an infection to be present.
Reassurance cannot establish infection status.
Pregnancy prevention and infection screening address different concerns.
questions.takeaway: Explain why asymptomatic clients may still benefit from STI screening.
questions.learningObjective: Explain why asymptomatic clients may still benefit from STI screening.

questions.title: Contraception and infection prevention
questions.stem: A client using an intrauterine contraceptive begins a new relationship. What should teaching emphasize?
options: The device protects against common sexually transmitted infections
Screening can replace all barrier use
Contraception should be stopped before discussing infection risk
Pregnancy prevention and infection prevention may require different strategies
why: An intrauterine contraceptive does not provide barrier protection from infection.
Testing does not prevent future exposure.
Effective contraception need not be stopped to assess infection prevention.
A separate discussion of condoms and testing addresses the new exposure context.
questions.takeaway: Distinguish contraceptive effectiveness from protection against infection.
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish contraceptive effectiveness from protection against infection.

questions.title: Adolescent self-management transition
questions.stem: Which actions support a teenager preparing to manage a chronic condition more independently? Select all that apply.
options: Practise describing the condition in their own words
Rehearse booking appointments with support
Develop a medication and refill plan
Transfer every task immediately because adult transfer is approaching
why: Clear explanation supports participation in future care.
Supported practice builds navigation skills before full independence.
Planning anticipates a common source of treatment interruption.
Abrupt transfer may exceed current skills and support.
questions.takeaway: Build health-management independence gradually before transfer to adult care.
questions.learningObjective: Build health-management independence gradually before transfer to adult care.

questions.title: Menstrual symptom assessment
questions.stem: A teenager reports missing school because of heavy menstrual bleeding and fatigue. What is the best nursing response?
options: Normalize all menstrual variation without assessment
Arrange clinical assessment of bleeding and possible anemia
Recommend waiting until cycles have continued for several years
Focus only on school attendance expectations
why: Functional impairment and fatigue warrant more than reassurance.
The pattern suggests a need to assess severity and consequences.
Delay may prolong treatable symptoms or anemia.
Attendance counselling alone does not address the health concern.
questions.takeaway: Assess heavy menstrual bleeding that impairs function or causes fatigue.
questions.learningObjective: Assess heavy menstrual bleeding that impairs function or causes fatigue.

questions.title: Exercise and menstrual change
questions.stem: An adolescent runner has increased training, restricted intake and stopped menstruating. What should the nurse prioritize?
options: Recommend a further training increase to improve endurance
Reassure that absent periods confirm athletic fitness
Arrange assessment of energy availability and overall health
Suggest tracking race results before seeking care
why: More training may worsen an energy imbalance.
Menstrual cessation is not a reliable marker of healthy fitness.
Training, restriction and amenorrhea warrant nutritional and medical review.
Performance data cannot establish the cause of menstrual change.
questions.takeaway: Recognize menstrual change with restricted intake as a health concern in athletes.
questions.learningObjective: Recognize menstrual change with restricted intake as a health concern in athletes.

questions.title: Vaping misconception
questions.stem: A student who has never smoked uses nicotine vapes to manage exam stress. Which response best supports health promotion?
options: Explore dependence and stress triggers while offering cessation support
Recommend continuing because smoking would be worse
Focus only on flavour preference
Advise switching brands before assessing use
why: Assessment can address nicotine exposure and the coping function of use.
Comparison with smoking does not make nicotine initiation beneficial.
Flavour alone does not characterize dependence or coping needs.
Brand changes do not address continued nicotine use.
questions.takeaway: Address nicotine use and the stress-related reasons for it together.
questions.learningObjective: Address nicotine use and the stress-related reasons for it together.

questions.title: Tanning and skin health
questions.stem: A young adult uses tanning beds before vacation to obtain a protective base tan. What should the nurse explain?
options: A base tan removes the need for sunscreen
Indoor tanning can safely prepare skin if sessions are brief
Skin protection matters only after redness develops
Tanning adds ultraviolet exposure; plan shade, clothing and sunscreen instead
why: Tanning does not provide reliable protection from further ultraviolet injury.
Brief sessions still add ultraviolet exposure.
Skin injury can occur before visible redness.
Multiple protective strategies reduce exposure without deliberate tanning.
questions.takeaway: Replace deliberate tanning with practical ultraviolet protection.
questions.learningObjective: Replace deliberate tanning with practical ultraviolet protection.

questions.title: Youth sleep routine
questions.stem: Which changes may help a teenager whose late-night phone use is reducing sleep? Select all that apply.
options: Establish a consistent wake time
Move stimulating screen use away from bedtime
Create a wind-down routine
Use energy drinks to replace lost sleep on weekdays
why: A regular wake time supports a stable sleep schedule.
Reducing bedtime stimulation supports settling for sleep.
Predictable quiet activity can signal the transition to sleep.
Stimulants do not replace sleep and can perpetuate sleep difficulty.
questions.takeaway: Develop consistent routines that protect adequate adolescent sleep.
questions.learningObjective: Develop consistent routines that protect adequate adolescent sleep.

questions.title: Interpreting screening results
questions.stem: An asymptomatic client receives an abnormal screening result and asks whether cancer is certain. What should the nurse explain?
options: Screening alone establishes the final diagnosis
Further diagnostic assessment is needed to clarify the result
A lack of symptoms proves the result is false
Repeating the same screening at home replaces follow-up
why: Screening identifies people needing further evaluation rather than confirming every diagnosis.
Diagnostic follow-up determines what an abnormal result means.
Some conditions are detectable before symptoms develop.
The recommended follow-up cannot automatically be replaced by repeat screening.
questions.takeaway: Distinguish an abnormal screening result from a confirmed diagnosis.
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish an abnormal screening result from a confirmed diagnosis.

questions.title: Symptoms despite recent screening
questions.stem: A client with recent normal colorectal screening now reports persistent rectal bleeding. What advice is best?
options: Wait until the next routine screening interval
Repeat the same screening without clinical review
Seek assessment of the new symptom
Assume hemorrhoids because screening was normal
why: Routine intervals apply to screening, not evaluation of new symptoms.
Symptom assessment may require a different diagnostic pathway.
New persistent bleeding warrants assessment despite a prior normal screen.
A normal screening result does not establish the cause of bleeding.
questions.takeaway: Evaluate new symptoms independently of routine screening schedules.
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate new symptoms independently of routine screening schedules.

questions.title: Family history and screening
questions.stem: A client reports several close relatives with early-onset cancer but has not reached the routine population screening age. What should the nurse do?
options: Arrange individualized risk review rather than applying age criteria alone
Reassure that age rules exclude all screening needs
Recommend every available tumour-marker blood test
Base advice only on the oldest affected relative
why: A significant family pattern can change risk assessment and planning.
Average-risk age criteria may not fit this family history.
Broad unselected testing is not a substitute for risk-based assessment.
Multiple relatives and ages contribute to the pattern.
questions.takeaway: Identify family histories that require individualized screening advice.
questions.learningObjective: Identify family histories that require individualized screening advice.

questions.title: Informed screening choice
questions.stem: A capable client is uncertain about an offered screening test. What should the nurse discuss?
options: Only the benefits to improve acceptance
Only the worst possible outcome of declining
The nurse's personal screening decisions
Potential benefits, harms, follow-up and the client's preferences
why: Benefits alone do not support a balanced informed choice.
Fear-based framing can distort rather than inform the decision.
The nurse's choices do not determine the client's values.
Balanced information and preferences support shared decision-making.
questions.takeaway: Support informed screening choices with benefits, harms and follow-up information.
questions.learningObjective: Support informed screening choices with benefits, harms and follow-up information.

questions.title: Vaccine assessment before a dose
questions.stem: Which information should be checked before administering a recommended vaccine? Select all that apply.
options: Prior serious vaccine reactions
Current relevant illness or immunosuppressive treatment
Pregnancy when relevant to vaccine selection
Only the client's age because the dose is already booked
why: Previous reactions may affect safety precautions or contraindications.
Health status can alter vaccine selection or timing.
Pregnancy can change which products are suitable.
A scheduled appointment does not replace pre-vaccination assessment.
questions.takeaway: Reassess vaccine-specific precautions before each dose.
questions.learningObjective: Reassess vaccine-specific precautions before each dose.

questions.title: A minor illness before vaccination
questions.stem: A well-appearing child has a mild runny nose without fever and is due for routine vaccines. What should the nurse do?
options: Cancel automatically until all nasal symptoms disappear
Assess against vaccine-specific guidance rather than assuming a contraindication
Begin antibiotics before vaccination
Require a negative respiratory panel for every vaccine
why: Mild illness alone is not generally a reason to defer routine immunization.
Clinical assessment and current guidance determine whether vaccination can proceed.
Antibiotics are not routinely indicated for this presentation.
Routine testing is not generally required solely for vaccination.
questions.takeaway: Distinguish minor illness from vaccine-specific precautions requiring deferral.
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish minor illness from vaccine-specific precautions requiring deferral.

questions.title: Vaccine record gaps
questions.stem: A newcomer has incomplete vaccine documentation and is unsure which doses were given. What is the best nursing approach?
options: Assume childhood infection provides complete protection
Restart every vaccine without checking recommendations
Review available records and arrange an individualized catch-up assessment
Defer discussion until records can be obtained from every previous residence
why: Infection history does not establish protection against all vaccine-preventable diseases.
Catch-up decisions should follow vaccine-specific guidance and verified information.
Review allows an appropriate plan despite uncertainty.
Indefinite delay may leave preventable protection gaps.
questions.takeaway: Use current catch-up guidance when immunization records are incomplete.
questions.learningObjective: Use current catch-up guidance when immunization records are incomplete.

questions.title: Vaccine reaction interpretation
questions.stem: After a previous vaccine, an adult had a sore arm for a day without systemic symptoms. They now believe all vaccines are contraindicated. What should the nurse do?
options: Clarify the reaction and explain how it differs from a severe allergic reaction
Confirm that any local pain prevents future vaccination
Recommend withholding all injections indefinitely
Advise taking leftover antibiotics before future doses
why: Reaction details support accurate safety assessment and appropriate counselling.
Brief local soreness is not equivalent to a severe allergy.
Indefinite avoidance is not justified by this history alone.
Antibiotics do not prevent routine local vaccine reactions.
questions.takeaway: Clarify prior reactions before labelling a vaccine contraindication.
questions.learningObjective: Clarify prior reactions before labelling a vaccine contraindication.

questions.title: Travel preparation timing
questions.stem: An adult with a chronic condition is planning international travel in two months. What is the most useful health-promotion advice?
options: Wait until departure week to review vaccines
Obtain antibiotics for every possible illness
Use the destination's general tourism rating as the medical guide
Arrange an early travel-health review with itinerary and medication information
why: Last-minute review may limit time for prevention or preparation.
Unselected antibiotics are not appropriate universal prevention.
Tourism ratings do not address individualized health risks.
Early itinerary-based review supports vaccines, medication planning and destination-specific prevention.
questions.takeaway: Arrange travel-health preparation early enough for individualized preventive measures.
questions.learningObjective: Arrange travel-health preparation early enough for individualized preventive measures.

questions.title: Adult vaccine review
questions.stem: Which factors help determine an adult's immunization needs? Select all that apply.
options: Age and previous doses
Health conditions and treatment
Occupational or travel exposures
Whether childhood records contain at least one vaccine
why: Age and dose history shape routine and catch-up recommendations.
Some conditions change risk, timing or product suitability.
Specific exposures may create additional indications.
One recorded dose does not establish complete current protection.
questions.takeaway: Review adult vaccination using history, health status and exposure risks.
questions.learningObjective: Review adult vaccination using history, health status and exposure risks.

questions.title: Selecting the teaching priority
questions.stem: A client starting home wound care has limited time before transport arrives. They can name supplies but cannot recognize complications. What should the nurse prioritize?
options: History of wound-healing research
Signs requiring help and whom to contact
Brand comparisons for dressings
The complete anatomy of skin layers
why: Background science is less urgent than safe home decisions.
Recognizing deterioration and accessing help addresses the demonstrated safety gap.
Brand details do not resolve the identified knowledge deficit.
Detailed anatomy is less immediately useful for home safety.
questions.takeaway: Prioritize teaching that enables safe action after discharge.
questions.learningObjective: Prioritize teaching that enables safe action after discharge.

questions.title: Assessing practical learning barriers
questions.stem: A client accurately describes medication timing but repeatedly misses morning doses while caring for a spouse. What should the nurse explore first?
options: Whether another written explanation is needed
Whether the client can repeat the drug names
How the regimen fits the caregiving routine
Whether a longer pharmacology discussion would help
why: The client already understands timing, so information may not be the barrier.
Name recall does not explain the routine-related missed doses.
Practical assessment can identify feasible reminders or support needs.
More theory does not directly address competing responsibilities.
questions.takeaway: Distinguish a practical barrier from a knowledge deficit.
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish a practical barrier from a knowledge deficit.

questions.title: Demonstration with limited dexterity
questions.stem: A client understands a new glucose device but cannot open its packaging because of arthritis. What is the best next step?
options: Assess an accessible method or device and repeat supervised practice
Provide a larger-print version of the same instructions only
Require more verbal recall before another attempt
Conclude that independent monitoring is impossible
why: Adaptation addresses the observed motor barrier and tests feasibility.
Print changes do not resolve packaging access.
Verbal recall does not improve hand function.
Independence may be possible with equipment or task modification.
questions.takeaway: Adapt self-care equipment to demonstrated physical ability.
questions.learningObjective: Adapt self-care equipment to demonstrated physical ability.

questions.title: Evaluating a practical skill
questions.stem: After catheter-care teaching, a client describes every step correctly but contaminates the equipment during practice. What is the most appropriate interpretation?
options: The teaching objective is met because recall is accurate
Another pamphlet is sufficient evidence of correction
Performance can be assumed to improve at home
Practical competence requires further coached practice and reassessment
why: Accurate recall does not establish safe task performance.
Receiving information is not evidence of corrected technique.
Unobserved future improvement cannot be assumed.
The observed error identifies a specific skill needing practice.
questions.takeaway: Evaluate demonstrated performance separately from verbal knowledge.
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate demonstrated performance separately from verbal knowledge.

questions.title: Interpreter-supported teaching
questions.stem: A client prefers a language the nurse does not speak. Which approaches support accurate teaching with a qualified interpreter? Select all that apply.
options: Speak directly to the client
Pause after short segments
Ask the interpreter to decide which care instructions matter
Use a family member to verify confidential answers without asking the client
why: Direct engagement preserves the therapeutic relationship.
Short segments support accurate interpretation and questions.
Clinical priorities remain the responsibility of the care team and client.
Involving relatives requires attention to client preference and privacy.
questions.takeaway: Use qualified interpretation while communicating directly with the client.
questions.learningObjective: Use qualified interpretation while communicating directly with the client.

questions.title: Numeracy and liquid measurement
questions.stem: A caregiver says 'one spoon' when discussing a prescribed liquid medicine. Which teaching best reduces measurement error?
options: Compare kitchen spoons visually
Provide the correct marked oral syringe and observe measurement in mL
Ask the caregiver to memorize the bottle colour
Explain the chemical concentration without practising measurement
why: Household spoon sizes are not reliably standardized.
Correct equipment and observed practice address the actual measurement task.
Colour recognition does not ensure a correct dose.
Concentration theory alone does not demonstrate accurate measurement.
questions.takeaway: Teach liquid measurement with appropriate equipment and observed practice.
questions.learningObjective: Teach liquid measurement with appropriate equipment and observed practice.

questions.title: Organizing complex instructions
questions.stem: A client with several new self-care tasks says, 'I cannot remember what matters most.' What should the nurse do?
options: Repeat all details more quickly
Add every possible complication to one page
Prioritize essential actions and organize them into manageable steps
Ask the client to memorize the discharge summary
why: Faster repetition increases cognitive load without clarifying priorities.
Excess detail can obscure essential actions.
Sequencing and prioritization make information easier to use.
A clinical summary is not necessarily an accessible action plan.
questions.takeaway: Reduce cognitive load by organizing essential self-care actions.
questions.learningObjective: Reduce cognitive load by organizing essential self-care actions.

questions.title: Teaching after a sensory change
questions.stem: A client newly using reading glasses is learning ostomy care and avoids the printed guide. What should the nurse assess first?
options: Whether the client can see the material and equipment comfortably
Whether the client agrees with every instruction
Whether the family will take over permanently
Whether the guide contains enough medical terminology
why: Visual access may explain avoidance and can often be improved.
Agreement does not establish access to the teaching materials.
Permanent transfer is premature before assessing a modifiable barrier.
More terminology would not address visual difficulty.
questions.takeaway: Assess sensory access before interpreting limited engagement as resistance.
questions.learningObjective: Assess sensory access before interpreting limited engagement as resistance.

questions.title: A missed learning goal
questions.stem: A client agreed to practise a dressing change but cannot complete it after teaching. What is the best nursing response?
options: Record the goal as achieved because teaching occurred
Label the client unwilling before reassessment
Repeat the identical session without examining the difficulty
Identify the difficult steps and adapt the teaching plan
why: Teaching delivery is not equivalent to learning achievement.
Difficulty may reflect a skill, access or readiness problem.
Unchanged repetition may leave the actual barrier untouched.
Step-specific assessment supports targeted coaching and reevaluation.
questions.takeaway: Revise teaching from observed learning difficulties.
questions.learningObjective: Revise teaching from observed learning difficulties.

questions.title: Health app appraisal
questions.stem: A client wants to use an app for symptom tracking. Which features should be reviewed? Select all that apply.
options: Whether the app's advice has an identifiable credible source
How personal health data are used and shared
Whether a high download count proves clinical reliability
Whether colour preferences can replace checking intended use
why: Credible authorship and evidence help assess the information offered.
Data practices matter when entering sensitive information.
Popularity alone does not establish safety or accuracy.
Appearance does not establish suitability for the clinical purpose.
questions.takeaway: Review information quality and privacy before recommending a health app.
questions.learningObjective: Review information quality and privacy before recommending a health app.

questions.title: Setting an activity goal
questions.stem: An inactive adult wants to walk more but becomes discouraged by large goals. Which goal is most useful initially?
options: Improve fitness as much as possible
Walk for a mutually agreed short period on specified days, then review
Reach the neighbour's distance immediately
Record weight daily as the sole activity measure
why: A vague goal is difficult to implement or evaluate.
A specific achievable plan allows progress review and adjustment.
Another person's performance may not fit this client's baseline.
Weight alone does not measure activity participation or tolerance.
questions.takeaway: Set activity goals that are specific, feasible and reviewable.
questions.learningObjective: Set activity goals that are specific, feasible and reviewable.

questions.title: Exploring ambivalence
questions.stem: A client says, 'I know smoking harms me, but it helps me get through work.' What response best supports motivation?
options: List complications until the client agrees to quit
Set a quit date without discussion
Ask what the client likes and dislikes about smoking
Focus on whether coworkers approve of smoking
why: More warnings may not address the competing value the client describes.
An imposed goal may not reflect readiness.
Exploring both sides helps the client articulate reasons for change.
Coworker approval is less relevant than the client's goals and barriers.
questions.takeaway: Explore ambivalence before prescribing a behaviour-change goal.
questions.learningObjective: Explore ambivalence before prescribing a behaviour-change goal.

questions.title: Learning from a smoking lapse
questions.stem: After two weeks without smoking, a client smoked during an argument and feels the attempt is ruined. What should the nurse emphasize?
options: Review the trigger and adjust the quit plan
Restart only after several months of smoking
Count the lapse as proof of poor motivation
Focus exclusively on the number of cigarettes smoked
why: A lapse can identify coping supports needed for the next attempt.
Delaying support may unnecessarily prolong tobacco exposure.
One event does not establish lack of motivation.
Quantity alone does not explain the trigger or recovery plan.
questions.takeaway: Use a lapse to refine cessation strategies rather than abandon the goal.
questions.learningObjective: Use a lapse to refine cessation strategies rather than abandon the goal.

questions.title: Changing sugary drink intake
questions.stem: A client chooses replacing one daily soft drink with water as a first goal. What is the best nursing response?
options: Replace the client's goal with total dietary restriction
Ask for daily weight targets before accepting the goal
Explain that small changes cannot affect habits
Confirm when the substitution will occur and how progress will be reviewed
why: A more restrictive imposed goal may undermine engagement.
Weight targets are not necessary to evaluate this chosen behaviour.
Repeated small feasible changes can support sustained routines.
A concrete cue and review plan strengthen implementation.
questions.takeaway: Turn a chosen health behaviour into a practical routine and review plan.
questions.learningObjective: Turn a chosen health behaviour into a practical routine and review plan.

questions.title: Supporting tobacco cessation
questions.stem: Which assessments help tailor a client's quit plan? Select all that apply.
options: Times and situations associated with smoking
Previous strategies that helped or failed
Whether the client meets the nurse's preferred quit date
Only the brand and purchase location
why: Trigger patterns identify where coping strategies are needed.
Past experience can reveal effective supports and barriers.
Goals should reflect collaborative planning rather than the nurse's preference.
Product details alone do not capture dependence or readiness.
questions.takeaway: Tailor cessation support using triggers and prior attempts.
questions.learningObjective: Tailor cessation support using triggers and prior attempts.

questions.title: Physical activity with joint pain
questions.stem: An adult with stable osteoarthritis wants to become active but walking aggravates knee pain. What should the nurse recommend?
options: Avoid all exercise until joints are painless
Explore tolerable lower-impact activity and appropriate professional guidance
Increase walking speed to finish sooner
Use pain severity as the sole measure of exercise benefit
why: Complete inactivity can worsen conditioning and function.
Adapted activity can support health within symptoms and abilities.
Faster walking may increase loading without improving tolerance.
Benefits and safety require broader assessment than pain alone.
questions.takeaway: Adapt activity type to joint symptoms and functional goals.
questions.learningObjective: Adapt activity type to joint symptoms and functional goals.

questions.title: Returning to activity after illness
questions.stem: After a prolonged illness, a client wants to resume their previous exercise level immediately. What is the best advice?
options: Restart at the old workload without review
Avoid activity until strength returns spontaneously
Plan a gradual return based on current function and clinical guidance
Replace all movement with stretching indefinitely
why: Previous ability may exceed current capacity after deconditioning.
Waiting without rehabilitation may delay recovery of function.
Gradual progression respects current tolerance and recovery needs.
Stretching alone may not address endurance and strength goals.
questions.takeaway: Base activity progression on current capacity after illness.
questions.learningObjective: Base activity progression on current capacity after illness.

questions.title: Prolonged sitting at work
questions.stem: A desk worker exercises on weekends but sits for most workdays. Which additional habit is most relevant?
options: Build regular movement breaks into the workday
Replace all weekend activity with a standing desk
Track only total calories eaten at work
Increase caffeine to reduce perceived fatigue
why: Frequent movement addresses the prolonged sedentary pattern directly.
A workstation change need not replace beneficial activity.
Diet tracking does not change uninterrupted sitting.
Stimulants do not provide the benefits of movement.
questions.takeaway: Address prolonged sedentary time as well as planned exercise.
questions.learningObjective: Address prolonged sedentary time as well as planned exercise.

questions.title: Food-label comparison
questions.stem: A client aims to reduce sodium and compares two soups. Which comparison is valid?
options: Choose the package with less advertising
Compare sodium numbers without checking serving size
Select the soup with the lower price per tin
Compare sodium for equivalent amounts actually eaten
why: Advertising style does not establish sodium content.
Different serving sizes can make unadjusted comparisons misleading.
Cost does not determine sodium intake.
Equivalent portions allow a meaningful nutrient comparison.
questions.takeaway: Compare nutrition-label values using equivalent consumed portions.
questions.learningObjective: Compare nutrition-label values using equivalent consumed portions.

questions.title: Planning nutritious meals on a budget
questions.stem: Which suggestions may help a client with limited income obtain balanced meals? Select all that apply.
options: Consider affordable frozen or canned foods with suitable labels
Plan meals using available low-cost protein foods
Recommend only fresh specialty produce
Assume all packaged foods have the same nutritional value
why: Appropriate frozen and canned options can be nutritious and affordable.
Feasible protein sources support nutrition within the budget.
Specialty-only advice may be financially inaccessible.
Labels and preparation vary, so blanket assumptions are inaccurate.
questions.takeaway: Adapt nutrition teaching to cost and available food options.
questions.learningObjective: Adapt nutrition teaching to cost and available food options.

questions.title: Hydration in heat with restrictions
questions.stem: An older adult with a prescribed fluid limit asks how to manage a heat wave. What is the best response?
options: Ignore the limit throughout the heat wave
Seek an individualized fluid and cooling plan from the treating team
Maintain the limit without considering new symptoms
Use sports drinks as unrestricted extra fluid
why: Unsupervised excess intake may worsen the condition requiring restriction.
The plan must balance heat risk with the client's clinical limitations.
Heat may change needs and symptoms requiring reassessment.
Sports drinks still contribute fluid and may add unwanted electrolytes.
questions.takeaway: Individualize heat advice when medical fluid restrictions apply.
questions.learningObjective: Individualize heat advice when medical fluid restrictions apply.

questions.title: Shift-work sleep planning
questions.stem: A night-shift worker has fragmented daytime sleep because family activities continue nearby. What intervention best addresses the stated problem?
options: Add evening caffeine to stay awake longer
Extend screen use before daytime sleep
Agree on a protected sleep period and a dark quiet environment
Restrict sleep to days off
why: Additional caffeine may interfere with later sleep.
Stimulating light and activity can delay settling.
Environmental and household planning target the actual sleep disruption.
Restricting sleep to days off worsens cumulative sleep loss.
questions.takeaway: Protect a consistent sleep opportunity within shift-work constraints.
questions.learningObjective: Protect a consistent sleep opportunity within shift-work constraints.

questions.title: Persistent snoring and sleepiness
questions.stem: A client reports loud snoring, witnessed breathing pauses and daytime sleepiness despite enough time in bed. What should the nurse recommend?
options: Clinical assessment for a sleep-related breathing disorder
A larger pillow as the only intervention
More time in bed before mentioning breathing pauses
Caffeine at each meal to improve alertness
why: The combined symptoms warrant evaluation beyond sleep-hygiene advice.
Position changes alone do not evaluate reported breathing pauses.
Adequate sleep opportunity with apnea symptoms still needs assessment.
Stimulants may mask sleepiness without treating its cause.
questions.takeaway: Refer breathing pauses with daytime sleepiness for assessment.
questions.learningObjective: Refer breathing pauses with daytime sleepiness for assessment.

questions.title: Alcohol discussion in primary care
questions.stem: A client says they drink 'socially' and asks whether that affects health. What should the nurse clarify first?
options: Preferred beverage brand
Whether friends drink more
Whether alcohol use is socially accepted
Amount, frequency, occasions and relevant health concerns
why: Brand alone does not quantify exposure or risk.
Peer consumption does not establish the client's health impact.
Social acceptability does not describe clinical risk.
Specific patterns and context support an individualized discussion.
questions.takeaway: Clarify alcohol quantity and pattern rather than relying on social labels.
questions.learningObjective: Clarify alcohol quantity and pattern rather than relying on social labels.

questions.title: Preventive care with limited transportation
questions.stem: Which approaches may improve preventive-care access for a rural client? Select all that apply.
options: Coordinate appropriate services during the same trip
Explore available transport assistance
Replace every examination with a phone call
Assume missed visits mean screening is unwanted
why: Coordinated visits can reduce travel burden when clinically feasible.
Practical transport support addresses an identified access barrier.
Some assessments require in-person examination or testing.
Access problems do not establish the client's preferences.
questions.takeaway: Organize preventive care around real transportation constraints.
questions.learningObjective: Organize preventive care around real transportation constraints.

questions.title: Menopause symptom discussion
questions.stem: A client experiencing bothersome hot flashes wants advice but is concerned about medication risks. What is the best initial approach?
options: Recommend one treatment for every menopausal client
Assess symptom impact, history and preferences before reviewing options
Recommend hormones before reviewing contraindications
Focus only on laboratory confirmation before discussing coping
why: Treatment should reflect symptoms and individual risks.
Assessment supports an informed discussion of suitable options.
Hormonal treatment requires individualized clinical review.
Practical support need not wait for routine laboratory confirmation.
questions.takeaway: Individualize menopause counselling to symptom burden and clinical history.
questions.learningObjective: Individualize menopause counselling to symptom burden and clinical history.

questions.title: Postmenopausal bleeding
questions.stem: A client who has had no periods for two years reports new vaginal spotting and asks if it can wait until a routine visit months away. What should the nurse advise?
options: Track it until it becomes heavy
Treat it as an expected menopause symptom
Arrange timely clinical assessment even if bleeding is light
Increase dietary iron before deciding on follow-up
why: Light bleeding still warrants evaluation after menopause.
New postmenopausal bleeding should not be presumed normal.
Assessment can identify the cause and appropriate follow-up.
Iron intake does not establish why bleeding occurred.
questions.takeaway: Arrange assessment for new postmenopausal bleeding.
questions.learningObjective: Arrange assessment for new postmenopausal bleeding.

questions.title: Bone-health prevention
questions.stem: A sedentary adult with a family history of osteoporosis asks what they can change. Which plan is most appropriate?
options: Review suitable weight-bearing and strengthening activity, nutrition and risk assessment
Begin high-impact exercise without assessing fracture risk
Focus exclusively on calcium supplements
Avoid all activity to prevent a possible fracture
why: Bone health requires a tailored combination of activity, nutrition and risk review.
Unassessed impact activity may be unsuitable for some clients.
Supplements alone do not address activity, falls or overall risk.
Inactivity can worsen strength and functional protection.
questions.takeaway: Combine individualized activity, nutrition and risk review for bone health.
questions.learningObjective: Combine individualized activity, nutrition and risk review for bone health.

questions.title: A height-loss report
questions.stem: An older adult reports becoming shorter and has new mid-back discomfort without a major injury. What should the nurse recommend?
options: Reassure that every height change is expected aging
Stretch vigorously before considering assessment
Wait until a fall occurs to evaluate bone health
Arrange assessment for a possible vertebral fracture or other cause
why: New pain with height loss may indicate more than expected aging.
Unassessed vigorous movement may aggravate an injury.
Fractures can occur without a reported major fall.
The combined changes justify clinical evaluation.
questions.takeaway: Assess height loss accompanied by new back pain.
questions.learningObjective: Assess height loss accompanied by new back pain.

questions.title: Vision and healthy aging
questions.stem: Which reported changes require evaluation rather than attribution to normal aging? Select all that apply.
options: New difficulty reading medication labels despite usual glasses
Gradual glare that limits night driving
Preference for brighter reading light without functional difficulty
Use of reading glasses prescribed at a recent examination
why: A new functional barrier may compromise medication safety.
Driving-limiting glare warrants assessment of vision and safety.
Lighting preference alone is less concerning without impairment.
Appropriate prescribed correction is not itself a warning finding.
questions.takeaway: Evaluate visual changes that impair important daily activities.
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate visual changes that impair important daily activities.

questions.title: Hearing-related social withdrawal
questions.stem: An older adult stops attending a discussion group because conversation is difficult in background noise. What is the best response?
options: Assume the client no longer enjoys social contact
Arrange hearing review and explore a quieter participation setting
Encourage lip-reading without discussing assessment
Replace all social interaction with written messages
why: Withdrawal may reflect a remediable communication barrier.
Hearing assessment and environmental changes may restore participation.
Lip-reading alone may not meet the client's needs.
A single communication mode unnecessarily narrows social options.
questions.takeaway: Address hearing barriers that reduce social participation.
questions.learningObjective: Address hearing barriers that reduce social participation.

questions.title: Urinary urgency and community activity
questions.stem: An older adult avoids outings because of urinary urgency but has not discussed it with a clinician. What should the nurse do?
options: Recommend accepting it as unavoidable aging
Suggest avoiding fluids before every outing
Encourage assessment and individualized continence strategies
Advise staying near home permanently
why: Urgency may have treatable contributors and warrants assessment.
Broad restriction can create dehydration without resolving the cause.
Evaluation can support continence and valued activities.
Avoidance reduces participation without addressing the problem.
questions.takeaway: Promote assessment of continence concerns that limit daily life.
questions.learningObjective: Promote assessment of continence concerns that limit daily life.

questions.title: Unintended weight loss in later life
questions.stem: An older adult living alone has loose clothing and reduced food intake since their partner died. What is the best initial nursing action?
options: Assess weight change, intake, oral function, mood and access to food
Offer only a generic low-fat diet sheet
Attribute the change solely to age
Recommend an appetite supplement without assessment
why: Multiple interacting causes may contribute and require targeted support.
Restrictive generic advice does not address reduced intake.
Unintended loss should not automatically be normalized as aging.
Unassessed supplementation may miss a treatable cause.
questions.takeaway: Assess physical and social contributors to unintended weight loss.
questions.learningObjective: Assess physical and social contributors to unintended weight loss.

questions.title: Driving and functional change
questions.stem: An older adult reports recent near misses and difficulty judging distances when driving. What should the nurse recommend?
options: Continue driving because no collision has occurred
Rely on age alone to decide fitness
Restrict driving only when family members insist
Arrange prompt assessment and discuss interim transport and safety plans
why: Near misses may indicate meaningful risk before a collision occurs.
Functional ability, not age alone, guides assessment.
Family concern is useful but not required to act on symptoms.
Assessment and practical alternatives address safety and independence together.
questions.takeaway: Respond to driving-related functional changes with assessment and transport planning.
questions.learningObjective: Respond to driving-related functional changes with assessment and transport planning.

questions.title: Maintaining independence at home
questions.stem: Which assessments help tailor health-promotion support for an older adult living alone? Select all that apply.
options: Ability to obtain and prepare food
Ability to manage appointments and medications
Chronological age as the sole measure of support need
Family preference without asking the client
why: Food access and preparation affect nutrition and independence.
Complex daily tasks reveal practical support needs.
Age alone does not establish functional ability.
The client's goals and choices remain central to planning.
questions.takeaway: Assess everyday function rather than assuming needs from age.
questions.learningObjective: Assess everyday function rather than assuming needs from age.

questions.title: Social connection after retirement
questions.stem: A recently retired client feels isolated and wants more contact but dislikes large groups. Which suggestion best fits the goal?
options: Enrol in the largest available senior club
Explore a small regular activity linked to an existing interest
Explain that retirement requires accepting loneliness
Arrange several unfamiliar activities without asking preferences
why: Group size may reproduce the barrier the client describes.
A preferred manageable activity supports feasible sustained connection.
Loneliness can be addressed rather than presumed inevitable.
Imposed unfamiliar activities may not support engagement.
questions.takeaway: Match social-connection opportunities to the client's interests and comfort.
questions.learningObjective: Match social-connection opportunities to the client's interests and comfort.

questions.title: Discussing sexuality in later life
questions.stem: An older adult asks about sexual activity after beginning a new relationship. What approach best supports health promotion?
options: Discuss only urinary symptoms
Assume infection prevention is unnecessary after menopause
Offer private, respectful assessment of sexual goals and prevention needs
Ask the adult's children to identify appropriate advice
why: Urinary symptoms do not cover sexual-health needs.
Infection exposure remains possible regardless of fertility.
Individual assessment avoids assumptions and supports relevant counselling.
The capable adult's privacy and preferences guide the discussion.
questions.takeaway: Include sexual health in older-adult assessment without age-based assumptions.
questions.learningObjective: Include sexual health in older-adult assessment without age-based assumptions.

questions.title: Advance-care conversations
questions.stem: A healthy older adult asks when to tell family what matters if serious illness occurs. What should the nurse suggest?
options: Begin values-based discussions while the client can participate fully
Wait until an emergency determines the available choices
Ask family to select preferences independently
Focus only on completing a form without discussion
why: Early discussion helps others understand values before a crisis.
Emergencies may reduce time and ability for considered conversation.
The client's values should guide planning.
Forms alone may not communicate the meaning behind choices.
questions.takeaway: Encourage early discussion of values for future health decisions.
questions.learningObjective: Encourage early discussion of values for future health decisions.

questions.title: Caregiver health maintenance
questions.stem: A caregiver misses their own appointments because the care recipient cannot stay alone. What is the best nursing response?
options: Remind them more firmly that appointments matter
Suggest permanently stopping all caregiving tasks
Provide another screening brochure only
Explore respite or replacement support for appointment times
why: The caregiver already identifies a practical rather than informational barrier.
A complete role change is not the necessary first response.
A brochure does not provide supervision for the care recipient.
Targeted replacement support can enable the caregiver's own preventive care.
questions.takeaway: Address caregiving barriers to the caregiver's health maintenance.
questions.learningObjective: Address caregiving barriers to the caregiver's health maintenance.

questions.title: Evaluating a community walking program
questions.stem: Which outcomes best indicate that a new accessible walking group is meeting its health-promotion goal? Select all that apply.
options: Participants attend regularly and report manageable exertion
Participants sustain agreed activity goals over time
The program printed many flyers
Staff purchased identical footwear for every participant
why: Participation with tolerable effort supports feasibility of the program.
Sustained behaviour is more informative than one-time interest.
Distribution volume measures promotion activity rather than participant outcomes.
Uniform equipment purchase does not establish participation or benefit.
questions.takeaway: Evaluate health-promotion programs using meaningful participation and behaviour outcomes.
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate health-promotion programs using meaningful participation and behaviour outcomes.

questions.title: A diabetes follow-up gap
questions.stem: A client with diabetes attends medication reviews but has never discussed retinal screening because vision seems normal. What should teaching emphasize?
options: Screening can identify changes before symptoms occur
Eye follow-up is needed only for blurred vision
Reading glasses provide equivalent screening
Stable glucose readings remove the need for eye review
why: Preventive screening may detect disease before noticeable visual change.
Waiting for symptoms can delay detection.
Corrective lenses do not assess diabetic retinal disease.
Glucose control reduces risk but does not replace recommended screening.
questions.takeaway: Explain the preventive purpose of diabetes eye screening.
questions.learningObjective: Explain the preventive purpose of diabetes eye screening.

questions.title: Assessing a written action plan
questions.stem: A client has an asthma action plan but cannot identify when to seek urgent help. What should the nurse do next?
options: Review inhaler colours again
Practise a symptom scenario using the plan's escalation instructions
Ask the client to copy the plan
File the plan because it is signed
why: Colour recall does not establish recognition of worsening illness.
Scenario practice tests the missing decision skill.
Copying does not demonstrate understanding of escalation.
A signature does not establish usable knowledge.
questions.takeaway: Evaluate whether clients can apply action-plan escalation instructions.
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate whether clients can apply action-plan escalation instructions.

questions.title: A symptom diary with purpose
questions.stem: A client with recurrent headaches asks how to make a diary useful for follow-up. Which entry is most helpful?
options: 'Bad day' without details
A pain rating without timing
Timing, associated symptoms, possible triggers and treatments used
A list of family members with headaches only
why: A vague label provides little information for pattern assessment.
Intensity alone omits relevant context and response.
Structured observations support assessment of patterns and treatment response.
Family history matters but does not describe current episodes.
questions.takeaway: Record symptom context and response when preparing for clinical review.
questions.learningObjective: Record symptom context and response when preparing for clinical review.

questions.title: Weight monitoring in an action plan
questions.stem: A client with heart failure weighs at different times in different clothing. The plan includes reporting weight changes. What should the nurse reinforce?
options: Weigh only when ankle swelling appears
Average the scale readings from different households
Record only the lowest reading each week
Use comparable daily conditions and follow the prescribed reporting plan
why: Symptom-only measurement may miss useful early trends.
Different scales may introduce measurement differences.
Selective recording hides rather than clarifies trends.
Consistency improves interpretation within the individualized action plan.
questions.takeaway: Standardize home measurements used to guide follow-up.
questions.learningObjective: Standardize home measurements used to guide follow-up.

questions.title: Planning ongoing self-management
questions.stem: Which elements make a chronic-condition action plan usable at home? Select all that apply.
options: Clear changes that should trigger contact
A reachable contact and backup route
A list of diagnoses without action instructions
Instructions that assume every client can access online portals
why: Specific triggers translate observations into action.
A practical contact route enables timely help-seeking.
Diagnosis names alone do not guide home decisions.
Digital access should be assessed rather than assumed.
questions.takeaway: Link self-monitoring findings to feasible action and contact instructions.
questions.learningObjective: Link self-monitoring findings to feasible action and contact instructions.

questions.title: Exercise confidence after rehabilitation
questions.stem: A client completes rehabilitation but fears exercising without staff present. Which nursing action best supports maintenance?
options: Repeat the full rehabilitation course automatically
Rehearse the agreed home plan and response to warning symptoms
Tell the client fear will disappear alone

questions.takeaway: Prepare clients to apply rehabilitation learning outside supervised settings.
questions.learningObjective: Prepare clients to apply rehabilitation learning outside supervised settings.

questions.title: A dietary goal and cultural foods
questions.stem: A client with hypertension wants to reduce sodium while continuing traditional family meals. What is the best approach?
options: Replace the entire cuisine with a standard menu
Ask the family to prepare separate meals indefinitely

Advise avoiding family gatherings involving food

questions.learningObjective: Adapt health goals within meaningful cultural food practices.

questions.title: Financial barriers to prescribed care
questions.stem: A client attends education but cannot afford transportation to laboratory monitoring. What should the nurse prioritize?
options: Explore accessible testing and financial or transport assistance

Ask for a commitment to try harder
Assume fewer tests are safe without consulting the plan
why: Practical access support targets the identified barrier.
More information does not make testing reachable.
Effort-based framing misattributes a material limitation.

questions.takeaway: Address access barriers to recommended preventive monitoring.
questions.learningObjective: Address access barriers to recommended preventive monitoring.

questions.title: Chronic pain and valued activity
questions.stem: A client with an established chronic-pain plan alternates doing all housework on good days and remaining inactive afterward. Which teaching is most relevant?
options: Finish as much as possible whenever pain is low
Stop all housework until pain resolves
Use pain alone to decide every day's workload
Plan manageable activity periods and breaks across days
why: Overactivity may contribute to the reported flare-and-rest cycle.
Complete avoidance can reduce function and participation.

questions.learningObjective: Use activity pacing to support sustainable function with chronic pain.

questions.title: Diabetes appointment preparation

Difficulties obtaining or using prescribed treatment
Only the most favourable glucose values
A medication list excluding nonprescription products

Access and technique problems may explain difficulties with the plan.
Selective results can hide clinically relevant patterns.
Nonprescription products may affect treatment and should be disclosed.
questions.takeaway: Prepare complete clinically relevant information for chronic-disease review.
questions.learningObjective: Prepare complete clinically relevant information for chronic-disease review.

questions.title: Food insecurity screening

questions.learningObjective: Recognize unreliable food access even when food is available today.

questions.title: Housing and asthma prevention
questions.stem: A parent follows the child's asthma plan but reports visible dampness and mould in rented housing. What action best complements self-care teaching?
options: Focus only on inhaler adherence
Help connect the family with housing and environmental-health resources
Recommend keeping all windows open in every season
Suggest the parent stop reporting symptoms until moving
why: Adherence does not remove a possible environmental contributor.

Ventilation advice alone may be ineffective or inappropriate in some conditions.

questions.takeaway: Address housing conditions that obstruct chronic-disease prevention.
questions.learningObjective: Address housing conditions that obstruct chronic-disease prevention.

questions.title: Designing a community program
questions.stem: A nurse plans a nutrition program for a neighbourhood with varied languages and food access. What should occur first?
options: Select a standard menu before consultation
Print materials in the nurse's preferred language
Ask residents about priorities, resources and barriers
Choose the venue with the most attractive kitchen

questions.learningObjective: Assess community priorities before designing health-promotion activities.

questions.title: Screening uptake disparity
questions.stem: A clinic finds lower screening completion among clients who need interpretation. What is the best next step?
options: Send the same reminder more often
Attribute the difference to cultural refusal
Remove these clients from the denominator
Explore communication and access barriers with affected clients

Group-level assumptions can conceal remediable system barriers.

questions.learningObjective: Investigate access barriers before explaining screening disparities as preference.

questions.title: Accessible group education
questions.stem: Which design features support participation in a community health class? Select all that apply.
options: Check transport and physical access
Provide language support that matches participants' needs
Require participants to disclose diagnoses publicly
Use attendance as the only measure of learning
why: Physical and transport access affect whether people can participate.

Public disclosure is not necessary for routine education and may deter attendance.
Attendance does not demonstrate understanding or skill.

questions.learningObjective: Design health education around access, privacy and meaningful learning.

questions.title: Understanding prevention levels

options: Rehabilitation after established complications
Early identification for assessment and management
Treatment of an acute hypertensive emergency
Confirmation of diagnosis from any single reading

questions.learningObjective: Explain screening as early detection requiring appropriate follow-up.

questions.title: Responding to a high screening reading

Dismiss it because exertion preceded measurement
Repeat appropriately after rest and arrange follow-up based on findings

questions.takeaway: Confirm screening measurements under suitable conditions and arrange appropriate follow-up.
questions.learningObjective: Confirm screening measurements under suitable conditions and arrange appropriate follow-up.

questions.title: Following up a referral
questions.stem: A nurse gives a client contact details for a smoking-cessation service. At review, the client has not called because telephone conversations are difficult. What is the best action?
options: Find an accessible referral route with the client's agreement
Reissue the same number without discussion
Mark the referral completed because information was provided
Stop offering support until the client calls independently

questions.learningObjective: Verify whether referral pathways are usable for the client.

questions.title: Choosing a program outcome
questions.stem: A prenatal education program aims to improve recognition of warning symptoms. Which measure best evaluates this objective?
options: Number of chairs filled
Number of handouts distributed
Satisfaction with refreshments
Ability to choose the appropriate action in symptom scenarios

Distribution measures activity rather than learning.

questions.learningObjective: Match program evaluation to the intended learning outcome.

questions.title: Community partnership

options: Ask whom the community wants involved in planning
Incorporate locally identified priorities and knowledge
Assume one program fits all Indigenous communities
Seek feedback about whether participation feels culturally safe

questions.learningObjective: Build wellness programs with community-defined participation and priorities.

questions.title: A culturally meaningful health goal

Require choosing one system of care before further discussion
Assume the family uses a particular ceremony
Refer elsewhere without exploring the request

questions.learningObjective: Ask how clients want traditional healing included in their care.

questions.title: A heat-risk plan

questions.learningObjective: Plan cooling access and social check-ins before heat illness develops.

questions.title: Noise exposure and hearing

Use protection only when ringing begins
Reduce leisure music but ignore work exposure
Arrange occupational hearing review and consistent suitable protection

questions.learningObjective: Respond to noise-related symptoms with assessment and reliable exposure protection.

questions.title: Preparing for medication storage away from home

options: Confirm product-specific storage requirements with the pharmacist
Plan transport that maintains required conditions
Assume every medication can be frozen

Labels support identification and safe use during travel.
questions.takeaway: Plan travel storage using the medication's actual requirements.
questions.learningObjective: Plan travel storage using the medication's actual requirements.

questions.title: Responding to a wellness supplement claim
