Try a larger dose to judge benefit quickly
Stop prescribed treatments while trying the supplement
why: Individual medications and conditions can alter supplement risks.
Universal marketing claims do not establish individual suitability.
Higher exposure can increase harm without establishing effectiveness.
Prescribed treatment changes require appropriate clinical review.
questions.takeaway: Review supplements in the context of the client's medications and conditions.
questions.learningObjective: Review supplements in the context of the client's medications and conditions.

questions.title: Testing understanding of an emergency plan
questions.stem: A client can recite emergency contact numbers but cannot explain which symptoms require emergency services. What teaching method best addresses the gap?
options: Ask for faster number recall
Work through realistic symptom examples and actions
Provide a second identical contact card
Add more nonurgent service numbers
why: Speed of recall does not clarify when to use each service.
Applied scenarios test the missing judgment skill.
Duplicate numbers do not resolve symptom interpretation.
Additional contacts may increase confusion without clarifying priorities.
questions.takeaway: Teach how to choose an emergency response, not only how to name contacts.
questions.learningObjective: Teach how to choose an emergency response, not only how to name contacts.

questions.title: Planning care during fasting
questions.stem: A client with diabetes plans a religious fast and asks about their usual medication schedule. What should the nurse do?
options: Recommend the usual regimen without reviewing intake changes
Advise abandoning the observance before discussing options
Arrange individualized medication, monitoring and safety planning before the fast
Suggest self-adjusting each dose according to hunger
why: Altered intake can change medication-related risks.
Respectful planning should explore goals and clinical constraints.
Proactive coordination can support informed choices and safer participation.
Hunger is not a reliable medication-adjustment guide.
questions.takeaway: Coordinate individualized care when fasting changes intake and treatment needs.
questions.learningObjective: Coordinate individualized care when fasting changes intake and treatment needs.

questions.title: Healthy eating with limited cooking facilities
questions.stem: A client living in temporary accommodation has only a refrigerator and microwave. Which approach is most useful?
options: Give recipes requiring a full kitchen
Focus on motivation to cook from scratch
Recommend skipping meals until housing changes
Build a nutritious plan using available storage and cooking equipment
why: Equipment-incompatible recipes cannot be implemented.
Motivation is not the identified barrier.
Skipping meals worsens rather than addresses the access problem.
A feasible plan adapts nutrition goals to actual resources.
questions.takeaway: Match food advice to available storage and preparation facilities.
questions.learningObjective: Match food advice to available storage and preparation facilities.

questions.title: Evaluating home-monitoring logs
questions.stem: Which patterns should a nurse discuss with a client who brings a symptom log? Select all that apply.
options: Repeated symptoms linked to a particular activity
Changes after a prescribed intervention
Missing entries as definite proof that symptoms were absent
Consistently worsening function despite similar numeric ratings
why: Activity relationships may help identify triggers and adaptations.
Before-and-after patterns support evaluation of the treatment plan.
Missing data cannot establish absence of symptoms.
Function provides important information beyond a single rating.
questions.takeaway: Interpret self-monitoring data with context, missing information and functional changes.
questions.learningObjective: Interpret self-monitoring data with context, missing information and functional changes.

questions.title: A client declines a preventive test
questions.stem: After balanced counselling, a capable client declines an offered screening test. What is the best health-promotion response?
options: Explore remaining questions, respect the choice and explain how to revisit it
Repeat risk statements until consent is obtained
Cancel all future preventive discussions
Ask a family member to approve the test instead
why: Informed choice can coexist with ongoing supportive access.
Repetition intended to secure agreement can become coercive.
Declining one test does not remove other preventive needs.
Family preference does not replace a capable client's decision.
questions.takeaway: Preserve informed choice and future access when screening is declined.
questions.learningObjective: Preserve informed choice and future access when screening is declined.

questions.title: A positive stool screening result
questions.stem: An asymptomatic client has a positive stool-based colorectal screening result and wants to repeat it until negative. What should the nurse explain?
options: A second negative result automatically cancels the first
Recommended diagnostic follow-up is needed rather than relying on repeated screening
The positive result confirms cancer without further tests
Symptoms must appear before further assessment is useful
why: A repeat negative screen does not reliably resolve the initial finding.
Diagnostic follow-up addresses the reason the screening test was positive.
Screening positivity is not itself a definitive diagnosis.
Follow-up is useful before symptoms develop.
questions.takeaway: Follow an abnormal screening result through the recommended diagnostic pathway.
questions.learningObjective: Follow an abnormal screening result through the recommended diagnostic pathway.

questions.title: Prevention after cancer treatment
questions.stem: A client completing cancer treatment assumes routine health care is no longer needed outside oncology. What should the nurse reinforce?
options: Only recurrence surveillance matters now
Preventive care can stop for all unrelated conditions
Coordinate survivorship follow-up with ongoing primary and preventive care
Wait for oncology discharge before addressing any new concern
why: General health needs continue alongside cancer surveillance.
Other conditions and prevention needs remain relevant.
Coordinated care can address treatment effects and general health maintenance.
New concerns should be assessed through appropriate routes when they arise.
questions.takeaway: Integrate survivorship care with ongoing general health maintenance.
questions.learningObjective: Integrate survivorship care with ongoing general health maintenance.

questions.title: Low confidence with new equipment
questions.stem: A client can safely use a home monitor under observation but says, 'I will fail when alone.' What intervention is most useful?
options: Repeat technical facts without practice
Have family take over all monitoring permanently
Remove monitoring from the plan without review
Rehearse the home routine and agree on support if difficulty occurs
why: Knowledge repetition may not address confidence in the real setting.
Permanent takeover may unnecessarily reduce autonomy.
Changing the clinical plan requires appropriate assessment.
Contextual practice and backup support promote confidence and independence.
questions.takeaway: Strengthen confidence by practising the actual home routine and backup plan.
questions.learningObjective: Strengthen confidence by practising the actual home routine and backup plan.

questions.title: Preventive care during unstable housing
questions.stem: Which adaptations may help a client without stable housing complete follow-up? Select all that apply.
options: Agree on a reliable contact method the client can access
Coordinate flexible or outreach-based services where available
Make portal access the only appointment route
Assume a mailed reminder will reach the client
why: A usable contact route supports continuity despite address changes.
Flexible access can reduce housing-related barriers.
Exclusive digital access may exclude someone without connectivity.
Mailing is ineffective if a stable address is unavailable.
questions.takeaway: Adapt follow-up routes to housing and communication realities.
questions.learningObjective: Adapt follow-up routes to housing and communication realities.

questions.title: Preparing a person with limited stamina
questions.stem: A client with fatigue must learn several home-care tasks. Which schedule best supports learning?
options: Several brief sessions timed to periods of better energy
One extended session after all daily care
A single rapid review immediately before transport
Independent reading without checking stamina or understanding
why: Short well-timed sessions match the client's available attention and energy.
A prolonged session may exceed stamina after other demands.
Last-minute rapid teaching leaves little opportunity for practice.
Reading alone may not meet the learning or fatigue needs.
questions.takeaway: Match teaching duration and timing to stamina.
questions.learningObjective: Match teaching duration and timing to stamina.

questions.title: A family member dominates education
questions.stem: A capable adult wants to manage their own care, but a relative answers every teaching question. What should the nurse do?
options: Direct all future teaching to the relative
Re-establish the client's goals and invite agreed family support
Exclude the family permanently without asking the client
Assess only the relative's recall before discharge
why: The client's desired participation remains central.
Clarifying roles preserves autonomy and useful support.
The client may still want family involvement.
Proxy recall does not establish the client's ability or preferences.
questions.takeaway: Keep the client central when involving family in self-care teaching.
questions.learningObjective: Keep the client central when involving family in self-care teaching.

questions.title: A changed learning need
questions.stem: A client previously managed injections independently but develops reduced vision. What is the best response?
options: Rely on the old competency record
Ask family to estimate doses from memory
Reassess technique and accessible support with the new visual limitation
Continue unchanged until an error occurs
why: Prior competence may not reflect current functional ability.
Dose estimation creates avoidable medication risk.
Changed abilities require renewed assessment and adaptation.
Preventive reassessment should precede a harmful error.
questions.takeaway: Reassess self-care competence when functional abilities change.
questions.learningObjective: Reassess self-care competence when functional abilities change.

questions.title: Health goals after disability
questions.stem: A client with a new mobility disability wants to return to community gardening. What should health-promotion planning emphasize?
options: Walking ability as the only marker of success
Delaying all goals until full recovery
Standard activity targets without adaptation
Accessible gardening tasks and supports aligned with the client's goal
why: Participation can be meaningful without restoration of walking.
Waiting may unnecessarily postpone valued activity.
Unadapted targets may not fit abilities or priorities.
Goal-directed adaptation supports health, participation and autonomy.
questions.takeaway: Define health-promotion outcomes around meaningful participation with disability.
questions.learningObjective: Define health-promotion outcomes around meaningful participation with disability.

questions.title: Checking a home plan's feasibility
questions.stem: Which questions identify whether a client can carry out a discharge self-care plan? Select all that apply.
options: 'Can you obtain the required supplies?'
'Where will you do this task at home?'
'Did you receive the discharge folder?' as the sole evaluation
'Will everyone in your household perform the task identically?'
why: Supply access affects whether the plan can be implemented.
The home setting can reveal practical barriers or needed adaptations.
Receiving paperwork does not establish practical readiness.
Consistent essential safety matters more than identical personal routines.
questions.takeaway: Check resources and setting when evaluating a home-care plan.
questions.learningObjective: Check resources and setting when evaluating a home-care plan.

questions.title: A changing prevention priority
questions.stem: A client has stable chronic conditions but recently lost access to food and heating. What should the nurse prioritize in the health-promotion plan?
options: Continue only the previous exercise targets
Address immediate basic-resource barriers alongside ongoing care
Delay all health contact until employment returns
Increase written instructions without discussing resources
why: Previous goals may be impractical while basic needs are threatened.
Food and safe housing conditions directly influence health and plan feasibility.
Delayed contact can worsen unmet needs and treatment gaps.
More instructions do not provide material resources.
questions.takeaway: Reprioritize health promotion when basic living conditions change.
questions.learningObjective: Reprioritize health promotion when basic living conditions change.

questions.title: Relating activity to personal values
questions.stem: A client dislikes formal exercise but wants stamina to play with grandchildren. What nursing response best supports engagement?
options: Insist on a gym program as the first step
Focus only on weight change
Develop enjoyable gradual activity linked to that valued role
Compare the client with more active peers
why: A disliked prescribed setting may reduce participation.
Weight may not be the client's motivating goal.
Personally meaningful benefits can support sustained behaviour change.
Social comparison may not address individual preferences or ability.
questions.takeaway: Connect health behaviours with the client's own valued activities.
questions.learningObjective: Connect health behaviours with the client's own valued activities.

questions.title: Preventive-care reminder consent
questions.stem: A clinic offers text reminders for sensitive screening appointments. What should the nurse confirm?
options: The client's preferred safe contact method and message privacy
The relative's phone number as a default
Only whether the phone can receive images
That detailed results may be included without further discussion
why: Contact preferences and privacy determine whether reminders are appropriate and safe.
A relative's number may not preserve the client's confidentiality.
Image capability is not the main access or privacy issue.
Detailed disclosures require appropriate consent and secure processes.
questions.takeaway: Confirm safe communication preferences for preventive-care reminders.
questions.learningObjective: Confirm safe communication preferences for preventive-care reminders.

questions.title: Interpreting a health trend
questions.stem: A client increased walking and reports better stamina, but their weight is unchanged after a month. What should the nurse explain?
options: Lack of weight loss proves the plan failed
The client should stop walking and reassess later
Weight is the only objective health-promotion outcome
Improved function can be a meaningful benefit even without weight change
why: Behaviour and functional gains can occur without immediate weight loss.
Stopping a tolerable useful activity is not supported by these findings.
Health outcomes include function, symptoms and sustained participation.
Better stamina is relevant to the activity goal.
questions.takeaway: Evaluate health behaviour using meaningful functional outcomes as well as weight.
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate health behaviour using meaningful functional outcomes as well as weight.

questions.title: Sustaining a new health habit
questions.stem: A client meets a walking goal for three weeks and asks how to maintain it through bad weather. Which strategies are useful? Select all that apply.
options: Identify an accessible indoor alternative
Link activity to a stable daily cue
Wait for motivation to return after winter
Review barriers and adjust the plan periodically
why: A backup setting reduces weather-related disruption.
A reliable cue can support repetition and routine.
Waiting may interrupt an established achievable habit.
Periodic review keeps the plan matched to changing circumstances.
questions.takeaway: Anticipate barriers and backup routines when maintaining behaviour change.
questions.learningObjective: Anticipate barriers and backup routines when maintaining behaviour change.

questions.title: Prenatal pica disclosure
questions.stem: A pregnant client quietly reports eating clay and craving ice. What is the most appropriate nursing response?
options: Explore the behaviour and arrange nutritional and clinical assessment
Recommend replacing clay with ice without further review
Treat the disclosure only as a cultural preference
Focus on calorie intake without discussing the substances
why: Nonfood ingestion and persistent cravings warrant assessment for nutritional and exposure concerns.
Substitution alone does not identify associated deficiencies or risks.
Cultural context matters but does not replace clinical assessment.
Calories alone do not address pica-related concerns.
questions.takeaway: Assess nonfood cravings during pregnancy without judgment.
questions.learningObjective: Assess nonfood cravings during pregnancy without judgment.

questions.title: Fish advice during pregnancy
questions.stem: A pregnant client stopped eating all fish after hearing about mercury. What should the nurse recommend?
options: Avoid every type of fish until breastfeeding ends
Review current Canadian advice to select lower-mercury options
Choose fish only by price
Eat any species if it is cooked thoroughly
why: Broad exclusion may unnecessarily remove nutritious foods.
Species-specific advice balances nutritional benefits and contaminant exposure.
Price does not establish mercury content.
Cooking does not reliably remove mercury from fish.
questions.takeaway: Use species-specific guidance rather than blanket fish avoidance.
questions.learningObjective: Use species-specific guidance rather than blanket fish avoidance.

questions.title: Prenatal supplement duplication
questions.stem: A pregnant client takes a prenatal vitamin and plans to add several 'pregnancy support' products. What should the nurse assess first?
options: Whether all packages use the same colour
Whether products have testimonials
Combined ingredients and total amounts already consumed
Whether products are sold near prenatal vitamins
why: Packaging colour does not identify duplicate nutrients.
Testimonials do not establish safe combined intake.
Multiple products may duplicate nutrients or introduce unsuitable ingredients.
Retail placement does not establish compatibility.
questions.takeaway: Review combined supplement ingredients before adding prenatal products.
questions.learningObjective: Review combined supplement ingredients before adding prenatal products.

questions.title: Persistent pregnancy vomiting
questions.stem: A pregnant client cannot retain fluids, feels dizzy on standing and urinates much less than usual. What should the nurse advise?
options: Continue dietary changes until the next prenatal visit
Try a larger meal before seeking help
Record symptoms for several days first
Obtain prompt clinical assessment for dehydration and treatment needs
why: Intake strategies alone are insufficient when dehydration signs develop.
A larger meal does not address poor fluid tolerance.
Delayed assessment may worsen volume depletion.
The combined findings require timely assessment and management.
questions.takeaway: Escalate pregnancy vomiting when fluid tolerance and hydration worsen.
questions.learningObjective: Escalate pregnancy vomiting when fluid tolerance and hydration worsen.

questions.title: Preparing for prenatal appointments
questions.stem: Which information should a client bring to a prenatal visit? Select all that apply.
options: Current prescription and nonprescription products
Previous pregnancy complications
Only symptoms that have lasted a full month
Questions about mood, sleep or coping
why: Product review identifies exposures and treatment questions.
Previous complications can influence current surveillance.
New concerns can merit assessment before a month passes.
Emotional wellbeing is part of comprehensive prenatal care.
questions.takeaway: Include treatment history, obstetric history and emotional concerns in prenatal review.
questions.learningObjective: Include treatment history, obstetric history and emotional concerns in prenatal review.

questions.title: Breastfeeding and return to work
questions.stem: A breastfeeding parent returns to work in a month and wants to continue providing milk. What planning is most useful?
options: Wait until the first workday to test the routine
Explore expressing, storage requirements and feasible breaks before returning
Assume longer workdays require immediate weaning
Recommend identical feeding times every day regardless of infant cues
why: Advance rehearsal can reveal practical barriers before the transition.
A realistic plan addresses milk provision and workplace constraints.
Continued breastfeeding may be possible with individualized support.
Rigid timing may not fit infant needs or work realities.
questions.takeaway: Plan milk expression and workplace feasibility before returning to employment.
questions.learningObjective: Plan milk expression and workplace feasibility before returning to employment.

questions.title: A breastfeeding parent's medication question
questions.stem: A parent taking a prescribed medicine is told by a friend to stop breastfeeding. What should the nurse do?
options: Recommend stopping medication immediately
Confirm that all medicines enter milk dangerously
Seek medication-specific lactation advice before changing feeding or treatment
Use the friend's experience to choose the plan
why: Abrupt treatment interruption can harm the parent.
Exposure and clinical relevance differ among medications.
Specific assessment balances parent treatment and infant feeding needs.
Another person's circumstances do not establish suitability here.
questions.takeaway: Obtain medication-specific lactation information before recommending changes.
questions.learningObjective: Obtain medication-specific lactation information before recommending changes.

questions.title: Gradual weaning
questions.stem: A parent chooses to wean and asks how to reduce breast discomfort. Which general approach is best when no urgent reason requires abrupt cessation?
options: Gradually replace feeds while monitoring comfort and intake
Stop every feed suddenly and avoid all breast assessment
Restrict fluids to suppress milk production
Add tighter breast binding whenever discomfort increases
why: Gradual change supports adjustment and observation of parent and infant needs.
Abrupt cessation can increase uncomfortable fullness and complications.
Fluid restriction is not a routine safe weaning strategy.
Tight binding may worsen discomfort and does not replace assessment.
questions.takeaway: Plan gradual weaning when circumstances allow.
questions.learningObjective: Plan gradual weaning when circumstances allow.

questions.title: Infant vitamin guidance
questions.stem: A parent exclusively breastfeeds and assumes no supplements should ever be discussed. What should the nurse do?
options: Recommend several supplements based only on advertising
Replace one breastfeed daily with juice
Wait until poor growth develops before reviewing nutrition
Review recommended infant vitamin D supplementation using current guidance
why: Unselected supplements may be unnecessary or inappropriate.
Juice does not address the relevant vitamin need.
Prevention can be addressed before a deficiency appears.
Breastfeeding counselling includes guideline-based vitamin D advice.
questions.takeaway: Include recommended vitamin supplementation in infant-feeding counselling.
questions.learningObjective: Include recommended vitamin supplementation in infant-feeding counselling.

questions.title: Infant food allergy planning
questions.stem: A caregiver delays every potentially allergenic food because an older sibling has food allergy. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Assess the infant's own eczema or allergy history
Arrange individualized introduction advice when risk concerns exist
Eliminate major food groups indefinitely without review
Explain what symptoms require urgent help when new foods are introduced
why: The infant's clinical history helps determine suitable guidance.
Risk-based advice supports safe nutritional planning.
Unnecessary broad exclusion can impair dietary variety and nutrition.
Caregivers need a clear response to possible reactions.
questions.takeaway: Individualize allergenic-food introduction and teach reaction recognition.
questions.learningObjective: Individualize allergenic-food introduction and teach reaction recognition.

questions.title: Choosing a milk substitute
questions.stem: A caregiver wants to replace a young infant's formula with an oat beverage because it is cheaper. What should the nurse explain?
options: Plant beverages are not nutritionally equivalent to infant formula
Any beverage labelled unsweetened provides equivalent infant nutrition
Adding cereal makes the substitution nutritionally complete
The substitution is suitable whenever the infant accepts its taste
why: Commercial infant formula is designed for infant nutritional requirements.
Lack of added sugar does not establish equivalent nutrient composition.
Cereal cannot reliably recreate complete infant nutrition.
Acceptance does not establish nutritional adequacy.
questions.takeaway: Distinguish ordinary plant beverages from nutritionally appropriate infant feeds.
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish ordinary plant beverages from nutritionally appropriate infant feeds.

questions.title: Bottle-to-cup development
questions.stem: A toddler uses a bottle throughout the day and shows little interest in meals. Which plan is most useful?
options: Increase bottle size to reduce feeding interruptions
Offer structured meals and snacks and practise an open cup
Replace meals with bottles until all teeth erupt
Restrict all fluids until the toddler eats a full meal
why: Larger milk volumes may further displace solid foods.
Structure and cup practice support feeding development and food intake.
Teeth do not justify replacing age-appropriate meals with bottles.
Restriction may create conflict and compromise hydration.
questions.takeaway: Support cup skills and structured meals when bottles displace food.
questions.learningObjective: Support cup skills and structured meals when bottles displace food.

questions.title: Preventing prolonged sugar exposure
questions.stem: A school-age child sips a sweet drink throughout the afternoon. Which change best targets dental risk?
options: Keep the drink but change the cup
Add a straw while maintaining continuous sipping
Choose water between meals and limit prolonged sugary sipping
Delay brushing until every adult tooth has erupted
why: Cup type alone does not remove sugar exposure.
A straw does not eliminate repeated sugar contact.
Water reduces repeated exposure that promotes decay.
Primary and newly erupted teeth both require cleaning.
questions.takeaway: Reduce the frequency and duration of sugary drink exposure.
questions.learningObjective: Reduce the frequency and duration of sugary drink exposure.

questions.title: Children's primary teeth
questions.stem: A caregiver asks whether treating decay in a primary tooth matters because it will fall out. What is the best explanation?
options: Treatment matters only if the tooth is visible
A primary tooth cannot affect eating comfort
Decay is harmless until the permanent tooth appears
Primary teeth support eating, speech and space for permanent teeth
why: Tooth function and infection risk matter beyond appearance.
Decay can cause pain and impair chewing.
Untreated decay can cause problems before permanent eruption.
Preserving primary tooth health supports several developmental functions.
questions.takeaway: Explain why primary teeth need treatment and preventive care.
questions.learningObjective: Explain why primary teeth need treatment and preventive care.

questions.title: Supporting infant motor exploration
questions.stem: Which activities support an awake infant's development? Select all that apply.
options: Supervised floor play with safe reaching opportunities
Brief supervised tummy-time practice as tolerated
Prolonged restraint in a seat for most waking hours
Responsive interaction during play
why: Floor play allows movement and exploration within a safe space.
Awake prone practice supports developing strength and control.
Prolonged restraint limits opportunities to practise movement.
Interaction supports social and communication development alongside movement.
questions.takeaway: Offer safe awake movement and responsive interaction.
questions.learningObjective: Offer safe awake movement and responsive interaction.

questions.title: Recognizing play readiness
questions.stem: During teaching, an infant repeatedly turns away, yawns and fusses after several minutes of stimulation. What should the nurse suggest?
options: Increase sound and movement to regain attention
Pause stimulation and allow a calming break
Continue until the infant smiles again
Change toys rapidly without stopping the session
why: Additional stimulation may intensify overload.
Disengagement cues can indicate a need for rest or reduced input.
Continuing despite cues does not respect the infant's regulation needs.
Rapid changes still maintain stimulation when a break is indicated.
questions.takeaway: Respond to infant disengagement cues during play.
questions.learningObjective: Respond to infant disengagement cues during play.

questions.title: Toddler tantrums in public
questions.stem: A caregiver reports tantrums when a tired toddler must leave the park. Which anticipatory strategy is most appropriate?
options: Negotiate a different departure time after every tantrum
Explain long-term consequences during peak crying
Plan around fatigue and give a brief predictable transition warning
Avoid all outings until tantrums stop
why: Inconsistent limits can make transitions less predictable.
Peak distress limits the toddler's ability to process complex explanation.
Planning and simple warnings address the identified trigger.
Avoidance limits family activity without building transition skills.
questions.takeaway: Use predictable transitions and fatigue awareness to reduce toddler distress.
questions.learningObjective: Use predictable transitions and fatigue awareness to reduce toddler distress.

questions.title: Preparing for a new sibling
questions.stem: A preschooler becomes clingy after a baby arrives. Which caregiver response is most helpful?
options: Maintain familiar routines and protected individual attention
Require immediate independence in every task
Remove usual comforts to encourage maturity
Compare the child's behaviour with the baby's needs
why: Predictability and connection support adjustment to a major family change.
Abrupt expectations may intensify insecurity.
Removing comforts may worsen regression or distress.
Comparison can increase perceived competition for attention.
questions.takeaway: Support sibling adjustment with routine and individual connection.
questions.learningObjective: Support sibling adjustment with routine and individual connection.

questions.title: School-age body privacy
questions.stem: A child entering school asks why a routine examination requires clothing removal. Which response is best?
options: Explain that clinicians do not need permission for examinations
Ask the caregiver to answer while ignoring the child
Promise that no examination will ever be uncomfortable
Explain the purpose, privacy protections and opportunity to ask questions
why: Children should be included in explanations and assent appropriate to development.
Direct engagement respects the child's developing participation.
Promising no discomfort can undermine trust.
Clear information supports bodily understanding and cooperation.
questions.takeaway: Explain examination purpose and privacy directly to children.
questions.learningObjective: Explain examination purpose and privacy directly to children.

questions.title: School health planning
questions.stem: Which preparations help a school-age child with a chronic condition participate safely in school? Select all that apply.
options: An individualized plan shared with appropriate staff and consent
Clear instructions for symptoms requiring help
Excluding the child from every physical activity automatically
Teaching age-appropriate ways to request assistance
why: A coordinated plan supports continuity and practical accommodations.
Escalation instructions guide timely responses to deterioration.
Participation should be individualized rather than universally prohibited.
Help-seeking skills support developing independence and safety.
questions.takeaway: Coordinate school participation with individualized support and escalation plans.
questions.learningObjective: Coordinate school participation with individualized support and escalation plans.

questions.title: Persistent childhood snoring
questions.stem: A parent reports nightly loud snoring, restless sleep and daytime behaviour changes in a child. What should the nurse recommend?
options: Assessment of possible sleep-disordered breathing
A later bedtime to increase tiredness
Ignoring snoring unless the child reports fatigue
Rewarding quiet sleep before discussing assessment
why: The combined sleep and daytime findings warrant clinical review.
Increasing sleep deprivation does not address possible airway-related sleep disruption.
Children may show behavioural changes rather than describing fatigue.
Rewards cannot evaluate or correct sleep-related breathing problems.
questions.takeaway: Assess persistent snoring with disrupted sleep or daytime effects.
questions.learningObjective: Assess persistent snoring with disrupted sleep or daytime effects.

questions.title: A sports concussion return question
questions.stem: A student with a recent diagnosed concussion feels better and wants to return to contact sport today. What should the nurse reinforce?
options: Symptom improvement permits immediate full-contact play
Follow the clinician's graduated return plan and required clearance
Take analgesics before play to test endurance
Skip schoolwork for a month regardless of recovery
why: Improvement alone does not establish readiness for contact exposure.
A staged individualized plan supports safe return to learning and sport.
Masking symptoms does not assess recovery.
Recovery planning should be individualized rather than imposing prolonged blanket restriction.
questions.takeaway: Reinforce a graduated assessed return after concussion.
questions.learningObjective: Reinforce a graduated assessed return after concussion.

questions.title: Adolescent health goal ownership
questions.stem: A parent wants the teenager to follow a diet plan the teenager has never discussed with staff. What should the nurse do first?
options: Adopt the parent's goals because meals are prepared at home
Ask the teenager only to sign the plan
Explore the teenager's priorities, health needs and willingness to participate
Schedule weigh-ins before establishing the purpose of change
why: Family involvement does not replace the adolescent's meaningful participation.
A signature does not establish understanding or ownership.
Collaborative assessment supports developmentally appropriate and relevant goals.
Measurement without agreed purpose can undermine engagement.
questions.takeaway: Include adolescents in defining their own health-promotion goals.
questions.learningObjective: Include adolescents in defining their own health-promotion goals.

questions.title: Preparing for first menstruation
questions.stem: A preadolescent worries that menstruation might begin at school. What teaching is most useful?
options: A detailed explanation of fertility treatment
Advice to avoid school around the expected date
Reassurance without a practical plan
Age-appropriate explanation, supplies and a trusted school contact
why: Fertility treatment is unrelated to the immediate preparation need.
Avoidance is unnecessary and does not build confidence.
Reassurance alone may leave practical concerns unresolved.
Concrete preparation supports coping with an expected developmental event.
questions.takeaway: Pair puberty information with a practical preparedness plan.
questions.learningObjective: Pair puberty information with a practical preparedness plan.

questions.title: Adolescent online health information
questions.stem: Which questions help a teenager evaluate online health advice? Select all that apply.
options: Who created it and what expertise do they have?
Is the claim supported by evidence and a current date?
Does a large number of likes prove the advice works?
Is the author selling the recommended product?
why: Identifiable expertise helps assess credibility.
Evidence and currency matter for health recommendations.
Popularity does not establish clinical effectiveness.
Commercial interests can influence how claims are presented.
questions.takeaway: Assess expertise, evidence and commercial influence in online health advice.
questions.learningObjective: Assess expertise, evidence and commercial influence in online health advice.

questions.title: Sexual consent education
questions.stem: During health teaching, a young adult asks whether agreement on a previous occasion means consent today. What is the best explanation?
options: Consent is ongoing and must apply to the current activity
A previous relationship establishes continuing consent
Lack of an objection always establishes consent
Consent is needed only when contraception is not used
why: A prior agreement does not replace voluntary current agreement.
Relationship status does not establish consent for every activity.
Silence or inability to respond does not reliably establish consent.
Consent is separate from contraceptive use.
questions.takeaway: Teach consent as voluntary, specific and ongoing.
questions.learningObjective: Teach consent as voluntary, specific and ongoing.

questions.title: New pain with sexual activity
questions.stem: A postpartum client reports pain during intercourse and is embarrassed to ask about it. What should the nurse do?
options: Recommend tolerating it until the annual examination
Offer private assessment and referral based on symptoms and healing
Assume the cause is solely emotional
Ask the partner to provide the history instead
why: Persistent discomfort deserves assessment rather than automatic delay.
A private review can identify physical and other contributors and suitable help.
Multiple causes are possible and should not be presumed.
The client's own account and preferences are central.
questions.takeaway: Invite assessment of postpartum sexual discomfort without assumptions.
questions.learningObjective: Invite assessment of postpartum sexual discomfort without assumptions.

questions.title: Menopause and pregnancy prevention
questions.stem: A client with irregular periods assumes contraception is no longer needed because hot flashes have begun. What should the nurse recommend?
options: Stop contraception at the first hot flash
Use cycle irregularity as proof of infertility
Review pregnancy-prevention needs using clinical history and current guidance
Replace contraception with symptom tracking alone
why: A symptom alone does not establish loss of fertility.
Irregular ovulation can still permit pregnancy.
Individual assessment can clarify appropriate contraception and timing.
Tracking symptoms alone does not reliably prevent pregnancy.
questions.takeaway: Do not equate early menopausal symptoms with established infertility.
questions.learningObjective: Do not equate early menopausal symptoms with established infertility.

questions.title: A new changing skin lesion
questions.stem: A client notices a mole becoming asymmetric and changing colour but has no pain. What should the nurse recommend?
options: Photograph it and wait a year before seeking help
Apply moisturizer and reassess only if itchy
Cover it and continue usual tanning habits
Arrange assessment of the evolving lesion
why: A long delay may postpone recognition of a concerning change.
Moisturizer does not evaluate changes in shape or pigmentation.
Covering one lesion does not address diagnosis or ongoing exposure.
Evolution warrants assessment even without pain.
questions.takeaway: Refer evolving skin lesions rather than waiting for discomfort.
questions.learningObjective: Refer evolving skin lesions rather than waiting for discomfort.

questions.title: Oral health with dry mouth
questions.stem: An older adult has persistent dry mouth after medication changes. Which approaches are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Review the medication contribution with the prescriber or pharmacist
Arrange dental guidance and oral-health prevention
Stop all prescribed medicines independently
Assess hydration and other contributing symptoms
why: Medication review can identify modifiable causes without abrupt cessation.
Dry mouth can affect comfort and dental health.
Unsupervised cessation may destabilize treated conditions.
A broader assessment can identify additional contributors.
questions.takeaway: Assess persistent dry mouth and protect oral health while reviewing causes.
questions.learningObjective: Assess persistent dry mouth and protect oral health while reviewing causes.

questions.title: Sun protection with a new medicine
questions.stem: A client is prescribed a medication whose information warns of photosensitivity. They garden outdoors daily. What should the nurse emphasize?
options: Adapt sun protection and activity timing to reduce exposure
Stop gardening indefinitely without discussing alternatives
Rely on a prior tan as protection
Take the medicine only on cloudy days
why: Practical protection can preserve activity while reducing exposure.
Permanent avoidance may be unnecessarily restrictive.
A tan does not provide dependable protection.
Unprescribed intermittent dosing can compromise treatment.
questions.takeaway: Adapt outdoor routines when medication increases sun sensitivity.
questions.learningObjective: Adapt outdoor routines when medication increases sun sensitivity.

questions.title: Financial strain and nutrition priorities
questions.stem: A client can afford either a marketed nutrition supplement or enough ordinary food for several days. No supplement is prescribed. What should the nurse do?
options: Recommend the supplement because it is labelled complete
Assess food access and affordable nutritious options before endorsing a product
Focus only on the supplement's flavour
Assume advertising has already addressed the client's needs
why: Marketing does not establish that this purchase best meets the client's needs.
Basic food access and individualized assessment guide a useful plan.
Flavour is secondary to adequacy and affordability.
Advertising cannot replace clinical and resource assessment.
questions.takeaway: Prioritize adequate feasible food access over unassessed commercial products.
questions.learningObjective: Prioritize adequate feasible food access over unassessed commercial products.

questions.title: Movement with a wheelchair
questions.stem: A client who uses a wheelchair wants to improve fitness but was given only walking goals. What should the nurse do?
options: Repeat the same goals with a longer deadline
Recommend waiting until walking returns
Develop accessible activity goals with appropriate rehabilitation input
Define success only by standing time
why: A deadline change does not make an inaccessible activity feasible.
Beneficial activity need not depend on regaining walking.
Tailored activity can address fitness within current ability.
Standing may not reflect the client's goals or capabilities.
questions.takeaway: Make physical-activity plans accessible to current mobility.
questions.learningObjective: Make physical-activity plans accessible to current mobility.

questions.title: Peer education and misinformation
questions.stem: A community participant confidently repeats an inaccurate health claim during a class. What should the nurse do?
options: Ignore it to preserve group harmony
Criticize the participant's intelligence
End the class immediately
Acknowledge the question and clarify the evidence respectfully
why: Uncorrected misinformation may influence others' decisions.
Personal criticism can undermine trust and participation.
Ending the class misses an opportunity for useful clarification.
Respectful correction supports learning without humiliating the participant.
questions.takeaway: Correct health misinformation while preserving participation and respect.
questions.learningObjective: Correct health misinformation while preserving participation and respect.

questions.title: Assessing health-program reach
questions.stem: A free clinic attracts mostly people who already use preventive services. Which changes may improve reach to underserved clients? Select all that apply.
options: Ask nonattenders about access barriers
Partner with trusted local organizations
Evaluate only satisfaction among current attenders
Adapt location or hours based on community feedback
why: Nonattender perspectives reveal barriers current users may not face.
Trusted partnerships can improve relevance and access.
Current satisfaction does not explain who remains unreached.
Practical adaptation can address barriers identified by intended users.
questions.takeaway: Evaluate who is missing from a program as well as who attends.
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate who is missing from a program as well as who attends.

questions.title: Newborn jaundice and feeding
questions.stem: During a home visit, a newborn appears increasingly yellow and is difficult to wake for feeds. What is the nurse's priority?
options: Arrange prompt clinical assessment rather than routine reassurance
Recommend sunlight at home as the sole treatment
Wait for jaundice to reach the feet before calling
Assume frequent sleep confirms adequate feeding
why: Increasing jaundice with poor feeding or lethargy needs timely evaluation.
Uncontrolled sunlight is not a substitute for appropriate assessment and treatment.
Visual spread alone should not determine whether to seek help.
Excessive sleepiness can interfere with intake and signal illness.
questions.takeaway: Escalate newborn jaundice associated with poor feeding or unusual sleepiness.
questions.learningObjective: Escalate newborn jaundice associated with poor feeding or unusual sleepiness.

questions.title: Postpartum infection warning
questions.stem: A client several days after birth reports fever, increasing pelvic discomfort and foul-smelling discharge. What should the nurse advise?
options: Continue usual hygiene and mention it at the routine visit
Obtain prompt clinical assessment
Increase activity to improve drainage
Use leftover antibiotics from a prior illness
why: The combination suggests possible infection requiring timely evaluation.
Prompt assessment can identify postpartum infection and appropriate treatment.
Activity does not address a possible infection.
Leftover antibiotics may be unsuitable and delay correct treatment.
questions.takeaway: Teach prompt assessment for postpartum fever with worsening pain or abnormal discharge.
questions.learningObjective: Teach prompt assessment for postpartum fever with worsening pain or abnormal discharge.

questions.title: Postpartum clot warning
questions.stem: A postpartum client reports new one-sided calf swelling and pain. They are otherwise comfortable. What should the nurse recommend?
options: Massage the calf and reassess later
Increase walking to test whether pain improves
Seek urgent clinical assessment for a possible clot
Compare swelling again at the next routine visit
why: Massage is not an appropriate response to suspected thrombosis.
Testing symptoms with exertion can delay needed assessment.
Postpartum thromboembolic risk makes this pattern an urgent concern.
A routine future visit is too delayed for this presentation.
questions.takeaway: Escalate unilateral postpartum leg swelling and pain promptly.
questions.learningObjective: Escalate unilateral postpartum leg swelling and pain promptly.

questions.title: Postpartum bleeding change
questions.stem: A client reports that vaginal bleeding suddenly became much heavier and they feel faint. What advice takes priority?
options: Lie down and wait for the usual follow-up call
Record pad use until the next morning
Increase oral fluids and continue routine activity
Activate urgent emergency help for possible significant blood loss
why: Waiting may delay treatment of a potentially serious hemorrhage.
Continued observation alone is insufficient with faintness and increased bleeding.
Fluids do not replace urgent assessment and treatment.
Heavy bleeding with faintness requires emergency evaluation.
questions.takeaway: Treat heavy postpartum bleeding with faintness as an emergency.
questions.learningObjective: Treat heavy postpartum bleeding with faintness as an emergency.

questions.title: Parent learning after discharge
questions.stem: Which statements indicate a caregiver knows when a newborn needs prompt assessment? Select all that apply.
options: 'I will seek help for unusual difficulty waking for feeds.'
'I will ask for assessment if breathing becomes persistently difficult.'
'A major feeding change can wait until the next monthly visit.'
'I will use our discharge contact instructions when I am concerned.'
why: Unusual lethargy can signal illness or inadequate intake.
Persistent respiratory difficulty requires timely evaluation.
Significant feeding changes can require earlier assessment.
A clear access route supports prompt help-seeking.
questions.takeaway: Include feeding, alertness and breathing warning signs in newborn teaching.
questions.learningObjective: Include feeding, alertness and breathing warning signs in newborn teaching.

questions.title: Childhood fever learning focus
questions.stem: A caregiver says, 'The thermometer number tells me everything about how sick my child is.' What should the nurse emphasize?
options: Include behaviour, breathing, hydration and age in assessing urgency
Use fever height alone to determine all care
Wait until fever medicine fails before assessing other symptoms
Assume a playful child can never deteriorate
why: Clinical context and associated symptoms guide urgency beyond one number.
Temperature alone cannot describe overall illness severity.
Assessment should not depend solely on antipyretic response.
Current activity is useful but does not remove the need for monitoring.
questions.takeaway: Teach assessment of the whole child rather than temperature alone.
questions.learningObjective: Teach assessment of the whole child rather than temperature alone.

questions.title: Preparing a child's hospital visit
questions.stem: A school-age child asks whether a planned procedure will hurt. What response best supports preparation?
options: Promise there will be no discomfort
Explain likely sensations honestly and discuss agreed coping support
Tell the caregiver to answer all questions
Describe only the equipment brand
why: Unrealistic reassurance can undermine trust if discomfort occurs.
Honest concrete preparation supports coping and participation.
The child's direct questions deserve developmentally appropriate answers.
Equipment branding does not address the child's concern.
questions.takeaway: Give honest age-appropriate information about expected procedural sensations.
questions.learningObjective: Give honest age-appropriate information about expected procedural sensations.

questions.title: A new caregiving arrangement
questions.stem: A grandparent will care for an infant and proposes practices different from the parents' updated health teaching. What should the nurse do?
options: Avoid discussing differences to preserve family harmony
Ask the grandparent to rely on memory alone
Review current guidance with all caregivers and agree on consistent safe routines
Exclude the grandparent from every teaching session
why: Unaddressed differences can produce inconsistent or unsafe care.
Previous experience may not reflect current guidance.
Shared teaching supports coordinated routines and respectful communication.
Inclusion can improve consistency if the family wants this involvement.
questions.takeaway: Update and coordinate health teaching across the infant's caregivers.
questions.learningObjective: Update and coordinate health teaching across the infant's caregivers.

questions.title: Choosing developmentally useful toys
questions.stem: A parent feels pressured to buy expensive electronic toys for an infant's brain development. What should the nurse explain?
options: Price predicts developmental benefit
Electronic prompts should replace caregiver interaction
Only specialized toys provide adequate stimulation
Safe simple play and responsive human interaction are valuable
why: Cost does not establish developmental effectiveness.
Responsive relationships are central to early learning.
Everyday safe materials can support exploration and interaction.
Development depends on experiences and relationships, not expensive products.
questions.takeaway: Emphasize responsive play over costly developmental marketing.
questions.learningObjective: Emphasize responsive play over costly developmental marketing.

questions.title: Evaluating a prevention plan over time
questions.stem: A client achieved an initial nutrition goal but a new work schedule makes the routine impractical. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Reassess available meal times and resources
Retain the health goal while adapting practical steps
Interpret the change as proof that previous learning failed
Agree on a new follow-up point to evaluate feasibility
why: Changed circumstances can alter what is feasible.
Adaptation can preserve the purpose while changing the method.
A new barrier does not erase previous learning or success.
Review allows the revised plan to be tested and refined.
questions.takeaway: Reassess and adapt health-promotion plans when circumstances change.
questions.learningObjective: Reassess and adapt health-promotion plans when circumstances change.
